RV infarct = preload-dependent → maintain RV filling

Warning: FOUR DRUGS THAT KILL in RV infarct:
1. Nitrates — ↓preload → profound hypotension
2. Diuretics — ↓preload → haemodynamic collapse
3. Morphine — vasodilation, ↓preload
4. ACEi/ARNi acutely — ↓afterload unmasks RV failure

- Fluid challenge: 200–300 mL NS boluses to optimise preload
- Maintain sinus rhythm — AF very poorly tolerated (loss of atrial kick)
- Right-sided ECG: ST elevation in V4R is diagnostic
- Reperfusion (pPCI) is the definitive treatment

Eisenmenger: L→R shunt reverses to R→L due to pulmonary vascular disease

- Mechanism: Longstanding high-flow/pressure → pulmonary vascular remodelling → ↑PVR → right heart pressure exceeds left → shunt reversal
- Defects that cause it: Large unrepaired VSD, ASD, PDA, AV canal (AVSD)
- Clinical: Cyanosis, polycythaemia, clubbing, haemoptysis, paradoxical embolism
- Why no repair: Lungs are the primary driver of disease — closing the defect removes the "pop-off valve" → acute RV failure and death

Tip: Treatment: Pulmonary vasodilators (bosentan - BREATHE-5 trial), oxygen, avoid pregnancy. Heart-lung transplant is definitive.

Tip: Example: 70-year-old patient → cutoff = 70 × 10 = 700 ng/mL. Increases specificity without compromising sensitivity.

| --- | --- |
| 0 YEARS items (no DVT signs, no haemoptysis, PE not most likely) | <1000 ng/mL → exclude PE |

| Either scenario exceeded | Proceed to CTPA |

| I. Morpho-functional (echo/CMR/RV angio) | RV akinesia/dyskinesia/aneurysm + ONE of: PLAX RVOT ≥32 mm, PSAX ≥36 mm, FAC ≤33% | Mild RV dysfunction; PLAX 29–31, PSAX 32–35, FAC 34–40% |
| II. Tissue characterisation (biopsy) | Fibrofatty replacement (<60% residual myocytes) in ≥2 samples | Fibrofatty replacement (60–75% residual myocytes) |
| III. Repolarisation (ECG) | T-wave inversion V1–V4 (age >14, no RBBB) | T-wave inversion V1–V3; or V1–V2 (age >14, no RBBB); or V4–V6 |
| IV. Depolarisation (ECG/SAP) | Epsilon wave in V1–V3 | Terminal activation duration >55 ms in V1–V3 (signal-averaged ECG) |
| V. Arrhythmia | Non-sustained or sustained VT with LBBB morphology + superior axis (right ventricular origin) | LBBB-VT (non-sustained); >500 VPBs/24h |
| VI. Family history | 1st-degree relative with definite ARVC OR pathogenic ARVC mutation | 1st-degree relative with suspected ARVC; SCD <35 y in 1st-degree relative |

Tip: Key genes: PKP2 (plakophilin-2) most common; also DSP, DSG2, DSC2, JUP, TMEM43. Autosomal dominant.

Diagnosis = Type 1 pattern (spontaneous OR provoked by Na-channel blocker)

- Provocative test: IV ajmaline, procainamide, or flecainide
- Best leads: V1–V2 in 2nd or 3rd intercostal space (superior placement)

Warning: Treatment: ICD for survivors of SCA or symptomatic patients. Quinidine for electrical storms. Avoid Na-channel blockers, fever (antipyretics promptly), cocaine.

HCM diagnosis: Maximal wall thickness ≥15 mm in ≥1 LV segment (echo or CMR) — unexplained by abnormal loading conditions

| Parameter | Threshold | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maximal LV wall thickness | ≥15 mm (≥13 mm in 1st-degree relative) | Any segment; typically asymmetric septal |
| LVOTO (obstructive HCM) | Peak LVOT gradient ≥30 mmHg at rest or provocation | ≥50 mmHg = haemodynamically significant |
| SAM (systolic anterior motion) | MV leaflet touching septum in systole | Causes dynamic LVOT obstruction |
| Mid-cavity obstruction | Gradient between LV apex and LVOT | Associated with apical HCM |

Warning: LVOTO intervention criteria: Symptoms (NYHA III–IV) + gradient ≥50 mmHg at rest or provocation → surgical myectomy (preferred) or alcohol septal ablation
Tip: Avoid: Digoxin (positive inotropy worsens obstruction), vasodilators (afterload ↓ worsens gradient), high-dose diuretics. Safe: Beta-blockers, verapamil (not in advanced HF), disopyramide.

back:
PPCM = New HF in last month of pregnancy or ≤5 months postpartum, LVEF <45%, no prior heart disease, no other cause

| Criterion | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Timing | Final month of pregnancy to 5 months postpartum |
| LVEF | <45% (or LVEF <55% + LV dilatation) |
| Exclusion | No identifiable cause of HF; no pre-existing LV dysfunction |

Tip: Recovery: ~50% recover LVEF ≥50% within 6 months. Associated with prolactin-mediated cardiotoxicity.
Warning: Treatment: Standard HF therapy BUT avoid ACEi/ARB in pregnancy (teratogenic). Use hydralazine + nitrates instead. Bromocriptine (anti-prolactin) — emerging evidence (ESC IIb recommendation).
Warning: Subsequent pregnancy: HIGH risk even if EF normalised. 30–50% relapse. Contraindicate in persistent LV dysfunction.
front: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy (PPCM) — HEART Failure Society definition and key distinguishing features

back:
MINOCA = Myocardial Infarction with Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries (<50% stenosis on angiography)

| Diagnostic Step | Findings/Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Coronary angiography | No obstructive disease (<50% stenosis in any epicardial artery) |
| LV angiography / echo | Rule out Takotsubo (apical ballooning), non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy |
| CMR (cardiac MRI) | Mandatory: LGE pattern distinguishes ischaemic vs non-ischaemic vs myocarditis |
| Intracoronary imaging (OCT/IVUS) | Detect SCAD, plaque rupture/erosion, coronary spasm |
| Hypercoagulability workup | APS, Factor V Leiden, antithrombin III deficiency |
| Coronary spasm test | Acetylcholine or ergonovine provocation if no other cause found |

Tip: Common causes: SCAD (especially young women), vasospasm, Takotsubo, myocarditis, Type 2 MI (supply/demand mismatch), coronary embolism, microvascular disease
Warning: 🇮🇩 MINOCA more common in women, younger patients — important in Indonesian context where RHD and hypercoagulable states are prevalent
front: MINOCA — definition, causes, and the required workup algorithm

CMR positive for myocarditis: ≥1 T2 criterion + ≥1 T1 criterion

| Category | Criterion (Major) |
| --- | --- |
| T2-based (oedema) | Regional or global myocardial T2 elevation OR T2-STIR signal intensity ratio >2.0 |
| T1-based (non-ischaemic injury) | Native T1 elevation OR ECV elevation OR LGE in non-ischaemic distribution (subepicardial or midwall) |

Tip: Myocarditis LGE distribution: Subepicardial or midmyocardial (lateral and inferior walls). Distinguishes from ischaemic (subendocardial / transmural following coronary territory).

| Cause | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| Viral (Coxsackievirus B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, enterovirus, COVID-19) | Most common |
| Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis | Emerging (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) |
| Giant cell myocarditis | Fulminant, poor prognosis — require heart transplant |

Warning: Fulminant myocarditis: Rapid haemodynamic compromise requiring mechanical support. Giant cell = specific histology; high mortality without transplant.

| Echo Criterion | Value |
| --- | --- |
| LVEDD (LV end-diastolic diameter) | >5.5 cm men / >5.0 cm women (or >2 SD indexed for BSA) |
| LVEF | <45% (many guidelines use <50%) |
| Left ventricular fractional shortening | <25% |

| Secondary Causes to Exclude | Investigation |
| --- | --- |
| Ischaemic (ischaemic CMP) | Coronary angiography / CT coronary angiogram |
| Alcohol / Toxins (chemotherapy) | History; TTE serial monitoring |
| Thyroid disease | TSH, T4 |
| Hypertensive heart disease | BP history |
| Viral / Post-myocarditis | CMR, viral serology |
| Genetic | Family history; genetic panel (lamin A/C, titin, MYH7) |

Tip: Lamin A/C (LMNA) mutations: DCM + conduction disease + arrhythmia → high risk SCA; ICD threshold is lower.

back:
Definite cardiac sarcoidosis: Histological confirmation from cardiac tissue OR non-cardiac sarcoid + ≥1 criterion below on cardiac evaluation

Criterion (any 1 of these)
Corticosteroid-responsive cardiomyopathy or AV block
Unexplained reduced LVEF (<40%)
Unexplained sustained VT or 2nd/3rd degree AV block
Patchy uptake on dedicated cardiac PET scan (FDG-PET)
Delayed enhancement on CMR in pattern consistent with sarcoid
Positive gallium uptake in the heart

Tip: CMR pattern of cardiac sarcoidosis: Basal septal and right ventricular LGE (different from HCM or ischaemic pattern). FDG-PET is the gold standard for active inflammation.
Warning: High-degree AV block + young patient = exclude cardiac sarcoidosis and Lyme disease before assuming idiopathic. Sarcoid can present as complete AV block as the first manifestation.
front: Cardiac Sarcoidosis — Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) 2014 diagnostic criteria

LFLG-AS = AVA ≤1.0 cm² + mean gradient <40 mmHg

| Subtype | EF | SVi | Pathomechanism |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Classic LFLG-AS | <50% | <35 mL/m² | LV systolic dysfunction → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ gradient despite severe stenosis |
| Paradoxical LFLG-AS | ≥50% (preserved) | <35 mL/m² | Restrictive LV filling, small LV cavity, ↓ flow despite preserved EF |

Dobutamine Stress Echo (DSE) — distinguishes true severe vs pseudo-severe AS

| Result | Interpretation | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AVA stays ≤1.0 cm² + gradient rises ≥40 mmHg + flow reserve present | True severe AS | Proceed to AVR/TAVI |
| AVA increases >1.0 cm² + gradient stays low when flow increases | Pseudo-severe AS (relative stenosis) | Medical management; treat HF |
| No flow reserve (EF doesn't rise >20%) | Very poor LV contractile reserve | High-risk; heart team decision |

| Echo (M-mode) | Septal bounce ("shudder") on inspiration; pericardial thickening/calcification |
| Echo (Doppler) | Mitral E variation with respiration ≥25%; hepatic vein expiratory diastolic flow reversal |

| Definite RHD | Pathological MR + ≥2 morphological features: anterior leaflet thickening ≥3 mm; chordal thickening; restricted leaflet motion; excessive leaflet tip motion |
| Definite RHD | MS with mean gradient ≥4 mmHg |

Warning: 🇮🇩 Indonesia context: RHD is the leading structural heart disease in young Indonesians. WHF echo criteria allow identification before symptoms develop — crucial for prophylaxis decisions.

back:
Two types: AL (light chain) and ATTR (transthyretin — hereditary or wild-type)

| Investigation | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| Echo | Concentric LVH + preserved or ↓ EF + "sparkling" myocardium + diastolic dysfunction (restrictive pattern) + thickened interatrial septum >7 mm + small pericardial effusion |
| ECG | "Voltage-mass discordance" — low QRS voltage despite echo LVH; pseudo-infarct pattern (Q waves in anterior leads without history of MI) |
| Bone scintigraphy (DPD/PYP scan) | Grade 2–3 cardiac uptake = ATTR amyloidosis (non-invasive diagnosis without biopsy) |
| CMR | Diffuse subendocardial LGE; abnormal gadolinium kinetics; ECV elevation >40% |
| Biopsy | Congo red staining → apple-green birefringence; fat pad or bone marrow biopsy for AL; endomyocardial biopsy for definitive typing |
| Serum/urine protein | Free light chains, SPEP, UPEP — exclude AL amyloidosis before treating as ATTR |

Tip: Key clue: Low-voltage ECG + echo showing thick walls. Also: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, biceps tendon rupture, lumbar spinal stenosis — all extracardiac ATTR manifestations. Tafamidis approved for ATTR-CM.
front: Cardiac Amyloidosis — diagnostic criteria and key clues to suspect it clinically

back:
Go through all 4 steps in order. First "YES" = VT diagnosis (stop)

| Step | Question | If YES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Is RS complex absent in ALL precordial leads? (All QRS are monophasic R or QS) | VT (100% specific) |
| 2 | Is the RS interval (onset R to nadir S) >100 ms in ANY precordial lead? | VT |
| 3 | Is there AV dissociation (P waves marching through, independent of QRS)? | VT (pathognomonic) |
| 4 | Morphology criteria in V1 and V6: RBBB-like: V1 monophasic R / Rr' / qR AND V6 R:S <1 LBBB-like: V1 R >30 ms / Notched S / RS >60 ms AND V6 Q or QS | VT |

If all 4 steps = NO → SVT with aberrancy (diagnosis of exclusion)
Warning: Clinical rule: ALL haemodynamically stable wide complex tachycardia with unknown origin should be treated as VT until proven otherwise. Verapamil/diltiazem in VT = catastrophic hypotension.
Tip: AV dissociation signs: Fusion beats (P+QRS partially merge); Capture beats (narrow QRS amidst wide complex — transient conduction); Independent P waves marching at different rate from QRS.
front: VT vs SVT with aberrancy — Brugada 4-step ECG algorithm for wide complex tachycardia

back:
| Feature | AVNRT (AV Nodal Reentry) | AVRT (AV Reentry via Accessory Pathway) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P wave location | Buried in / immediately after QRS (RP <70 ms, short RP); pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-s in II/III/aVF | P wave visible AFTER QRS (RP >70 ms, long RP typical) |
| RP interval | <70 ms (short RP) — P behind QRS | RP >70 ms (usually); P follows T wave |
| Mechanism | Reentry within AV node (slow-fast pathway) | Reentry using AV node + accessory pathway (Kent bundle) |
| Retrograde P axis | Negative in II, III, aVF (retrograde conduction) | Negative in II, III, aVF (retrograde via AP) |
| WPW on sinus rhythm ECG | No delta wave | Delta wave present (unless concealed AP) |
| Frequency | Most common SVT (60%) | Second most common (30%) |

Tip: Key differentiator: P wave timing. RP <70 ms → buried in QRS → AVNRT most likely. Long RP (>RP < PR) → AVNRT atypical (fast-slow), AVRT, or atrial tachycardia.
Atrial tachycardia: Long RP with visible distinct P wave morphology different from sinus P wave.
front: AVNRT vs AVRT — ECG features to differentiate the two most common regular narrow-complex SVTs

back:
| Feature | Typical Flutter (CTI-dependent) | Atypical Flutter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Counterclockwise (90%) or clockwise (10%) reentry around the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) | Reentry around other circuits (scar, mitral annulus, pulmonary veins) |
| Flutter rate | Atrial rate ~300 bpm | Variable (200–350 bpm) |
| Ventricular rate (2:1) | ~150 bpm (typical 2:1 block) | Variable depending on AV conduction |
| Flutter wave morphology | Counterclockwise: Negative sawtooth in II, III, aVF; positive in V1. Clockwise: Positive in II, III, aVF | Variable |
| Isoelectric baseline | Absent — continuous sawtooth undulation | May have isoelectric segments |

Classic clue: Regular tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm → flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise
Tip: Definitive treatment of typical flutter: Catheter ablation of cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI ablation) — very high cure rate (95%). Rate control alone rarely sufficient long-term.
Warning: Antiarrhythmic drugs (especially flecainide) can slow flutter rate to 200 bpm → 1:1 conduction → extremely rapid ventricular response. Always add AV blocker before AAD in flutter.
front: Atrial Flutter — ECG features of typical (isthmus-dependent) vs atypical flutter. What is the classic ventricular rate in untreated flutter?

back:
LBBB requires ALL of the following:

| Criterion | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| QRS duration | ≥120 ms (complete LBBB) / 110–119 ms (incomplete LBBB) |
| Broad, notched or slurred R wave in lateral leads | I, aVL, V5–V6 (absent q waves in I, V5–V6) |
| Rsr', rsR' or rSR' in V1 | Usually small r followed by deep S (rS pattern) |
| Absent septal q waves | No q in I, V5, V6 (septal activation reversed) |
| Secondary ST-T changes | Discordant — ST/T in OPPOSITE direction to QRS deflection |

Tip: LBBB + ACS: New LBBB with chest pain = treat as STEMI equivalent. Use Sgarbossa criteria (Vol.1, card 44) to detect ischaemia within LBBB pattern. Sgarbossa concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm = strongly specific for MI.
Warning: New LBBB criteria for CRT eligibility: QRS ≥150 ms for Class I benefit. LBBB 130–149 ms = Class IIa. Non-LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms = Class IIa.
front: LBBB diagnostic ECG criteria — what are the five essential features?

back:
RBBB = QRS ≥120 ms + rSR' in V1–V2 + wide S in I, V5, V6

| Criterion | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| QRS duration | ≥120 ms |
| rSR' (or rsR' or rsr') in V1–V2 | Terminal R' wave — "rabbit ears" morphology |
| Wide, slurred S wave in I, aVL, V5–V6 | S wave duration > R wave; or >40 ms |

| Block Type | ECG Pattern | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bifascicular block | RBBB + LAFB (left axis deviation −30 to −90°) OR RBBB + LPFB (right axis deviation) | Low risk of progression without symptoms |
| Trifascicular block | Bifascicular + 1st degree AV block (↑PR) OR alternating LBBB/RBBB | High risk → pacing if symptomatic |
| Alternating BBB | Spontaneous alternation between LBBB and RBBB | High risk → pacing Class I |

Tip: Isolated RBBB: Often benign. In PE → new RBBB is a sign of acute RV strain. In post-MI → suggests large anteroseptal infarct (proximal LAD). Monitor closely.
front: RBBB diagnostic ECG criteria — the three core features. Also: bifascicular and trifascicular block

back:
Epsilon wave: Small positive deflection AFTER the QRS complex, before the T wave — in V1–V3

| ECG Feature | Leads | Prevalence in ARVC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Epsilon wave | V1–V3 | ~30–50% (specific but insensitive) |
| T-wave inversion (right precordial) | V1–V3 ± V4 | ~60–80% — most common ECG finding |
| Prolonged terminal activation (TAD >55 ms) | V1–V3 | Detected on signal-averaged ECG (SAECG) |
| QRS duration >110 ms in V1–V3 | V1–V3 | Common |
| VPBs with LBBB morphology + superior axis | Any | RV-origin arrhythmia |

Tip: Mechanism: Epsilon wave represents delayed depolarisation of a small island of viable myocardium surrounded by fibrofatty replacement → conduction delay. Think of it as a very late "notch" in the QRS tail. Filtered QRS on SAECG detects even smaller versions.
Warning: ARVC is a genetic disease with autosomal dominant inheritance. Competitive sport SIGNIFICANTLY accelerates disease progression → ban from competitive sport is mandatory upon diagnosis.
front: Epsilon wave — what is it, in which condition is it seen, and what other ECG changes characterise ARVC?

back:
| Feature | Early Repolarisation (Benign) | STEMI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distribution | Lateral (V4–V6) and/or inferior | Territory-specific (LAD, RCA, LCx) |
| ST morphology | Concave (upward) — "smiling face" | Convex (upward) — "frowning face" or horizontal/downsloping |
| J-point notch | Notch/slur at J-point ("fishhook") | Less common |
| Reciprocal changes | Absent | Present (highly specific for STEMI) |
| PR depression | Absent | Absent (present in pericarditis) |
| Evolution over serial ECGs | Stable (unchanged) | Dynamic (ST rises, then Q waves, then T inversion) |
| Q waves | Absent | May develop (>30 min ischaemia) |
| Clinical context | Young, asymptomatic or non-cardiac pain | Chest pain, diaphoresis, haemodynamic changes |

Warning: High-risk early repolarisation: Horizontal or descending slur, high amplitude in inferior leads, short QT — associated with idiopathic VF. Not truly "benign" in all cases.
front: Early repolarisation vs inferior/lateral STEMI — what ECG features help differentiate them?

back:
ECG progression correlates roughly with serum K⁺ level (though individual variation is large)

| K⁺ Level | ECG Change |
| --- | --- |
| 5.5–6.5 mEq/L | Tall, peaked, narrow (tented) T waves — "tall T" especially in precordial leads (V1–V4) and inferior leads |
| 6.5–7.5 mEq/L | PR interval prolongation; P wave flattening/widening |
| 7.0–8.0 mEq/L | QRS widening (bundle branch block pattern) |
| >8.0 mEq/L | P waves disappear (sinoventricular conduction); QRS further widens; sine-wave pattern |
| >9.0 mEq/L | VF or asystole |

Emergency treatment: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation — immediate but temporary)
Tip: Then: Insulin + dextrose (shift K into cells, 15 min onset); salbutamol nebulisation (shift, 30 min); sodium bicarbonate (if acidosis); kayexalate or patiromer (eliminate). Dialysis for refractory cases.
Warning: Peaked T waves in STEMI can mimic hyperkalaemia (hyperacute T waves). Context critical: STEMI → reciprocal depression; K⁺ → no reciprocals, uniform T morphology.
front: Hyperkalaemia ECG changes — describe the sequential progression from mild to severe

back:
| Stage | Timing | ECG Changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | Hours to days (acute) | Diffuse ST elevation (concave) in multiple territories + PR depression in II, V4–V6; PR elevation in aVR |
| Stage 2 | Days to 1 week | ST returns to baseline; T waves flatten |
| Stage 3 | 1–2 weeks | Diffuse T-wave inversion |
| Stage 4 | Weeks to months | ECG normalises (or T inversions persist) |

| Feature | Pericarditis | STEMI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ST distribution | Diffuse (all territories) — "saddle-shaped" | Focal (coronary territory) |
| ST morphology | Concave (upward-sloping) | Convex (dome-shaped) or straight |
| PR depression | Present (atrial involvement) | Usually absent |
| Reciprocal ST depression | Absent (except aVR: ST elevation) | Present (opposite territory) |
| Q waves | Absent | May develop |
front: Pericarditis — the four ECG stages. How does pericarditis ECG differ from STEMI?

back:
S1Q3T3 = S wave in lead I + Q wave in lead III + T-wave inversion in lead III

| ECG Finding | Frequency in PE | Specificity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sinus tachycardia | ~40% (most common) | Low — non-specific |
| S1Q3T3 | ~20% | Moderate (~70%) |
| New RBBB (complete or incomplete) | ~12% | Moderate — acute RV overload |
| T-wave inversion V1–V4 | ~30% | Moderate — RV strain |
| ST depression (inferior/lateral) | ~15% | Low |
| Normal ECG | ~20–30% | — |
| AF (new) | ~5% | Low |

Tip: Most suggestive pattern for massive PE: Sinus tachycardia + new RBBB + T inversion V1–V4 + S1Q3T3. RV strain pattern predicts poor outcome and right heart failure.
Warning: Normal ECG does NOT exclude PE. PE is a clinical + imaging diagnosis — ECG guides risk stratification, not diagnosis.
front: PE ECG changes — S1Q3T3 pattern and other right heart strain changes. How common and specific is S1Q3T3?

back:
| Feature | Digoxin Effect (therapeutic) | Digoxin Toxicity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ST depression | "Scooped" / Salvador-Dali-moustache ST — V4–V6 | Similar but more pronounced; new changes |
| T wave | Flat or slightly inverted | Inverted, may be biphasic |
| QT interval | Shortened (QTc often <400 ms) | Further shortened or prolonged if toxic rhythm |
| PR interval | Slightly prolonged (vagotonic effect) | Prolonged → AV block (1st, 2nd, 3rd degree) |
| Arrhythmias | Minimal; rate controlled AF | Bidirectional VT (pathognomonic); junctional tachycardia with AV dissociation; regularisation of AF (AV junctional escape); paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with block |

Pathognomonic toxic arrhythmia = Bidirectional VT (alternating QRS axis beat-to-beat)
Tip: Other toxic arrhythmias: Frequent PVCs (bigeminism, trigeminy); Junctional tachycardia; PAT with 2:1 AV block. Any arrhythmia + AV block combination is highly suggestive of digoxin toxicity.
front: Digoxin effect vs digoxin toxicity ECG — distinguish the two and describe the characteristic signs

back:
Posterior MI = MIRROR IMAGE pattern in V1–V3

| Standard V1–V3 finding (posterior MI) | What it represents |
| --- | --- |
| ST depression in V1–V3 | Mirror of posterior ST elevation |

| Class effect | Mechanism | ECG result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I (Na block) | ↓ Phase 0 upstroke in His-Purkinje | ↑ QRS slightly |

| III (K block) | ↓ IKr, ↓ IKs → ↑ AP duration → ↑ ERP | ↑ QTc (often significantly) |
| IV (Ca block) | ↓ ICaL in SA and AV node | ↑ PR, ↓ HR |

| Pharmacokinetics | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Half-life | 40–55 days (longest of any drug) |
| Volume of distribution | 60 L/kg (extremely lipophilic — accumulates in fat, lung, liver, thyroid) |
| Iodine content | 37% iodine by weight → thyroid effects |

| Organ | Side Effect | Monitoring |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thyroid | Hypothyroidism (more common) or hyperthyroidism (via Jod-Basedow or destructive thyroiditis) | TFT every 6 months |
| Lung | Pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis/fibrosis) — insidious | Annual CXR, PFTs; any new respiratory symptom → CT chest |
| Liver | Hepatotoxicity (transaminase elevation; cirrhosis) | LFT every 6 months |
| Eye | Corneal microdeposits (virtually all patients — usually asymptomatic); optic neuropathy (rare but vision-threatening) | Annual ophthalmology exam |
| Skin | Photosensitivity; blue-grey discolouration (chronic) | Sun protection counselling |
| Nerve | Peripheral neuropathy, proximal myopathy | Symptom review |

Coronary Perfusion Pressure (CPP) = Aortic Diastolic Pressure − LVEDP

| Determinant | Effect on Coronary Flow |
| --- | --- |
| Aortic diastolic pressure ↑ | ↑ CPP → ↑ coronary flow |
| LVEDP ↑ (e.g. HF, AS) | ↓ CPP → ↓ subendocardial flow → ischaemia |
| Heart rate ↑ | ↓ diastolic time → ↓ coronary filling time → ↑ ischaemia risk |
| Myocardial compression during systole | LV flow occurs mainly in DIASTOLE (subendocardium especially). RV can receive flow during systole (lower wall tension). |

Tip: Concept: Optimal sarcomere length = 2.2 μm. Beyond this, actin-myosin overlap decreases → force decreases. The descending limb is rarely reached in intact hearts (pericardial constraint limits over-distension) but becomes relevant in acute severe HF.

| Step | Hypotension response | Hypertension response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stretch receptor firing | ↓ stretch → ↓ afferent firing | ↑ stretch → ↑ afferent firing |
| NTS in medulla | ↓ NTS activation → ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic tone | ↑ NTS → ↓ sympathetic, ↑ parasympathetic |

Re-entry requires ALL THREE simultaneously:

| Requirement | Explanation | Example in AVNRT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Two anatomically or functionally distinct pathways | Parallel conduction routes with different properties | Fast pathway (short ERP, fast conduction) + Slow pathway (long ERP, slow conduction) |
| 2. Unidirectional block in one pathway | Impulse can travel in one direction only (e.g. premature beat finds one pathway refractory) | PAC finds fast pathway refractory → conducts slowly via slow pathway |
| 3. Slow conduction in the other pathway | Allows time for the blocked pathway to recover and allow retrograde conduction | Slow pathway conduction gives fast pathway time to recover → anterograde loop |

Tip: Breaking re-entry: ↑ refractoriness (Class IA, III — eliminate the excitable gap) OR ↑ conduction block in one limb (adenosine, Class IV — block AV node → terminate AVNRT/AVRT) OR ↑ wavelength (wavelength = ERP × conduction velocity; longer wavelength → less room for re-entry circuit).

Therapeutic digoxin level: 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (HF). Toxic: >2.0 ng/mL but toxicity can occur at lower levels with hypokalaemia.

| Type of Arrhythmia | Mechanism | Specificity for toxicity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequent PVCs (bigeminy) | ↑ DAD-triggered automaticity in Purkinje fibres | Common early sign |
| Bidirectional VT | Alternating pacemakers in Purkinje + fascicles (alternating QRS axis) | Pathognomonic for digoxin toxicity |
| Junctional tachycardia with AV dissociation | ↑ AV nodal automaticity + ↑ AV block simultaneously | Highly specific |
| PAT (atrial tachycardia) with 2:1 AV block | ↑ atrial automaticity + AV block (vagotonic) | Specific — "regularisation of AF" also seen |
| High-degree AV block | ↑ vagotonic effect on AV node | Common but non-specific |

Hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity: K⁺ and digoxin compete for the same binding site on Na-K-ATPase. ↓ K⁺ → more digoxin binding → ↑ toxicity at same plasma level.
Warning: Treatment: Digoxin-specific Fab antibodies (Digifab). Correct K⁺, Mg²⁺. Temporary pacing if severe AV block. Phenytoin for digitalis VT (Class IB suppresses ectopy). Magnesium for digitalis-induced VT. AVOID cardioversion in digitalis toxicity (↑ VF risk).

CPVT: Bidirectional or polymorphic VT triggered by catecholamine surge (exercise, emotion) in absence of structural disease or QTc prolongation

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Mutation in RyR2 (ryanodine receptor 2, AD) or CASQ2 (calsequestrin 2, AR) → abnormal SR Ca²⁺ release during adrenergic stimulation → DADs → triggered VT |
| ECG at rest | NORMAL — this is key. No QT prolongation, no structural disease, no resting ECG findings |
| ECG during exercise | Bidirectional VT (alternating QRS axis 180°) or polymorphic VT — TRIGGERED BY CATECHOLAMINES |
| Diagnosis | Exercise stress test: Reproduces bidirectional/polymorphic VT. IV epinephrine/isoproterenol infusion (provocation). Genetic testing (RyR2 mutation). |

| Treatment | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Beta-blockers (high dose) | Nadolol preferred (non-selective, long-acting, Class I). Target HR <110 bpm during exercise. |
| Flecainide | Directly blocks RyR2 channel (additional effect beyond beta-blockade). Class IIa — CPVT-specific use of an IC drug. |
| ICD | Survivors of cardiac arrest or breakthrough VT despite OMT |
| Activity restriction | Mandatory — ban competitive sports. Avoid intense emotional/physical stimuli. |

WPW ECG: Short PR (<120 ms) + Delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) + Wide QRS (≥120 ms)

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Accessory pathway (Kent bundle) bypasses AV node → pre-excites ventricle (delta wave) + forms AVRT re-entry circuit |
| Pathway location | Left free wall (most common), right free wall, posterior septal, anteroseptal. Location predicted from delta wave polarity. |
| AVRT types | Orthodromic AVRT (anterograde AV node, retrograde AP) → narrow QRS. Antidromic AVRT (anterograde AP, retrograde AV node) → wide QRS (maximally pre-excited). |

Pre-excited AF: AF + WPW = MOST DANGEROUS combination → extremely rapid ventricular rate → VF risk

| Drug | Effect in WPW + AF | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verapamil/diltiazem | Block AV node → more conduction via AP → ↑ ventricular rate → VF | ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED |
| Digoxin | ↑ AP conduction (→ faster pathway) + blocks AV node → same catastrophic effect | ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED |
| Adenosine | Blocks AV node → pre-excited wide complex VT may worsen; avoid in pre-excited AF (use only for narrow complex orthodromic AVRT) | Avoid in pre-excited AF |
| Procainamide IV | Slows AP conduction (Na channel block) → slows ventricular rate → safe | Drug of choice |
| DC cardioversion | If haemodynamically unstable | Immediate cardioversion |

Mechanism: Activates A₁ adenosine receptors in SA node + AV node → ↑ IKACh → hyperpolarisation → transient AV block

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Route/Dose | 6 mg IV rapid push (large antecubital vein or central line); if no response in 1–2 min → 12 mg; then 12 mg again (max 3 doses) |
| Half-life | <10 seconds (taken up by RBCs and endothelium — extremely short) |
| Chest flush proximal vein | Must flush rapidly with 20 mL NS — otherwise inactivated before reaching heart |

| Arrhythmia | Response to Adenosine |
| --- | --- |
| AVNRT | Terminates (blocks AV node → breaks re-entry circuit) — diagnostic and therapeutic |
| AVRT (WPW orthodromic) | Terminates (AV node is part of circuit) |
| AF/AFL | Transient rate slowing → unmasks flutter waves/atrial activity. Does NOT terminate AF/AFL. |
| Atrial tachycardia | Transient AV block → reveals atrial tachycardia continuing. Terminates if AV node-dependent AT. |
| VT | Rarely terminates VT (except idiopathic fascicular VT). No effect on scar-related VT. Can worsen pre-excited AF. |

Warning: Contraindications: Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) — block AV node → more AP conduction → VF. 2nd/3rd degree AV block. Sick sinus syndrome. Active bronchospasm/asthma (→ bronchospasm via A₂B receptor). Use with caution in transplanted hearts (denervated — exaggerated response; use 50% dose).
Tip: Dipyridamole blocks adenosine reuptake → potentiates adenosine effect → ↑ duration. Theophylline/caffeine are A₁ receptor antagonists → block adenosine effect. Caffeine reduces adenosine sensitivity in stress testing.

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism of short half-life | Metabolised by red blood cell esterases (not hepatic) → extremely rapid offset regardless of renal/hepatic function |
| Route | IV only (loading 500 mcg/kg over 1 min → maintenance 50–200 mcg/kg/min) |

| Indication | Dose | Expected response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Symptomatic sinus bradycardia | 0.5 mg IV; repeat every 3–5 min; max 3 mg total | ↑ HR within 1–2 min |
| 2nd degree AV block (Type I / Mobitz I) | 0.5 mg IV | ↑ AV conduction (vagally mediated block) |

Use temporary pacing instead. Also avoid in acute glaucoma (dilates pupil), urinary retention (↓ detrusor tone), tachycardia.

Lidocaine: Class IB — Na-channel blocker with FAST on/off kinetics; preferential affinity for INACTIVATED channels

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Channel kinetics | Binds Na channel in inactivated state (phase 0 complete) → dissociates quickly during phase 3–4. Rate-dependent: more binding at fast rates (↑ inactivated time). Preferentially suppresses depolarised/ischaemic tissue. |
| ECG effects | Minimal QRS widening; SHORTENS action potential (↓ APD) — opposite to Class IA/III. Shortens QTc (useful in LQT3). |
| Route / PK | IV only (significant first-pass hepatic metabolism → oral bioavailability <30%). Half-life ~90 min. Hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4). Accumulates in hepatic failure. |
| Dose | 1–1.5 mg/kg IV bolus; repeat 0.5–0.75 mg/kg at 5 min if needed; maintenance 1–4 mg/min infusion |

| Indication | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Acute VT/VF in MI (historically) | Largely replaced by amiodarone (ARREST, ALIVE trials) |
| Ventricular arrhythmia during cardiac surgery/catheterisation | Still used (local/prophylactic) |
| VT in LQT3 (mexiletine oral equivalent) | Class IIa — shortens QT via late INa block |
| Local anaesthesia | Primary non-cardiac use |

Q = (ΔP × π × r⁴) / (8 × η × L)

| Variable | Symbol | Clinical correlate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow | Q | Cardiac output / organ perfusion |
| Pressure gradient | ΔP | MAP − venous pressure; perfusion pressure |
| Vessel radius | r⁴ | Most powerful determinant — doubling radius → 16× ↑ flow. Vasodilation/constriction is the main flow regulator. |
| Blood viscosity | η | Haematocrit is primary determinant. Polycythaemia ↑ η → ↑ resistance. Anaemia ↓ η → ↓ resistance. |
| Vessel length | L | Fixed in arteries; relevant in coronary microcirculation diffuse disease |

Resistance R = 8ηL / πr⁴ — therefore SVR ∝ 1/r⁴
Tip: Key insight: Arteriolar radius is the dominant regulator of SVR. 10% ↓ in radius → 46% ↑ in resistance. This is why vasodilators (ACEi, CCB, hydralazine) are so effective at reducing afterload and why arteriolar spasm causes severe hypertension.
Tip: At low shear rates (capillaries, venous stasis), RBCs aggregate (rouleaux) → ↑ viscosity → ↑ thrombosis risk (Virchow's triad — abnormal flow). Aspirin particularly effective when TXA₂/rouleaux formation is the thrombotic mechanism.

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ΔP | Pressure gradient across stenosis or regurgitation (mmHg) |
| V | Peak Doppler velocity (m/s) measured by continuous-wave Doppler |

Clinical examples:

| Application | Doppler velocity | Calculation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aortic stenosis mean gradient | V_peak = 4 m/s | ΔP = 4 × 4² = 64 mmHg peak gradient |
| TR velocity → sPAP | V_TR = 3.5 m/s | ΔP (RV-RA) = 4 × 3.5² = 49 mmHg. sPAP = 49 + RAP (e.g. 10) = 59 mmHg |
| VSD gradient | V_VSD = 5 m/s | ΔP (LV-RV) = 4 × 25 = 100 mmHg |
| Mitral inflow E velocity | V_E = 1.2 m/s | ΔP (LA-LV) = 4 × 1.44 = 5.8 mmHg |

Tip: Modified Bernoulli: ΔP = 4(V₂² − V₁²). Used when proximal velocity V₁ is ≥1.5 m/s (LVOT obstruction, valvular disease with high proximal flow). Ignoring V₁ when it is high overestimates the true gradient.

| Component | Measurement |
| --- | --- |
| LVOT area | π × (LVOT diameter/2)² — measured in PLAX view |
| LVOT VTI | Pulsed-wave Doppler in LVOT (subcostal or apical 5-chamber) |

Gorlin formula (Cath): AVA = CO / (44.3 × HR × SEP × √ΔP_mean)

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| CO | Cardiac output (mL/min) |
| HR | Heart rate (beats/min) |
| SEP | Systolic ejection period (s/beat) |
| √ΔP_mean | Square root of mean transvalvular gradient (mmHg) |

Normal AVA: 3–4 cm². Mild AS: 1.5–2.9 cm². Moderate: 1.0–1.4 cm². Severe: <1.0 cm². Very severe: <0.6 cm²

MVO₂ ∝ Heart Rate × Systolic BP × Contractility (tension–time index)

| Determinant | Effect on MVO₂ | Drugs that reduce it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heart rate | ↑ HR → ↑ frequency of contraction → ↑ total O₂ demand/min. Also ↓ diastolic time → ↓ coronary filling. DOUBLE JEOPARDY in ischaemia. | Beta-blockers, ivabradine, non-DHP CCBs, digoxin (rate in AF) |
| Systolic wall stress (afterload) | Laplace law: Wall stress = (P × r) / (2h). ↑ SBP → ↑ wall stress → ↑ MVO₂ | ACEi, ARB, DHP CCB, hydralazine, nitroprusside |
| Contractility (inotropy) | ↑ Force of contraction → ↑ Ca²⁺ cycling → ↑ ATP consumption | Beta-blockers (↓ inotropy is not desirable in HF but reduces MVO₂) |
| Preload (wall tension) | ↑ LVEDV → ↑ wall radius → ↑ wall stress (Laplace) | Nitrates (↓ preload), diuretics |

Tip: Angina treatment targets: Beta-blockers ↓ HR + contractility. Nitrates ↓ preload. CCBs ↓ HR (non-DHP) or ↓ SVR (DHP). Ranolazine ↓ late INa without HR/BP change. All reduce MVO₂ by different mechanisms — combination is complementary.

| State | Primary Fuel | ATP yield | O₂ efficiency |

| Fasting / resting | Fatty acids (60–70%) | 129 ATP/palmitate | Lower (more O₂ per ATP) |

| --- | --- | --- |
| Cardiac function curve (Starling curve) | ↑ RAP → ↑ RV preload → ↑ CO (up to plateau) | Upward shift: ↑ contractility, ↓ afterload. Downward shift: ↓ inotropy, ↑ afterload, arrhythmia. |
| Venous return curve | ↑ RAP → ↓ venous return (↓ venous-atrial pressure gradient). At RAP = mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP ≈ 7 mmHg), flow = 0. | Rightward shift (↑ MSFP): ↑ blood volume, venoconstriction. Leftward shift: hypovolaemia, vasodilation, venodilation (nitrates). |

Intersection = operating point = equilibrium CO and RAP of the patient
Tip: Clinical application: IV fluids → ↑ MSFP → venous return curve shifts right → new intersection at higher CO and higher RAP. Dobutamine → cardiac function curve shifts up → new intersection at higher CO and LOWER RAP (unlike fluids). This explains why inotropes are effective in cardiogenic shock without causing fluid overload.
front: Guyton's model of cardiac output and venous return — what are the two curves and what do their intersections represent?

| Zone | Location | Pressure relationship | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zone 1 (apex) | Top of lung | PA alveolar > PA arterial > PA venous (in upright position) | Alveolar pressure collapses capillaries → No perfusion (dead space). Clinically: PEEP, hypovolaemia, high altitude can expand Zone 1. |
| Zone 2 (middle) | Middle of lung | PA arterial > PA alveolar > PA venous | Intermittent flow (alveolar pressure intermittently exceeds venous). Flow = arterial − alveolar pressure (Starling resistor). |
| Zone 3 (base) | Bottom of lung | PA arterial > PA venous > PA alveolar | Continuous flow. Flow = arterial − venous pressure. Normal physiology (blood pools at base due to gravity). |

Tip: V/Q mismatch: At base (Zone 3), perfusion > ventilation → V/Q <1 (shunt-like). At apex (Zone 1), ventilation > perfusion → V/Q >1 (dead space-like). Normal overall V/Q ratio ≈ 0.8.
Warning: PCWP measurement: Swan-Ganz catheter drifts to dependent (Zone 3) lung — accurately reflects LAP. If in Zone 1 (tip above LA): PCWP overestimates LAP. Most balloon-flotation catheters naturally drift to Zone 3 (highest flow). Confirm with lateral CXR (tip at or below LA level).

| Feature | Normal value / Detail |

| Pericardial pressure | Normally subatmospheric (−5 to +5 mmHg), closely tracks pleural pressure |
| Pericardial fluid volume | 10–50 mL of serous fluid (lubricant) |

Tip: Acute vs chronic effusion: Acute (e.g. haemopericardium, aortic dissection): even 200 mL can cause tamponade (no time for pericardial stretch). Chronic (e.g. malignancy, myxoedema): >2,000 mL may accumulate slowly without tamponade (pericardium stretches gradually).
Tip: Pericardial restraint: Prevents acute ventricular dilation and limits excessive preload. Ventricular interdependence is mediated by pericardium — filling of one ventricle reduces compliance of the other. This is most pronounced in tamponade and constrictive pericarditis.
Warning: Post-cardiac surgery: Pericardium often left open or partially closed → tamponade physiology may present atypically (posterior effusion compressing LA/RA rather than global effusion).
front: Pericardial physiology — normal pericardial pressure, restraint function, and the concept of pericardial reserve volume

22% ↓ in composite endpoint (death, MI, ischaemia-driven revascularisation, stent thrombosis) at 48h.

20% ↓ CV death/HHF; 16% ↓ CV death; 21% ↓ HHF; 16% ↓ all-cause mortality

Resistant HTN: BP >140/90 mmHg despite ≥3 drugs (including diuretic) at optimised doses

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Confirm true resistance | Rule out white-coat HTN (24h ABPM), pseudoresistance (wrong cuff, poor adherence), secondary HTN |
| 2. Address adherence | Pill count, urine drug levels, direct observed therapy; non-adherence is #1 cause of apparent resistance |
| 3. Lifestyle optimisation | Reduce salt (<2g Na/day), alcohol, weight. DASH diet. Exercise. |
| 4. Eliminate aggravating drugs | NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, decongestants, stimulants, ciclosporin, erythropoietin, licorice, cocaine |
| 5. Screen for secondary HTN | Primary aldosteronism (most common — plasma aldosterone/renin ratio), RAS (duplex renal US), obstructive sleep apnoea (STOP-BANG), phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, coarctation |

Drug strategy for true resistant HTN (on ACEi/ARB + DHP-CCB + thiazide): Add spironolactone 25 mg (PATHWAY-2 trial — most effective 4th agent, ↓ BP ~10 mmHg systolic in primary aldosteronism/sodium-avid patients)

front: Resistant hypertension — definition, causes, workup, and specific drug strategies

Digoxin mechanism: Inhibits Na-K-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → ↑ Na-Ca exchange → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → positive inotropy. Also ↑ vagal tone → ↓ HR, ↑ AV block.

DIG Trial (1997): Digoxin vs placebo in HFrEF patients on ACEi + diuretic
No mortality benefit (neutral). ↓ HF hospitalisation by 28%. At higher plasma levels (>1.2 ng/mL) → ↑ mortality in women especially.

| Feature | Current recommendation |
| --- | --- |
| Indication in HF | Symptomatic HFrEF + persistent AF with rapid rate uncontrolled by BB/CCB (Class IIb, ESC 2021). Not for maintaining sinus rhythm. |
| Target plasma level | 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (lower is safer; benefit occurs at lower levels) |
| Dose | 0.125 mg OD (reduced in elderly, CKD, low body weight). Avoid loading in chronic HF (start low). |
| Monitoring | Serum digoxin level (trough, ≥6h post-dose), K⁺, Mg²⁺, renal function |
| Modern role | Reserved for patients in sinus rhythm with HFrEF on full OMT with persistent symptoms — Class IIb. Less used now that SGLT2i/ARNi/ivabradine available. |
front: Digoxin in heart failure — DIG trial findings, mechanism, correct use, and what has changed in modern HF management

Diuretic resistance: Inadequate natriuresis/diuresis despite high-dose loop diuretics

| Mechanism of resistance | Clinical example |
| --- | --- |
| ↓ Renal perfusion | Cardiorenal syndrome → ↓ furosemide delivery to tubule |
| Compensatory Na absorption | Distal tubule (DCT) hypertrophy → absorbs Na that loop diuretic dumps |
| Neurohormonal RAAS activation | Diuretic → ↓ volume → ↑ RAAS → ↑ Na retention (counteracts diuresis) |
| Hypoalbuminaemia | Furosemide protein-bound → ↓ free drug → ↓ tubular secretion → ↓ effect |
| Gut oedema | ↓ Oral bioavailability of furosemide (40–80% normally → lower in oedematous gut) |

| Strategy | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Switch oral to IV furosemide | IV bioavailability 100% vs oral 40–80%; faster onset |
| Higher IV dose or continuous infusion | Continuous infusion superior to bolus in DOSE trial (trend to better urine output) |
| Add thiazide/thiazide-like | "Sequential nephron blockade" — metolazone or chlorothiazide IV before furosemide → blocks DCT compensation. Very potent — monitor K⁺ closely. |
| Add MRA (spironolactone) | Blocks aldosterone-driven Na absorption in collecting duct |
| SGLT2i | Independent osmotic diuresis via glucosuria — different tubular mechanism; additive to loop diuretics |
| Ultrafiltration | Mechanical fluid removal — CARRESS-HF trial (not superior to pharmacologic strategy + worse creatinine) |
front: Diuretic resistance in HF — causes and stepwise management strategy

Aldosterone escape: Despite ACEi/ARB therapy, aldosterone levels rise back to near-baseline within months in many patients

| Mechanism | Details |
| --- | --- |
| ACEi/ARB block Ang II → initial ↓ aldosterone | At initiation of therapy, aldosterone suppressed (Ang II is primary aldosterone stimulus) |
| Alternative aldosterone stimuli bypass ACEi/ARB | ↑ K⁺ (direct adrenal stimulus), ACTH, angiotensin II from tissue renin (non-ACE pathways — chymase), neurohormonal adaptation |
| Frequency | Up to 40% of patients on long-term ACEi show aldosterone escape within 6–12 months |
| Consequence | Persistent aldosterone → continued Na retention, K⁺ wasting, fibrosis, LV remodelling despite ACEi/ARB |

Therapeutic implication: This is why adding MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) on top of ACEi/ARB is independently beneficial — directly blocks aldosterone receptor regardless of circulating Ang II level
Tip: The RALES trial showed spironolactone benefit even in patients on ACEi — confirming that residual aldosterone activity is clinically significant. MRA provides "complete RAAS blockade" at the aldosterone receptor level that ACEi/ARB cannot achieve alone.

Friedewald formula: LDL-C = Total cholesterol − HDL-C − (TG/5) [mg/dL units]
Or in mmol/L: LDL-C = Total-C − HDL-C − (TG/2.2)

| Limitation | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Unreliable when TG >400 mg/dL (4.5 mmol/L) | TG/5 coefficient assumes fixed TG:VLDL ratio — not true at high TG. Friedewald UNDERESTIMATES LDL at high TG. |
| Type III hyperlipoproteinaemia (dysbetalipoproteinaemia) | IDL accumulation → TG/5 overestimates VLDL → underestimates LDL |
| Fasting vs non-fasting | Non-fasting sample → higher TG → lower estimated LDL (may miss statin indication) |

Alternatives when Friedewald unreliable:

| Method | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Martin-Hopkins equation | Uses adjustable TG:VLDL divisor based on non-HDL and TG — more accurate than Friedewald, especially at high TG |
| Direct LDL measurement | By ultracentrifugation or homogeneous assay — accurate at any TG level; gold standard |
| Non-HDL cholesterol | Does not require TG level assumption; useful alternative treatment target when TG elevated |

Tip: ESC 2019 guideline: Measure Lp(a) at least once in everyone; ≥180 mg/dL is equivalent lifetime risk to heterozygous FH. Consider in recurrent CV events despite statin therapy at LDL target — Lp(a) is the hidden driver.

CCBs are only indicated in PAH if the patient is a "responder" on vasoreactivity testing

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Vasoreactivity test | Performed during right heart catheterisation: inhaled NO (10–20 ppm) OR IV adenosine OR IV epoprostenol OR inhaled iloprost is administered to test acute vasodilator response |
| Positive response (responder) | ↓ mPAP ≥10 mmHg to absolute value ≤40 mmHg AND preserved/improved CO (without ↓ CO) |
| Frequency of responders | ~10–15% of idiopathic PAH only (rarely see response in associated PAH — connective tissue disease, HIV, etc.) |
| CCB used in responders | Nifedipine (high dose, up to 240 mg/day) OR diltiazem (360–720 mg/day) OR amlodipine. Verapamil AVOIDED (excessive negative inotropy). |
| Response on CCB at 3–4 months | Must reassess haemodynamics. ~50% of initial responders sustain long-term response. If not sustained → switch to PAH-specific therapy. |

Warning: NEVER give CCBs to non-responders — may cause acute deterioration (↓ SVR, ↑ RV afterload, ↓ CO). Vasoreactivity testing is REQUIRED before prescribing CCBs in PAH. Only applicable to Group 1 PAH (not Group 2 PH from left heart disease — where CCBs are dangerous).

Takotsubo = Transient LV systolic dysfunction with apical ballooning (occasionally mid-ventricular or atypical variants) triggered by physical or emotional stress

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| InterTAK Diagnostic Criteria | Transient LV/RV dysfunction (hyper- or hypokinesis); Preceded by neurological/psychological trigger; No obstructive CAD or acute plaque rupture (angiography); New ECG changes or modest troponin rise; No myocarditis; Postmenopausal women (90%) |
| ECG features | Initially: ST elevation (V3–V6, similar to anterior STEMI). Then: Deep T inversions + QTc prolongation (days 2–4). QTc >500 ms → TdP risk |
| Echo pattern | Apical ballooning (hypokinesis/akinesis/dyskinesis) + basal hyperkinesis. Non-coronary territory (crosses LAD distribution). |
| Catecholamine hypothesis | Catecholamine surge → coronary spasm + direct myocardial toxicity via β-adrenoceptor-mediated cAMP-driven Ca²⁺ overload. Apical region has highest catecholamine sensitivity (↑ sympathetic innervation density). |

Management — supportive:

- Remove the triggering stressor if possible
- Beta-blockers: reduce catecholamine-mediated injury (no RCT but logical)
- ACEi/ARNi: for LV recovery and remodelling prevention
- Avoid catecholamines (dobutamine, dopamine): paradoxically worsen (LVOTO can occur in hypovolaemic phase). Use levosimendan if inotrope needed.
- LVOTO in Takotsubo: Phenylephrine (↑ afterload) + IV fluids + beta-blocker. Avoid vasodilators + diuretics.
- Anticoagulation if LV thrombus (40% apical thrombus formation risk)

Correct: Prognosis: Generally excellent — LV function recovers fully in 90% within 4–8 weeks. In-hospital mortality ~2–3% (complications: LVOTO, VT/VF, cardiogenic shock, LV thrombus). Recurrence: 1–2%/year.
front: Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopathy) — diagnosis, management, and prognosis

Remodelling = progressive structural changes: LV dilatation, wall thinning, sphericalization, fibrosis, myocyte loss → sustains and worsens HF independent of haemodynamic triggers

back:
Remodelling = changes in LV size, shape, and composition in response to sustained load or injury

| Type | Stimulus | Sarcomere change | Shape | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Eccentric hypertrophy | Volume overload (MR, AR, DCM, HFrEF) | Sarcomeres added in SERIES → ↑ myocyte length | LV enlarges, wall relatively thin → ↑ radius, ↓ relative wall thickness (RWT) | ↑ EDV, ↑ SV (Starling), ↓ EF over time |
| Concentric hypertrophy | Pressure overload (HTN, AS, HCM) | Sarcomeres added in PARALLEL → ↑ myocyte width | LV walls thicken, cavity normal/small → ↑ wall thickness, ↑ RWT | ↑ stiffness, ↓ compliance, diastolic dysfunction → HFpEF |
| Concentric remodelling | Mild pressure overload (early HTN) | Parallel sarcomere addition without ↑ LV mass | ↑ RWT but normal LV mass | Early diastolic dysfunction; precedes concentric hypertrophy |

Tip: Laplace's law explains both: Wall stress = (P × r) / (2h). Eccentric: ↑ r → ↑ wall stress → further dilatation cycle. Concentric: ↑ h → normalises wall stress → but ↓ compliance. HFpEF = predominantly concentric; HFrEF = predominantly eccentric.
Warning: Reverse remodelling: Treatment with GDMT (BB + RAAS inhibitors + SGLT2i) → ↓ LV volume, ↑ EF over months → "LV reverse remodelling." Echocardiographic response at 3–6 months is a positive prognostic sign.

Ross's response-to-injury hypothesis: Atherosclerosis = chronic inflammatory disease triggered by endothelial dysfunction

| Step | Event | Key molecules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Endothelial dysfunction | Risk factors (HTN, smoking, DM, LDL) → ↓ NO production + ↑ oxidative stress + ↑ adhesion molecules | ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, ↑ ROS |
| 2. LDL entry and oxidation | LDL enters subendothelial space → oxidised LDL (ox-LDL) by ROS → pro-inflammatory | ox-LDL is the key atherogenic particle |
| 3. Monocyte recruitment | MCP-1 recruits monocytes → differentiate into macrophages → ingest ox-LDL via scavenger receptors (SR-A, CD36) | MCP-1, M-CSF, SR-A, CD36 |
| 4. Foam cell formation | Macrophages engorged with lipid → foam cells → fatty streak (earliest lesion, reversible) | Foam cells = hallmark of early atherosclerosis |
| 5. Fibrous cap formation | PDGF from macrophages → smooth muscle cell migration from media → collagen deposition → fibrous cap over lipid core | PDGF, TGF-β, collagen I and III |
| 6. Vulnerable plaque | Large necrotic lipid core + thin fibrous cap + macrophage infiltration + ↓ smooth muscle → HIGH RISK of rupture | MMPs degrade cap (macrophage-derived) |
| 7. Plaque rupture/erosion | Thrombosis at rupture site → ACS. 70% of MI from plaques with <70% stenosis (non-obstructive but vulnerable) | Tissue factor → thrombin → fibrin |
front: Atherosclerosis pathophysiology — describe the key steps from endothelial injury to vulnerable plaque rupture

Virchow's Triad: Stasis + Endothelial injury + Hypercoagulability → Thrombosis

| Component | Mechanism | Clinical examples | Contributing drugs/conditions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stasis (abnormal flow) | ↓ Flow → ↑ contact time of clotting factors with vessel wall; ↑ rouleaux formation | AF (atrial), DVT (venous), mechanical heart valve, HF, immobility, long flights | Dehydration, bed rest, varicose veins, pregnancy (uterus compresses IVC) |
| Endothelial injury | Exposed subendothelial collagen + tissue factor → vWF + platelet activation → intrinsic pathway | Atherosclerotic plaque rupture, PCI (balloon), MI, surgery, trauma, sepsis (endotoxin) | Catheters/lines, radiation, chemotherapy (bevacizumab, cisplatin), HTN |
| Hypercoagulability | ↑ Clotting factors, ↓ anticoagulants, ↑ platelets | Malignancy (Trousseau's), APS, protein C/S deficiency, Factor V Leiden, pregnancy, nephrotic syndrome (loss of AT-III, protein C/S) | OCP (↑ clotting factors, ↓ AT-III), HRT, tamoxifen, thalidomide, JAK inhibitors |

Tip: AF: All three components — stasis in LA/LAA + endothelial dysfunction from atrial fibrosis + hypercoagulable state (↑ TF, ↑ fibrinogen). This is why CHA₂DS₂-VASc risk ≥1 (men) or ≥2 (women) requires anticoagulation, not antiplatelet (thrombosis mechanism is primarily stasis-driven, not platelet-driven).

back:
Paradox: Restoring blood flow to ischaemic myocardium causes additional cell death beyond the ischaemia itself

| Mechanism | Pathology |
| --- | --- |
| Calcium overload | During ischaemia: ↑ intracellular Na⁺ (↑ H⁺ → NHE-1 activation → Na⁺ influx) → ↑ NCX reverse mode → ↑ Ca²⁺. At reperfusion: pH normalises rapidly → NHE-1 activates again → massive Ca²⁺ influx → hypercontracture + mitochondrial damage |
| Reactive oxygen species (ROS) | Reoxygenation → xanthine oxidase + NADPH oxidase burst → massive ROS → lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, protein oxidation → myocyte death |
| Mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) | Opening of mPTP at reperfusion → dissipation of mitochondrial membrane potential → energy failure → apoptosis/necrosis. Major driver of reperfusion cell death. |
| Neutrophil infiltration | Activated by complement + cytokines → ROS + proteases → "no-reflow" (microvascular obstruction) |
| No-reflow phenomenon | Microvascular obstruction despite epicardial vessel patency. Seen in 30–40% of primary PCI. ECG: persistent ST elevation after PCI. Echo: wall motion abnormality without flow. |

Tip: Therapeutic targets: Cyclosporin A (mPTP inhibitor — CIRCUS/CYCLE trials: negative in humans). Ischaemic post-conditioning (brief cycles of ischaemia/reperfusion at time of PCI). GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors may reduce no-reflow. No definitive pharmacological therapy proven to reduce reperfusion injury in humans to date.
front: Reperfusion injury — what are the mechanisms, and what interventions reduce it?

back:
AF initiation vs maintenance involves two distinct mechanisms

| Phase | Mechanism | Clinical relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initiation (triggering) | Focal discharges from pulmonary vein (PV) sleeves — ectopic automaticity or triggered activity (EADs/DADs) from PV cardiomyocytes with shorter APD + ↑ automaticity | PV isolation is the basis of catheter ablation (Class I for paroxysmal AF) |
| Maintenance (perpetuation) | Multiple re-entry wavelets (multiple wavelet hypothesis) + rotor activity (rotational drivers) within the atrium, sustained by electrical and structural remodelling | Longer AF duration → more remodelling → harder to cardiovert ("AF begets AF") |
| Electrical remodelling | Rapid firing → ↓ L-type Ca²⁺ current, ↓ APD, ↓ ERP → shorter wavelength → more stable re-entry | Occurs within days of sustained AF |
| Structural remodelling | Atrial fibrosis (via TGF-β + Ang II), ↑ atrial size → ↑ substrate for multiple re-entry | Longer AF → more fibrosis → less chance of successful cardioversion. CMR/electroanatomic mapping shows fibrosis burden. |

Tip: Why PVs? PV sleeves contain cardiomyocytes extending 1–3 cm into the PV lumen. These cells have unusual electrophysiology (shorter APD, steep repolarisation gradients) making them prone to triggered activity especially at PV-LA junctions.
Warning: EAST-AFNET 4 trial: Early rhythm control (within 1 year of diagnosis) vs rate control in AF with ≥1 CV complication → 21% ↓ in CV death/stroke/hospitalisation. Changed paradigm: aggressive early rhythm control now preferred (ESC 2020).
front: AF pathophysiology — focal triggering vs re-entrant maintenance. What is the role of pulmonary veins?

PAH = progressive obliteration of pulmonary arterioles by three pathological mechanisms acting simultaneously

| Pathway | Imbalance | Consequence | Drug target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Prostacyclin/Thromboxane | ↓ PGI₂ (anti-aggregatory, vasodilatory) + ↑ TXA₂ (pro-aggregatory, vasoconstrictive) | Vasoconstriction + platelet aggregation → micro-thrombosis in small PAs | Prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost, selexipag) |
| 2. Endothelin pathway | ↑ Endothelin-1 (ET-1) — most potent vasoconstrictor; acts on ET_A receptor → vasoconstriction + smooth muscle proliferation | Sustained vasoconstriction + vascular remodelling + smooth muscle hypertrophy | Endothelin receptor antagonists: bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan |
| 3. NO/cGMP pathway | ↓ eNOS expression + activity → ↓ NO → ↓ cGMP → loss of vasodilatory and anti-proliferative signalling | Vasoconstriction + vascular smooth muscle proliferation + fibrosis | PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil), sGC stimulators (riociguat) |

Tip: Pathological changes in PAH vessels: Intimal hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, adventitial fibrosis, plexiform lesions (hallmark — disordered angiogenesis creating a vascular "plexus"). Plexiform lesions are irreversible — reason why advanced PAH does not fully reverse even after treatment.
Warning: Genetic link: BMPR2 mutation (bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2) is present in ~75% of heritable PAH and ~25% of apparently sporadic PAH. BMPR2 normally inhibits smooth muscle cell proliferation — loss-of-function → uncontrolled proliferation.

| 1. MI/HF precipitant | ↓ Myocardial function → ↓ CO → ↓ BP |
| 2. Compensatory sympathetic activation | ↑ HR + ↑ SVR → maintains BP short-term but ↑ MVO₂ + ↑ afterload → worsens ischaemia |

Torsades = polymorphic VT with QRS amplitude twisting around the isoelectric baseline — in context of prolonged QTc

| Precipitating factor | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| QT-prolonging drugs (see Vol.4 card 66) | IKr block → ↑ APD → ↑ EAD → triggered activity |
| Hypokalaemia | ↓ K⁺ → ↓ IKr activity → ↑ APD. K⁺ acts as agonist for hERG channel. Hypo-K⁺ potentiates all QT-prolonging drugs. |
| Hypomagnesaemia | Mg²⁺ stabilises cardiac membranes; deficiency → ↑ EAD amplitude |
| Bradycardia | Slower rate → longer cycle length → longer repolarisation time (reverse use-dependence) → ↑ EAD risk |
| Pause-dependent initiation | Long-short initiating sequence: Long R-R (pause) → ↑ APD → EAD → short coupling interval to next beat → TdP |
| LQT syndromes (congenital) | Baseline prolonged APD → easy EAD formation |

Acute management:

| Intervention | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| MgSO₄ 2g IV over 5–15 min | First-line regardless of Mg level — suppresses EADs. Works even with normal Mg²⁺. |
| Correct K⁺ to 4.5–5.0 mEq/L | ↑ IKr activity → ↓ APD → ↓ EAD risk |
| Stop all QT-prolonging drugs | Remove precipitant |
| Temporary overdrive pacing (100–120 bpm) | Removes pause-dependence; ↑ rate → ↓ APD → ↓ EAD. Drug of choice for refractory TdP. |
| Isoproterenol infusion (drug-induced TdP) | ↑ HR → ↓ pause → ↓ EAD; used while awaiting pacemaker |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aspirin | 750–1000 mg TID (or 2–4g/day total) | 1–2 weeks then taper | Preferred if post-MI pericarditis or on anticoagulation |

| Colchicine (add to NSAID) | 0.5 mg BD (or 0.5 mg OD if <70 kg) | 3 months (first attack); 6 months (recurrent) | Mandatory add-on; ↓ recurrence 50–70% |

| Agent | Mechanism | Evidence |

| Anakinra (anti-IL-1α/β) | IL-1 receptor antagonist → blocks inflammasome-mediated pericardial inflammation | AIRTRIP trial: anakinra → 83% ↓ recurrence over 14 months. ESC Class IIa for refractory recurrent pericarditis. |
| Rilonacept (anti-IL-1α/β) | Soluble IL-1 trap (decoy receptor) | RHAPSODY trial: 96% ↓ recurrence. FDA-approved for recurrent pericarditis. |

Warning: Activity restriction during acute pericarditis: Athletes must not compete for 3 months minimum (myocarditis coexistence risk). Non-athletes: restrict to sedentary activity until symptom-free + normalised CRP.
front: Pericarditis treatment algorithm — NSAIDs, colchicine, steroids, and when to add IL-1 inhibitors

back:
Tamponade = pericardial pressure exceeds intracardiac pressure → impaired diastolic filling → ↓ CO

| Physiology | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ Pericardial pressure | Fluid accumulation → pericardial pressure rises (non-linear) → compresses all cardiac chambers |
| Equalisation of pressures | RVEDP = LVEDP = RAP = PCWP = pericardial pressure — hallmark on cath (usually within 5 mmHg of each other) |
| Ventricular interdependence ↑↑ | Fixed pericardial constraint → any volume entering RV must displace IVS leftward → ↓ LV filling. Respiratory variation exaggerated. |
| Pulsus paradoxus | Inspiration → ↑ venous return to RV → IVS bows further left → ↓ LV filling → ↓ SBP >10 mmHg. Echo: E velocity variability >25%. |

Beck's Triad: Hypotension + Muffled heart sounds + Elevated JVP (↑ CVP)

| Pericardiocentesis | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Approach | Subxiphoid (most common) — needle at 45° angle toward left shoulder. Parasternal (echo-guided for loculated effusions). |
| Guidance | Echo-guided PREFERRED — identifies safe window, guides needle. ECG-guidance (ST elevation = ventricular contact) is historical. |
| Drainage | Catheter left in situ; drain until dry; fluid sent for cytology/culture (aetiology). Remove when <25 mL/24h. |
| Pericardiodesis | For malignant effusion — instil sclerosant after drainage to prevent recurrence |

Warning: Avoid pericardiocentesis in: Aortic dissection with haemopericardium (↓ tamponade → may release tamponade effect → ↑ haematoma → surgery is the answer). Bleeding diathesis (relative CI). Posterior loculated effusion → surgical drainage preferred.
front: Cardiac tamponade — pathophysiology, Beck's triad, and management (pericardiocentesis technique)

back:
Complete (3rd degree) AV block: No impulses conduct from atria to ventricles — total electrical dissociation

| Escape rhythm location | QRS width | Rate | Stability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Junctional (His bundle) escape | Narrow (≤120 ms) | 40–60 bpm | Relatively stable |
| Ventricular (Purkinje/myocardial) escape | Wide (>120 ms) | 20–40 bpm | Unstable — prone to arrest |

| Cause | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Ischaemic | Inferior STEMI (RCA occlusion → AV nodal artery) — usually reversible. Anterior STEMI → infra-Hisian block → worse prognosis |
| Congenital | Isolated congenital CHB (maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies) |
| Infiltrative | Sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, Lyme disease |
| Iatrogenic | Post-TAVI (especially if pre-existing LBBB — 20–30% need PPM), post-cardiac surgery |
| Drug-induced | Digoxin toxicity, beta-blockers, CCBs (non-DHP), amiodarone |

Permanent pacing indications (ESC Class I):

- Symptomatic 3rd degree AV block — pacemaker Class I regardless of cause
- 3rd degree AV block with asystole >3s or escape rate <40 bpm even if asymptomatic
- 3rd degree AV block post-MI if persistent (>7 days post-MI)
- Symptomatic Mobitz II AV block
- Alternating LBBB/RBBB
front: Complete AV block — causes, haemodynamic consequences, and permanent pacing indications

back:
Cardiac rehabilitation (CR): Structured comprehensive programme of exercise + education + psychological support + risk factor modification

| Component | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Exercise training | Aerobic exercise 3–5× per week, 20–60 min, 60–85% peak HR. Resistance training added. Home-based or centre-based. |
| Risk factor management | BP control, lipid management, DM optimisation, smoking cessation, weight management |
| Psychological support | Anxiety/depression management (20–30% of post-MI patients have depression). CBT or pharmacotherapy if needed. |
| Education | Medication adherence, symptoms recognition, nutrition, sexual activity guidance, return to work/driving |
| Duration | Typically 8–12 weeks (36 sessions), then home programme |

| Evidence | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
| Post-MI CR | 20–25% ↓ all-cause mortality, 26% ↓ CV mortality, 25% ↓ re-hospitalisation (Cochrane meta-analysis) |
| Post-CABG/PCI CR | ↑ Exercise capacity, ↑ QoL, ↓ readmissions |
| HFrEF CR (HF-ACTION trial) | 4% ↓ all-cause mortality/hospitalisation, significant ↑ functional capacity and QoL. CR safe in stable HFrEF. |
| Post-TAVI | Emerging evidence: ↑ functional independence, ↑ 6MWT |

Warning: CR is severely underutilised globally and especially in Indonesia. Only ~20% of eligible post-MI patients participate. Barriers: cost, access, awareness. Telerehabilitation (home-based with digital monitoring) may overcome access barriers in Indonesia.
front: Cardiac rehabilitation — components, evidence for mortality reduction, and who benefits most

Post-MI secondary prevention: ABCDE mnemonic

| Element | Drug | Duration | Key evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A — Antiplatelet + ACEi/ARB | Aspirin 75–100 mg lifelong + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor/prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel for 12 months). ACEi (all post-MI, especially if EF <40%). | Aspirin: lifelong. P2Y12: 12 months minimum. | PLATO (ticagrelor), ISIS-4 (ACEi) |
| B — Beta-blocker | Metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, or carvedilol. Target HR 55–60 bpm. | Minimum 1 year. Lifelong if EF <40% or HF. | COMMIT, CAPRICORN |
| C — Cholesterol (statin) | High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg). LDL target <55 mg/dL (very high risk). Add ezetimibe if not at target. | Lifelong | 4S, HPS, PROVE-IT |
| D — DM/Diet | SGLT2i if DM + ASCVD (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin). GLP-1RA if DM + ASCVD (liraglutide, semaglutide). Diet: Mediterranean. | Indefinitely | EMPA-REG, LEADER |
| E — Exercise/Education + RAAS | Cardiac rehabilitation (Class I). Add MRA (spironolactone) if EF ≤40% + HF symptoms. Add ARNi if HF develops. | Cardiac rehab: 8–12 weeks program | Cochrane CR meta-analysis, RALES |

Tip: Post-MI EF assessment: Reassess EF at 6–12 weeks. If EF improves to >40%: stop ICD programming (if prescribed). If EF remains ≤35% at 40 days post-MI: ICD eligible (ESC Class I, MADIT-II territory).

Ref: PERKI 2024 §6.1, §6.2, §6.3 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.1.b · ESC 2023 §13.1, §13.2, §13.3 · ACC/AHA 2025 §10.5.3, §11.1, §11.2, §11.3, §11.4, §11.5
front: Post-MI care — complete evidence-based management: all drug classes, duration, and monitoring

| Class | Clinical findings | Haemodynamic | 30-day mortality |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class I | No heart failure — no rales, no S3, no JVP elevation | Normal CO, normal filling pressures | ~5–6% |
| Class II | Mild HF — bibasilar rales up to 50% of lung fields, S3 gallop, ↑ JVP | Mild ↑ filling pressures, mildly ↓ CO | ~17% |
| Class III | Acute pulmonary oedema — bibasilar rales >50%, severe dyspnoea | PCWP >18 mmHg, significantly ↓ CO | ~38% |
| Class IV | Cardiogenic shock — SBP <90 mmHg, cold/clammy skin, oliguria, altered consciousness | CI <2.2 L/min/m², PCWP >18 mmHg | ~60–80% |

Tip: Killip class on presentation is a powerful independent predictor of in-hospital and 30-day mortality in STEMI. Used in TIMI-STEMI score (Killip class 2–4 = +2 points). Simple clinical classification requiring only physical examination — no haemodynamic monitoring needed.
Tip: Haemodynamic equivalent (Forrester classification): Both classify acute MI HF severity but Killip uses clinical signs while Forrester uses invasive measurements (CI, PCWP). Forrester Profile IV ≈ Killip IV (cardiogenic shock). In clinical practice Killip is used at presentation; Forrester when PA catheter is placed.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §1.8, §2.1 · ESC 2023 §8.2.2.1, §8.2.2.4 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.3

GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events): Predicts in-hospital and 6-month mortality in ACS

| Variable | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Age | Continuous variable (0–100 points for age range) |
| Killip class | I=0, II=20, III=39, IV=59 points |
| Systolic BP | ↓ SBP = ↑ points (inverse relationship) |
| Serum creatinine | ↑ creatinine = ↑ points |
| Cardiac arrest on admission | +43 points if present |
| ST-segment deviation | +28 points |
| Elevated cardiac biomarkers | +14 points |
| Heart rate | ↑ HR = ↑ points |

Available online: gracescore.org (calculator — cannot manually compute easily)

| GRACE Risk Category | In-hospital death (%) | ESC ACS recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low (<108) | <1% | Conservative/selective invasive approach acceptable |
| Intermediate (108–140) | 1–3% | Early invasive (within 24h) |
| High (>140) | >3% | Immediate/urgent invasive (within 2h if very high risk features) |

Tip: GRACE >140 + ANY of: haemodynamic instability, refractory ischaemia, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complications → IMMEDIATE PCI (within 2h). GRACE >140 without above → early invasive within 24h.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §1.8, §2.1 · ESC 2023 §8.2.2.1, §8.2.2.4 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.3
front: GRACE Score — variables, how to calculate, and what risk categories guide ACS management

| Letter | Risk factor | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H | Hypertension (uncontrolled, SBP >160 mmHg) | 1 |
| A | Abnormal renal/liver function (creatinine >200 μmol/L OR dialysis OR hepatic disease with bilirubin >2× ULN or ALT >3× ULN) | 1 or 2 |
| S | Stroke history (prior ischaemic stroke) | 1 |
| B | Bleeding history or predisposition (anaemia, thrombocytopenia) | 1 |
| L | Labile INR (TTR <60%) | 1 |
| E | Elderly (age >65) | 1 |

HAS-BLED ≥3 = High bleeding risk. Does NOT mean STOP anticoagulation — means CORRECT modifiable bleeding risk factors.

| Modifiable HAS-BLED risk factors | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled HTN (H) | Optimise antihypertensives |
| Labile INR (L) | Switch to DOAC (more predictable) or intensive INR monitoring |
| Drugs: NSAIDs/aspirin (D) | Stop NSAIDs; review antiplatelet need |
| Alcohol (D) | Alcohol cessation counselling |

Warning: HAS-BLED is widely misused to deny anticoagulation. The ESC explicitly states: High HAS-BLED does NOT justify stopping OAC. Stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) generally outweighs bleeding risk when CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (M) or ≥3 (F). Address modifiable risk factors, then anticoagulate.
front: HAS-BLED score — components and what a high score means for anticoagulation decisions in AF

ESC 2019 Dyslipidaemia Guidelines — risk-stratified LDL-C targets

| Cardiovascular Risk | LDL-C Target | Statin initiation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Very high risk Established ASCVD, DM with TOD/multiple RF, eGFR <30, FH + major RF, SCORE >10% | <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) AND >50% reduction from baseline | Initiate high-intensity statin |
| High risk Markedly elevated single RF (LDL >310 mg/dL, SBP >180), DM without TOD, CKD eGFR 30–59, SCORE 5–10% | <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) AND >50% reduction | Initiate statin therapy |
| Moderate risk SCORE 1–5%, no other high-risk features | <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) | Consider statin if LDL not at target with lifestyle |
| Low risk SCORE <1% | <116 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) | Lifestyle modification first; statin only if lifestyle fails |

Tip: For secondary prevention (very high risk): high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg OR rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) regardless of baseline LDL. Add ezetimibe if target not reached. Add PCSK9i if still not at <55 mg/dL. Treat-to-target approach is now endorsed (vs previous "fire-and-forget" high-intensity statin).
Warning: 🇮🇩 Indonesia context: Simvastatin 10–40 mg is the most commonly BPJS-prescribed statin. For post-MI or high-risk patients, advocate strongly for atorvastatin 40–80 mg (now available as generic). Rosuvastatin 10–20 mg is also available but less consistently BPJS-covered. Document indication clearly for formulary access.
front: Statin therapy initiation — primary prevention decision making: ESC LDL targets and when to initiate

Diabetic nephropathy = leading cause of ESRD worldwide. RAAS inhibition is the cornerstone of nephroprotection.

| Drug class | Mechanism of nephroprotection | Key trial | Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ACEi (ramipril, lisinopril) | ↓ Ang II → ↓ efferent arteriolar resistance → ↓ intraglomerular pressure → ↓ proteinuria → ↓ glomerulosclerosis | HOPE (ramipril), MICRO-HOPE | ↓ Proteinuria, ↓ ESRD, ↓ CV events in DM |
| ARBs (losartan, irbesartan) | Same mechanism as ACEi via AT1 blockade. Preferred if ACEi-intolerant (cough). | RENAAL (losartan), IDNT (irbesartan) | ↓ Doubling of creatinine, ↓ ESRD, ↓ proteinuria. NOT in Type 1 DM (less data). |
| SGLT2i (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) | ↓ Tubuloglomerular feedback (↓ glucose absorption in PCT → ↑ Na delivery to macula densa → afferent arteriole constriction → ↓ glomerular pressure). Also reduces proteinuria, inflammation, and oxidative stress. | CREDENCE (canagliflozin), DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin), EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin) | ↓ Progression to ESRD + 30–40% ↓ renal outcomes regardless of DM. ESC Class I for DM CKD. |
| Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) | Selective MRA → ↓ aldosterone-driven fibrosis and inflammation in glomerulus | FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD | ↓ ESRD + ↓ MACE in DM CKD. ESC Class I. |

Tip: Gold-standard triple therapy for DM nephropathy: ACEi/ARB + SGLT2i + finerenone. Max renoprotection with additive mechanisms.
front: RAAS inhibitor nephroprotection in diabetic nephropathy — which drug, what target, and key trials

| Feature | VT (sustained) | VF |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Re-entry (scar-related most common), focal automaticity (idiopathic), triggered activity (CPVT, digitalis) | Multiple wavelet re-entry or rotor activity — chaotic, disorganised electrical activity |
| ECG rate | 100–250 bpm; regular | >300 bpm (unmeasurable); irregular, chaotic |
| Haemodynamics | Stable or unstable depending on rate, duration, underlying function | Always haemodynamically unstable — no meaningful output |
| Immediate management (unstable/pulseless) | Unsynchronised DC shock (200J biphasic) | CPR + unsynchronised defibrillation ASAP (200J biphasic) |
| Stable VT (pulse present) | Synchronised cardioversion (100–200J) OR IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min | N/A — always pulseless |
| Post-resuscitation | IV amiodarone 1 mg/min × 6h then 0.5 mg/min. Treat reversible causes (ischaemia, electrolytes). ICD if structural disease. | Post-ROSC care: TTM (target temperature management 32–36°C × 24h), urgent cath if STEMI, aggressive resuscitation of causes |

VF defibrillation timing: Every minute of VF without defibrillation → 10% ↓ survival. AED within 3–5 min → survival 50–70%. Public access defibrillation (PAD) is the most impactful intervention for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
front: Ventricular tachycardia vs ventricular fibrillation — distinguish mechanisms, management, and key ACLS protocol steps

back:
TTM: Controlled hypothermia 32–36°C for 24h after resuscitation from cardiac arrest (primarily VF/pulseless VT)

| Trial | Design | Key result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HACA (2002) | 32–34°C × 24h vs normothermia after OHCA (VF only) | ↓ Poor neurological outcome (55% vs 69%). TTM established as standard. |
| TTM Trial (2013, n=950) | 33°C vs 36°C × 24h in all rhythms | NO difference in mortality or neurological outcome. Conclusion: target 36°C (avoids hypothermia complications without losing benefit). |
| TTM-2 Trial (2021, n=1,900) | 33°C (hypothermia) vs normothermia (37.5°C) + fever prevention | NO benefit of 33°C over fever-prevention normothermia. Trend toward harm with hypothermia. |

Current recommendation (2021): Prevent fever (T <37.7°C) for all comatose post-arrest survivors. Active cooling to 33°C no longer mandated. Key goal = prevent fever, NOT achieve hypothermia.

| TTM complications (if 33°C used) | Management |
| --- | --- |
| Shivering (most common — worsens outcomes) | Sedation + muscle relaxants (magnesium, meperidine, vecuronium) |
| Hypokalaemia (K⁺ shifts into cells) | Monitor K⁺ frequently; supplement. Risk of rebound hyperkalaemia on rewarming. |
| Coagulopathy + bleeding (↓ clotting factor activity) | Avoid during hypothermia if possible |
| Bradycardia | Usually well tolerated if adequate CO. Pacing if symptomatic. |
front: Targeted temperature management (TTM) after cardiac arrest — current evidence, protocol, and complications
