| Condition | Best BB | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thyroid storm | IV propranolol (1 mg over 10 min, repeat q5min) OR PO propranolol 40–80 mg q4h | Non-selective (blocks β₂ → prevents peripheral T₄→T₃ conversion). Also controls: tachycardia, hypertension, tremor, anxiety, hyperpyrexia. Rate control for AF in thyroid storm. |
| Phaeochromocytoma | Non-selective BB (propranolol, atenolol) — only AFTER alpha-blockade established | NEVER use BB without prior alpha-blockade → unopposed α → hypertensive crisis. After phenoxybenzamine: add propranolol 10–40 mg TID to control reflex tachycardia. |
| Aortic dissection (acute) | IV labetalol (α + β) OR IV esmolol (short-acting, titratable) | Goal: HR <60 + SBP <120 mmHg in 20 min. β-blockade reduces aortic dP/dt (rate of pressure rise) = reduces wall shear force driving dissection propagation. |
| HCM with LVOTO | Beta-blockers (metoprolol, bisoprolol, propranolol) | ↓ HR → ↑ diastolic filling time + ↓ inotropy → ↓ LVOT gradient. Start at low dose. Avoid ISA-containing BB (partial agonism worsens obstruction). |
| Right heart failure | Use with extreme caution or AVOID (carvedilol may be tolerated) | Negative inotropy in RV failure → ↓ RV CO → worse PH. Avoid in acute decompensated RV failure. |

Tip: Propranolol unique properties: Non-selective β → blocks peripheral T₄ to T₃ conversion (via inhibition of Type I deiodinase). This makes it the preferred BB specifically in thyroid storm where T₃ levels need suppression. Atenolol or metoprolol (selective) do NOT have this effect.
front: Beta-blockers in specific conditions — thyroid storm, phaeochromocytoma, aortic dissection, and HCM: what to use and why

back:
PDE5 inhibitors: Block phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) → ↓ cGMP degradation → ↑ cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation

| Feature | Sildenafil (Viagra/Revatio) | Tadalafil (Cialis/Adcirca) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Half-life | ~4 hours | ~17.5 hours (much longer) |
| Dosing for PAH | 20 mg TID (Revatio) | 40 mg OD (Adcirca) |
| Dosing for erectile dysfunction | 25–100 mg PRN 1h before sex | 5–20 mg PRN; or 5 mg daily (allows spontaneous activity) |
| PDE selectivity | PDE5 > PDE6 (in retina → visual disturbance, blue tinge) | PDE5 = PDE11 (in testis/skeletal muscle → myalgia) |
| Food/alcohol interaction | High-fat meal ↓ absorption; alcohol enhances hypotension | Food: minimal effect |
| Key adverse effects | Flushing, headache, nasal congestion, visual disturbance (blue tinge) | Myalgia, back pain, lower limb oedema (PDE11 inhibition) |

Warning: ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION: Organic nitrates (GTN, ISDN, ISMN) + PDE5i → synergistic ↑ cGMP → profound fatal hypotension. Wait ≥24h after sildenafil/vardenafil or ≥48h after tadalafil before giving nitrates. If patient takes PDE5i → do NOT give nitrate in emergency (use IV morphine, IV fluids, IABP instead for ischaemia).
Tip: PAH mechanism: Pulmonary smooth muscle has high PDE5 activity. PDE5i preferentially dilate pulmonary vasculature (high local PDE5 density) + ↓ smooth muscle proliferation → ↓ PVR → ↑ exercise capacity.
front: PDE5 inhibitors — sildenafil, tadalafil: mechanism, clinical uses in PAH and ED, and the critical nitrate contraindication

| Factor | Impact on survival |
| --- | --- |
| Initial rhythm: VF/pulseless VT | Survival 20–40% (shockable, reversible). Non-shockable (PEA/asystole): <5–10% |
| Time to CPR (bystander CPR) | Bystander CPR within 1 min: 3–4× ↑ survival. Without CPR: 10% ↓ survival per minute of VF |
| Time to defibrillation | Every 1 min delay in defibrillation → 10% ↓ survival. AED in 3 min → 50–70% survival |

OHCA survival: 10–12% in most systems (varies 5–30%). IHCA: 20–25% to discharge.
Tip: Best-performing OHCA systems (Seattle, Copenhagen): 15–30% survival to discharge. Common features: High bystander CPR rates (>60%), widespread AED availability, mobile dispatch CPR instruction, short EMS response times (<6 min). Public access defibrillation (PAD) is the most cost-effective intervention.
Warning: 🇮🇩 Indonesia context: Bystander CPR rates very low (<5%). AED availability essentially absent in public spaces. BCLS/ACLS training expansion and public awareness campaigns are urgent public health priorities.
front: Sudden cardiac arrest survival chain — OHCA vs IHCA, prognostic factors, and what determines survival

back:
AF + ischaemic stroke: DUAL risk — re-stroke without OAC, haemorrhagic transformation with early OAC

| Stroke severity | Timing of OAC initiation |
| --- | --- |
| TIA | Start OAC within 1 day (after excluding haemorrhage by CT) |
| Minor ischaemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) | Start OAC within 3 days |
| Moderate ischaemic stroke (NIHSS 4–15) | Start OAC within 6 days (after CT to confirm no haemorrhagic transformation) |
| Severe ischaemic stroke (NIHSS ≥15) | Start OAC within 12 days (repeat CT at 7–10 days to confirm no haemorrhage) |

"1-3-6-12 day rule" (ESC 2020): TIA → 1 day; minor stroke → 3 days; moderate → 6 days; severe → 12 days
Tip: Key exceptions: Large infarct (>1/3 MCA territory) → individual assessment (often delay 2–4 weeks due to higher haemorrhagic transformation risk). Haemorrhagic transformation already present → delay OAC further. Always consult neurology + repeat brain imaging before OAC initiation.
Tip: DOAC preferred over VKA post-stroke in AF (ARISTOTLE, ROCKET-AF: lower ICH risk than warfarin). Avoid bridging with LMWH/UFH (↑ haemorrhagic transformation risk). Start DOAC directly when timing window opens.
front: Anticoagulation in AF post-stroke or TIA — when to start, and what is the 1-3-6-12 rule?

back:
RV infarction: Complicates 30–50% of inferior STEMIs (proximal RCA occlusion before RV marginal branches)

| ECG finding | Details |
| --- | --- |
| ST elevation in V4R (or V3R) | ≥1 mm = diagnostic of RV infarction. Most sensitive and specific. V4R is at right 5th intercostal space mid-clavicular line. |
| Right precordial leads (V1–V3R) | ST elevation may appear; often more apparent with right-sided leads |
| Inferor ST elevation + elevated JVP + clear lungs + hypotension | Clinical triad of RV infarction (Kussmaul's sign may be present) |

Specific management of RV infarction:

| Intervention | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| IV fluids (normal saline) — CAREFUL preload management | RV failure → ↓ RVEDP and preload → IV fluids maintain RV preload. BUT: over-hydration → RV overdistension → septal shift → ↓ LV filling. Goal: JVP optimisation. |
| AVOID diuretics and nitrates | Venodilators ↓ preload → catastrophic ↓ in CO in RV infarction. CONTRAINDICATED. |
| Restore sinus rhythm (AV synchrony) | Atrial kick contributes 30–50% of RV filling in RV infarction. Treat AF/AV block aggressively. Temporary AV sequential pacing if complete AV block develops. |
| Primary PCI (reperfusion) | Restores flow to RV marginal branch → RV often recovers function (RV is thin-walled, resilient) |
| Inotropes (dobutamine) | If hypotension persists despite fluids + reperfusion → dobutamine 2–5 mcg/kg/min |

Ref: PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.1, §3.6 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.a, Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §3.2.1, §12.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2, §9
front: ECG diagnosis of right ventricular infarction — clinical significance and specific management

back:
HFmrEF: HF symptoms + EF 40–49% (ESC definition). Also called "borderline" or "mid-range" EF.

| Feature | HFmrEF |
| --- | --- |
| Prevalence | ~10–20% of all HF patients |
| Clinical profile | Intermediate phenotype between HFrEF and HFpEF. More similar to HFrEF (ischaemic aetiology common, male predominance). |
| Natural history | May transition to HFrEF or HFpEF. Dynamic EF — reassess at 3–6 months. |

| Treatment | Evidence | ESC Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diuretics (symptom control) | Expert consensus | Class I |
| ACEi/ARB or ARNi | Post-hoc analysis CHARM-Preserved (candesartan) + TOPCAT (spironolactone) subgroup: benefit in EF 40–50% range. PARAGON-HF subgroup: sacubitril/valsartan benefit in EF ≤57%. | Class IIb |
| Beta-blockers | MERIT-HF subgroup, meta-analyses: possible benefit | Class IIb |
| MRA (spironolactone) | TOPCAT Americas subgroup benefit | Class IIb |
| SGLT2i (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) | EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER both included EF 40–49% → significant benefit | Class IIa |

Tip: The inclusion of EF 40–49% in EMPEROR-Preserved (empagliflozin) and DELIVER (dapagliflozin) means SGLT2i benefit extends to the FULL spectrum of HF (HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF). SGLT2i are now the only Class I-adjacent treatment across all EF ranges.

| Population | Differences in CAD presentation/management |

| Women | Atypical symptoms more common (dyspnoea, fatigue, nausea, jaw pain vs classic chest pain). Higher prevalence of MINOCA, microvascular disease, Takotsubo. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) — predominantly young women. Troponin upper reference limits lower in women (smaller myocardial mass). Underprescibed GDMT post-MI historically. |
| Elderly (>75 years) | Atypical symptoms (dyspnoea, confusion, fatigue). Higher procedural risk. Frailty and bleeding risk more prominent. Aspirin primary prevention: NOT recommended (ASPREE). More diffuse atherosclerosis — less "focal" lesion-based approach. |

PMC (balloon mitral valvuloplasty): Catheter-based dilation of stenotic mitral valve — treatment of choice for appropriate severe MS

| Wilkins Score Component | Score 1–4 per variable (4 = worst) |
| --- | --- |
| Leaflet mobility | 1 = highly mobile → 4 = rigid |
| Subvalvular thickening | 1 = minimal → 4 = extensive |
| Leaflet thickening | 1 = minimal → 4 = severe, marked |
| Leaflet calcification | 1 = none → 4 = fluoroscopic brightness throughout |

Total Wilkins score: max = 16. Score ≤8 = favourable anatomy for PMC → good results expected. Score >8 = unfavourable → ↑ post-PMC MR risk, ↓ success rate → consider surgery.

| PMC Indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Severe MS (MVA <1.5 cm²) + symptoms + favourable anatomy (Wilkins ≤8) | Class I |
| Severe MS + symptoms + unfavourable anatomy (Wilkins >8) + high surgical risk | Class IIa |
| Severe MS + no symptoms + favourable anatomy + no LA thrombus | Class IIa (to prevent progression) |
| Severe MS + pregnancy (to avoid surgery) | Class IIb (if appropriate anatomy, no LA thrombus) |

Warning: Contraindications: LA thrombus (mandatory TOE to exclude before PMC — thrombus → embolism on balloon dilation). MR >grade 2. Severe/bicommissural calcification. Concomitant severe AR (↑ risk). Active rheumatic carditis.
front: Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy (PMC) — indications, Wilkins score, and contraindications

CIED infection = one of the most serious device complications — carries ~35% 1-year mortality if untreated

| Classification | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Superficial (pocket) infection | Erythema, warmth, tenderness at device pocket. No systemic signs. Organism tracking to device. |
| Generator pocket infection | Deep infection to generator/leads. Purulent discharge, erosion, or adherent vegetations on leads (TOE). |
| Lead endocarditis (CDRIE) | Systemic signs (fever, bacteraemia). Vegetation on lead(s) or tricuspid valve on TOE. PE may occur (septic emboli to lungs). |

| Management | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Complete device and lead extraction | MANDATORY for lead endocarditis (ERT Class I). No antibiotic suppression without extraction — relapse rate nearly 100%. Surgical extraction if lead too large for transvenous. |
| Antibiotics | Prolonged IV antibiotics (4–6 weeks for bacteraemia/endocarditis). Target organism-guided therapy. S. aureus/CoNS most common. |
| Re-implantation timing | At least 72h of culture-negative blood cultures before new device at contralateral site. Longer if S. aureus (>14 days) or endocarditis. |

Tip: Prevention: Single pre-operative antibiotic dose (cefazolin 2g IV 30 min before) reduces pocket infection rate by 80% (PADIT trial). Antimicrobial envelope (Tyrx/AIGISRX) — absorbable antibiotic-eluting mesh — Class IIa for high-risk patients (WRAP-IT trial: 40% ↓ infection).
front: Cardiac implantable device infection — prevention, diagnosis, and management of CIED infection

Tip: NYHA vs ACC/AHA staging: NYHA reflects CURRENT FUNCTIONAL STATUS (can change with treatment). ACC/AHA reflects STRUCTURAL DISEASE PROGRESSION (only moves forward — cannot de-stage). A patient in Stage C NYHA I (asymptomatic post-MI with ↓ EF) remains Stage C even if fully asymptomatic.

IE Surgery: ~50% of IE patients require surgical intervention — high-risk category. Heart failure is the primary indication.

| Category | Specific indication | Urgency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Heart failure (most common indication ~60%) | Severe AR or MR + acute pulmonary oedema + cardiogenic shock (Class I emergency). Severe AI/MR + refractory HF despite medical Rx (Class I urgent). Moderate AI/MR causing progressive HF (Class IIa elective) | Emergency/Urgent/Elective |
| 2. Uncontrolled infection (~40%) | Perivalvular extension (abscess, fistula, false aneurysm) [Class I urgent]. Persistently positive blood cultures despite appropriate antibiotics >7–10 days. Fungal endocarditis. Multi-resistant organism (VRSA, MDR-GNB). | Urgent/Emergency |
| 3. Prevention of embolism ~20% | Large mobile vegetation (>10 mm) + prior embolic event. Very large vegetation >15 mm regardless of emboli if expected mortality acceptable. Vegetation on mitral valve (higher emboli risk than AV IE). | Urgent/Elective |

Warning: Stroke is NOT a contraindication to IE surgery if neurological deficit is mild/improving. Recent cerebral haemorrhage: delay surgery ≥4 weeks (surgical anticoagulation → ↑ haemorrhagic transformation). Coma: very high surgical mortality — individual assessment.
Tip: Perivalvular extension (abscess): Best detected by TOE (>90% sensitivity vs 50% TTE). Occurs in ~25–30% of IE. Especially: aortic root abscess (↑ AVB risk), sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. Almost always requires surgery.

| Newly diagnosed NICM (non-ischaemic DCM) + EF ≤35% | 40–90 days while waiting to see if EF improves (reverse remodelling on OMT) | Avoid premature ICD implant — 30–40% of NICM recover EF with OMT |

HFpEF = Preserved EF (≥50%) + HF symptoms + ↑ filling pressures. 50% of all HF is HFpEF.

| Why difficult to treat | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| No single unifying mechanism | HFpEF is a syndrome of multiple pathologies: obesity, HTN, DM, AF, CKD — each contributing differently |
| Mostly diastolic dysfunction | ↑ LV stiffness → impaired filling → symptoms without reduced EF. No drug proven to improve myocardial compliance. |
| Neurohormonal activation less prominent | RAAS/sympathetic less activated than in HFrEF → ACEi/BB less effective |

| Trial | Drug | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PARAGON-HF (2019) | ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) vs valsartan alone in EF ≥45% | Primary endpoint MISSED (p=0.059). Subgroup: women + EF 45–57% may benefit. ESC: Class IIb to consider ARNi to ↓ HF hospitalisation in HFpEF. |
| EMPEROR-Preserved (2021) | Empagliflozin vs placebo in EF >40% | 21% ↓ CV death + HHF (p<0.001). FIRST positive trial in HFpEF. Benefit regardless of DM status. |
| DELIVER (2022) | Dapagliflozin vs placebo in EF >40% | 18% ↓ CV death + worsening HF. Confirmed SGLT2i benefit in HFpEF across full spectrum of EF. |

ESC 2021 (updated): SGLT2i Class IIa in HFpEF to reduce HHF. Diuretics for congestion (Class I). Treat comorbidities (HTN, AF, DM, obesity) aggressively.

Pharmaco-invasive strategy: Fibrinolysis when PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes of STEMI diagnosis → mandatory angiography 2–24h later

| Scenario | Action |
| --- | --- |
| PCI-capable centre within 120 min | Primary PCI (standard of care) |
| PCI NOT available within 120 min | IV fibrinolysis (streptokinase or alteplase) within 10 min of diagnosis |
| Fibrinolysis given → transfer to PCI centre | Coronary angiography 2–24h post-fibrinolysis (pharmaco-invasive strategy) |
| Fibrinolysis fails (persistent symptoms + <50% ST resolution at 60–90 min) | Rescue PCI immediately |

Streptokinase: 1.5 million units IV over 60 min. Available in BPJS formulary in Indonesia. LOWER cost than alteplase/tenecteplase.

| Streptokinase consideration | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Antigenicity | Do NOT repeat within 6 months (antibodies neutralise). If re-MI within 6 months → use alteplase instead. |
| Hypotension | Common (20%) — slow rate of infusion reduces risk. Position supine. IV fluids if severe. |
| Concomitant antithrombotics | Add enoxaparin (preferred over UFH) + aspirin + clopidogrel 300 mg loading (if age <75 years) |

Warning: 🇮🇩 Indonesian context: Many hospitals lack 24/7 cath lab. Primary PCI availability is concentrated in major cities (Jakarta, Surabaya, Bali, Makassar). Pharmaco-invasive strategy is the standard approach for STEMI in peripheral hospitals. BPJS covers streptokinase (Streptase) — ensure no prior SK within 6 months.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §3.2.2.1, §3.2.2 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §5.3.1.2, §5.3 · ACC/AHA 2025 §5.3.2, §5.3
front: Pharmaco-invasive strategy for STEMI in Indonesia — when and how to use it in settings without primary PCI

| Drug Class | BPJS-covered drugs | NOT typically BPJS-covered |
| --- | --- | --- |

| Lipid-lowering | Simvastatin, atorvastatin (generic), fenofibrate | Rosuvastatin (limited), PCSK9 inhibitors, ezetimibe (limited) |

Tip: BPJS formulary is updated periodically. In practice, BPJS covers basic cardiac drugs at primary care (FKTP) and specialist (FKRTL) levels. Expensive drugs (DOACs, ticagrelor, ARNi) require specialist prescription and may be available at top-tier referral hospitals (RSUD level 4 or academic centres).

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Myocarditis | Defervescence (day 3–6) | Dengue virus directly infects cardiomyocytes + immune-mediated T-cell myocardial injury | Supportive. Avoid NSAIDs (↑ bleeding). Corticosteroids — no proven benefit; use only for haemodynamically significant myocarditis. Mechanical support if fulminant. |

🇮🇩 Indonesia has one of the highest TB burdens globally. TB pericarditis and myocarditis are relatively common in Indonesia and SE Asia.

| Condition | Prevalence / Features | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TB pericarditis | ~70% of pericarditis in TB-endemic regions. Large haemorrhagic effusion. Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fever, night sweats). ADA (adenosine deaminase) ↑ in pericardial fluid (>35 U/L = suggestive). | Anti-TB therapy (HRZE × 2 months → HR × 4 months). Corticosteroids (prednisone 1–2 mg/kg × 6 weeks then taper) — IMPI trial: ↓ hospitalisation + ↓ pericardial constriction, but no ↓ mortality. |
| Constrictive pericarditis (TB) | Most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in Indonesia. Pericardial calcification on CXR/CT (calcific constriction). Presents months to years after TB pericarditis. | Anti-TB therapy (if active). Surgical pericardiectomy — definitive treatment. Steroids for recent-onset (CMR gadolinium enhancement) transient constrictive form. |
| TB myocarditis | Rare. Miliary spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to myocardium. VT, AV block, cardiac failure in context of miliary TB. | Anti-TB therapy. Standard HF drugs. ICD if sustained VT. |

Tip: Workup for TB pericarditis: Pericardial fluid ADA, culture, PCR (GeneXpert). If effusion accessible: diagnostic pericardiocentesis. FNAC/biopsy if lymphadenopathy accessible. HIV test (co-infection common). Sputum AFB and culture. Do NOT await culture result (weeks) — start empiric TB treatment if clinical suspicion high.
front: Tuberculosis-related cardiac disease in Indonesia — pericarditis, constrictive pericarditis, and myocarditis: management

ARF = Systemic inflammatory disease post-GAS pharyngitis. Carditis in 40–60% → RHD if recurrent attacks

| Phase | Treatment | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eradicate GAS | Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM single dose OR amoxicillin × 10 days | Even if throat culture negative — assume GAS to prevent ongoing antigenic stimulation |
| Anti-inflammatory therapy (arthritis) | Aspirin 100 mg/kg/day (children) or 4–8 g/day (adults) in 4 divided doses × 4–8 weeks | Dramatic response in 24–48h (diagnostic feature). Naproxen is alternative. |
| Anti-inflammatory therapy (carditis) | Prednisone 2 mg/kg/day (max 80 mg) × 2–4 weeks → taper over 4 weeks → overlap with aspirin 6–8 weeks | Steroids for moderate-severe carditis (HF, cardiomegaly). No proven benefit for mild carditis (only arthritis benefit). |
| HF management | Digoxin + furosemide + ACEi for acute HF. Bed rest during active phase. | Avoid physical exertion during acute carditis (may worsen valve damage) |
| Choreic movement (Sydenham's) | Carbamazepine or valproate or haloperidol | Self-limiting (months). Address if severe/disabling. |

Warning: KEY: Aspirin/NSAIDs do NOT prevent development of carditis or RHD — they reduce symptoms. Secondary prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks) is the only intervention proven to prevent recurrent ARF and progression to RHD. Start immediately and continue lifelong (if severe RHD).
front: Acute rheumatic fever management in Indonesia — treatment of the acute attack and prevention of permanent valve damage

back:
Leptospirosis: Spirochetal infection (Leptospira spp.) — endemic in Indonesia, particularly during floods

| Cardiac complication | Features | Prevalence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Myocarditis | Troponin ↑, ECG changes (ST changes, T-wave abnormalities, QTc prolongation), ↓ EF | ~5–10% of Weil's disease (severe leptospirosis) |
| Pericarditis/pericardial effusion | Chest pain, friction rub, echo effusion | Uncommon |
| Arrhythmias | AF, AV block, VT — especially in severe disease with multi-organ failure | Variable |
| Sudden death | Malignant arrhythmia from myocarditis/electrolyte disturbance | Rare |

Diagnosis: Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT) — gold standard. Leptospira PCR in early phase. Leptospira IgM ELISA.
Treatment: Penicillin G 1.5 million units IV every 6h × 7 days (severe). Or amoxicillin PO for mild. Early treatment ↓ severity.
Tip: 🇮🇩 Indonesia context: Post-flood leptospirosis is common in urban Indonesia (Jakarta, Surabaya, etc.). Young patients presenting with fever + jaundice + AKI + myocarditis → suspect leptospirosis. Weil's disease (icterohaemorrhagic leptospirosis) = severe form with jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage + cardiac involvement. Notifiable disease in Indonesia.
front: Leptospirosis cardiac involvement — a rare but important cause of myocarditis in tropical Indonesia

back:
IABP: Helium-filled balloon in descending aorta (distal to left subclavian); triggers on ECG (R-wave) or arterial pressure

| Phase | Action | Haemodynamic effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diastole (inflation — after dicrotic notch/T-wave) | Balloon inflates → displaces blood proximally → ↑ aortic diastolic pressure | ↑ Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP = aortic DBP − LVEDP); ↑ cerebral perfusion |
| Systole (deflation — before QRS) | Balloon deflates rapidly → vacuum created in descending aorta → ↓ LV afterload | ↓ SVR → ↓ LVEDP → ↑ SV; ↓ MVO₂; ↑ CO by 10–20% |

IABP-SHOCK II Trial (NEJM 2012, n=600): IABP vs no IABP in cardiogenic shock complicating STEMI → NO difference in 30-day mortality (39.7% vs 41.3%). Downgraded from Class I to Class IIb/III.

| Current ESC indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| CS-STEMI (routine use) | Class III (no benefit — IABP-SHOCK II) |
| Mechanical complications of MI (acute VSD, severe MR) | Class IIa (haemodynamic stabilisation bridge to surgery) |
| High-risk PCI (selected cases) | Class IIb |
| Refractory ventricular arrhythmias with haemodynamic instability | Class IIa |

Warning: Contraindications: Significant AR (inflation worsens regurgitation), aortic dissection, severe aortoiliac occlusive disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm. Complications: Limb ischaemia (5%), thrombocytopenia, aortic perforation, infection.
front: IABP (Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump) — mechanism of diastolic augmentation and systolic unloading, and current evidence

back:
| Feature | Impella | VA-ECMO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Axial flow pump (Archimedes screw) in LV → aspirates from LV and expels into aorta → LV unloading + ↑ CO | Centrifugal pump drains venous blood (RA via femoral vein) → oxygenator → returns to femoral artery (retrograde aortic flow) |
| LV unloading | Excellent (directly reduces LVEDP and wall stress) | Poor (retrograde aortic flow increases LV afterload → worsens LV distension unless combined with Impella or vent) |
| CO support | Impella 2.5: +2.5 L/min. CP: +3.7 L/min. 5.0: +5 L/min | Up to 6–7 L/min full cardiopulmonary support |
| Oxygenation | Does NOT oxygenate blood (no oxygenator) | Full gas exchange support (oxygenation + CO₂ removal) |
| Indication | CS without respiratory failure; high-risk PCI; LV unloading in refractory VT | Refractory CS + respiratory failure; cardiac arrest (ECPR); bridge to VAD/transplant; massive PE |
| Access | Retrograde transaortic via femoral or axillary artery | Femoral artery + vein (peripheral); or central cannulation (cardiac surgery) |
| Complications | Haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, limb ischaemia, aortic regurgitation, device migration | Limb ischaemia (distal perfusion cannula essential), haemolysis, HIT, systemic emboli, LV distension |

Tip: ECPR (ECMO-CPR): VA-ECMO during refractory cardiac arrest — restores perfusion while treating reversible cause (STEMI, PE, hypothermia, OD). Prague and ARREST pilot trials: ECPR survival advantage in selected refractory arrests. Requires rapid cannulation team.
front: Impella and VA-ECMO — compare mechanisms, haemodynamic effects, and when to use each

back:
LVAD: Continuously assists or replaces LV function by pumping blood from LV apex to ascending aorta

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Current generation | 3rd generation: centrifugal continuous-flow (HeartMate 3, HVAD — now withdrawn). Magnetically levitated impeller → low haemolysis, ↓ thrombosis. |
| Pulsatility | Continuous flow → no palpable pulse, no korotkoff sounds. Use MAP by Doppler ultrasound (target MAP 70–90 mmHg). |
| Heart rate | Native HR has little effect on CO (pump provides baseline flow regardless) |
| Destinations | Bridge to transplant (BTT): most common. Destination therapy (DT): for patients not eligible for transplant. Bridge to recovery (BTR): rare. |

| LVAD emergency | Signs | Cause | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pump thrombosis | ↓ Flow + ↑ power consumption (alarms) + haemolysis (↑ LDH, ↑ free Hb) | Thrombus in pump | IV heparin + thrombolytics vs urgent pump exchange |
| RV failure | ↑ CVP, ↓ LVAD flow, ↓ BP — most common post-implant complication | LV unloading → IVS shifts left → ↓ RV function; inadequate RV output to fill LV | Vasopressors (vasopressin/NE) + pulmonary vasodilators (inhaled NO) + temporary RVAD if severe |
| Suction event | VT, ↓ flow, alarms | Hypovolaemia or arrhythmia → LV collapses around inflow cannula | IV fluids; correct arrhythmia; ↓ pump speed temporarily |
| Drive-line infection | Erythema, purulent discharge at exit site | Staphylococcal most common | Wound care + antibiotics; device exchange if systemic |
| Stroke | Neurological deficit | Embolic (inadequate anticoagulation) or haemorrhagic (over-anticoagulation) | Optimise INR target 2.0–3.0; aspirin 81 mg |
front: LVAD (Left Ventricular Assist Device) — principles, types, complications, and management of LVAD emergencies

back:
Temporary transvenous pacing (TVP): Emergency rate support when pharmacological therapy fails or not appropriate

| Indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Complete (3rd degree) AV block with haemodynamic compromise | Class I |
| Symptomatic Mobitz II (infranodal) 2nd degree AV block | Class I |
| Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to atropine | Class I |
| Bifascicular/trifascicular block post-anterior MI | Class I (high risk of complete block) |
| Drug-induced bradycardia refractory to pharmacotherapy | Class I |
| Post-cardiac surgery conduction block | Class I (often epicardial wires already placed) |

Approach: RV bipolar lead via subclavian, femoral, or jugular vein under fluoroscopy or ICU/bedside guidance. Target: RV apex position. Rate: 60–80 bpm (VVI). Pacing threshold <1 V. Sensing threshold >5 mV.

| Complication | Prevention |
| --- | --- |
| Cardiac perforation/tamponade | Use soft-tip catheter; stiff catheters ↑ risk |
| Lead dislodgement | RV apex placement; limit patient movement |
| Pneumothorax (subclavian approach) | CXR post-insertion mandatory |
| Pacemaker-induced VT | Competition between native and paced rhythm; adjust sensing |
| Infection/endocarditis | Strict sterile technique; remove as soon as permanent pacing can be arranged |
front: Temporary transvenous pacing — indications, approach, and complications

back:
LBBB dyssynchrony: Delayed activation of lateral LV wall → LV contracts segmentally rather than synchronously → ↓ CO + ↑ MR + ↑ wall stress

| LBBB consequence | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Intraventricular dyssynchrony | Septal activation first (via right bundle) → septal shortening → bulging OUTWARD when lateral wall is still contracting (wasted work). IVS swings like pendulum. |
| Interventricular dyssynchrony | RV activated first → septal bowing → ↓ LV preload during isovolumetric contraction |
| Diastolic mitral regurgitation | Prolonged PR interval + delayed lateral wall → MR begins during late diastole ("pre-systolic MR") |
| ↓ EF + ↑ LV volume | Cumulative effect of dyssynchronous contraction → ↓ effective SV → ↑ EDV over time (eccentric remodelling) |

CRT corrects ALL of the above by simultaneously pacing RV + LV lateral wall

| CRT haemodynamic benefit | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ EF (+5–10% absolute) | Synchronised contraction → ↑ effective SV per beat |
| ↓ LV volume (reverse remodelling) | ↑ CO → ↓ compensatory preload; ↓ MR → ↓ volume overload |
| ↓ Mitral regurgitation | Synchronised papillary muscle activation → improved MV coaptation |
| ↓ MVO₂ per unit output | More efficient contraction → ↓ wall stress and energy waste |
front: CRT biventricular pacing — how does it correct LBBB-related dyssynchrony and improve haemodynamics?

back:
Vorapaxar (Zontivity): PAR-1 (protease-activated receptor-1) antagonist → blocks thrombin-mediated platelet activation

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Thrombin activates PAR-1 on platelets → platelet aggregation. Vorapaxar blocks PAR-1 → ↓ thrombin-mediated aggregation (complementary to P2Y12 block) |
| Half-life | 3–4 days; active metabolite ~5–8 days (very long — irreversible functional effect) |
| Route | Oral 2.5 mg OD (no loading dose needed — very long half-life) |

TRA 2P-TIMI 50 Trial: Vorapaxar + standard antiplatelet therapy vs placebo in stable atherosclerosis
12% ↓ CV death/MI/stroke (primary endpoint at 3 years). BUT: 66% ↑ ICH (1.0% vs 0.6%). Trial pre-specified stopping vorapaxar in prior stroke subgroup (unacceptably high ICH).

| Current indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Prior MI (not stroke/TIA) on aspirin ± clopidogrel — to further reduce thrombotic events | ESC Class IIb |
| CONTRAINDICATED | Prior stroke or TIA (3× ↑ ICH risk), active bleeding, severe liver disease |

Tip: Vorapaxar represents a novel antiplatelet mechanism (thrombin pathway) beyond traditional COX-1 (aspirin) and P2Y12 (clopidogrel/ticagrelor). Adds incremental benefit with incremental bleeding risk. Very limited current use — reserved for very high-risk post-MI on aspirin + stable tolerating triple antiplatelet.
front: Vorapaxar — mechanism, TRA 2P-TIMI 50 trial, and when it is used today

back:
Tranexamic acid (TXA): Competitive inhibitor of plasminogen and plasmin → prevents fibrinolysis → ↓ bleeding

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | TXA binds to lysine binding sites on plasminogen → prevents attachment to fibrin → ↓ plasmin activation → ↓ clot dissolution |
| Indication in cardiac surgery | Routine use in cardiac surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) → reduces bleeding and transfusion requirements |
| Dose (cardiac surgery) | 30 mg/kg loading → 15 mg/kg/h maintenance + 2 mg/kg pump prime (multiple dosing regimens exist) |
| ATACAS Trial (NEJM 2017) | TXA vs placebo in cardiac surgery: ↓ red cell transfusion (17.7% vs 25.5%). No ↑ in MI, stroke, kidney failure, or seizures at 30 days. |

Tip: Epsilon-aminocaproic acid (EACA, Amicar): Older antifibrinolytic — same mechanism as TXA but lower potency and less evidence. Aprotinin: Serine protease inhibitor (broader anti-fibrinolytic) — withdrawn due to renal toxicity (BART trial 2008) → TXA is now the standard antifibrinolytic in cardiac surgery.
Warning: TXA seizures: High doses (especially with renal impairment) → inhibit GABA-A and glycine receptors → seizures. Reduce dose in renal failure. Do NOT exceed recommended dosing protocols.
front: Tranexamic acid and antifibrinolytics in cardiac surgery — mechanism, dose, and the ATACAS trial

back:
Methylene blue: Inhibits guanylate cyclase → ↓ cGMP → ↑ vascular tone → reverses pathological vasodilation

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | 1. Blocks soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) → ↓ cGMP → vasoconstriction. 2. Scavenges nitric oxide directly. 3. Inhibits NO synthase (NOS) at high doses. |
| Indication | Vasodilatory shock refractory to catecholamines: Post-cardiac surgery vasoplegia, anaphylactic shock refractory to epinephrine, septic shock, drug-induced vasodilation (overdose) |
| Dose | 1–2 mg/kg IV over 15–60 min. Repeat in 1–2h if needed. Infusion: 0.5–1 mg/kg/h. |
| Contraindications | G6PD deficiency (→ haemolytic anaemia), severe renal failure, ↑ PAP (↑ PVR as side effect) |
| Side effects | Blue/green urine (harmless). Pulse oximetry interference (SpO₂ reads low — check ABG). ↑ PVR (avoid in PAH/RV failure). Serotonin syndrome risk if serotonergic drugs used concurrently. |

Tip: Post-cardiac surgery vasoplegia: Occurs in 5–25% after CPB. Pathophysiology: CPB triggers ↑ NO production + RAAS depletion + vasopressin depletion → refractory hypotension despite adequate CO. Methylene blue is the "rescue vasopressor" of choice. Add vasopressin and hydroxocobalamin as alternatives.
front: Methylene blue for vasodilatory shock — mechanism, indication, and dose

back:
GLP-1 RAs: Initially developed for T2DM — proven CV benefit in high-risk patients, including non-diabetics

| Drug | Trial | CV benefit | Weight loss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Liraglutide (Victoza) | LEADER: 13% ↓ MACE (CV death/MI/stroke) vs placebo. Driven by ↓ CV death. 27% ↓ CV death specifically. | Strong | ~3 kg |
| Semaglutide SC (Ozempic) | SUSTAIN-6: 26% ↓ MACE. SELECT: 20% ↓ MACE in non-diabetic obese patients (BMI ≥27, ASCVD — first non-DM CV outcome trial). 28% ↓ CV death/MI/stroke. | Strong | ~9–15 kg |
| Dulaglutide (Trulicity) | REWIND: 12% ↓ MACE. Longest follow-up. | Moderate | ~3 kg |
| Semaglutide PO (Rybelsus) | PIONEER 6: non-inferior for MACE | Neutral | ~4 kg |

Tip: Mechanisms of CV benefit (NOT just weight/glucose): Direct anti-atherosclerotic effects (↓ VCAM-1, ↓ macrophage infiltration), ↓ BP, ↓ inflammation (↓ CRP, ↓ IL-6), modest diuresis, direct cardioprotective signalling via GLP-1R in cardiomyocytes and endothelium. Benefit in non-diabetic SELECT trial confirms direct CV mechanisms beyond glycaemia.
Warning: HFpEF + obesity: STEP-HFpEF (semaglutide 2.4 mg vs placebo in obese HFpEF without DM) → ↑ 6MWT +21m, ↓ KCCQ symptoms, ↓ NT-proBNP. Obesity-phenotype HFpEF may respond dramatically to GLP-1RA. First Class I-equivalent treatment recommendation emerging for obesity-related HFpEF.
front: GLP-1 receptor agonists in cardiovascular disease — LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, SELECT trials and cardioprotective mechanisms

back:
Brugada pattern: ST elevation in V1–V2 with RBBB morphology — three types based on ECG shape

| Type | ST morphology in V1–V2 | T-wave | Diagnostic? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 (coved) | ST ≥2 mm with descending convex/coved upstroke → negative T | Negative | YES — diagnostic of Brugada pattern. Only type that constitutes "Brugada ECG" |
| Type 2 (saddle-back) | ST ≥2 mm with high take-off then concave saddle shape → positive/biphasic T | Positive or biphasic | NO — suggestive but not diagnostic. Type 1 on provocative testing = Brugada syndrome |
| Type 3 | Type 1 or 2 pattern with <2 mm ST elevation | Variable | NO — non-specific |

Brugada Syndrome diagnosis = Type 1 Brugada pattern (spontaneous OR drug-provoked) + ≥1 clinical feature:

- Documented VF or polymorphic VT
- Family history of Brugada syndrome or sudden unexplained nocturnal death
- Inducible VF at EP study
- Syncope (unexplained)
- Nocturnal agonal respiration

Tip: Provocative testing: IV sodium channel blocker (ajmaline 1 mg/kg IV, or procainamide, flecainide) → unmasks concealed type 1 pattern. Fever also unmasks Brugada pattern — counsel patients to treat fever aggressively. SCN5A mutation in 20–30%.
Warning: High-risk features requiring ICD: Prior cardiac arrest, spontaneous type 1 pattern + syncope. Treatment: ICD. Quinidine (↑ Ito block) for recurrent VF episodes. Isoproterenol IV for acute VF storm in Brugada (↑ cAMP → ↓ Ito → ↓ ST elevation).
front: Brugada syndrome — ECG pattern types 1, 2, 3, and criteria for Brugada syndrome diagnosis

back:
Wellens syndrome: ECG pattern indicating critical proximal LAD stenosis — a "pre-infarction" warning

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Context | Patient with recent chest pain that has RESOLVED. ECG changes during the pain-FREE period (not during active ischaemia). |
| Type A (25%) | Biphasic T waves in V2–V3 (upright then negative) — more subtle |
| Type B (75%) | Deeply symmetrically inverted T waves in V2–V3 (sometimes V1–V4) |
| Key features | Normal or minimal ST changes. Minimal/no troponin elevation. No new Q waves. Suggests reperfused proximal LAD stenosis. |
| Mechanism | Transient ischaemia → altered repolarisation in anterior wall → characteristic T-wave changes persist after pain relief |

Warning: CRITICAL clinical implication: Wellens pattern = proximal LAD stenosis → RISK of anterior STEMI if untreated. These patients should NOT have stress testing (may precipitate anterior MI). → Urgent coronary angiography is required.
Tip: Common pitfall: Patient presents with resolved chest pain, normal troponin, Wellens ECG → wrongly reassured and discharged → returns with massive anterior STEMI within days. Recognise and act immediately. Admit + urgent cath.
front: Wellens syndrome — what is it, ECG patterns, and why does it matter clinically?

back:
De Winter T waves: Hyperacute ECG sign of proximal LAD occlusion — STEMI equivalent (but lacks classic ST elevation)

| ECG Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| T-wave morphology | Tall, prominent, symmetrically upright (hyperacute) T waves in precordial leads V1–V6 |
| ST segment | Upsloping ST depression (1–3 mm) in precordial leads — NOT typical ST elevation. Key distinction from STEMI. |
| aVR | ST elevation in aVR (reciprocal to diffuse anterior ischaemia) |
| Mechanism | Acute proximal LAD occlusion → subendocardial ischaemia creates reciprocal pattern. May represent occlusion without collateral filling. |
| Prevalence | 2% of acute LAD occlusions present as De Winter pattern (not classic STEMI) |

Warning: STEMI EQUIVALENT: De Winter T waves = proximal LAD total occlusion → treat as STEMI. Activate cath lab immediately for primary PCI. Do NOT give thrombolytics alone. The lack of ST elevation should NOT delay reperfusion — this is a well-recognised STEMI equivalent pattern.
Tip: Other STEMI equivalents (STEMI without classic elevation): Left bundle branch block (new or presumed new) + ischaemic symptoms. Posterior STEMI (ST depression V1–V3, ST elevation V7–V9). DeWinter T waves. sgarbossa criteria in LBBB. All require same urgency as classic STEMI.
front: De Winter T waves — ECG pattern, mechanism, and why urgent intervention is required

back:
ARVC (Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy): Progressive fibro-fatty replacement of RV myocardium → RV arrhythmias + SCD

| ECG finding | Description | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Epsilon wave | Small deflection after QRS in V1–V3 (delayed depolarisation of RV remnants). Seen in 30% of ARVC. | Pathognomonic for ARVC when present |
| T-wave inversions V1–V3 | Inverted T waves in right precordial leads beyond V2 (after age 14, excluding RBBB) | Most sensitive ECG finding (~85%). Major diagnostic criterion. |
| RBBB (incomplete or complete) | Right bundle branch block morphology | Minor criterion |
| Terminal activation delay | Duration of QRS from S nadir to end of QRS >55 ms in V1–V3 (not RBBB) | Minor criterion |
| VT morphology (LBBB pattern) | VT with LBBB morphology = RV origin. Positive axis = inferior RVOT; negative axis = RV free wall or apex | Major criterion for VT/VF in ARVC |

Tip: ARVC diagnosis (2010 Task Force): Major/minor criteria in 5 categories: Structural RV dysfunction, tissue characterisation (CMR fibrosis), repolarisation (T inversions), depolarisation (epsilon wave/TAD), arrhythmia (LBBB VT), family history/genetics. Definite = 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, or 4 minor criteria.
Warning: Exercise is harmful in ARVC — physical exertion accelerates fibro-fatty replacement and ↑ VT/VF risk. ALL ARVC patients should be disqualified from competitive athletics. ICD for high-risk patients. Sotalol/amiodarone for symptomatic VT. Beta-blockers for exercise-related arrhythmias.
front: Epsilon wave and ARVC — ECG findings, diagnostic criteria, and arrhythmia risk

back:
Progressive ECG changes with rising potassium — know the sequence: Peaked T → wide QRS → sine wave → VF

| K⁺ level | ECG change | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5.5–6.5 mEq/L (mild) | Peaked, tall, narrow, symmetrical T waves (especially V2–V5, II) | ↑ IK1 → faster phase 3 repolarisation → narrow, tall T waves (reverse of hypokalaemia) |
| 6.5–7.0 mEq/L (moderate) | PR prolongation + loss of P waves (atrial standstill) | Atria more sensitive to ↑ K⁺ → ↓ automaticity → slow then absent P waves |
| 7.0–7.5 mEq/L | Wide QRS (↑ intraventricular conduction time) | ↑ K⁺ → ↓ resting potential → ↓ INa availability → slow ventricular depolarisation |
| >7.5 mEq/L (severe) | Sine wave pattern (merging P + QRS + T into undulating wide complex) | P waves merge into widening QRS; terminal phase |
| >8–9 mEq/L (critical) | VF or asystole | Complete membrane instability |

Emergency treatment (guided by ECG severity):

| ECG finding | Immediate action |
| --- | --- |
| Peaked T only (mild) | Calcium resonium ± furosemide; treat cause |
| Wide QRS, sine wave (severe) | IV calcium gluconate (10 mL 10% over 2 min) → membrane stabilisation. THEN: insulin + dextrose; NaHCO₃; salbutamol. THEN: dialysis. |

Warning: Calcium gluconate does NOT lower K⁺ — it STABILISES the cardiac membrane. Onset 2–5 min, lasts 30–60 min. Must be followed by definitive K⁺-lowering measures. In patients on digoxin: give calcium slowly (10 min) — rapid calcium + digoxin → arrhythmia.
front: Hyperkalaemia ECG — progressive changes from mild to severe, and how to use ECG for emergent management

back:
ECG criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy — voltage and pattern-based

| Criterion | Formula | Threshold | Sensitivity / Specificity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sokolow-Lyon | S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 (whichever taller) | ≥35 mm | Sensitivity ~20–45%; Specificity ~90–95% |
| Cornell voltage (limb) | R in aVL + S in V3 | ≥28 mm (men) / ≥20 mm (women) | Sensitivity ~42%; Specificity ~95% |
| Cornell voltage-duration | (R aVL + S V3) × QRS duration | ≥2440 mm·ms | Higher sensitivity than voltage alone |
| R in aVL | R wave in aVL | ≥11 mm | Simple; best single lead for LVH |

| ECG feature suggesting LVH strain | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ST depression + T-wave inversion in I, aVL, V5–V6 | "LV strain pattern" or "LVH repolarisation abnormality" — downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion in lateral leads |
| Increased R wave amplitude V5–V6 | Tall R wave in lateral leads reflecting hypertrophied LV |

Warning: Limitations: ECG LVH has LOW sensitivity (misses ~50–60% of LVH confirmed by echo or CMR). Obesity, emphysema, and small stature cause false negatives. Young slim males with tall voltage = normal variant (athlete's voltage). ECHO or CMR is the gold standard for LVH diagnosis (LV mass index).
front: LVH ECG criteria — Sokolow-Lyon and Cornell voltage criteria, their sensitivity/specificity, and limitations

back:
Acute RV strain from massive PE → ECG pattern of acute right-sided overload

| ECG finding | Details | Frequency in PE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S₁Q₃T₃ (McGinn-White sign) | S wave in Lead I + Q wave in Lead III + inverted T in Lead III | 20–25% (not specific) |
| Sinus tachycardia | Most common ECG finding in PE | ~40–50% |
| New RBBB (complete or incomplete) | Acute RV pressure overload → right bundle stretch | 25–30% in massive PE |
| T-wave inversions V1–V4 | RV ischaemia from acute RV pressure overload — often mistaken for anterior ischaemia | ~50% in massive PE |
| Atrial fibrillation | New AF from RV distension + catecholamine surge | ~10% |
| Right axis deviation | Acute RV dilatation shifts axis rightward | ~15–20% |
| P pulmonale (peaked P in II) | RA dilatation from ↑ RAP | Variable |
| Normal ECG | Even in significant PE | ~25% |

Tip: T inversions V1–V4 + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia → consider PE vs anterior STEMI. Key differentiator: PE = T inversions without ST elevation in V1–V4, usually with tachycardia + pleuritic component + risk factors (DVT, immobility, cancer). Do D-dimer and/or CTPA.
front: Right heart strain ECG in acute PE — the S1Q3T3 pattern, what other ECG findings occur, and their clinical significance

back:
| Feature | Digitalis effect (therapeutic) | Digitalis toxicity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ST changes | Scooping/sagging ST depression ("reverse tick" or "Salvador Dali's moustache") in lateral leads. Normal pattern at therapeutic levels. | Similar ST changes but with arrhythmias |
| T-wave | Flattened or inverted, asymmetric | Variable, may have new changes |
| QT interval | SHORTENED QT (↑ Ca²⁺-mediated faster repolarisation) | QT may lengthen if toxicity alters repolarisation |
| PR interval | Mildly prolonged (↑ vagal tone → ↓ AV conduction) | Markedly prolonged or AV block |
| Heart rate | Slightly decreased (vagal) | Bradyarrhythmias OR paradoxical tachyarrhythmias |
| Arrhythmias | None (or controlled AF rate) | Pathognomonic: Bidirectional VT, PAT with 2:1 AV block, junctional tachycardia with AV dissociation, frequent PVCs/bigeminy |

Digitalis effect = expected findings at therapeutic levels (no intervention needed). Toxicity = arrhythmias at any level — STOP digoxin, check K⁺/Mg²⁺, consider Digifab.
Tip: Shortened QT: If QT appears shorter than expected for rate → think digitalis, hypercalcaemia. Digitalis is the most common cause of drug-induced QT shortening. Bidirectional VT: Alternating QRS axis 180° → pathognomonic for digoxin toxicity or CPVT.
front: Digitalis effect vs digitalis toxicity on ECG — how to tell them apart

back:
Dextrocardia: Heart located in right side of chest with apex pointing right — mirror image of normal cardiac anatomy

| ECG Feature in Dextrocardia | Appearance |
| --- | --- |
| Lead I | Inverted (negative P, QRS, T — "global inversion") |
| Leads II and III | Swapped (Lead II looks like Lead III and vice versa) |
| aVR and aVL | Swapped (aVR looks like normal aVL) |
| Precordial leads V1–V6 | Progressive R wave DECREASE from V1 to V6 (inverse of normal progression). P, QRS, T all become smaller moving left. |
| Overall | All leads effectively mirror-imaged |

Correct ECG for dextrocardia: Place right-sided precordial leads (V1R–V6R) + reverse limb leads (right arm → left, left arm → right)
Tip: Dextrocardia vs limb lead reversal: Both cause global inversion in Lead I. KEY difference: In pure limb lead reversal, precordial leads (V1–V6) are NORMAL (normal R wave progression). In dextrocardia, precordial leads are ABNORMAL (decreasing R wave V1→V6). CXR confirms position of heart and gastric bubble.
Tip: Situs inversus totalis: All organs mirror-imaged. Dextrocardia + situs solitus (normal organ position) = rare, associated with complex congenital heart disease (not mirror image, but malpositioned).
front: ECG features of dextrocardia — what changes occur and how to distinguish from lead reversal

back:
ESC 2020: hs-cTnT or hs-cTnI at presentation + 1h or 2h can rapidly rule in or rule out NSTEMI

| Algorithm | Rule-OUT (safe discharge) | Rule-IN (high probability NSTEMI) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0/1h algorithm (preferred) | 0h hs-cTnT <5 ng/L (or hs-cTnI <2 ng/L) = "very low" → rule out. OR 0h <12 ng/L + Δ1h <3 ng/L | 0h ≥52 ng/L OR Δ1h ≥5 ng/L = rule in NSTEMI |
| 0/2h algorithm | 0h <12 ng/L + Δ2h <3 ng/L | 0h ≥52 ng/L OR Δ2h ≥6 ng/L |
| 0/3h algorithm (for older assays) | 0h below 99th percentile URL AND low pre-test probability | 0h above 99th percentile URL OR rise ≥20% at 3h |

OBSERVE zone: Patients not meeting rule-in or rule-out criteria → observation zone. Serial testing at 3h (0/1h algorithm) or additional clinical assessment needed.
Tip: hs-cTnT 99th percentile URL = 14 ng/L. hs-cTnI varies by assay (typically 16–26 ng/L for women, 30–34 ng/L for men — sex-specific references in hs-cTnI). hs-cTnT cutoff is same for men and women.
Warning: Rule-out requires BOTH low concentration AND no significant rise (delta). Low absolute level alone is insufficient — a rising troponin from very low baseline is more specific for MI than a moderate stable elevation from chronic disease.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §1.5.2.2 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.B.4.b · ESC 2023 §3.3.4 · ACC/AHA 2025 §3.1.2
front: High-sensitivity troponin algorithms — ESC 0/1h, 0/2h, and 0/3h protocols for NSTEMI rule-in and rule-out

back:
BNP/NT-proBNP: Released from ventricular myocytes in response to ↑ wall stress (↑ filling pressures) — key biomarker for HF diagnosis and prognosis

| Cutoff | BNP | NT-proBNP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rule OUT acute HF (dyspnoea) | <100 pg/mL → HF very unlikely (<2%) | <300 pg/mL → HF very unlikely |
| Rule IN acute HF | >400 pg/mL → HF likely (>79%) | Age-adjusted: <50y: >450; 50–75y: >900; >75y: >1800 pg/mL |
| Grey zone | 100–400 pg/mL | 300–age threshold |
| Ambulatory HF management target | <200–400 pg/mL (GUIDE-IT) | <1000 pg/mL guided strategy |

Causes of elevated BNP/NT-proBNP BEYOND HF
AF (↑ atrial and ventricular wall stress)
Pulmonary hypertension (RV pressure overload)
Acute PE (RV strain)
Renal failure (↓ clearance — NT-proBNP predominantly renally cleared)
Sepsis (direct myocardial depression)
Cardiac amyloidosis (severe wall stress)
STEMI / ACS (acute wall stress)

Tip: Obesity paradox: BNP/NT-proBNP are LOWER in obese patients with HF (adipose tissue clears BNP). Use obesity-adjusted thresholds or interpret with caution. NT-proBNP rises more sharply with CKD (↓ renal clearance) — age-adjusted cutoffs account for this partially.
front: NT-proBNP and BNP — cutoffs by age and clinical context, and what causes elevation beyond HF

back:
| Biomarker | What it measures | Clinical role | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sST2 (soluble suppression of tumorigenicity 2) | Soluble decoy receptor for IL-33. ↑ In cardiac fibrosis and mechanical stress. Reflects IL-33/ST2 signalling pathway (anti-fibrotic, anti-apoptotic pathway — sST2 blocks it). | Prognostication in HF: ↑ sST2 → ↑ HF mortality + hospitalisation. Additive to BNP for risk stratification. NOT useful for HF diagnosis. Guides MRA therapy titration? | Less well-studied than BNP. Cutoff (>35 ng/mL = high risk) not age-adjusted. Little change with medications. |
| Galectin-3 | Secreted by activated macrophages. Promotes myocardial fibrosis via macrophage-driven TGF-β signalling. ↑ In HF with fibrotic phenotype. | Prognostication in HF: ↑ galectin-3 → ↑ HF hospitalisation + mortality. May identify patients who will NOT respond to spironolactone (fibrotic phenotype — worse with MRA?). Additive to BNP. | Elevated in renal failure (↓ renal clearance). Limited therapeutic guidance. Not used to guide drug therapy. |

Tip: Combined biomarker panel (BNP + hs-troponin + sST2 + galectin-3): Greater prognostic power than any single marker. However, no trial has demonstrated outcome benefit from a multi-biomarker strategy over BNP-guided treatment alone. Currently, only BNP/NT-proBNP has sufficient evidence to guide HF management decisions.
front: sST2 and Galectin-3 — what they measure in heart failure, their clinical role, and limitations

back:
Any elevation of hs-troponin above 99th percentile URL = myocardial injury. MI requires injury + ischaemia evidence.

| MI Type | Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 | Atherosclerotic plaque rupture/erosion → coronary thrombosis | Classic ACS (NSTEMI, STEMI) |
| Type 2 | O₂ supply-demand mismatch without plaque rupture: coronary spasm, tachyarrhythmia, hypo/hypertension, anaemia, respiratory failure | Post-surgery, severe tachycardia, coronary spasm |
| Type 3 | Cardiac death with symptoms suggesting ischaemia but death before biomarker sampling | OHCA before blood draw |
| Type 4a | Periprocedural MI within 48h of PCI (>5× URL if baseline normal, or >20% rise if elevated) | Side branch occlusion, distal embolisation at PCI |
| Type 4b | Stent thrombosis (confirmed by angiography or autopsy) | Acute/subacute/late/very late stent thrombosis |
| Type 4c | Restenosis-related MI | In-stent restenosis with occlusion |
| Type 5 | Periprocedural MI within 48h of CABG (>10× URL if baseline normal) | Graft failure, air embolism during CABG |

Ref: PERKI 2024 §1.2, §1.4 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.A · ESC 2023 §2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §2.1
front: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction — myocardial injury vs MI, and the five MI types

back:
Cardiac amyloidosis: Infiltration of amyloid fibrils into myocardium → restrictive CMP + HFpEF phenotype

| Feature | AL (light chain) | ATTR (transthyretin) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protein source | Immunoglobulin light chains (plasma cell dyscrasia — plasma cell myeloma or MGUS) | Transthyretin (TTR) protein — produced in liver |
| Subtypes | One type | Wild-type (ATTRwt): age-related, elderly men. Hereditary (ATTRv): mutation in TTR gene (Val122Ile common in African Americans; Val30Met neuropathy) |
| Age | 50–80 years | ATTRwt: >65 years (men predominantly). ATTRv: 50–70 years |
| Prognosis without treatment | Median survival 6 months (very aggressive) | ATTRwt: 2–6 years. ATTRv: variable |
| Cardiac symptoms | Rapidly progressive HF, orthostatic hypotension (autonomic), macroglossia, periorbital bruising | HFpEF, carpal tunnel syndrome (often bilateral, preceding cardiac disease by years), lumbar stenosis, bicipital tendon rupture |

Diagnostic pathway:

- Echo: Sparkling granular myocardium, biventricular thickening, small LV cavity, diastolic dysfunction, RV involvement, atrial dilatation, low voltage despite wall thickness
- ECG: Classic "voltage-mass discordance" — low QRS voltage despite thickened walls (opposite of HCM/LVH)
- Technetium scintigraphy (PYP/DPD/HMDP scan): ↑ uptake = ATTR (not AL). Grade 2–3 uptake = highly specific for ATTR. Avoids biopsy if negative serum/urine protein electrophoresis + plasma cell studies.
- CMR: LGE with diffuse subendocardial or transmural enhancement + abnormal gadolinium kinetics (early washout)
- Biopsy: Abdominal fat pad (60–80% positive in AL). Bone marrow. Endomyocardial biopsy (gold standard) if fat pad negative.
front: Cardiac amyloidosis — types, clinical features, and the diagnostic pathway

back:
Tafamidis (Vyndaqel/Vyndamax): TTR stabiliser — prevents dissociation of TTR tetramer into monomers → prevents amyloid fibril formation

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Binds to thyroxine-binding sites on TTR tetramer → stabilises tetramer → reduces monomer misfolding and amyloid deposition |
| Route/Dose | Oral: Tafamidis meglumine 80 mg OD (ATTR-CM indication). Tafamidis 61 mg OD = bioequivalent. |
| Effect | Slows fibril formation → slows cardiac infiltration. Does NOT dissolve existing amyloid. Must treat early. |

ATTR-ACT Trial (NEJM 2018): Tafamidis vs placebo in wild-type or hereditary ATTR cardiomyopathy (NYHA I–III, EF ≥40%)

| Endpoint | Result (80 mg arm, 30 months) |
| --- | --- |
| All-cause mortality | 29% ↓ RRR (p<0.001) |
| CV hospitalisations | 32% ↓ |
| Functional capacity (6MWT, KCCQ) | Significantly preserved |

Correct: ESC 2021: Tafamidis Class I for ATTR-CM (wild-type or hereditary) with NYHA I–II symptoms. First disease-modifying therapy proven to reduce mortality in ATTR cardiomyopathy.
Tip: ATTR-CM is vastly underdiagnosed. Prevalence estimates: ATTRwt in elderly HFpEF patients may be ~10–15%. Technetium scintigraphy is now the non-invasive standard for diagnosis — must exclude AL (plasma cell studies) before accepting ATTR diagnosis. Earlier diagnosis = more benefit from tafamidis.
front: Tafamidis — mechanism, ATTR-ACT trial, and who should receive treatment

back:
RNA-silencing agents: Target TTR mRNA → ↓ TTR protein production in liver → ↓ substrate for amyloid formation (NOT a stabiliser — reduces production)

| Drug | Mechanism | Route | Key trial | Indication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patisiran (Onpattro) | Lipid nanoparticle siRNA → silences TTR mRNA in hepatocytes → ↓ TTR production ~80% | IV every 3 weeks | APOLLO: ↓ TTR levels + ↓ neurological impairment in ATTRv polyneuropathy. APOLLO-B: cardiac outcomes in ATTR-CM (ongoing) | ATTRv polyneuropathy (FDA/EMA approved). ATTR-CM — awaiting outcome data |
| Vutrisiran (Amvuttra) | GalNAc-conjugated siRNA → targeted hepatocyte delivery → ↓ TTR ~80–90% | SC every 3 months (improved adherence vs patisiran) | HELIOS-A (polyneuropathy): superior to inotersen. HELIOS-B (cardiac): ↓ CV events in ATTR-CM (results 2024) | ATTRv polyneuropathy. ATTR-CM indication pending outcome data |
| Eplontersen (Wainua) | Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) → binds TTR mRNA → RNase H degradation → ↓ TTR | SC monthly | NEURO-TTRansform: superior to inotersen in ATTRv polyneuropathy | ATTRv polyneuropathy (FDA-approved 2023) |

Tip: Key concept: TTR stabilisers (tafamidis) prevent existing TTR from misfolding. RNA-silencing agents prevent TTR from being made. Combined approach (stabiliser + silencer) may become standard in future — CARDIO-TTRansform investigating.
front: RNA-silencing therapy for ATTR amyloidosis — patisiran, vutrisiran, and eplontersen

back:
Cardiac amyloidosis is frequently missed — up to 5–10-year diagnostic delay. Recognise the constellation of clues.

| Red flag | Type of amyloidosis |
| --- | --- |
| HFpEF with disproportionate wall thickness (LV ≥14 mm) without adequate hypertension history | Both AL and ATTR |
| Low QRS voltage on ECG despite echocardiographic wall thickening (voltage-mass discordance) | Both (more common in AL) |
| Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (often operated years earlier) | ATTRwt and ATTRv |
| Lumbar spinal stenosis (bilateral) | ATTRwt |
| Bicipital tendon rupture | ATTRwt |
| Senile ("benign") cardiac amyloid findings in autopsy of elderly men >80 | ATTRwt |
| MGUS + HF (plasma cell dyscrasia) | AL amyloidosis (assume until proven otherwise) |
| Macroglossia, periorbital purpura, shoulder pad sign (amyloid deposits) | AL amyloidosis |
| Autonomic neuropathy (postural hypotension, GI symptoms) + cardiac involvement | ATTRv polyneuropathy-cardiac overlap |
| Intolerance to standard HF drugs: hypotension on ACEi/ARB/BB even at low doses | Both (rigid restrictive physiology) |

Tip: ACEi/ARB hypotension in amyloid: Amyloid deposits in walls of arterioles → autonomic failure + fixed compliance → ACEi/ARB cause profound hypotension. Use with extreme caution; start at very low dose or avoid.
front: "Red flags" suggesting cardiac amyloidosis — clinical and echocardiographic warning signs

back:
Sotagliflozin: Inhibits BOTH SGLT2 (kidney) AND SGLT1 (gut and heart) — broader mechanism than other SGLT inhibitors

| Feature | Sotagliflozin | Standard SGLT2i |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SGLT1 inhibition | Yes — blocks intestinal glucose absorption + cardiac SGLT1 | No (SGLT2-selective) |
| GI glucose absorption | ↓ Post-prandial glucose surge (SGLT1 in gut) | Normal |
| Cardiac SGLT1 | Direct cardiac anti-hypertrophic effect? (mechanism being studied) | Not applicable |

SOLOIST-WHF Trial (NEJM 2020): Sotagliflozin vs placebo started BEFORE HOSPITAL DISCHARGE in worsening HF (EF any range, DM)

| Endpoint | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Primary: CV death + HHF + urgent HF visits | 33% ↓ RRR (p<0.001) — stopped early for funding issues (COVID) |
| HFrEF subgroup | Significant reduction. HFpEF subgroup: also significant. |
| In-hospital initiation | Benefit seen even when started during acute HF hospitalisation — supports early initiation strategy |

Correct: SOLOIST-WHF demonstrated: 1) SGLT1 inhibition adds value over SGLT2 alone? (uncertain — no head-to-head); 2) Early in-hospital initiation is SAFE and beneficial (aligned with EMPULSE trial showing empagliflozin safe in-hospital). ESC recommends starting SGLT2i before discharge from HF hospitalisation.

Aficamten: Next-generation cardiac myosin inhibitor — more selective than mavacamten with different binding properties

| Result | Details |
| --- | --- |

Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound): Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist — more potent weight loss than GLP-1 RA monotherapy

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Activates BOTH GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) and GLP-1 receptors → synergistic appetite suppression, ↑ insulin secretion, ↓ glucagon, delayed gastric emptying → greater weight loss than GLP-1 RA alone |

Finerenone (Kerendia): Non-steroidal, highly selective MRA — structurally and pharmacologically distinct from steroidal MRAs

| Structure | Non-steroidal | Steroidal | Steroidal |
| MR selectivity | Highly selective (no androgen/progestogen cross-reactivity) | Non-selective (→ gynaecomastia, sexual dysfunction) | Selective (limited SE) |

PARAGON-HF (NEJM 2019): Sacubitril/valsartan vs valsartan in EF ≥45%, symptomatic HF, elevated NP

| Result | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Primary endpoint | CV death + HHF: Rate ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.75–1.01, p=0.059) — JUST MISSED significance |
| HHF component | Significant ↓ in HHF (driven by ↓ first HHF) |

ESC 2021 guidance: Consider ARNi (Class IIb) to ↓ HHF in HFpEF + EF below normal range (near 40–50%) especially in women. FDA 2021: expanded ARNi label to include all HF regardless of EF.

HFpEF has impaired cGMP signalling (↓ NO-cGMP pathway in hypertensive heart) → ARNi restores this signalling. The sex-differential response (women > men) may relate to sex-differences in NP biology and ARNi pharmacokinetics.

back:
Residual inflammatory risk: Even after statin treatment, hsCRP >2 mg/L predicts ↑ CV events. Anti-inflammatory strategies target this independently of LDL.

| Trial | Drug | Mechanism | Key result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CANTOS (2017) | Canakinumab (anti-IL-1β monoclonal antibody) | Blocks IL-1β → ↓ CRP → ↓ residual inflammatory risk | 15% ↓ MACE in post-MI patients with hsCRP >2 mg/L. BUT: ↑ fatal infections → neutral all-cause mortality. Drug too expensive for routine CV use. Proof-of-concept for inflammatory pathway. |
| COLCOT (2019) | Colchicine 0.5 mg OD | NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition + neutrophil inhibition → ↓ IL-1β and IL-18 → ↓ inflammation | 23% ↓ MACE post-MI (including ↓ stroke 46%). Same mechanism as CANTOS at fraction of cost. Generic, widely available. |
| LoDoCo2 (2020) | Colchicine 0.5 mg OD | Same | 31% ↓ MACE in stable CAD (chronic coronary syndrome). 36% ↓ stroke. |

Correct: CANTOS proved the inflammatory hypothesis. COLCOT/LoDoCo2 showed colchicine achieves similar (or better) benefit at vastly lower cost and with an acceptable safety profile. Colchicine has emerged as a practical anti-inflammatory CV therapy endorsed by ESC (Class IIa after acute MI).
front: Anti-inflammatory therapies for residual cardiovascular risk — canakinumab and colchicine in CANTOS vs COLCOT

| --- | --- | --- |
| SERCA2a gene therapy (AAV1-SERCA2a) | Restores SR calcium pump (SERCA2a is downregulated in HF) → improves Ca²⁺ cycling → ↑ contractility. CUPID trial: early promise but CUPID-2 (large RCT) negative. | Phase II — failed to demonstrate benefit in large trial. Further development paused. |

Aldosterone synthase inhibitors (CYP11B2 inhibitors): Block the PRODUCTION of aldosterone at adrenal level — a fundamentally different mechanism from MRAs (which block the receptor)

| Feature | Aldosterone synthase inhibitors | MRAs (spironolactone, eplerenone) |

CHIP: Age-related expansion of haematopoietic stem cells carrying somatic mutations in cancer-driver genes (most commonly DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, JAK2) — detected in peripheral blood

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Prevalence | ~10% of people >70 years; rare <40 years |
| Definition | Variant allele frequency ≥2% in any haematopoietic gene without overt haematological malignancy |
| Haematological risk | ~0.5–1%/year progression to haematological cancer (leukaemia, myeloma) — small absolute risk |
| CV risk | Much larger CV risk: 2× ↑ coronary heart disease, 4× ↑ HF (specifically TET2 mutations), 2× ↑ stroke. Independent of traditional CV risk factors. |

Tip: CHIP as a new CV risk factor: Larger MACE risk than several traditional Framingham factors. Future CV risk prediction models will likely incorporate CHIP status. CHIP testing (targeted blood sequencing) is becoming feasible but not yet routinely used outside research.

HOCM (obstructive HCM): Rest gradient ≥30 mmHg. Severe obstruction ≥50 mmHg. Dynamic obstruction worsened by dehydration, exercise, drugs that ↓ preload/afterload or ↑ inotropy

| Step | Intervention | Mechanism/Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (First-line) | Non-vasodilating beta-blockers (metoprolol, propranolol) | ↓ HR → ↑ diastolic filling time → ↑ LV volume → ↓ obstruction. ↓ Inotropy. Avoid ISA-containing BB. |
| 2 (Alternative/add-on) | Verapamil or diltiazem (if BB intolerant) | ↓ HR + ↓ inotropy. AVOID in severe obstruction + low BP (↓ SVR → haemodynamic collapse). Use verapamil with caution in severe LVOTO + pulmonary oedema. |
| 3 (Add-on for refractory) | Disopyramide (Class IA antiarrhythmic) | Potent negative inotrope + anti-cholinergic → ↓ gradient. Significant anticholinergic SE (dry mouth, urinary retention). MUST combine with BB (disopyramide increases AV conduction — risk of AF with rapid ventricular response). |
| 4 (New — Disease-modifying) | Mavacamten (cardiac myosin inhibitor) | ↓ Actin-myosin cross-bridge formation → ↓ hypercontractility → ↓ LVOTO gradient. EXPLORER-HCM: 45% ↓ gradient, ↑ exercise capacity, ↑ KCCQ. FDA-approved 2022. |
| 5 (Invasive — Refractory symptoms) | Septal reduction therapy: Surgical myectomy OR Alcohol septal ablation (ASA) | Myectomy: Gold standard; long-term durable relief; lower SCD risk. ASA: Catheter-based; less invasive; creates controlled septal MI → scar → ↓ septal thickness. |

Warning: Avoid in HOCM: Vasodilators (ACEi, ARB, nitrates, hydralazine, DHP-CCB) — ↓ preload/afterload → ↑ obstruction. Diuretics (excessive) — ↓ LV volume → ↑ obstruction. Positive inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine) — ↑ obstruction. Vasopressin useful for hypotension.

Mavacamten (CAMZYOS): First cardiac myosin inhibitor approved for obstructive HCM — reduces hypercontractility that causes LVOTO

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Selectively binds to cardiac myosin heavy chain → stabilises myosin in actin-free (super-relaxed) state → ↓ number of actin-myosin cross-bridges → ↓ force of contraction → ↓ LVOTO gradient. Targets the fundamental pathophysiological mechanism of HCM. |
| Effect | ↓ LVOT gradient, ↓ LV wall thickness (mild), ↓ NT-proBNP, ↓ troponin, ↑ exercise capacity |
| Route/Dose | Oral 5 mg OD → uptitrate based on LVOT gradient and LVEF (REMS program). Echocardiographic monitoring every 4–12 weeks. |

EXPLORER-HCM Trial (NEJM 2020, n=251): Mavacamten vs placebo in symptomatic obstructive HCM on BB/verapamil

| Endpoint | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Primary (pVO₂ improvement + NYHA class) | 37% vs 17% response (p<0.001) |
| LVOT gradient reduction | Resting gradient: −47 mmHg vs −10 mmHg. 45% ↓ gradient. |
| Quality of life (KCCQ) | Significant improvement |
| Reduction in septal reduction therapy need | 11% vs 27% — fewer patients needed invasive intervention |

Warning: LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF <50%): Mavacamten reduces contractility — must monitor LVEF carefully. If LVEF falls <50% during treatment → reduce dose or stop. REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) programme required in USA for prescribing. CYP2C19 metabolises mavacamten — PMs may have higher plasma levels.

1 MET = oxygen consumption at rest (3.5 mL O₂/kg/min) — unit of metabolic equivalent of task

| MET Level | Activities |
| --- | --- |
| 1–4 METs (poor) | Self-care, eating, dressing, walking on flat at 3–4 km/h, light housework |

| >10 METs (excellent) | Swimming fast, running ≥10 km/h, competitive sports |

Clinical threshold: ≥4 METs (can climb one flight of stairs or walk on level ground at 6 km/h without symptoms) = adequate functional capacity → proceed to surgery without further cardiac testing in most cases
Warning: <4 METs = poor functional capacity → high MACE risk. If RCRI ≥1 + poor functional capacity + surgery will be altered by test results → non-invasive stress testing (dobutamine stress echo or nuclear perfusion imaging). Exercise stress test preferred if patient can exercise.
Tip: Duke Activity Status Index (DASI): Validated questionnaire scoring METs. Used when objective treadmill assessment not available. Single question "Can you climb a flight of stairs?" has good predictive value.

| Starting new BB pre-operatively | Only if clear indication (high cardiac risk surgery + strong indication); start weeks before surgery and titrate. Class IIb. |
| Starting BB on day of surgery | NOT recommended — POISE showed harm. Class III. |

Tip: Other perioperative medications: Continue statins (Class I — abrupt discontinuation → ↑ CV events). Continue aspirin only if dual indication (recent stent <6 months). Hold ACEi/ARB morning of surgery (↑ intraoperative hypotension). SGLT2i: hold 3 days before major surgery (euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk).

Step-by-step ESC 2022 algorithm for elective non-cardiac surgery:

| Step | Question | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Emergency surgery? | Yes → proceed immediately with perioperative cardiac monitoring. No → continue. |
| 2 | Active cardiac condition? (ACS, decompensated HF, severe arrhythmia, severe valve disease) | Yes → postpone surgery + treat condition. No → continue. |
| 3 | Low-risk surgery? (minor procedure, superficial, endoscopic) | Yes → proceed without further cardiac testing. No → continue. |
| 4 | Good functional capacity (≥4 METs) without symptoms? | Yes → proceed. No → continue. |
| 5 | RCRI ≥3 or individual high-risk factors? | Consider non-invasive stress testing if it will CHANGE management. If negative: proceed. If positive: coronary angiography ± revascularisation. |

Warning: Prophylactic revascularisation: Routine pre-operative PCI/CABG in stable CAD does NOT reduce perioperative MACE (CARP trial). Revascularisation is indicated only if patient meets standard criteria independent of surgery (e.g. left main disease, severe 3-vessel disease with reduced EF, refractory angina).
Tip: Biomarker strategy: Pre-op NT-proBNP/BNP is recommended in intermediate-high risk patients — NT-proBNP >300 ng/L (or BNP >92 ng/L) → enhanced perioperative monitoring (HDU/ICU observation) regardless of RCRI. ESC 2022 Class IIa.
front: ESC pre-operative cardiac assessment algorithm — when is cardiac testing or revascularisation indicated before elective non-cardiac surgery?

MINS = Myocardial Injury after Non-cardiac Surgery: hs-troponin elevation within 30 days post-surgery without an obvious non-ischaemic cause

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Prevalence | ~20% of patients ≥45 years undergoing non-cardiac surgery (VISION study, n>15,000) |
| Most are asymptomatic | 80% of MINS episodes have no symptoms — detected only by routine troponin monitoring |
| Definition threshold | hs-cTnT ≥20 ng/L (rising or falling within 30 days post-surgery) |
| 30-day mortality | 10% vs 1.8% in those without MINS (VISION study) |

VISION study recommendation: Post-op hs-troponin monitoring on days 1, 2, 3 for patients ≥65 years or ≥45 years with atherosclerotic disease undergoing major surgery

| MINS management | Details |
| --- | --- |
| MINS without CAD features | Aspirin + statin initiation; cardiology referral |
| MINS with suspected ACS features | Treat as per ACS (anticoagulation, coronary angiography) |
| Dabigatran for MINS (MANAGE trial) | Dabigatran 110 mg BD in MINS patients → 28% ↓ vascular events. ESC Class IIb. |

Tip: MINS vs type 2 MI: Both cause troponin elevation post-surgery. Type 2 MI = demand-supply mismatch (no plaque rupture, often tachycardia/hypotension-related). Pure MINS = troponin elevation without definite MI criteria. All require cardiology evaluation.

PPCM: HF due to LV dysfunction occurring from last month of pregnancy to 5 months post-partum, without another identifiable cause

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Incidence | 1:1,000–1:3,000 deliveries. Higher in Africa, Haiti, and multiparous older women. |
| Diagnostic criteria | LVEF <45% + onset in last month of pregnancy to 5 months post-partum + no other identifiable cause + no pre-existing LV dysfunction |
| Pathogenesis | Prolactin hypothesis: Oxidative stress in late pregnancy → 16-kDa cleaved prolactin (pro-apoptotic, anti-angiogenic) damages myocardium. STAT3 pathway impaired in pregnancy. Genetic predisposition (TTN mutations). |
| Prognosis | 50–75% recover LV function to EF >50% within 6–12 months. 10–15% progress to severe refractory HF. Risk factors for non-recovery: LVEF <30% at diagnosis, Black race, delayed diagnosis. |

IPAC Registry/BSTP-II trial: Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist → ↓ prolactin secretion) + standard HF therapy vs standard therapy alone → improved LVEF recovery at 6 months in PPCM

| Treatment | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Bromocriptine | 2.5 mg OD × 6 weeks (mild-moderate PPCM) or 2.5 mg BD × 2 weeks then OD × 4 weeks (severe). ESC Class IIb. Requires anticoagulation (LMWH) as prolactin inhibition + immobilisation → ↑ VTE risk. |
| Standard HF therapy | BB, ACEi/ARBi (post-partum), diuretics, SGLT2i (post-partum, avoid in breastfeeding). Avoid ACEi/ARB in pregnancy (teratogenic). |

| Drug | Fetal risk | Maternal risk | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Warfarin | Embryopathy if used 6–12 weeks (nasal hypoplasia, epiphyseal stippling). CNS anomalies in 2nd/3rd trimester. Dose-dependent: <5 mg/day → lower risk. | Best valve protection — lowest thromboembolism risk | ESC: Warfarin throughout (≤5 mg/day) or switch to LMWH at 6–12 weeks to avoid embryopathy period. |
| LMWH | Does not cross placenta — safe for fetus | Higher valve thrombosis risk than warfarin. Must monitor anti-Xa levels rigorously (target 0.8–1.2 IU/mL 4–6h post-dose). | Option for 1st trimester (embryopathy avoidance) or if warfarin dose >5 mg/day. Close monitoring essential. |

| DOACs | Teratogenic — animal data. Very limited human data. | RE-ALIGN: dabigatran ↑ thromboembolic events vs warfarin in mechanical valves | ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in mechanical valves. No role in pregnancy. |

Warning: Delivery plan: Switch to IV UFH at 36 weeks. At labour onset: stop UFH 4–6h before delivery (short half-life). Restart anticoagulation 4–6h post-delivery (if no excessive bleeding). Never deliver while anticoagulated (maternal haemorrhage risk).

Duke Criteria: Validated diagnostic framework for IE — major and minor criteria combined to classify likelihood

MAJOR criteria
1. Blood culture: Typical organism in ≥2 cultures (S. viridans, S. bovis, HACEK, S. aureus, Enterococcus) OR persistently positive cultures ≥12h apart OR single positive for Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)
2. Imaging (echo/CMR): Vegetation, abscess/pseudoaneurysm/fistula, new valvular regurgitation, new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve. OR PET/CT: Abnormal uptake around prosthetic valve (>3 months post-implant)

MINOR criteria
1. Predisposing cardiac condition OR IV drug use
2. Fever ≥38°C
3. Vascular phenomena: arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages, Janeway lesions
4. Immunological phenomena: glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor
5. Microbiological evidence not meeting major criteria

| Diagnosis | Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Definite IE | 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor criteria |
| Possible IE | 1 major + 1 minor OR 3 minor criteria |
| Rejected IE | Firm alternative diagnosis OR resolution of symptoms ≤4 days antibiotics OR none of above met |
front: Duke criteria for infective endocarditis — major and minor criteria, and diagnostic categories

| Trial | COAPT (USA) | MITRA-FR (France) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MR type | Secondary (functional) MR | Secondary (functional) MR |
| Patient selection | Strict: EROA ≥0.2 cm², RV ≥30 mL, EF 20–50%, symptom despite OMT >3 months | Less strict: EROA ≥0.2 cm², EF 15–40%, symptoms despite OMT |
| MR severity | Disproportionate MR (relative to LV dilation — "MR begets MR") | Proportionate MR (appropriate to LV dilation — compensatory) |
| Primary endpoint | 29% ↓ HHF + 62% ↓ HHF over 2 years. 38% ↓ mortality. | No significant difference in death or HHF |
| Why different? | COAPT selected patients where MR was the DRIVER of worsening (disproportionate). OMT was maximally optimised before enrolment (≥3 months). | MITRA-FR included compensatory MR where fixing MR doesn't change outcome. Less rigorous OMT optimisation. |

Grayburn's Proportionality Concept: EROA/(LVEDV/100) <1 = proportionate (don't clip). >1 = disproportionate → MR driving LV dysfunction → clip will help (COAPT phenotype).
Correct: ESC 2021: MitraClip Class IIa for symptomatic severe secondary MR despite OMT, suitable anatomy, ≥1 year life expectancy, COAPT-like patient selection. Heart Team required.

| PROTECT-AF (2009) | WATCHMAN non-inferior to warfarin for stroke/embolism/CV death. But ↑ procedural complications (effusion, embolisation, haemorrhage). After learning curve: outcomes improved. |
| PREVAIL (2013) | Met non-inferiority for stroke/embolism. Confirmed lower haemorrhagic stroke + bleeding. Short-term (7-day) complication rate ↑ but 18-month outcomes favourable. |
| PRAGUE-17 (2023) | WATCHMAN vs NOACs in patients who survived major bleeding or had contraindication to OAC: Non-inferior for MACE. First head-to-head vs DOACs data. |

Tip: Post-WATCHMAN: 45 days of dual antithrombotic (aspirin + clopidogrel or OAC) while device endothelialises → then aspirin alone lifelong. TOE at 45 days to confirm device seal. ESC Class IIb for patients with AF + absolute CI to OAC (bleeding risk too high).
