Low-flow, low-gradient (LFLG) AS: AVA <1.0 cm² + mean gradient <40 mmHg + either low EF or low flow — two distinct entities

| Feature | Classical LFLG (reduced EF) | Paradoxical LFLG (preserved EF) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LVEF | <50% (reduced) | ≥50% (preserved) |
| Stroke volume index | ↓ (<35 mL/m²) — from pump dysfunction | ↓ (<35 mL/m²) — from small, concentric, hypertrophied LV |
| Pathophysiology | DCM/ischaemic CMP + AS. Low flow through valve → artificially low gradient despite severe stenosis. "True severe" vs "pseudo-severe" AS. | Severely concentric hypertrophy → small cavity → ↓ SV despite preserved EF. Often elderly hypertensive women. |
| Dobutamine stress echo (DSE) | Used to distinguish true severe (AVA stays <1.0 cm², gradient ↑) from pseudo-severe (AVA increases >1.0 cm² at higher flow — not truly severe). Flow reserve: ↑ SV ≥20% = reserve. | CT calcium scoring: Aortic valve calcium score ≥1600 (men) or ≥800 (women) = confirms severity. DSE less useful in preserved EF. |
| Prognosis without AVR | Very poor — surgical mortality ↑ but so is untreated mortality. | High mortality if untreated; AVR beneficial. |

Tip: TAVI preferred for LFLG AS: Surgically high risk, but medical management has poor prognosis. TAVR outcomes in LFLG AS are good (PARTNER 2S3i registry).
front: Low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis — two subtypes and how to distinguish them

back:
BAV (bicuspid aortic valve): Most common congenital cardiac malformation — prevalence 0.5–2% of population (male predominance 3:1)

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Morphological types | Type 1 (most common, 70%): Right-left coronary leaflet fusion. Type 2 (20%): Right-non-coronary fusion. Type 3 (10%): Left-non-coronary fusion. Raphe = fused commissure remnant. |
| Associated aortopathy | Aortic dilatation in 50–80% (ascending aorta most common; also root, arch). NOT just post-stenotic dilatation — intrinsic aortic wall disease (↓ fibrillin, ↑ MMP-2/-9). Independent of valve function. |
| Genetic associations | NOTCH1 mutation most common. Associated with Turner syndrome (45,XO). Familial clustering → screen 1st-degree relatives with echo. |
| Natural history | AS: More rapid progression than tricuspid AS (calcification faster). AR: 20–25% develop significant AR. Mean age of AS surgery: BAV ~50–60 years vs tricuspid AS 65–75 years. |

| Aortic diameter threshold for surgery in BAV (ESC 2021) | Indication |
| --- | --- |
| ≥55 mm | Class I — elective aortic root/ascending aorta replacement |
| ≥50 mm | Class IIa if additional risk factors (family history dissection, HT, coarctation, rapid growth >3 mm/year) |
| ≥45 mm | Class IIa if BAV + aortic valve surgery already planned (concomitant repair) |
front: Bicuspid aortic valve — prevalence, associated aortopathy, risk stratification, and surveillance

| ASD type | Location | Frequency | Closure approach |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Secundum (most common) | Fossa ovalis | 75% | Transcatheter device closure (Amplatzer) if adequate rims ≥5 mm. Avoid if ≤5 mm posterior/inferior rim or very large defect. |
| Primum | Lower IAS, adjacent to AV valves | 15–20% | Surgical repair only (AV valve involvement — often cleft mitral valve repair needed) |
| Sinus venosus (superior) | Upper IAS near SVC-RA junction | 5–10% | Surgical only. Often associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) |

Indications for ASD closure (ESC Class I):

- Significant shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5) + evidence of RV volume overload ± symptoms
- Any age if the above criteria met (including elderly)
- Paradoxical embolism (PFO/ASD as mechanism of cryptogenic stroke)

Warning: Eisenmenger: PVR ≥5 WU → ASD closure contraindicated (would remove the pressure release valve — closure → acute RV failure). Assess PVR with RHC before closure in any patient with signs of PAH. Vasoreactivity testing required if PVR elevated.
Tip: Transcatheter ASD closure (Amplatzer): Fluoroscopy + TOE guidance. Rim adequacy: ≥5 mm all around (especially posterior/aortic rim). Device size = defect + 8–14 mm. Antiplatelet (aspirin 100 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg) × 6 months post-closure.

| Type | Location | Frequency | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Membranous (perimembranous) | Membranous IVS adjacent to tricuspid annulus | 70% | Most common. May partially close spontaneously. Risk of AR from aortic cusp prolapse (right or non-coronary cusp falls into defect). |
| Muscular (trabecular) | Muscular IVS — may be multiple (Swiss cheese) | 20% | Spontaneous closure common in childhood. Device closure possible for large single muscular VSDs. |

- Significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs ≥2) causing LV volume overload
- History of IE (prevent recurrence)
- Outlet (supracristal) VSD regardless of size — to prevent progressive AR
- Progressive AR from aortic cusp prolapse in membranous VSD

Warning: Small restrictive VSD in adults with normal LV, no history of IE, no AR: Can observe. VSD jet creates Venturi effect → risk of IE (jets traumatise endocardium). Long-term risk of IE even in small VSD (~0.3%/year) — counsel about IE prophylaxis for high-risk dental procedures.

Eisenmenger syndrome: Uncorrected large left-to-right shunt → progressive pulmonary vascular disease → PVR ≥ SVR → shunt reversal to right-to-left → cyanosis

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Cyanosis mechanism | PVR ↑ progressively → when PVR ≥ SVR, shunt reverses to R→L → deoxygenated blood enters systemic circulation → central cyanosis (fingers, lips, tongue) |
| Erythrocytosis | Chronic hypoxia → ↑ EPO → secondary erythrocytosis → haematocrit 60–75%. Compensatory — do NOT routinely phlebotomise (unless symptomatic hyperviscosity AND Hct >65%). |
| Paradoxical embolism | R→L shunt allows venous thrombi/emboli to cross directly to systemic circulation → stroke, peripheral embolism. IV air embolism also possible. |
| Iron deficiency | Secondary erythrocytosis depletes iron (microcytic red cells ↑ viscosity more than normal RBCs). Iron deficiency WORSENS hyperviscosity. Supplement iron if iron-deficient. |

Management:

| Intervention | Details |
| --- | --- |
| PAH-specific therapy | Bosentan (BREATHE-5 trial: ↑ 6MWT + ↓ PVR in Eisenmenger patients). ERAs/PDE5i are Class I for symptomatic Eisenmenger. |
| Avoid | Unnecessary dehydration (↑ viscosity). Iron deficiency. Vigorous exercise. Pulmonary vasodilators without PAH expertise. Pregnancy (very high maternal mortality — WHO IV risk). |
| Closure of defect | CONTRAINDICATED once Eisenmenger physiology established (PVR ≥ 5 WU) |
| Heart-lung transplant | Only curative option. Limited availability. |
front: Eisenmenger syndrome — pathophysiology, management goals, and PAH-specific therapy

back:
CoA: Narrowing of the aorta, most commonly at the isthmus (junction of arch and descending aorta, near ductus arteriosus insertion)

| Clinical feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Hypertension | Upper body HTN + lower body relative hypotension. Radio-femoral delay. Arm-leg BP gradient >20 mmHg. |
| Associated defects | Bicuspid aortic valve (50–85%), VSD, transposition, PDA, Turner syndrome (30% of females with Turner have CoA) |
| Cerebral aneurysms | Berry aneurysm of Circle of Willis in ~10% — risk of SAH. Screen with MRA brain in all confirmed CoA. |
| Collateral vessels | Intercostal artery collaterals → rib notching on CXR (inferior surface of ribs 3–9). "3" sign on CXR (pre- and post-stenotic aortic dilatation). |
| Echo | Suprasternal notch view: Turbulence in descending aorta + increased gradient. Doppler: Prolonged systolic acceleration with diastolic tail (diastolic run-off = high gradient). Abdominal aortic pulsatility ↓. |

| Intervention indication | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| Peak-to-peak gradient at cath OR CT/CMR diameter | Gradient ≥20 mmHg OR aortic diameter <50% of normal descending aorta diameter at diaphragm |
| Preferred approach (adults) | Transcatheter balloon dilation ± stenting (preferred for discrete native CoA or re-CoA). Surgery for complex arch, long segment, aneurysm formation. |
front: Coarctation of the aorta — ECG and echo findings, adult complications, and indications for intervention

ToF = 4 components: VSD + overriding aorta + RVOTO + RVH. Total surgical repair in childhood: VSD patch + RVOTO relief (valvotomy ± transannular patch)

| Late complication | Mechanism | Significance | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pulmonary regurgitation (PR) | Transannular patch leaves free pulmonary regurgitation → RV volume overload → RV dilatation → RV failure. Most important late problem. | Progressive — develops over decades. 25–50 year survivors have severe PR in majority. | Pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) when RVEDVi >160 mL/m² or RVEF <47% or symptoms. Transcatheter PVR (MELODY/SAPIEN) if conduit present. |
| RV dilatation and dysfunction | Chronic PR volume overload → RV dilatation → ↓ RVEF → symptoms and arrhythmia | Predictor of SCD and HF | Pulmonary valve replacement before irreversible RV dysfunction |
| Ventricular arrhythmia (VT/VF) | QRS prolongation ≥180 ms predicts sustained VT. Re-entry circuits at patch borders (RVOT, VSD patch). | Risk of SCD — 2%/decade | ICD if sustained VT. Catheter ablation for specific circuits. |
| Aortic root dilatation and AR | Congenitally abnormal aortic root with ↑ RV outflow → ↑ aortic flow preoperatively → progressive dilatation. Bicuspid AV in 10%. | Aortic root >55 mm → intervention risk | Serial imaging + consider aortic root replacement if symptomatic or rapidly enlarging |
| AF/AFL | RA enlargement from TR or Fontan physiology. 10–25% of adults with repaired ToF by age 40. | Haemodynamic compromise + thromboembolism risk | Rate/rhythm control + anticoagulation (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) |
front: Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) late complications in adults — what to monitor and when to re-intervene

back:
Fontan procedure: Single ventricle palliation — systemic venous blood flows passively (no pumping chamber) from IVC/SVC directly to pulmonary arteries

| Fontan physiology | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Passive pulmonary flow | No RV pump. Pulmonary blood flow driven entirely by systemic venous pressure (CVP) − left atrial pressure gradient. Normal CVP ~8–12 mmHg in Fontan (much higher than normal 2–8 mmHg). |
| Low cardiac output | CO ~60–70% of normal. Single ventricle runs at higher filling pressures but lower CO. Exercise tolerance severely limited. |
| Venous hypertension | Chronically elevated CVP → systemic venous congestion → hepatic congestion → protein-losing enteropathy, ascites, varices |

| Late Fontan complications | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) | Intestinal lymphatic hypertension → protein leaks into gut lumen → hypoalbuminaemia + oedema. Severe (10-year mortality ~50%). Treat: Sildenafil + fenestration creation + transplant consideration. |
| Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) | Chronic hepatic congestion → fibrosis → cirrhosis → HCC (rare). All Fontan patients develop FALD over time. Monitor with AFP + imaging. |
| Arrhythmias | AF/AFL common (50% by age 40). Intra-atrial re-entrant tachycardia (IART) most common. ↑ Stroke risk. |
| Plastic bronchitis | Lymphatic cast formation in bronchi → airway obstruction. Related to elevated lymphatic pressure. |
| Thromboembolic events | Thrombosis in Fontan pathway or PA. Anticoagulation or antiplatelet recommended in all Fontan patients. |

Warning: Fontan failure: Progressive → heart-lung transplant is only curative option. Median survival after complete Fontan: ~50–60 years in ideal cases; shorter with complications. All Fontan patients need lifelong follow-up at specialized ACHD centres.
front: Fontan circulation — physiology, haemodynamics, and long-term complications

PDA: Persistence of ductus arteriosus (fetal connection between PA and aorta) beyond 3 months of age

| Classification | Haemodynamic effect | Symptoms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silent PDA | No haemodynamic effect, detected on echo only | Asymptomatic — no treatment needed but IE risk (controversial) |
| Small PDA | Qp:Qs <1.5 — minimal LV overload | Continuous machine murmur. Close to prevent IE. |
| Moderate PDA | Qp:Qs 1.5–2.0 — LV volume overload | Symptomatic — fatigue, reduced exercise |
| Large PDA | Qp:Qs >2 — severe LV overload; pulmonary HTN | HF, PAH, Eisenmenger risk |

Indication for PDA closure: Any haemodynamically significant PDA with LV overload OR any PDA to prevent IE. Absolute CI: Eisenmenger physiology (PVR ≥ SVR).

| Closure approach | Preferred use |
| --- | --- |
| Transcatheter coil/device (Amplatzer ductal occluder) | Most adults with PDA — First choice; avoidance of surgery |
| Surgical ligation (video-assisted thoracoscopy) | Large/calcified PDA; failed device; coexisting cardiac surgery needed |

Tip: Adult PDA complications not seen in children: Calcification of ductus (↑ rupture/dissection risk at closure); severe PAH; IE (typically on PA endothelium at jet impact); aneurysm of ductus (rare). Adults with large PDA and ↑ PA pressures need pre-closure RHC to assess PVR.
front: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in adults — when to close, approach, and Eisenmenger risk

Ebstein's anomaly: Apical displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets (septal + posterior) into RV → "atrialization" of RV → small functional RV + large RA + tricuspid regurgitation

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| TV leaflet displacement | Septal and posterior TV leaflets displaced apically into RV (normal TV annulus position = AV junction). Anterior leaflet typically elongated and "sail-like." Displacement ≥8 mm/m² body surface area on apical 4-chamber view = significant. |
| Atrialized RV | Proximal RV becomes functionally part of RA (large dilated RA) → massive RA/atrialized RV → "massively enlarged RA" on CXR (boot-shaped heart) |
| Associated anomalies | ASD/PFO (80%) with R→L shunt → cyanosis. WPW accessory pathway (25%) — often right-sided. Maternal lithium exposure association (mild increased risk). |
| Arrhythmias | WPW (SVT, pre-excited AF — high risk given right-sided AP). AF/AFL from enlarged RA. Complete heart block (rare) |
| Severity | Carpentier classification A–D: D = most severe (fully atrialized RV, sail anterior leaflet, complete TV obstruction) |

Surgical intervention (Class I): Symptoms or cyanosis + RV dilatation. Cone repair (cone reconstruction of TV) is the preferred surgical approach — reconstructs native TV from available leaflet tissue.
Warning: Pre-excited AF in Ebstein/WPW: Very high SCD risk (rapid conduction via AP → VF). Urgent ablation of AP should precede or accompany any surgical repair.
front: Ebstein's anomaly — anatomy, haemodynamic consequences, and specific treatment

| Feature | IVUS (Intravascular Ultrasound) | OCT (Optical Coherence Tomography) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technology | High-frequency ultrasound (40–60 MHz) | Near-infrared light (1310 nm) reflected |
| Axial resolution | 100–150 μm | 10–20 μm (10× better than IVUS) |
| Imaging depth (penetration) | 5–10 mm (can image through calcium, plaque) | 1–2 mm (shallow — limited in large vessels/plaque) |
| Blood clearance needed | Not required (ultrasound penetrates blood) | Yes — must flush vessel with contrast/saline to clear blood (light attenuated by blood) |
| Calcium assessment | Identifies calcified lesions (acoustic shadow). Good for assessing calcium distribution. | Best for calcium thickness quantification (arc measurement). Better for thin calcium sheets. |
| Plaque characterisation | Identifies lipid (echolucent), fibrous, calcified plaques | Superior tissue characterisation: Identifies thin-cap fibroatheroma (TCFA) — plaque vulnerability |
| Stent assessment | Stent expansion, apposition, edge dissection | Superior stent apposition assessment (malapposition detection), stent strut coverage, neointima |
| Best use | CTO PCI, calcified lesions, renal failure (less contrast), large vessels (LM) | Stent failure (thrombosis/restenosis work-up), complex anatomy (bifurcation, LM), thin calcium, plaque rupture visualisation |

Tip: IVUS-guided PCI trials: IVUS-XPL, ULTIMATE: IVUS-guided PCI → ↑ MSA (minimum stent area) → ↓ MACE vs angiography-guided PCI. ILUMIEN ONYX: OCT-guided PCI non-inferior to IVUS with fewer contrast reactions. Both are superior to angiography-alone guidance for complex PCI.
front: IVUS vs OCT — what each measures, imaging depth vs resolution, and when to use each in PCI

Coronary perforation: Rare (0.4–0.5%) but potentially catastrophic PCI complication — immediate haemopericardium risk

| Ellis Class | Angiographic appearance | Haemodynamic risk | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class I | Extraluminal crater without extravasation. Contrast staining of adventitia/extravascular tissue but NO free extravasation. | Low — usually benign | Prolonged balloon inflation at perforation site × 10–20 min. Protamine if on UFH. Observe × 30 min angio. Echo × 2–4h. |
| Class II | Pericardial or myocardial blush. Limited extravasation into pericardium — "dye staining" appearance. | Moderate — watch closely for tamponade | Prolonged balloon inflation. Protamine if anticoagulated. Covered stent if accessible. Pericardiocentesis if tamponade develops. |
| Class III | Jetting into pericardium, pleural cavity, or free extravasation (≥1 mm diameter perforation). Active blood loss clearly visible. | HIGH — immediate tamponade risk | Emergency: Balloon inflation (seals leak). Covered stent (PTFE-covered stent = "sealing stent" e.g. BeGraft, PK Papyrus). Pericardiocentesis immediately if tamponade. Reversal of anticoagulation. Emergency cardiac surgery if stent cannot seal or surgical anatomy. |
| Class IV (Cavity spilling) | Perforation into cardiac chamber (ventricle, LV) | Variable — often lower tamponade risk than Class III since blood drains into ventricle | Usually conservative — seal perforation; monitor. |

Warning: Highest risk: Guidewire-induced distal vessel perforation (PTFE-covered stent too large for distal vessel) → coil embolisation of distal perforated vessel as last resort. Emergency surgery if haemopericardium + haemodynamic instability not controlled by catheter measures.
front: Coronary perforation during PCI — Ellis classification and management of each class

| Trial | Design | Primary endpoint | Key result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EXCEL (2016, n=1,905) | LM disease + SYNTAX ≤32; PCI (Xience EES) vs CABG | Death/MI/stroke at 3 years | Non-inferior (15.4% vs 14.7%, p=0.02 for non-inferiority). PCI had more spontaneous MI; CABG more periprocedural stroke. At 5 years: CABG numerically better (22% vs 19%, not significant). Controversy: MI definition differences. |

| ESC 2018/2019 Recommendation | SYNTAX Score | PCI vs CABG |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LM distal bifurcation, complex anatomy | High (>32) | CABG preferred (Class I) |

back:
Rotational atherectomy (RA): Ablation of calcium-containing plaque by a diamond-studded burr rotating at 140,000–180,000 rpm — allows stent delivery and expansion in severely calcified lesions

| Mechanism | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Differential cutting | Burr preferentially ablates inelastic (calcified/fibrotic) tissue, not elastic (healthy) tissue. Creates smooth channel for balloon/stent. |
| Micro-particle size | Ablated particles <10 μm → pass through capillary bed → absorbed. Larger particles → "slow flow" or "no-reflow." |
| Guide wire | Rotawire (specific floppy guide wire) required — standard guide wires incompatible. |

| Indication | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Severely calcified coronary lesions (Class II in ACC/AHA PCI guidelines) | When calcium prevents balloon expansion or stent delivery. IVUS calcium arc >270° or CT calcium arc >270° = severe. |
| Undilatable lesions ("balloon failure") | When pre-dilation balloon cannot expand to nominal pressure (rigid calcium prevents expansion) |
| CTO PCI (selected) | When CTO entry requires plaque modification |

Warning: Major complications: Slow flow/no-reflow (5–10% from platelet activation + micro-debris) → treat with IC adenosine + IC nitroprusside + GP IIb/IIIa. Coronary perforation (especially if too large a burr). Coronary dissection. Vessel spasm. Use smallest burr first, then upsizing. Burr:artery ratio should NOT exceed 0.6. Avoid in thrombus-containing lesions or cardiogenic shock.
front: Rotational atherectomy — mechanism, indications, and procedural considerations

WHO PH Classification (Revised 6th World Symposium 2018): 5 groups based on pathological mechanism — treatment varies completely between groups

| Group | Category | Key causes | PAH-specific drugs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Group 1 — PAH | Pulmonary ARTERIAL hypertension — small vessel obliterative disease | Idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), CTD (scleroderma), HIV, portal HTN, congenital heart disease, drugs/toxins (aminorex, dasatinib) | YES — ERA + PDE5i + prostacyclin analogues |
| Group 2 — Left heart disease | Post-capillary PH — elevated left-sided filling pressures transmitted to pulmonary circulation | HFpEF, HFrEF, mitral/aortic valve disease | NO — treat underlying left heart disease. PAH drugs may cause pulmonary oedema (↑ venous return without adequate LV output). |
| Group 3 — Lung disease / hypoxia | PH from chronic hypoxia or lung parenchymal disease | COPD, ILD (especially SSc-ILD), OSA, high altitude | NO — treat hypoxia (long-term O₂, CPAP for OSA). Sildenafil may benefit SSc-ILD + PH (INCREASE trial). |
| Group 4 — CTEPH | Chronic thromboembolic PH — organised thrombus obstructs PAs | Incomplete resolution of PE → fibrotic obstruction | Riociguat (Class I). Macitentan (Class IIa). Surgical: pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA). Interventional: balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA). |
| Group 5 — Multifactorial / unclear | Heterogeneous mechanisms | Haematological (myeloproliferative, sickle cell), systemic (sarcoidosis, Gaucher), metabolic (Pompe), complex CHD | Individualised — treat underlying disease |
front: WHO pulmonary hypertension classification — groups 1–5, causes, and why grouping matters for treatment

back:
CTEPH: Incomplete PE resolution → organised fibrous obstruction of PAs → PH. Develops in 0.5–4% of acute PE survivors.

| Diagnostic step | Details |
| --- | --- |
| V/Q scan | First-line screening. Characteristic: Mismatched perfusion defects (absent perfusion in ventilated segments). V/Q is MORE sensitive than CTPA for CTEPH. |
| CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) | Shows organised clot as filling defects, webs, bands, pouches, or smooth tapering. RV enlargement, mosaic attenuation pattern. |
| Right heart catheterisation | Confirms PH: mPAP >20 mmHg. CTEPH has pre-capillary PH (PCWP normal). |
| Pulmonary angiography | Essential before surgery or BPA — defines operability and extent of disease. |

| Treatment | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Surgical PEA (pulmonary endarterectomy) | Gold standard. Removes organised thrombus from PAs under deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. Perioperative mortality ~5% at expert centres. Near-curative for proximal disease. Requires lifelong anticoagulation post-op. |
| Balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) | Catheter-based dilation of stenotic PA segments — for inoperable CTEPH (distal disease, high surgical risk, or post-PEA residual). Multiple sessions needed. Reperfusion oedema risk. |
| Riociguat (Adempas) | sGC stimulator → ↑ cGMP → pulmonary vasodilation. CHEST-1 trial: ↑ 6MWT +46m vs placebo in inoperable or residual CTEPH. Only PAH drug with Class I in CTEPH. Also used post-BPA for residual PH. |

Warning: Lifelong anticoagulation: All CTEPH patients require lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin preferred — most data; DOACs increasingly used). VKA target INR 2.5–3.5. The underlying thrombophilia/prothrombotic state persists — recurrent thrombosis risk without anticoagulation.
front: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) — diagnosis, surgical vs balloon approaches, and riociguat

back:
| Feature | Group 1 PAH | Group 2 PH (left heart disease) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PCWP | <15 mmHg (pre-capillary PH) | >15 mmHg (post-capillary PH from ↑ left-sided filling pressures) |
| DPG (diastolic pressure gradient) | DPG = PADP − PCWP ≥7 mmHg indicates "out-of-proportion" or combined pre + post-capillary PH | DPG <7 mmHg = isolated post-capillary PH (purely from transmitted left-sided pressure) |
| PVR | ↑↑ (>3 WU — often 5–20 WU) | Normal or mildly ↑ (<3 WU); ↑↑ = "combined" PH (Group 2 + secondary vascular changes) |
| Right heart catheterisation | mPAP >20, PCWP <15, PVR ≥2 WU | mPAP >20, PCWP >15 |

Warning: WHY PAH drugs dangerous in Group 2 PH: Group 1 PAH drugs (sildenafil, bosentan, ERAs, prostacyclins) cause pulmonary vasodilation → ↑ pulmonary blood flow → ↑ return to already-congested left heart → ACUTE PULMONARY OEDEMA. Sildenafil in HFpEF + PH (RELAX trial, SilHF) showed NO benefit + possible harm. ERAs in HFrEF worsened outcomes. Group 2 PH MUST be treated by addressing the left heart disease (diuretics, GDMT for HF, valve surgery).
Tip: Exception: Sildenafil for SSc-ILD associated PH (Group 3/mixed): INCREASE trial showed modest benefit. Small group — limited data. Expert centre decisions only.
front: Group 2 PH (left heart disease) — how to distinguish from Group 1 PAH and why PAH drugs are dangerous in Group 2

LGE = zones of fibrosis/necrosis with slow gadolinium washout → appear bright on inversion recovery sequences ~10 min post-contrast

| LGE Pattern | Disease | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subendocardial (ischaemic) — coronary territory | Myocardial infarction (old or acute) | Infarction starts subendocardially → extends outward with severity. Territory corresponds to occluded coronary artery. |
| Transmural LGE in coronary territory | Large/complete MI | Full-thickness infarction |
| Mid-wall (non-ischaemic) "stripe" | DCM (dilated cardiomyopathy), myocarditis, sarcoidosis | Mid-wall fibrosis from chronic inflammation or fibrosis — does NOT follow coronary distribution |
| Subepicardial (patchy) | Myocarditis, ARVC, pericarditis | Epicardial/subepicardial inflammation; characteristic in viral myocarditis (inferolateral wall) |
| Diffuse subendocardial (global) | Cardiac amyloidosis | Diffuse subendocardial/transmural with inability to null myocardium (myocardium appears bright, blood pool dark = inverted pattern) |
| Patchy, non-ischaemic, multiple foci | Cardiac sarcoidosis | Multifocal granulomatous infiltration; any location but often basal septum and lateral wall |
| RV insertion points (bilateral) | HCM, PAH | Fibrosis at right ventricular insertion points — high mechanical stress zones |
| Diffuse "hazy" low-level enhancement | Fabry disease | Glycosphingolipid infiltration → mid-wall lateral LV LGE (pathognomonic pattern) |

Tip: LGE quantification in HCM: ≥15% of LV mass by LGE → Class IIa indication for ICD in primary prevention. CMR is superior to echo for HCM risk stratification — detects fibrosis burden which echo cannot. Every HCM patient should have CMR once.

Lake Louise Criteria (CMR Working Group 2018 update): Diagnoses myocarditis based on tissue characterisation

| Category | Criterion | Score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T2-based (oedema) | Regional or global ↑ T2 signal (or ↑ T2 mapping values) in myocardium vs skeletal muscle (T2 ratio ≥2.0). Or T2 mapping: ≥59 ms (1.5T) or ≥52 ms (3T). | +1 major |
| T1-based (injury/fibrosis) | LGE in non-ischaemic pattern OR ↑ T1 mapping values OR ↑ extracellular volume (ECV) fraction | +1 major |

Positive CMR: ≥1 major criterion present (sensitivity ~87%, specificity ~85%)
Supportive (minor) criteria: Pericardial effusion + ↑ LGE of pericardium (myopericarditis). LVEF <50% or regional wall motion abnormality in absence of obvious structural cause.

| Myocarditis CMR pattern | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Oedema (T2) | Acute phase <2 weeks: typically subepicardial or mid-wall, inferolateral location. Represents active inflammation. |
| LGE pattern | Subepicardial/mid-wall, non-coronary distribution — KEY distinguishing feature from MI (which is subendocardial/transmural in coronary territory) |
| T1/ECV mapping | Increased T1 relaxation time and ECV indicates diffuse fibrosis + oedema |

Tip: CMR timing: Ideally perform within 14 days of symptom onset for T2 oedema detection. After 4 weeks: T2 abnormalities resolve but LGE may persist (fibrosis). Repeat CMR at 3–6 months: LGE resolution = favourable prognosis for LV recovery.
front: CMR Lake Louise criteria for myocarditis — original and updated (2018) criteria

back:
Parametric mapping: Quantitative pixel-by-pixel T1 and T2 relaxation times → detect diffuse myocardial disease missed by conventional LGE

| Mapping | Measures | Normal values (1.5T) | Diseases with abnormal values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Native T1 mapping | Intrinsic T1 relaxation time of myocardium without contrast. ↑ T1 = more water content (oedema, fibrosis, infiltration). | ~950–1000 ms (1.5T); ~1050 ms (3T) | ↑ T1: Amyloidosis (very high), myocarditis, haemochromatosis (↓ T1!), Anderson-Fabry (↓ T1 in early, ↑ late) |
| ECV (extracellular volume) | Pre- and post-contrast T1 maps + haematocrit → fractional ECV = proportion of interstitium. Normal ~25%. | ~25% | ↑ ECV: Amyloidosis (60–70%), fibrosis, oedema; ↓ ECV: Anderson-Fabry (glycosphingolipid fills cells) |
| T2 mapping | Free water content (oedema, acute inflammation) | ~52–55 ms (1.5T) | ↑ T2: Myocarditis (acute), Takotsubo, acute MI, sarcoidosis (active) |

Tip: Amyloidosis CMR signature: Very ↑ native T1 + very ↑ ECV (sometimes >50%) + diffuse subendocardial LGE with abnormal gadolinium kinetics (early myocardial washout = elevated ECV). Combined T1 mapping + LGE pattern is diagnostic in most cases without biopsy.
Tip: Anderson-Fabry: Native T1 is DECREASED (↓) in early disease — the only infiltrative cardiomyopathy with ↓ T1. This is because α-galactosidase A deficiency → glycosphingolipid accumulates intracellularly → replaces high-T1 water with low-T1 lipid. T1 <940 ms at 1.5T in posterior/inferolateral wall suggests Fabry cardiomyopathy.
front: T1 mapping and T2 mapping on CMR — what they measure and in which diseases are they abnormal

back:
Viability CMR: Transmural extent of LGE predicts functional recovery after revascularisation

| LGE transmurality | Myocardial status | Likelihood of functional recovery post-revascularisation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0% transmurality (no LGE) | Normal or stunned/hibernating — all viable | Very high (>80%) |
| <25% transmurality | Predominantly viable (small subendocardial scar) | High (>70%) |
| 25–50% transmurality | Mixed — partial viability | Moderate (~50%) |
| 50–75% transmurality | More scar than viable tissue | Low (~25%) |
| >75% transmurality (near-transmural/transmural LGE) | Predominantly scar — minimal viable tissue | Very low (<10%) — revascularisation unlikely to improve function |

Stunning: Acute reversible dysfunction post-ischaemia. No LGE. Recovers spontaneously within days to weeks.
Hibernation: Chronic ischaemic LV dysfunction — myocytes downregulate function to survive chronic low flow. No/minimal LGE. Recovers after revascularisation.
Tip: CMR viability vs dobutamine stress echo: CMR provides direct anatomical information about scar burden; DSE provides functional information (contractile reserve). Both predict recovery. CMR has higher spatial resolution for thin-walled segments; DSE preferred when claustrophobia or contraindications to CMR. Combined assessment improves accuracy.
front: CMR for myocardial viability — hibernation vs stunning vs scar: what CMR reveals and how it guides revascularisation

back:
ARVC CMR: Provides structural, functional, and tissue characterisation of RV — key diagnostic modality for ARVC

| CMR finding | Task Force criterion | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RV end-diastolic volume index (RVEDVi) | Major: ≥110 mL/m² (males), ≥100 mL/m² (females) Minor: 100–109 (M), 90–99 (F) | RV dilatation without another cause |
| RV ejection fraction (RVEF) | Major: ≤40% Minor: 41–45% | Global RV systolic dysfunction |
| Regional RV wall motion abnormality | Major criterion (any): Akinesis, dyskinesis, or dyssynchronous RV contraction | Typically RV free wall (ARVC triangle of dysplasia: inflow, outflow, apex) |
| RV fatty infiltration (LGE/fat signal) | Supportive finding (not standalone criterion) | Fat within RV myocardium on FIESTA or T1 gradient; subepicardial/mid-wall LGE of RV free wall. Must be distinguished from normal epicardial fat. |

Warning: CMR pitfalls in ARVC: Normal individuals can have RV fat (especially anterior wall epicardial fat). LGE in RV is technically challenging (thin wall). Breathhold artefacts. Criteria require careful measurement — over-diagnosis can lead to inappropriate ICD. Diagnosis requires integration of all Task Force criteria (ECG, Holter, familial, histology, signal abnormalities).
Tip: CMR is best imaging test for ARVC but TOE or CT can also demonstrate RV structural changes. Genotyping (DSP, PKP2, DSG2, DSC2, JUP, TMEM43 mutations) is positive in ~60% of ARVC — confirms diagnosis when Task Force criteria borderline.
front: CMR in ARVC — Task Force CMR criteria and what findings confirm the diagnosis

back:
Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin, daunorubicin): Type I cardiotoxicity — irreversible myocardial damage

| Mechanism | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2β) inhibition | Nuclear enzyme responsible for DNA unwinding. Anthracyclines form a ternary complex (drug-TOP2β-DNA) → DNA double-strand breaks → cardiomyocyte apoptosis. This is the CARDIAC mechanism — different from anti-cancer (TOP2α) mechanism. |
| Free radical generation | Anthracyclines undergo redox cycling → reactive oxygen species → mitochondrial damage → cardiomyocyte death. Dexrazoxane (cardioprotectant) inhibits TOP2β and scavenges iron that catalyses free radical generation. |
| Ca²⁺ overload | Disruption of SR Ca²⁺ handling → Ca²⁺ overload → mitochondrial dysfunction |

| Cumulative dose thresholds (doxorubicin equivalent) | Risk of cardiotoxicity |
| --- | --- |
| <300 mg/m² | <1% |
| 300–400 mg/m² | 1–3% |
| 500 mg/m² | ~5–10% |
| >600 mg/m² | 30–40% symptomatic HF |

Tip: Dexrazoxane: Iron chelator + TOP2β inhibitor → cardioprotective. FDA-approved for patients receiving >300 mg/m² doxorubicin. No reduction in anti-cancer efficacy. ESC cardio-oncology guidelines 2022: Consider dexrazoxane for patients receiving high cumulative anthracycline doses or with cardiac risk factors.
Tip: Liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil/Caelyx): Encapsulated in liposome → preferential tumour uptake → reduced cardiac exposure → lower cardiotoxicity at equivalent anti-tumour doses. Preferred in patients with cardiac risk factors.
front: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity — type I cardiotoxicity mechanism, risk factors, dose thresholds, and primary prevention

back:
| Feature | Type I cardiotoxicity | Type II cardiotoxicity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Irreversible myocyte death (apoptosis and necrosis). Structural damage — cardiomyocytes lost permanently. | Reversible myocyte dysfunction without structural cell death. "Hibernation-like" — LV function impairs but cells remain viable. |
| Examples | Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin), cyclophosphamide (high-dose), alkylating agents | Trastuzumab (Herceptin), pertuzumab, lapatinib (HER2-targeted); imatinib (rare); immune checkpoint inhibitors (myocarditis — separate mechanism) |
| Dose-dependence | Cumulative dose-dependent (thresholds matter) | NOT dose-dependent — can occur at any dose |
| Reversibility | Permanent — EF may partially improve but cardiomyocyte loss is not recovered | Largely reversible (80%) — EF usually recovers when drug stopped ± HF therapy |
| Electron microscopy | Vacuolisation, myofibril loss, sarcomere disruption | Normal or near-normal ultrastructure |
| Combined toxicity | Prior anthracycline ↑ risk of trastuzumab Type II toxicity dramatically (synergistic harm) | Avoid sequential anthracycline + trastuzumab without cardiac monitoring |
| Re-challenge | Use alternative agent; dose reduction if needed | Often rechallengeable after EF recovery + HF treatment (decision with oncology) |
front: Type I vs Type II chemotherapy cardiotoxicity — distinguish mechanism, reversibility, and which drugs cause each

back:
ICI myocarditis: Rare (0.04–1.14%) but potentially FATAL (case fatality rate 25–50%). Highest of any ICI adverse event.

| Causative ICIs | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Anti-PD-1: Pembrolizumab, nivolumab | Highest incidence — most widely used |
| Anti-PD-L1: Atezolizumab, durvalumab | Less common |
| Anti-CTLA-4: Ipilimumab | Lower individual risk but combination ICI (nivolumab + ipilimumab) → 5× ↑ myocarditis risk vs monotherapy |
| Combination ICI regimens | Dramatically ↑ risk vs monotherapy. Combination is the highest-risk scenario. |

| Diagnosis | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical presentation | Dyspnoea, chest pain, fatigue. Often within first 3 months of ICI (sometimes first dose). May have normal echo with elevated troponin (inflammation without global dysfunction). |
| Troponin | Elevated in >90% — most sensitive marker. Serial monitoring recommended if on ICI. |
| ECG | Conduction abnormalities (AV block, BBB), VT. New ECG changes + ↑ troponin in ICI patient = suspect myocarditis. |
| CMR | Lake Louise criteria (T2 + LGE) — confirms active myocarditis. May be negative (false negative up to 30%). Endomyocardial biopsy if CMR negative but high suspicion. |

Warning: URGENT TREATMENT: HOLD ICI immediately (most important step). High-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY: Methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day IV × 3–5 days → oral prednisone taper over 4–6 weeks. Fulminant (haemodynamic instability): 1 mg/kg methylprednisolone IV PLUS additional immunosuppression (mycophenolate, abatacept, anti-thymocyte globulin in refractory). MCS if needed. Do not wait for biopsy to start steroids — delay worsens outcome.
front: Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis — which drugs cause it, diagnosis, and emergency treatment

back:
Radiation-induced cardiac disease (RICD): Occurs years to decades after mediastinal/chest radiation (Hodgkin lymphoma, breast cancer, lung cancer, oesophageal cancer)

| Manifestation | Typical onset | Mechanism | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pericardial disease (most common) | Months to years post-RT | Fibrous pericardial thickening → pericarditis → effusion → constrictive pericarditis | Constrictive pericarditis may appear 10–20 years later. Pericardiectomy required. |
| Accelerated CAD | 5–20 years post-RT | Radiation fibrosis of coronary intima + adventitia → accelerated atherosclerosis. Proximal coronary arteries (LAD in left-sided breast RT) | Typically involves proximal/ostial coronary arteries. Higher risk than age-matched controls. Screen with CT calcium score or stress testing. |
| Valvular disease | 10–20 years post-RT | Fibrosis and calcification of valve leaflets + subvalvular apparatus | AS + AR + MR in same patient ("panvalvular disease"). TAVI may be challenging (poor tissue quality, radiation aortitis). |
| Cardiomyopathy | Variable | Diffuse myocardial fibrosis → restrictive CMP | HFpEF pattern, diastolic dysfunction, low EF in severe cases |
| Conduction disease | Years to decades | Fibrosis of conduction system → bundle branch blocks, AV block | Permanent pacing may be needed |

Tip: Heart dose reduction: Modern RT planning limits mean heart dose <5 Gy (ideal <2 Gy) for left-sided breast cancer. Deep inspiration breath hold (DIBH) moves heart away from field. Proton beam therapy reduces cardiac dose. Despite advances, RICD remains a major long-term mortality cause in Hodgkin survivors.
front: Radiation-induced cardiac disease — what types occur, timeline, and clinical presentation

ESC Cardio-Oncology Guidelines 2022: Risk-stratified cardiac monitoring before, during, and after cancer therapy

| Chemotherapy agent | Baseline | During treatment | Follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anthracyclines (low-risk doses) | Echo + ECG + troponin + BNP | Echo at midpoint (if >250 mg/m² cumulative doxorubicin); troponin each cycle (optional) | Echo 1 year and 5 years post-treatment |
| Anthracyclines (high-risk or cumulative >300 mg/m²) | Echo + ECG + troponin | Echo before every 2 cycles or 100 mg/m² increments; troponin each cycle | Echo at 1, 2, 5 years post-treatment |
| Trastuzumab/HER2 agents | Echo + ECG | Echo every 3 months during 12-month treatment | Echo 1 year post-treatment if baseline function normal |
| VEGF inhibitors (sunitinib, sorafenib) | Echo + ECG + BP + lipids | BP monitoring every visit; Echo every 3 months | Discontinue if EF <50% |
| ICIs (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) | ECG + troponin + BNP | Troponin + ECG before each cycle (first 6–12 weeks). Any symptom → immediate work-up. | — |

Tip: CARDIOTOX Score: Baseline risk stratification score for cardiotoxicity (age, CV risk factors, prior cardiac history, prior cardiotoxic chemotherapy, radiation). High-risk = more intensive monitoring. ESC 2022 uses simplified risk categories (low/medium/high/very high) based on clinical + therapy factors.

Posterior MI: Infarction of posterior LV wall — supplied by RCA (right dominant) or LCx (left dominant). Standard 12-lead shows RECIPROCAL changes.

| ECG finding | Lead location | Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tall R wave (R > S) in V1–V2 | Anterior leads (mirror of posterior Q wave) | Posterior Q waves are invisible on standard 12-lead — appear as tall R waves in V1–V2 (180° reciprocal). R:S ratio >1 in V1 in the context of inferior MI = posterior extension. |
| ST depression in V1–V4 | Anterior leads (mirror of posterior ST elevation) | Posterior ST elevation appears as ST depression in V1–V4 on standard leads. Horizontally depressed ST with upright T waves in V1–V2 = classic posterior injury pattern. |
| Tall, upright T waves V1–V2 | Anterior leads | Reciprocal of posterior T wave inversions in the evolving phase |

Posterior leads V7–V9 confirm the diagnosis:

| Lead placement | V7: left posterior axillary line; V8: left midscapular line; V9: left paraspinal area |
| --- | --- |
| Diagnostic criterion | ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V7–V9 (lower threshold than standard leads) = posterior STEMI |

Warning: Posterior MI is a STEMI equivalent — must activate cath lab. Easily missed when only looking at standard anterior leads. Any inferior STEMI should have posterior leads done — 20–25% of inferior STEMIs have posterior extension. V4R for RV infarction; V7-V9 for posterior involvement.
front: Posterior MI — how to recognise it on standard 12-lead ECG and with right-sided/posterior leads

back:
Sgarbossa criteria (1996) + Modified Sgarbossa (Smith, 2012): Identify STEMI in the presence of LBBB or ventricular pacing (which normally distorts ST segments)
LBBB normally causes: Secondary ST-T changes opposite to QRS direction (ST ↓ + T inversion where QRS is positive; ST ↑ + upright T where QRS is negative). This OBSCURES ischaemic changes.

| Criterion | Threshold | Points (original) | Specificity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. ST elevation ≥1 mm concordant with QRS direction (both same direction) | Any concordant ST elevation | 5 points | Highly specific (~94%) |
| 2. ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3 (concordant) | ≥1 mm ST↓ in leads with negative QRS (concordant) | 3 points | High |
| 3. ST elevation ≥5 mm discordant in leads with negative QRS (excessive ST elevation in discordant direction) | ≥5 mm (original) / modified: ST/S ratio ≥0.25 | 2 points | Low with 5 mm; better with ratio |

Original threshold: Score ≥3 points = STEMI. But sensitivity only ~36%.
Modified Sgarbossa (Smith, 2012): Criterion 3 replaced by ST/S ratio (ST elevation / depth of preceding S wave). If ST/S ratio ≥0.25 in ANY lead with negative QRS → positive. Sensitivity ↑ to ~80% with modified criteria.
Tip: Any new LBBB + chest pain in the right clinical context = STEMI equivalent (Sgarbossa or not) — activate cath lab. If LBBB is old and known, use Sgarbossa to evaluate new changes.
front: Sgarbossa criteria — diagnosing MI in LBBB or paced rhythm

back:
Pericarditis ECG: Diffuse ST elevation from pericardial inflammation → 4 evolutionary stages over days to weeks

| Stage | Timing | ECG changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 (Acute) | Hours to days | Diffuse concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation in MULTIPLE leads (I, II, III, aVL, aVF, V2–V6) + PR depression (in leads with ST elevation). ST elevation in aVR and PR elevation in aVR (reciprocal). No Q waves. |
| Stage 2 | Days | ST returns to baseline. T waves flatten. |
| Stage 3 | Weeks | T-wave inversions develop in same leads where ST was elevated |
| Stage 4 (Resolution) | Weeks to months | ECG normalises or T inversions persist (chronic pericarditis) |

Differentiating pericarditis ST from STEMI
Pericarditis: ST elevation is CONCAVE (saddle-shaped) / diffuse in multiple territories. STEMI: ST elevation is CONVEX (domed/tombstone) in a coronary territory.
Pericarditis: PR segment depression (in leads with ST elevation) — pathognomonic. Absent in STEMI.
Pericarditis: No reciprocal ST depression (except aVR). STEMI: Reciprocal ST depression in opposite leads.
Pericarditis: Spodick's sign = downsloping TP segment in STEMI mimics ST elevation — not seen in STEMI.
Pericarditis: ST/T ratio in V6 ≥0.25 favours pericarditis vs early repolarisation

Warning: If any doubt: treat as STEMI until ACS excluded. Chest pain + pericarditis ECG + elevated troponin = myopericarditis — most have benign course but monitor and rest from activity.
front: ECG in acute pericarditis — four stages and differentiating from STEMI

back:
Fascicular blocks affect the fascicles of the left bundle branch (anterior + posterior). Normal QRS duration (unless combined with RBBB).

| Feature | LAFB (Left Anterior Fascicular Block) | LPFB (Left Posterior Fascicular Block) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial activation | Posterior fascicle activates inferiorly first | Anterior fascicle activates superiorly first |
| QRS axis | Left axis deviation (LAD): −30° to −90° | Right axis deviation (RAD): +90° to +180° |
| Lead I, aVL | Positive (qR or R pattern) | Negative (rS pattern) |
| Lead II, III, aVF | Negative (rS pattern) | Positive (qR or R pattern) |
| QRS duration | Normal (<120 ms) | Normal (<120 ms) |
| Frequency | COMMON (most common conduction defect in adults, ~1–4%) | RARE (requires excluding other causes of RAD) |
| Cause | Fibrosis, ischaemia, HCM, cardiac surgery | Must exclude: RVH, lateral MI, vertical heart, COPD/PE before diagnosing LPFB |

Bifascicular block: RBBB + LAFB (most common) = right axis deviation of right ventricle + left axis deviation. RBBB + LPFB = rare. Risk of progression to complete AV block: ~1%/year.
Tip: Trifascicular block: RBBB + LAFB/LPFB + 1st degree AV block OR alternating LBBB/RBBB. Implies disease in all three fascicles. Class I indication for PPM implantation if symptoms (syncope/presyncope).
front: Fascicular blocks — left anterior fascicular block (LAFB) and left posterior fascicular block (LPFB): ECG criteria and clinical significance

back:
Pre-excited ECG in WPW: Delta wave polarity and QRS axis reflect location of accessory pathway (AP) along the AV groove

| Delta wave pattern | AP location |
| --- | --- |
| Positive delta in V1–V6, negative in aVR | Left free wall — most common (60–70%). Positive delta V1 = left-sided AP. |
| Negative delta in V1–V2 (QS or rS in V1) | Right free wall or right anteroseptal AP. |
| Positive delta in I, aVL; negative in III, aVF | Posteroseptal or right posterior AP |
| Isoelectric or negative delta in V1, negative in III, aVF | Posteroseptal (most common septal location) |
| Negative delta in I, aVL; positive in inferior leads | Left lateral or left posterior AP |

Simplified rule for ablation planning:

| V1 delta wave | Location |
| --- | --- |
| Positive (R wave) in V1 | LEFT-sided AP (left free wall or posteroseptal) |
| Negative (QS/rS) in V1 | RIGHT-sided AP (right free wall, right anteroseptal, or true posteroseptal) |

Tip: Mahaim fibre (nodoventricular/nodofascicular): Conducts from AV node to RV → atypical LBBB-pattern wide QRS with delta wave. Unlike classic WPW — only anterograde conduction (no retrograde = no AVRT). Treated with RF ablation at the RA end (ventricular attachment near RV base).
front: WPW delta wave localization — how to determine accessory pathway location from the 12-lead ECG

| Phenomenon | Definition | Mechanism | Clinical significance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical alternans (QRS alternans) | Beat-to-beat alternation in QRS axis/amplitude — QRS complex changes every other beat | Large pericardial effusion → heart swings with each beat → alternating electrical axis. Can also occur in VT at fast rates. | CLASSIC sign of cardiac tamponade (large effusion). Also seen in fast VT. When combined with sinus tachycardia + low voltage = tamponade triad. |
| T-wave alternans (TWA) | Beat-to-beat alternation in T-wave amplitude or polarity | Alternating Ca²⁺ cycling → alternating repolarisation. Reflects dispersion of repolarisation — substrate for VF. | Microvolt TWA (MTWA): Non-invasive marker of VF susceptibility. Positive MTWA predicts ↑ risk of SCA in HF, LQTS, Brugada. ABCD trial: MTWA predicts ICD benefit. Not yet widely used in clinical guidelines. |
| ST alternans | ST elevation alternates beat-to-beat | Variant of T/QRS alternans | May represent severe ischaemia (Prinzmetal variant) or hyperkalemia pattern |

Tip: Electrical alternans in tamponade: Swinging heart in pericardial fluid → alternating QRS axis. "Classic triad" of tamponade on ECG: Sinus tachycardia + low QRS voltage + electrical alternans. This triad is highly specific (but insensitive). Echo confirmation always needed.
front: QRS and T-wave alternans — what they mean and clinical significance

back:
Early repolarisation (ER): J-point elevation ≥0.1 mV in ≥2 contiguous inferior or lateral leads — historically considered benign but some forms carry VF risk

| Feature | Benign ER | High-risk ER (malignant) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location | Lateral leads (V4–V6, I, aVL) | Inferior or inferolateral leads (II, III, aVF) |
| Morphology | Notch (or slur) at J point + positive ST slope (rapidly ascending ST) | Horizontal or descending ST after J point elevation (slurred J point + flat or down-sloping ST) |
| Amplitude | <1 mm J elevation | ≥2 mm J elevation in inferior leads |
| Demographics | Young athletes, black patients, males | Middle-aged males, family history SCD, previous VF |
| Prevalence | 5–13% of general population | <0.1% of ER patterns are truly malignant |
| Associated arrhythmia | No significant VF risk (same as general population) | Idiopathic VF (ER pattern found in 15–30% of idiopathic VF patients) |

Tip: Pattern evolution with standing or tachycardia: ER that DISAPPEARS at faster heart rates = lower risk (benign, vagally mediated). ER that ACCENTUATES at slow HR or with vagal manoeuvres = more concerning. Quinidine can suppress VF storms in ER syndrome (same as Brugada — increases Ito-countering effect).
front: Early repolarisation pattern — distinguish benign from malignant (increased VF risk) forms

back:
ST depression morphology characterises the underlying cause — not all ST depression is ischaemia

| Morphology | Appearance | Clinical significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal ST depression | ST segment flat (0° slope) for ≥80 ms after J point | Most specific for ischaemia. Ischaemic ST depression criteria: ≥1 mm horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥80 ms from J point in ≥2 contiguous leads. |
| Downsloping ST depression | ST segment slopes downward (negative slope) | Highly suggestive of ischaemia. Also seen in digoxin effect (scooping = "reverse tick"), LVH repolarisation abnormality. |
| Upsloping ST depression | ST rises from J point (positive slope) | Less specific for ischaemia. May be normal variant. If ≥1.5 mm at J+80 ms = borderline significant for ischaemia on exercise stress test. Also: tachycardia with rapid repolarisation. |
| Digoxin "scooping" | Sagging, asymmetric downsloping curve ("Salvador Dali's moustache") | Therapeutic digoxin effect — not ischaemia. Does not predict arrhythmia or toxicity alone. |
| J-point depression (0 ms) | ST depression at the J point only, quickly normalising | Often benign — normal variant in tachycardia; also in LVH. Not significant for ischaemia without additional slope criteria. |

Tip: In exercise stress testing: Horizontal/downsloping ST ↓ ≥1 mm at J+80 ms = positive for ischaemia. Upsloping ST ↓ <1.5 mm at J+80 ms = negative. Upsloping ≥1.5 mm = borderline (grey zone — continue test or refer for imaging). ST location: Depression in multiple territories = diffuse ischaemia (LM or 3-vessel disease). Isolated V5–V6 depression = circumflex territory.
front: ST depression morphology — horizontal vs downsloping vs upsloping: significance and differential diagnosis

back:
ASE 2016 diastolic dysfunction grading: Based on 4 key parameters assessed when E/A ratio is <0.8 (or 0.8–2 with E <50 cm/s)

| Parameter | Normal / Impaired relaxation | Pseudonormal / Elevated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average E/e' ratio | <14 (normal septal E/e' <15, lateral <13) | ≥14 (↑ filling pressure) |
| Septal e' velocity | ≥7 cm/s (septal); ≥10 (lateral) | <7 cm/s (septal) |
| LA volume index (LAVI) | <34 mL/m² | ≥34 mL/m² (↑ chronic filling pressure) |
| TR velocity (sPAP estimation) | <2.8 m/s | ≥2.8 m/s (↑ PAP → ↑ LVEDP) |

Grading with ≥50% parameters abnormal:

| Grade | E/A ratio | Interpretation | Filling pressures |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grade I (Impaired relaxation) | E/A <0.8 + E <50 cm/s | Impaired relaxation, normal filling pressure. <50% parameters abnormal. | Normal |
| Grade II (Pseudonormal) | E/A 0.8–2 with E ≥50 cm/s OR E/A >0.8–2 with <50% criteria OR E/A >2 | ≥50% criteria abnormal (E/e' ≥14, LAVI ≥34, TR vel ≥2.8) | Elevated |
| Grade III (Restrictive) | E/A ≥2 + DT <160 ms | Restrictive filling — all parameters show very elevated LVEDP | Markedly elevated |
| Indeterminate | E/A 0.8–2 with ≤50% and ≥50% criteria each | Cannot determine grade — insufficient agreement between parameters | Uncertain |

Tip: DT (deceleration time): Normal 160–240 ms. Grade III <160 ms (rapid LV pressure equalisation in stiff LV). Valsalva: E/A ratio ↓ ≥0.5 with Valsalva → pseudonormal converts to Grade I (unmasking).
front: Diastolic dysfunction grading — ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm: how to classify Grade I, II, and III, and when is it indeterminate?

RV dysfunction is an independent predictor of mortality in HF, PE, PAH, and post-cardiac surgery

| Parameter | Measurement | Normal | Abnormal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TAPSE (Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion) | M-mode at lateral tricuspid annulus — longitudinal RV excursion | ≥17 mm | <17 mm = RV systolic dysfunction |
| RV S' velocity (tissue Doppler) | Peak systolic velocity at lateral RV annulus by TDI | ≥9.5 cm/s | <9.5 cm/s = RV dysfunction |
| FAC (RV Fractional Area Change) | (RV end-diastolic − end-systolic area) / end-diastolic area | ≥35% | <35% = RV dysfunction |
| RV GLS (Global Longitudinal Strain) | Speckle tracking of RV free wall | ≥−20% | Less negative = ↓ RV longitudinal function |
| RIMP/MPI (Myocardial Performance Index) | (IVCT + IVRT) / ET (tissue Doppler) | <0.54 | >0.54 = global RV dysfunction |
| RV end-diastolic diameter (basal) | A4C view, basal RV | <41 mm | ≥41 mm = dilated RV |
| IVC diameter + respiratory variation | Subcostal view | <21 mm + >50% collapse = RAP 0–5 mmHg | >21 mm + <50% collapse = RAP 10–20 mmHg |

Tip: sPAP estimation: 4 × TR velocity² + RAP (estimated from IVC). Normal sPAP <35 mmHg. sPAP = 4 × 2.8² + 5 = 36 mmHg (borderline). TR velocity >2.8 m/s warrants further PH workup (add other PH signs for probability assessment).
front: TAPSE and other RV function parameters — normal values and what each measures

back:
GLS: Speckle-tracking echo measure of myocardial deformation in the longitudinal direction. Expressed as % (negative = shortening).

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Measurement | Software tracks myocardial speckles from apical views (A4C, A2C, APLAX) → calculates strain (% shortening) at each segment → averages all 17 segments → Global LV GLS |
| Normal LV GLS | −20% or more negative (e.g. −22%). Absolute value ≥20%. |
| Subclinical dysfunction threshold | GLS between −16% and −20% = subclinical LV dysfunction (EF may still be normal!) |
| Severe dysfunction | GLS > −16% (less negative) |

| Clinical application | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Cardio-oncology monitoring | GLS ↓ ≥15% relative reduction during chemotherapy = subclinical cardiotoxicity (predicts later EF decline). Detected BEFORE EF falls. Standard monitoring parameter in CARDIOTOX protocols. |
| HCM | Abnormal GLS in apical regions despite preserved EF indicates early disease |
| HFpEF | GLS often ↓ even when EF normal — reflects subclinical longitudinal dysfunction |
| Aortic stenosis | GLS ↓ in AS predicts worse outcomes post-TAVI; helps identify those needing earlier intervention |
| Post-cardiac surgery | Early GLS recovery predicts long-term LV remodelling after CABG or valve surgery |

Warning: Vendor variability: GLS values differ between echo software platforms by ~2%. Use the same vendor for serial measurements. The relative change (≥15% decline) is more reliable than absolute thresholds across vendors.
front: Global Longitudinal Strain (GLS) — what it measures, reference values, and clinical applications in cardiology

back:
Aortic stenosis echo assessment: CW Doppler across AV + LVOT pulsed wave Doppler + LVOT diameter measurement

| Parameter | Mild AS | Moderate AS | Severe AS | Very severe AS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Peak velocity (Vmax) | <3 m/s | 3–4 m/s | >4 m/s | >5 m/s |
| Mean gradient (ΔP̄) | <20 mmHg | 20–40 mmHg | ≥40 mmHg | ≥60 mmHg |
| AVA (continuity equation) | >1.5 cm² | 1.0–1.5 cm² | <1.0 cm² | <0.6 cm² |
| AVA index (cm²/m²) | >0.85 | 0.6–0.85 | <0.6 | <0.4 |
| Velocity ratio (Vmax LVOT/Vmax AV) | >0.50 | 0.25–0.50 | <0.25 | — |

Continuity equation: AVA = (LVOT area × LVOT VTI) / AV VTI = (π × [LVOT diameter/2]² × LVOT VTI) / AV VTI
Tip: Dimensionless velocity index (DVI) = LVOT Vmax / AV Vmax. Does NOT require LVOT diameter measurement (avoids the squared error of diameter). DVI <0.25 = severe AS. Useful when LVOT diameter difficult to measure accurately.
Warning: Discordant grading: If AVA <1.0 cm² but mean gradient <40 mmHg → suspect LFLG severe AS (low flow, low gradient). Check SV index, flow state (dobutamine stress echo), and CT calcium score. Do not dismiss small AVA when gradient is "not severe" — LFLG AS carries high mortality without intervention.
front: Echo assessment of aortic stenosis — key parameters, severity thresholds, and the continuity equation

back:
MR grading: Qualitative (colour Doppler) + Semi-quantitative (vena contracta, PISA) + Quantitative (EROA, RVol) — integrated approach recommended

| Parameter | Mild MR | Moderate MR | Severe MR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Colour Doppler jet | Small, narrow central jet <4 cm² | Intermediate | Large jet >10 cm² or wall-hugging jet (Coanda effect) |
| Vena contracta (VC) | <3 mm | 3–6.9 mm | ≥7 mm |
| EROA (effective regurgitant orifice area) | <0.2 cm² | 0.2–0.39 cm² | ≥0.4 cm² |
| Regurgitant volume (RVol) | <30 mL | 30–59 mL | ≥60 mL |
| Regurgitant fraction | <30% | 30–49% | ≥50% |
| Pulmonary vein flow | Normal systolic flow | ↓ Systolic flow | Systolic flow reversal (S wave reversal) |

Tip: PISA (Proximal Isovelocity Surface Area): Hemispheric shell of blood converging toward MV orifice. EROA = 2π r² × aliasing velocity / MR peak velocity. Vena contracta is the simplest and most reproducible single measure of MR severity.
Warning: Eccentric jets (wall-hugging / Coanda): Colour Doppler underestimates severity — jet appears smaller than it is because it adheres to atrial wall. Always use vena contracta and quantitative methods for eccentric jets. Severe MR missed by colour Doppler alone in eccentric jets.
front: Mitral regurgitation grading by echo — integrated approach with colour Doppler, quantitative, and supportive criteria

back:
TOE: Semi-invasive echo with 4–8 MHz probe in oesophagus → superior posterior cardiac structures (LA, LAA, mitral valve, aorta)

| Indication | Why TOE superior to TTE |
| --- | --- |
| LA/LAA thrombus (pre-cardioversion, stroke workup) | TTE sensitivity ~60%; TOE sensitivity ~95% for LAA thrombus |
| Infective endocarditis | TOE detects vegetations <5 mm; perivalvular abscess (sensitivity 87% vs 50% TTE); prosthetic valve assessment |
| Mitral valve anatomy (pre-MitraClip/PMC) | Detailed leaflet anatomy, chordae, subvalvular apparatus — inaccessible by TTE |
| Aortic dissection (haemodynamically unstable) | TOE bedside assessment; midesophageal long-axis view for ascending aorta and arch |
| Intraoperative monitoring | Real-time cardiac function during cardiac surgery, valve repair assessment, post-bypass evaluation |
| Prosthetic valve dysfunction | Acoustic shadow from prosthetic valve blocks TTE assessment of adjacent structures |
| Poor TTE windows | COPD, obesity, mechanical ventilation — TOE overcomes acoustic barriers |
| PFO / ASD assessment | Interatrial septum anatomy; bubble contrast with Valsalva to demonstrate shunting |

Warning: Contraindications to TOE: Oesophageal/gastric disease (varices, stricture, fistula, recent surgery, active GI bleed), severe cervical arthritis (limited neck flexion), uncooperative patient. Relative CI: Oesophageal dysmotility, diverticulum.
front: TOE (transoesophageal echocardiography) — indications, standard views, and what it detects that TTE misses

back:
| Feature | Exercise stress echo | Dobutamine stress echo (DSE) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preferred when | Patient can exercise adequately (≥85% MPHR) | Cannot exercise; LFLG AS assessment; viability (low-dose) |
| Stress agent | Treadmill (Bruce protocol) or bike; image post-exercise immediately | Dobutamine 5–40 mcg/kg/min + atropine if needed to reach MPHR |
| Target heart rate | ≥85% predicted maximum (220 − age) | ≥85% MPHR OR wall motion abnormality OR limiting symptoms or arrhythmia |

Positive (ischaemic) stress echo findings:

- New wall motion abnormality (hypokinesis, akinesis, dyskinesis) at stress in ≥2 adjacent segments
- Worsening of pre-existing wall motion abnormality
- Cavity dilatation at peak stress (ischaemic cardiomyopathy pattern)
- Fall in LVEF at peak stress

Viability assessment (low-dose DSE 5–10 mcg/kg/min):

- Biphasic response (↑ contractility at low-dose → worsens at high-dose) = hibernating myocardium — predicts recovery post-revascularisation
- Sustained improvement at all doses = stunned myocardium (recently ischaemic, viable)
- No improvement = scar (non-viable)

Warning: Dobutamine SE: Tachyarrhythmias (VT 1–2%), hypertension, hypotension, ischaemia. Have atropine, beta-blocker, nitrates, and defibrillator available. Stop if: WALL MOTION ABNORMALITY develops, VT/VF, fall in BP >20 mmHg, severe symptoms.
front: Stress echocardiography — dobutamine vs exercise protocols, what findings are diagnostic, and indications

| Echo sign | Specificity | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RV free wall diastolic collapse | High (94%) | RV collapses when pericardial pressure > RV diastolic pressure. First chamber affected. Seen in subcostal/PLAX views. |
| RA systolic inversion/collapse | Moderate (sensitive) | RA collapses during systole when pericardial pressure ≥ RA pressure. Duration >1/3 cardiac cycle = significant. |
| IVC plethora (↓ respiratory variation) | Moderate | Dilated IVC >21 mm + <50% inspiratory collapse → ↑ RAP (tamponade/constrictive physiology). Non-specific alone. |
| Swinging heart / pendular motion | Variable | Heart swings to-and-fro in large effusion → electrical alternans on ECG (alternating QRS axis). |
| Respiratory variation in valve flows (Doppler) | High | Mitral E velocity: >25% respiratory variation (↓ inspiration = ↓ LV filling while RV filling ↑). Tricuspid E: >40% variation. This is the Doppler equivalent of pulsus paradoxus. |
| LA collapse | High | Seen in post-surgical localised tamponade (posterior effusion compressing LA — atypical tamponade) |

Pericardiocentesis guidance: Identify the safest window (largest echo-free space closest to transducer). Subcostal most common. Parasternal for loculated. Mark entry site. Needle advancement: Aspirate continuously until fluid → check with agitated saline (bubbles confirm pericardial space, not intracardiac).

ESC/ERS 2022: PH probability on echo based on TR velocity + indirect signs → categorises probability LOW/INTERMEDIATE/HIGH

| TR velocity (m/s) | No additional PH signs | Additional PH signs present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ≤2.8 or not measurable | Low probability | Intermediate probability |
| 2.9–3.4 | Intermediate probability | High probability |
| >3.4 | High probability | High probability |

Indirect echo signs of PH (grouped A, B, C):

| Group | Signs |
| --- | --- |
| A — RV/RA morphology | RV/LV basal area ratio >1.0; flattening of IVS (D-shaped LV in short axis); RA area >18 cm²; RV outflow tract acceleration time <105 ms or mid-systolic notch |
| B — Pulmonary artery | PA diameter >25 mm; PA/Ao ratio >1.0; RVOT early systolic notch on pulsed Doppler |
| C — IVC + RA pressure | IVC >21 mm + <50% collapse → RAP ≥15 mmHg |

Tip: D-shaped LV (septal flattening): Eccentricity index >1 in systole = pressure overload (IVS bows into LV during systole). >1 in diastole = volume overload. Both in systole AND diastole = both. The D-shaped LV in systole is a hallmark of severe PAH/RV pressure overload.
front: Echo assessment of pulmonary hypertension — beyond TR velocity: indirect signs and probability classification

| Type | Agent | Indications | Findings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agitated saline (bubble study) | 10 mL saline + 1 mL air agitated × 3 → IV push | PFO/ASD detection; intrapulmonary shunt; Hepatopulmonary syndrome | Bubbles in RA → immediate <3 beats in LA = intracardiac shunt (PFO/ASD). Bubbles appear after >3 beats = intrapulmonary AVM or hepatopulmonary syndrome. |
| Ultrasound contrast agents (UCA) | Sonovue, Optison, Definity (microbubble agents — gas + lipid shell) | Suboptimal endocardial border; LV thrombus detection; non-compaction diagnosis; stress echo LV opacification; perfusion imaging | LV opacification → improved wall motion assessment. LV thrombus: appears as filling defect. LV non-compaction: deep trabeculations opacified. |

Tip: PFO vs ASD distinction: Both show early bubble passage to LA. PFO: bubbles appear on first 2–3 beats, often requires Valsalva or coughing to increase RA pressure transiently. ASD: bubbles cross without Valsalva; also shows colour Doppler left-to-right flow at interatrial septum. TOE is more sensitive for both (95% vs 50% TTE).
Warning: UCA contraindications: Known right-to-left shunt (PE from coronary arterioles described with right-to-left shunt); known hypersensitivity to agent. Relative: Unstable cardiopulmonary disease. Most UCAs are well tolerated — serious adverse events <0.01%.
front: Contrast echocardiography — agitated saline bubble study and ultrasound contrast agents: indications and findings

back:
Critical differentiation — both cause similar symptoms (dyspnoea, oedema, elevated JVP, ascites) but treatment is completely different

| Feature | Constrictive pericarditis | Restrictive cardiomyopathy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Septal bounce / ventricular interdependence | YES — IVS rapid back-and-forth motion in early diastole (pathognomonic). Marked respiratory variation in Doppler flows (>25% mitral E). | No septal bounce. Minimal respiratory variation. |
| Tissue Doppler e' (lateral and septal) | Lateral e' LESS than septal e' (annulus reversus) — lateral annulus tethered by scar. Both typically >8 cm/s. | Both lateral and septal e' markedly ↓ (<8 cm/s). Septal < lateral (normal pattern). |
| E/e' ratio | <15 (relatively preserved e' despite elevated E due to annulus reversus) | ≥15 (severely reduced e' → high E/e') |
| Pericardial thickness | ≥4 mm on CMR or CT (but normal thickness in ~20% of CP!) | Normal |
| Hepatic vein Doppler | Expiratory diastolic flow reversal (↑ intrathoracic pressure during expiration compresses heart → ↑ RV pressure → reversal) | Inspiratory diastolic flow reversal |
| Myocardial appearance | Normal myocardium | Thickened, bright (amyloid "granular sparkling"), diffuse infiltration |

Tip: Annulus reversus: In CP, the pericardial scar restrains the lateral annulus more than septal → lateral e' < septal e'. This is the OPPOSITE of normal (where lateral e' > septal e'). Finding lateral e' < septal e' strongly favours CP over RCM.
front: Constrictive pericarditis vs restrictive cardiomyopathy — echo and Doppler features that distinguish them

back:
Speckle tracking: Software tracks natural acoustic markers (speckles) frame-to-frame → quantifies myocardial deformation (strain)

| Deformation type | Measurement | Clinical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Longitudinal strain (LS) | Shortening in the long axis (base to apex) during systole. GLS = average of all 17 segments from apical views. | Subclinical LV dysfunction, cardiotoxicity monitoring, HCM, amyloidosis, HFpEF. Most widely used and validated. |
| Circumferential strain (CS) | Circumferential shortening (outer circumference decreases during systole). Measured from short-axis views. | Regional ischaemia detection; differences between endo and epicardial strain layers |
| Radial strain (RS) | Wall thickening during systole (inward radial motion). Complements circumferential but high variability. | Less clinically used; wall motion analysis |
| Twist/Torsion | Base rotates clockwise, apex counterclockwise during systole → LV twisting (like wringing a towel). Measured in short-axis views at base and apex. | Diastolic function (untwisting in early diastole drives early filling). Reduced twist in HCM, DCM. Preserved in HFpEF despite ↓ GLS. |

Tip: Amyloid pattern: GLS with characteristic "apical sparing" — apex has normal GLS while base is severely reduced. Bull's-eye map shows: dark (abnormal) base + light (preserved) apex. Sensitivity and specificity ~90% for differentiating cardiac amyloidosis from other causes of LVH when apical sparing present.
front: Speckle tracking echocardiography — four types of cardiac deformation and their clinical applications

back:
Cardiac sarcoidosis: Non-caseating granulomatous infiltration of myocardium → conduction disease, VT, and cardiomyopathy

| Clinical manifestation | Frequency | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conduction abnormalities | Most common (60%) | AV block (complete AV block in young patient = cardiac sarcoid until proven otherwise), RBBB, LBBB. Granulomas in His-Purkinje system. |
| Ventricular arrhythmia | 23% | Sustained VT from scar-mediated re-entry. High SCD risk. VT often with LBBB morphology (from RV involvement or inferior LV). |
| Cardiomyopathy | Variable | DCM or HCM-like. Regional wall motion abnormality. Can mimic myocarditis (perimyocarditis pattern). |

Diagnosis: Japanese Ministry of Health (2006) criteria or Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) criteria (2014)

| Diagnostic approach | Sensitivity |
| --- | --- |
| CMR: LGE (multifocal, non-ischaemic, basal septum + lateral wall common) | 75–100% |
| FDG-PET: Patchy uptake in active granulomatous disease | ~80% (best for active inflammation) |
| Technetium scintigraphy | Variable |
| Endomyocardial biopsy | ~30% (patchy distribution — false negative common) |
| Extra-cardiac biopsy (lymph node, lung, skin) | High — diagnose systemic sarcoidosis first |

Management: Corticosteroids (prednisone 40–60 mg/day → taper) for active myocarditis and conduction abnormalities. ICD for VT/complete AV block. PPM for complete AV block if no VT risk. Standard HF therapy.
Warning: Sarcoidosis + complete AV block in patient aged 40–60 + no other obvious cause = cardiac sarcoidosis until proven otherwise. Screen systemic sarcoidosis markers (ACE, serum calcium, CXR for hilar adenopathy, HRCT chest).
front: Cardiac sarcoidosis — diagnostic criteria, clinical manifestations, and management

back:
Giant cell myocarditis (GCM): Rare, rapidly progressive fulminant myocarditis with characteristic multinucleated giant cells on biopsy — high mortality without aggressive treatment

| Feature | GCM | Lymphocytic (viral) myocarditis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Age | Young/middle-aged adults (median 42 years) | Any age; often young adults post-viral illness |
| Onset | Rapidly progressive HF or VT | Variable; often subacute |
| LV function | Severe biventricular failure; often mechanically supported | Variable — mild to severe |
| VT | Common (>50%); refractory | Less common |
| AV block | Common | Less common |
| CMR LGE | Non-ischaemic, often extensive | Subepicardial inferolateral (viral pattern) |
| Biopsy | Required for diagnosis: Multi-nucleated giant cells + eosinophilic infiltrate + myocyte necrosis. Dallas criteria positive. | Lymphocytes + myocyte necrosis; no giant cells |
| Response to steroids | Partial — requires multi-drug immunosuppression | Often spontaneous recovery; steroids uncertain |

GCM treatment: Combined immunosuppression mandatory. Standard regimen: Cyclosporin + prednisone + azathioprine (or mycophenolate). MCS (Impella/ECMO) as bridge. 50% require MCS. 1-year mortality WITHOUT treatment ~90%. WITH treatment: ~70% 1-year survival. Heart transplant for refractory GCM — recurs in 20–25% of allografts.
front: Giant cell myocarditis — what distinguishes it from lymphocytic myocarditis, diagnosis, and treatment

back:
Fabry disease: X-linked lysosomal storage disorder. GLA gene mutation → α-galactosidase A deficiency → globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulates in cells

| Cardiac manifestation | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Cardiomyopathy (LVH) | Concentric LVH (mimics HCM). Symmetric wall thickening, often massive. LV mass ↑ progressively. Short PR interval (↓ AV conduction from Gb3 in conduction system). |
| Native T1 ↓ on CMR | Pathognomonic: Native T1 <940 ms at 1.5T (inferolateral). Only cardiomyopathy with ↓ T1 (Gb3 replaces water → ↓ T1). Later: ↑ T1 when fibrosis supervenes. |
| LGE | Mid-wall LGE in inferolateral wall — characteristic. Develops as Gb3 replaced by fibrosis. LGE presence = advanced disease; predicts arrhythmia + HF. |
| Arrhythmias | Short PR interval, SVT, AF, VT (with advanced fibrosis) |
| Angina/ACS | Coronary endothelial Gb3 accumulation → microvascular disease. Normal epicardial coronaries with TIMI reduced flow or IMR elevation. |

Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT): Agalsidase alfa (Replagal) or agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme) — IV biweekly. Replace missing enzyme → clear Gb3 from organs.

ERT effect on cardiac manifestations
↓ LV mass index (if started before LGE develops)
Prevents further fibrosis progression (partial)
Does NOT reverse established LGE/fibrosis — irreversible once present
Best cardiac outcomes: Start ERT before significant LGE (<1% LV mass LGE)

Tip: Migalastat (oral pharmacological chaperone): For patients with amenable GLA mutations — oral tablet, fewer infusion reactions. Non-inferior to ERT in certain mutations.
front: Fabry disease cardiac manifestations and treatment — what enzyme replacement therapy does and does not do

back:
Iron overload cardiomyopathy: Excess iron deposits in myocardium → reactive oxygen species → cellular damage → DCM and arrhythmias

| Feature | Hereditary haemochromatosis (HH) | Thalassaemia major |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | HFE gene mutation (C282Y/H63D) → ↑ GI iron absorption → tissue iron overload | Chronic transfusion requirement → 200 mg iron/unit pRBC → iron loading without adequate elimination → massive iron overload |
| Cardiac iron deposition | Less severe cardiac involvement than liver. Heart affected in ~15% (if untreated). | Frequent and severe. Heart failure is the leading cause of death in thalassaemia major. |
| CMR T2* (gold standard) | T2* reflects iron content. T2* <20 ms = cardiac iron overload. T2* <10 ms = severe — imminent HF risk. | Annual CMR T2* mandatory for monitoring. T2* <10 ms → intensify chelation. |

Treatment:

| Drug | Route | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Desferrioxamine (DFO) | SC infusion (8–12h) × 5–7 nights/week | Gold standard iron chelator. Burden of administration is high. Subcutaneous pump. IV for severe/acute iron overload. |
| Deferasirox (Exjade/Jadenu) | Oral once daily | Equivalent efficacy to DFO. Better QoL. Risk of renal impairment — monitor creatinine. |
| Deferiprone | Oral TID | Best cardiac penetration (most lipophilic). Used when cardiac iron overload predominates. Risk of agranulocytosis — weekly FBC. LVEF improves most with deferiprone. |
| Combination (DFO + deferiprone) | Combined | Severe cases or T2* <10 ms — combination most potent chelation |
front: Iron overload cardiomyopathy — hemochromatosis and thalassaemia major: detection, monitoring, and treatment
