back:
Chagas disease: Trypanosoma cruzi infection (vectored by triatomine "kissing bug"). Endemic Latin America; Southeast Asian immigrants from endemic areas. 6–7 million infected globally.

| Phase | Features | Cardiac involvement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acute phase (0–2 months) | Romaña sign (unilateral eyelid oedema), fever, myocarditis. Most resolve; 5–10% die from acute myocarditis/meningoencephalitis. | Acute myocarditis with T. cruzi in myocardium |
| Indeterminate phase | 20–30 years; serology positive; no cardiac/GI symptoms; normal ECG and echo. ~30% progress to cardiac form. | No symptoms; ECG/echo surveillance |
| Chronic cardiac form (~30%) | CCC (chronic Chagasic cardiomyopathy): DCM + conduction disease + VT + thromboembolic events | Posterior-apical aneurysm (LV apex — pathognomonic), AV block, RBBB+LAHB, VT |

ECG in chronic Chagas: RBBB (most common finding) + LAHB (bifascicular block in young patient from endemic area = Chagas until proved otherwise). AV block. VPBs (often LBBB morphology from LV involvement).

| Treatment | Drug | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anti-parasitic (acute + indeterminate) | Benznidazole (first-line) or nifurtimox × 60 days | Cures ~80% in acute phase; reduces seroconversion in chronic indeterminate (BENEFIT trial: benznidazole did not slow cardiac progression in established CCC) |
| HF treatment (CCC) | Standard GDMT (ACEi/BB/MRA/SGLT2i) | Same as other DCM aetiologies; ICD for VT/VF |
| Anticoagulation | Warfarin (DOACs less data) for AF or apical aneurysm | High thromboembolic risk from apical thrombus |
front: Chagas disease cardiac manifestations — mechanism, ECG features, and treatment in the chronic phase

back:
Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS): Bidirectional interaction — heart disease causing kidney dysfunction (or vice versa)

| CRS Type | Cause | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 (Acute CRS) | Acute cardiac disease → acute kidney injury | Acute decompensated HF → ↓ renal perfusion → AKI |
| Type 2 (Chronic CRS) | Chronic cardiac disease → progressive CKD | Chronic HF → ↓ renal perfusion + venous congestion → progressive CKD |
| Type 3 (Acute RCS) | Acute kidney disease → acute cardiac disease | Acute kidney injury → ↑ fluid retention → pulmonary oedema + arrhythmia |
| Type 4 (Chronic RCS) | Chronic CKD → progressive cardiac disease | CKD stage 3–5 → LVH, accelerated CAD, cardiomyopathy, sudden death |
| Type 5 (Secondary CRS) | Systemic disease → both cardiac and renal | Sepsis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, diabetes |

Tip: Management of Type 2 CRS (HF + CKD): ACEi/ARB: ↑ creatinine acceptable up to 30% — this is the haemodynamic effect, not nephrotoxicity. Continue if K⁺ <5.5. SGLT2i: renal + cardiac protection (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY). Diuretics: Furosemide dose ↑ in CKD (GFR ↓ → ↓ tubular secretion → ↓ effect). Spironolactone: caution at eGFR <30 (↑ K⁺). Phosphate binders, ESA for anaemia → secondary benefits on cardiac load.
Warning: Acute worsening of renal function (WRF) during aggressive diuresis in acute HF: Minor ↑ creatinine (≤0.3 mg/dL) = acceptable ("tolerable WRF") and does NOT predict worse outcomes if clinical decongestion achieved. Maintain decongestion — stopping diuretics for minor creatinine rise harms outcome more than helps.
front: Heart failure with CKD (cardiorenal syndrome) — types, mechanisms, and management approach

back:
LVNC (Left Ventricular Non-Compaction): Failure of myocardial compaction during fetal development → prominent trabeculations + deep intertrabecular recesses in LV

| Diagnostic criteria | Echo (Jenni 2001) | CMR (Petersen 2005) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main criterion | Non-compacted to compacted layer ratio >2:1 in end-systole. Two-layer structure: outer compacted layer (NC) + inner non-compacted layer (C). | NC/C ratio >2.3 in diastole. Or trabeculation extent ≥20% of LV myocardium. |
| Distribution | Apex, mid-lateral, mid-inferior walls. Spares basal segments. | Isolated LV NCCC vs congenital heart disease associated |
| Colour Doppler | Blood flow into deep intertrabecular recesses from LV cavity | — |

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Genetics | ~30–40% have identified mutation. TAZ (Barth syndrome — X-linked, boys), LMNA, MYH7, ACTC1, NKX2-5. Familial in ~25%. |
| Clinical presentation | HF (DCM phenotype, often with low EF), arrhythmias (VT, AF), thromboembolic events (LA/LV thrombus), sudden death. |
| Anticoagulation | Controversial. Consider if: EF <40%, AF, prior thromboembolic event, spontaneous echo contrast. Most guidelines: OAC or aspirin for EF <40% or AF. |
| ICD | Standard HF ICD criteria apply (EF ≤35% + NYHA II–III). Family history SCD may lower threshold. |

Warning: LVNC is over-diagnosed: Prominent trabeculations are common in athletes, pregnant women, and certain ethnic groups (Afro-Caribbean) as a physiological variant. The key is: prominent trabeculations + LV dysfunction + family history + genetic testing to confirm. Over-diagnosis leads to inappropriate restriction from sport and anxiety.
front: Non-compaction cardiomyopathy — diagnostic criteria, genetic associations, and management

back:
OSA prevalence: 25–30% of general adult population; 40–60% of HF patients; 50–60% of AF patients — a major treatable CV risk factor

| Cardiovascular effect | OSA mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Hypertension | Intermittent hypoxia + sympathetic surges → chronic ↑ SVR + ↓ baroreceptor sensitivity. OSA is a major cause of resistant HTN (~30% of resistant HTN have significant OSA). |
| Coronary artery disease | Repeated arousal → catecholamine surge → ↑ HR + ↑ BP + platelet activation → endothelial dysfunction + inflammation → accelerated CAD |
| Heart failure | Hypoxia → LV dysfunction. Negative intrathoracic pressure oscillations → ↑ LV transmural pressure → ↑ afterload. Cardiac CPAP trial: CPAP ↑ EF in sleep apnoea + HF. |
| Atrial fibrillation | OSA → atrial dilatation + fibrosis → AF substrate. OSA is associated with ↑ AF recurrence after cardioversion/ablation. CPAP ↓ AF recurrence post-ablation. |
| Sudden cardiac death | VT/VF during REM sleep — nocturnal SCD timing peak in OSA (opposite of general population morning peak) |

Screening: STOP-BANG score (Snoring, Tired, Observed apnoea, Blood Pressure, BMI, Age, Neck, Gender). Score ≥3 = high risk → formal sleep study (polysomnography or home oximetry/WatchPAT).
Warning: SERVE-HF trial: Adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) for central sleep apnoea + HFrEF → INCREASED mortality. ASV should NOT be used in HFrEF with EF <45% and central apnoea. CPAP for OSA remains beneficial in HF. The distinction between OSA (↓ O₂ = obstruction) and CSA (↑ CO₂ = central dysregulation) is critical — requires sleep study.
front: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) and cardiovascular disease — OSA pathophysiology, screening, and cardioprotective effects of CPAP

back:
Dynamic LVOTO may be caused by conditions other than HCM — important differential diagnosis since treatment differs

| Cause | Mechanism | Key differentiator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HCM (HOCM) | Asymmetric IVS hypertrophy + systolic anterior motion (SAM) of mitral valve → LVOTO. Dynamic — worsens with ↓ preload, ↓ afterload, ↑ inotropy. | Asymmetric IVH on echo, SAM, family history, sarcomere gene mutation, LGE on CMR |
| Takotsubo cardiomyopathy | Mid-ventricular obstruction from catecholamine surge → hypercontractile basal LV + apical akinesis → dynamic LVOTO in mid-cavity region | Acute onset post-stress, apical ballooning, basal hypercontractility, no IVS asymmetry. Levosimendan (not dobutamine) if inotrope needed. Resolves. |
| Severe hypovolaemia / underfilling | Small LV cavity + hyperdynamic function → "physiological" LVOTO in sepsis, blood loss, dehydration. SAM can develop acutely. | Context: acute illness, volume-responsive, no LVH. IV fluids → resolves gradient. |
| Post-TAVI obstruction (LVOTO from TMVR) | Transcatheter valve implantation → neo-LVOT obstruction from valve strut or anterior leaflet displacement → LVOTO. | Post-procedural context. Requires immediate intervention (LAMPOON technique if anticipated). |
| Infiltrative cardiomyopathy (amyloid) | Diffuse wall thickening → ↓ LV cavity → physiological LVOTO in advanced amyloid | Low voltage ECG, diffuse thickening, T1 mapping abnormal, no SAM typically |
| Athlete's heart | Symmetric hypertrophy + high flow → mild resting LVOTO possible at peak exercise | Regresses with detraining, no symptoms, normal E/e', no LGE, full genetic screening negative |
front: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy vs other causes of LVOTO — differential diagnosis

back:
Cardiac cachexia: Unintentional weight loss >6% of previous stable weight within 6 months (non-oedematous) in chronic HF — severe negative prognostic marker

| Pathophysiological mechanism | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Neurohormonal activation | ↑ Cortisol + ↑ TNF-α + ↑ IL-6 + ↑ angiotensin II → catabolic state → muscle breakdown. ↓ Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) → ↓ anabolic signalling. |
| Cardiac anorexia | Gut oedema (from ↑ mesenteric venous pressure) → malabsorption + anorexia. Early satiety from hepatomegaly pressing on stomach. Ascites → further gastric restriction. |
| Metabolic shift | ↑ Resting energy expenditure despite ↓ physical activity. Skeletal muscle wasting = sarcopenia. Fat catabolism. |
| GI malabsorption | Protein-losing enteropathy from elevated venous pressures → ↓ albumin → ↑ oedema → further gut congestion. |

| Management approach | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Optimise decongestion (GDMT) + reduce gut oedema | ↑ Gut perfusion → ↑ absorption |
| Nutritional support (enteral preferred) | High-protein diet; oral nutritional supplements. No evidence from RCTs but expert consensus. |
| Exercise rehabilitation (cardiac rehab) | Preserves skeletal muscle mass, ↑ metabolic efficiency. HF-ACTION subgroup: exercise ↑ lean mass. |
| Ghrelin analogues / growth hormone | Small trials — ↑ LBM + ↓ catabolism. Not yet standard of care. |
| GLP-1 RAs in obesity-HF | STEP-HFpEF: Semaglutide → ↑ lean-to-fat ratio. Concerns about sarcopenic obesity — muscle preservation important. |
front: Cardiac cachexia — definition, pathophysiology, and management in advanced heart failure

Both are pulmonary complications of liver disease — completely opposite pathophysiology and treatment

| Feature | Hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS) | Portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pathophysiology | Intrapulmonary vascular DILATATION → R→L shunt at capillary level → hypoxaemia. Endothelin + NO excess → vasodilatation of pulmonary capillaries → V/Q mismatch + diffusion impairment. | Pulmonary VASOCONSTRICTION + vascular remodelling → ↑ PVR → PAH. Portal hypertension → splanchnic vasoactive mediators bypass liver → reach pulmonary circulation → injury. |
| O₂ saturation | ↓ SpO₂ — orthodeoxia (worse sitting/standing → gravity causes more blood through dilated basal vessels) | Normal or ↓ only with severe PH |
| Platypnoea | YES — dyspnoea worsens upright (orthodeoxia + platypnoea = HPS-specific) | No characteristic positional component |
| mPAP | Normal or mildly elevated (from ↑ CO in cirrhosis) | ≥25 mmHg (PAH by definition) |
| PVR | Normal or ↓ | ↑ (>3 WU for PoPH diagnosis) |
| Bubble study (TOE) | Positive — bubbles appear >3 cardiac cycles after RA (intrapulmonary shunt). Normal: bubbles absorbed in lung. | Negative (no intrapulmonary or intracardiac shunt) |
| Treatment | Liver transplantation (reverses HPS in 85%). O₂ supplementation for symptoms. | PAH-specific drugs (ERA, PDE5i). Liver transplant considered if mPAP <35 mmHg (mPAP >50 = contraindication to transplant). |
front: Hepatopulmonary syndrome vs portopulmonary hypertension — pathophysiology and diagnosis in cirrhosis

back:
Anaemia in HF: Prevalence ~30–60%. Defined as Hb <13 g/dL (men) or <12 g/dL (women) — commonly coexists and worsens HF outcomes

| Mechanism | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Iron deficiency (most common) | Functional (↑ ferritin but ↑ hepcidin blocks iron release from stores) OR absolute (depleted stores). Present in ~50% of HF regardless of Hb level. |
| Cardiorenal anaemia syndrome | ↓ Renal EPO production (CKD) + ↑ EPO resistance (inflammation) → ↓ erythropoiesis |
| Haemodilution | ↑ Plasma volume in decompensated HF → dilutional anaemia (Hb may ↓ even without true anaemia) |
| Inflammation/cytokine-mediated | TNF-α, IL-6 → ↑ hepcidin → ↓ iron availability; direct suppression of erythropoiesis |

| Treatment | Evidence | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) | FAIR-HF, CONFIRM-HF, AFFIRM-AHF: ↑ QoL, ↑ 6MWT, ↓ HHF. ESC Class IIa. | First-line for iron-deficient HFrEF (ferritin <100 OR 100–299 with TSAT <20%) |
| ESA (erythropoietin-stimulating agents) | RED-HF trial (darbepoetin): ↑ Hb but NO ↓ MACE + ↑ thromboembolic events (↑ stroke) | NOT recommended routinely. Consider only if EPO-deficient anaemia + severe symptoms + no response to IV iron. |
| Blood transfusion | Benefit outweighed by volume load and alloimmunisation. Use only if Hb <7 g/dL OR acute haemodynamic instability. Avoid in chronic stable HF anaemia. | Last resort — acute situation only |

Tip: IV iron improves QoL and reduces HF hospitalisation even in non-anaemic iron-deficient HF patients (CONFIRM-HF, FAIR-HF). Benefit is from cellular iron deficiency correction (not just Hb), suggesting muscle/mitochondrial function improvement independent of anaemia correction.
front: Anemia in heart failure — prevalence, mechanisms, and specific treatment (IV iron vs ESA vs transfusion)

HCM genetics: Autosomal dominant in ~60% of cases. Sarcomere protein gene mutations are the most common identified cause.

| Gene | Protein | Frequency in HCM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MYH7 | β-myosin heavy chain | ~15–20% |
| MYBPC3 | Myosin-binding protein C | ~15–20% |
| TNNI3 | Troponin I | ~5% |
| TNNT2 | Troponin T | ~5% |
| TPM1 | α-tropomyosin | ~2% |
| MYL2, MYL3 | Myosin light chain | ~1–2% |
| ACTC1 | Cardiac α-actin | Rare |
| No identified mutation ("sarcomere negative" HCM) | — | ~40–50% of HCM index cases |

Family screening protocol:

- If gene mutation identified in proband: Cascade genetic testing of first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children). Genetic carrier + no phenotype = continue surveillance (echo + ECG every 1–5 years).
- If no mutation identified (sarcomere-negative): Clinical screening of first-degree relatives with echo + ECG. Cannot use genetic testing to rule out. Screen every 2–3 years during childhood; every 5 years in adulthood.
- Children of HCM patients: Screen from puberty (when phenotype can develop). Penetrance is age-dependent — some not expressed until 40–50 years.

Tip: Mimics of HCM on echo (phenocopies — must be excluded before diagnosing sarcomere-mutation HCM): Anderson-Fabry disease (X-linked, α-galactosidase A deficiency — ↓ T1 on CMR); ATTR amyloidosis (elderly, ↑ T1 on CMR, ↑ ECV); Danon disease (X-linked, LAMP2 mutation, associated with WPW); Pompe disease (lysosomal glycogen storage — associated with skeletal myopathy); Noonan syndrome (RASopathy); Friedreich's ataxia.
front: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — genetic causes, family screening, and genetic testing strategy

| Feature | Hypertensive LVH | HCM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall thickness distribution | Symmetric, concentric hypertrophy (all walls equally thickened) | Asymmetric — IVS typically thicker than posterior wall. IVS/PW ratio >1.3. |
| Degree of hypertrophy | Rarely >15 mm (unusual to see >15 mm in hypertension alone) | Often >15 mm, sometimes >30 mm (massive hypertrophy) |
| LVOT obstruction | Rare (only in severe LVH + small cavity) | Present in 70% at rest or provocation |
| SAM | Absent | Present (systolic anterior motion of mitral valve) |
| Family history | Often hypertension history | Often positive for HCM or SCD in family |
| Genetics | Negative sarcomere mutation | Positive in ~60% |
| LGE on CMR | No or minimal (strain-related at RV insertion points) | Mid-wall fibrosis, RV insertion point LGE, patchy |
| Response to BP treatment | Regression of LVH with BP control (over 6–12 months) | LVH does NOT regress with antihypertensives |
| Diastolic dysfunction | Grade I–II typical | Grade II–III typical; may be more severe |

Tip: Grey zone patients: Hypertension + wall thickness 14–15 mm + no family history + no LVOTO = genuinely difficult. Genetic testing (negative = leans toward hypertensive), detraining (regression with antihypertensives leans toward HTN), CMR (LGE absent leans toward HTN), serial imaging (no progression with BP control = HTN).
front: Hypertensive heart disease vs HCM — key distinguishing features and management differences

back:
🇮🇩 Cardiac surgery in Indonesia: Available primarily at Type C/D referral hospitals and academic medical centres. BPJS Kesehatan covers most cardiac surgical procedures through INA-CBGs (Indonesian Case Based Groups) payment system.

| Category | BPJS-covered procedures |
| --- | --- |
| Coronary revascularisation | CABG (all techniques). BPJS covers on-pump and off-pump CABG. Wait times may be extended at some centres. |
| Valve surgery | Mechanical valve replacement (mitral, aortic, tricuspid). Tissue valves (bioprosthetic). Valve repair. RHD is the most common valvular indication in Indonesia. |
| Congenital heart disease repair | ASD, VSD, ToF repair, and other CHD repairs. Paediatric cardiac surgery available at designated national centres. |
| Aortic surgery | Ascending aorta and aortic root replacement. Emergency Type A dissection — covered but limited by centre availability. |
| Cardiac transplantation | NOT currently available in Indonesia. Patients requiring transplant are referred abroad (Singapore, Malaysia, Japan) — not covered by BPJS. |

Tip: Key Indonesian surgical considerations: RHD-related surgery is far more common than in high-income countries (young patients with rheumatic MV disease). Primary TAVI and MitraClip are available at select centres but NOT universally BPJS-covered — significant cost to patient. Streptokinase remains first-line thrombolytic for ST-elevation MI where primary PCI is not accessible (pharmaco-invasive strategy is the standard model).
Warning: Emergency cardiac surgery (Type A dissection, acute mechanical MI complication): Transport time from peripheral hospitals to surgical centres is a critical limiting factor. Haemodynamically unstable patients — stabilise first, then arrange urgent transfer with ICU-level transport.
front: Cardiac surgery in Indonesia — BPJS coverage, common procedures, and unique considerations

back:
Normal aging produces predictable cardiovascular changes — distinguishing these from pathological findings is critical in elderly patients

| Parameter | Change with normal aging | Clinical implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aortic stiffness | ↑ Arterial stiffness → ↑ pulse wave velocity → ↑ SBP + ↓ DBP → widened pulse pressure. Isolated systolic HTN common. | Systolic HTN in elderly is NOT due to arteriosclerosis alone but ↑ pulse pressure from stiffness. Treat SBP target <130 mmHg in elderly if tolerated. |
| LV wall thickness | Mild ↑ (1–2 mm) in LV wall thickness and mass — "physiological" with ↑ afterload from arterial stiffness | Wall thickness >12 mm in elderly without other cause → investigate (HCM, HTN, amyloid) |
| LV filling (diastolic function) | ↑ LV stiffness → ↓ early LV relaxation → ↓ E wave → ↑ A wave → E/A ratio reversal (A > E in elderly >70 years is normal) | Grade I diastolic dysfunction (E/A <0.8) is NORMAL in elderly. Don't over-label as "diastolic dysfunction" without clinical correlation. |
| Resting heart rate | Minimal change | HR response to exercise ↓ (↓ β-receptor sensitivity) → lower MPHR. Use MPHR formula adjusted for age: 220 − age (or 208 − 0.7×age for adults). |
| SV/CO reserve | ↓ Maximum CO during exercise (↓ HR + ↓ SV reserve) | Exercise tolerance declines with age — partially trainable with exercise. VO₂ max ↓ ~1% per year from age 25. |
| Calcification | Aortic valve sclerosis (thickening without obstruction) in >50% of people >80. Mitral annular calcification (MAC) common. NOT aortic stenosis unless ↑ velocity. | Aortic sclerosis ≠ AS. Sclerosis: no significant gradient. AS: gradient ≥20 mmHg mean + symptoms. |
front: Normal aging and cardiovascular physiology — changes in cardiac structure and function with age

back:
Digoxin: The oldest cardiac drug (from foxglove plant, 1785). Not first-line for most conditions but retains specific indications where no superior alternative exists.

| Indication | Evidence level | Mechanism and dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rate control in AF + HFrEF (when BB/CCB inadequate or contraindicated) | Class IIb (ESC 2020) | ↑ Vagal tone → ↓ AV conduction → ↓ ventricular rate. Effective at rest; less effective during exercise (vagal tone ↓ with exercise). Target plasma level 0.5–0.9 ng/mL. Dose: 0.125–0.25 mg OD. |
| Symptom control in HFrEF on optimal GDMT (sinus rhythm) | Class IIb (ESC 2021) | DIG trial: ↓ HHF; neutral mortality. Useful add-on for symptom reduction when quadruple therapy incomplete or not tolerated. Target low plasma level (0.5–0.9 ng/mL). |
| Acute rate control during decompensated HF + AF | Useful in acute setting | IV digoxin 0.5 mg load → 0.25 mg q4–6h (max 1.5 mg in 24h). Effective when BB/diltiazem not tolerated in decompensated HF. |

Warning: Digoxin in 2024 — important cautions: Avoid plasma levels >1.0 ng/mL (↑ mortality confirmed in post-hoc analyses). Narrow therapeutic index — monitor closely in elderly, CKD, hypokalaemia, hypothyroidism. NOT first-line for anything. Interactions: Amiodarone and verapamil ↑ digoxin levels dramatically — halve dose when combining. Digoxin has lost much of its previous prominent role with the availability of safer and more effective treatments (ivabradine, SGLT2i, beta-blockers).
Tip: Key teaching point for PPDS exam: When asked about HFrEF treatment, list the four GDMT pillars + ivabradine + digoxin as add-on options. Don't skip digoxin entirely — it remains in guidelines for specific scenarios. Know DIG trial: neutral mortality but ↓ hospitalisations. Lower is better for plasma target.
front: Digoxin use in modern cardiology — clinical contexts where digoxin still has a role in 2024

back:
Syncope: Transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) due to global cerebral hypoperfusion — sudden onset, brief, complete recovery

| Type | Mechanism | Key features | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neurally-mediated (reflex) syncope | Abnormal cardiovascular reflex → vasodilation + bradycardia → ↓ BP → ↓ cerebral perfusion. Includes vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus syncope. | Triggered by standing, emotion, pain, Valsalva, micturition, coughing. Prodrome: nausea, diaphoresis, pallor, warmth. Lying down prevents/aborts. Younger patients typical. | ~50% |
| Orthostatic hypotension (OH) syncope | Inadequate BP rise on standing → cerebral hypoperfusion. Primary (autonomic failure) or secondary (drugs, volume depletion). | Standing up → ↓ SBP ≥20 or DBP ≥10 mmHg within 3 min. Drug-related OH most common. | ~15–20% |
| Cardiac syncope | Arrhythmia (most common) or structural (outflow obstruction, MI, tamponade). Sudden ↓ CO → ↓ cerebral perfusion. | No prodrome (sudden), during exertion (structural), palpitations before loss, ECG abnormality. Supine position does not protect. Associated with chest pain or HF symptoms. | ~10% |
| Unexplained syncope | — | ~40% remain unexplained after full workup | ~40% |

Warning: High-risk features warranting hospitalisation and urgent evaluation: Syncope during exertion, new ECG abnormality (AV block, LBBB, QTc prolongation, Brugada, ischaemia), HF or structural disease, family history SCD, syncope without prodrome, age >60 + cardiac disease.
front: Syncope classification — three main types, key distinguishing features, and the initial evaluation approach

back:
Tilt table test (TTT): Provokes neurally-mediated syncope by passive orthostatic stress. Used when non-invasive evaluation inconclusive.

| Phase | Protocol |
| --- | --- |
| Supine baseline | 5–10 min supine; ECG + continuous non-invasive BP monitoring |
| Passive phase | Head-up tilt to 60–70° for 20–45 min (Italian protocol). If negative → proceed to pharmacological provocation. |
| Drug provocation | Sublingual NTG 400 mcg spray (Westminster protocol) OR IV isoprenaline 1–3 mcg/min (some centres). Increases sensitivity. |
| Endpoint | Syncope or pre-syncope with haemodynamic changes → positive. Or completion of protocol without symptoms → negative. |

VASIS classification of positive TTT (Vasovagal International Study):

| Type | BP + HR response | Treatment implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 (Mixed) | ↓ BP (syncope) + mild ↓ HR (>40 bpm but not <40 bpm >10s) | Vasodepressor predominant — physical manoeuvres, avoid triggers |
| Type 2A (Cardioinhibitory with asystole) | Asystole >3s + BP ↓ before HR ↓ | Pacing may benefit (SPAIN trial — subcutaneous Holter-guided pacing) |
| Type 2B (Cardioinhibitory without asystole) | ↓ HR to <40 bpm for >10s but <3s asystole | Moderate — consider pacing if recurrent |
| Type 3 (Vasodepressor) | ↓ BP at syncope, HR ↓ <10% | Vasodepressor — fludrocortisone, midodrine |
front: Tilt-table testing — protocol, positive response types, and clinical interpretation

back:
| Intervention | Evidence/Detail | Class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Education and reassurance | Understanding triggers + prodrome recognition → preventive action. Fundamental first step. | Class I |
| Physical counter-pressure manoeuvres (PCMs) | Leg crossing + muscle tensing, hand grip + arm tensing at prodrome → ↑ venous return → aborts syncope. PC-Trial: ↓ syncope frequency 39%. | Class I (during prodrome) |
| Orthostatic training (tilt training) | Prolonged standing periods progressively increased (30–40 min daily) → reduces frequency. Requires motivation; dropouts high. | Class IIa |
| Increased salt and fluid intake | ↑ Plasma volume → ↑ venous return → raises syncopal threshold. 2–3 L fluid/day + additional salt (especially athletes, young patients). | Class IIa |
| Fludrocortisone | Mineralocorticoid → ↑ Na/water retention → ↑ plasma volume. 0.1–0.2 mg/day. Most useful in orthostatic/vasovagal with volume depletion. POST trial: no benefit in paediatric VVS vs placebo. | Class IIb |
| Midodrine | Alpha-1 agonist → ↑ venous/arterial tone → ↑ BP. 2.5–10 mg TID. Effective in vasodepressor predominant syncope. Avoid supine HTN (take during the day only). | Class IIa (vasodepressor type) |
| Beta-blockers | Previously thought to prevent reflex activation. MULTIPLE NEGATIVE TRIALS (PREsyncope Study, randomised controlled trials). NOT recommended. | Class III (harm) |
| Cardiac pacing | ISSUE-3 and SPAIN trials: Closed-loop stimulation pacing in documented asystolic VVS (ILR-confirmed asystole ≥3s). ↓ Syncope by ~50%. Class IIa in patients ≥40 years with ILR-confirmed asystolic VVS. | Class IIa (selected) |
front: Vasovagal syncope treatment — evidence for non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches

back:
ILR (Implantable Loop Recorder): Subcutaneous device that continuously records rhythm and stores events. Modern devices transmit wirelessly. Battery life ~3 years.

| Indication | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Unexplained recurrent syncope with high injury risk and standard evaluation negative | Class I — ILR provides rhythm correlation in 35–60% of patients over 1 year |
| High-risk syncope patients with negative comprehensive evaluation (including EP study) | Class I — identifies arrhythmic cause missed by other means |
| Suspected neurally-mediated syncope to guide pacemaker therapy (ISSUE-3 approach) | Class IIa — identifies asystolic pauses that predict pacing benefit |
| Cryptogenic stroke workup (suspected AF as source) | CRYSTAL-AF and EMBRACE trials: ILR detects AF in 30% within 3 years vs 3.7% standard monitoring. Class IIa for cryptogenic stroke — changed AF detection paradigm. |
| Palpitations of unknown aetiology | Class IIa |

Tip: ISSUE-3 trial strategy: All unexplained syncope → ILR implant → wait for documented event. If asystole ≥3s → pace. If tachyarrhythmia → ICD or ablation. If no arrhythmia → vasovagal or neurological cause likely. This "mechanism-guided therapy" is more effective than empirical treatment.
Warning: ILR does not eliminate the need for initial comprehensive evaluation. Standard evaluation: History + physical exam + lying/standing BP + 12-lead ECG + ECHO (if cardiac risk factors) → ILR if still unexplained. ILR is a DIAGNOSTIC tool — does not treat syncope itself.
front: Implantable loop recorder (ILR) — indications in syncope, when to implant, and major trials

back:
TAA = Aortic diameter exceeding 1.5× expected normal for body size, or a fixed threshold — location matters for threshold

| Aortic segment | Normal diameter | Elective surgery threshold (normal anatomy) | Modified threshold (high-risk features) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ascending aorta | ≤40 mm | ≥55 mm | ≥50 mm (bicuspid AV or connective tissue disorder) |
| Aortic root (sinus of Valsalva) | ≤40 mm | ≥55 mm | ≥45 mm (Marfan); ≥50 mm (BAV) |
| Aortic arch | ≤30 mm | ≥55 mm | Concomitant other aortic surgery |
| Descending thoracic | ≤30 mm | ≥60 mm (TEVAR) or ≥55 mm (open) | Rapid growth >10 mm/year |

Surveillance imaging: Annual CTA or MRA if aorta 45–54 mm. Every 6 months if 50–54 mm or rapid growth. Once <45 mm: every 2–5 years.

| Condition | Threshold for surgery | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marfan syndrome | ≥45 mm root/ascending (class IIa at 40–45 mm if rapid growth or FH dissection) | Intrinsic aortic wall disease — high rupture/dissection risk at lower diameters |
| BAV aortopathy | ≥50 mm (or ≥45 mm if risk factors: FH, HT, rapid growth, CoA) | BAV + aortopathy = ↑ dissection risk vs age-matched controls at any diameter |
| Loeys-Dietz syndrome | ≥42–45 mm or Z-score ≥3.0 | Very aggressive aortopathy — dissections at small diameters |

Warning: Rapid growth (>5–10 mm/year) = surgery at any diameter regardless of absolute size. Growth rate is a major independent risk factor for acute aortic events.
front: Thoracic aortic aneurysm — surveillance intervals, surgery thresholds, and Marfan vs BAV vs normal thresholds

back:
Acute aortic syndrome (AAS): Three conditions presenting with acute severe chest/back pain + aortic pathology on imaging

| Condition | Mechanism | CT appearance | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type A dissection | Intimal tear → false lumen in ascending aorta | True + false lumen in ascending aorta. Intimal flap visible. | Emergency surgery within hours |
| Type B dissection | Dissection confined to descending aorta (distal to L subclavian) | Intimal flap in descending aorta only | Uncomplicated: Medical (BB + SBP <120 mmHg). Complicated: TEVAR |
| Intramural haematoma (IMH) | Haemorrhage within aortic wall without intimal tear. Vasa vasorum rupture. | Crescent-shaped hyperattenuation in aortic wall on non-contrast CT. No intimal flap. No false lumen. | Type A IMH: Surgery (similar to Type A dissection). Type B IMH: Medical → follow. Progression to dissection/aneurysm possible. |
| Penetrating aortic ulcer (PAU) | Atherosclerotic ulceration through intima into media → pseudoaneurysm formation | Contrast-filled outpouching beyond aortic wall. Typically in descending thoracic or abdominal aorta in elderly atherosclerotic patients. | Symptomatic/enlarging PAU: TEVAR. Incidental stable: medical (BB) + surveillance. |

Tip: IMH vs dissection: IMH has NO intimal flap and NO false lumen — just wall haematoma. Both require same urgency assessment. Type A IMH = surgical emergency. Type B complicated (rapidly expanding, end-organ ischaemia, rupture) = TEVAR.
front: Acute aortic syndrome — three entities (dissection, intramural haematoma, penetrating aortic ulcer): diagnosis and management

back:
Uncomplicated Type B: Medical management (BB + BP <120 mmHg). Complicated Type B: TEVAR or surgery.

Complicated Type B features (any one = TEVAR indication)
Malperfusion syndrome: Ischaemia of kidneys, gut, limbs, spinal cord from false lumen compressing true lumen branch vessels
Rupture or impending rupture (haemothorax, haemopericardium on CT)
Rapid expansion: Aortic diameter increase >10 mm on serial imaging within days
Uncontrollable pain or hypertension despite maximal medical therapy
False lumen diameter >22 mm (predictor of late adverse events)

Medical management of uncomplicated Type B:

- IV beta-blocker first (labetalol or esmolol) → target HR <60 + SBP 100–120 mmHg
- Add IV nicardipine or SNP if SBP still >120 after BB
- Transition to oral BB + oral CCB for long-term
- Serial imaging: CT at 48h, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, then annually

Tip: INSTEAD trial: Pre-emptive TEVAR in uncomplicated Type B vs medical therapy → 2-year aortic remodelling ↑ with TEVAR. At 5 years: similar survival. Ongoing debate — TEVAR for uncomplicated Type B now Class IIb (selective use). PETTICOAT concept: TEVAR + bare metal stent in distal aorta → ↑ true lumen flow → better malperfusion outcomes.
front: Type B aortic dissection — complicated vs uncomplicated: how to distinguish and when to use TEVAR

back:
AAA: Dilatation of abdominal aorta ≥3.0 cm (or ≥1.5× normal diameter). Normal infrarenal aorta ≤2.0 cm in women, ≤2.5 cm in men.

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Prevalence | Men >65: 2–5%. Women: less common (lower prevalence but higher rupture risk per size). |
| Risk factors | Male sex, age >65, smoking (strongest modifiable RF), family history (↑ 8× with 1st-degree relative), HTN, atherosclerosis. DM is PROTECTIVE (↓ AAA via altered glycosylation). |
| Screening | UK/USPSTF: One-time ultrasound screening for men aged 65–74 who have ever smoked → ↓ AAA mortality 50%. |

| Diameter | Surveillance | Annual rupture risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <3 cm | Normal — no follow-up | <0.5% |
| 3.0–3.9 cm | Ultrasound every 2–3 years | 0.5% |
| 4.0–4.9 cm | Ultrasound every 6–12 months | 1–3% |
| 5.0–5.4 cm | Ultrasound every 3–6 months + surgical referral | 5–10% |
| ≥5.5 cm (men) / ≥5.0 cm (women) | Surgical repair recommended | 20–40%/year |
| Rapid growth >10 mm/6 months | Surgical repair regardless of size | High |

Correct: EVAR vs Open repair: EVAR-1 and DREAM trials: EVAR → ↓ 30-day mortality vs open repair (1.7% vs 4.7%). But at 8 years: no long-term mortality benefit. EVAR requires lifelong CT surveillance (endoleak risk). Open repair: more durable, fewer re-interventions, no endoleak.
front: Abdominal aortic aneurysm — epidemiology, screening, surveillance, and intervention thresholds

| Revised Ghent nosology (2010) — cardiovascular features | Score |
| --- | --- |
| Aortic root dilatation (Z-score ≥2) OR aortic dissection | Major criterion (2 points) |
| Ectopia lentis (dislocated lens upward — FBN1 mutation) | Major criterion (2 points) |
| Systemic score ≥7 (skeletal: arachnodactyly, pectus, scoliosis, arm-to-height ratio >1.05) | — |
| Mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration) | Systemic score 1 point |

Diagnosis: ≥1 major criterion + FBN1 pathogenic mutation OR ≥2 major criteria (aortic root + ectopia lentis) OR major + systemic score ≥7

| Cardiovascular management | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Beta-blockers (class I) | Slow aortic root growth rate. Atenolol or propranolol. Start at diagnosis in all Marfan patients with aortic disease. |
| Losartan (class IIa) | ARB → ↓ TGF-β signalling (Marfan pathomechanism). COMPARE trial: Losartan ≈ atenolol for rate of aortic root growth. Combination (losartan + BB) may be superior. |
| Elective root replacement | Aortic root ≥45 mm (or 40–45 mm + rapidly growing or family history of dissection at <50 mm). |
| Pregnancy | WHO Class III. High-risk: root >40 mm → discourage pregnancy. Root >45 mm → Class IV (contraindicated). C-section preferred to avoid Valsalva during labour. |

Takayasu arteritis: Large vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting the aorta and its major branches. Young women of Asian descent (including Indonesia). Mean age onset 15–25 years.

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Affected vessels | Aorta and major branches: subclavian (most common), carotid, renal, mesenteric, pulmonary arteries. Coronary ostia in ~10%. |
| Phases | Pre-occlusive: Non-specific systemic (fever, weight loss, elevated ESR/CRP). Occlusive: Claudication, carotid bruits, absent pulses, Arm BP discordance >10 mmHg. |
| ACR diagnostic criteria | Age <40 + claudication + brachial artery BP discordance >10 mmHg + subclavian/aortic bruit + CTA/MRA showing narrowing of aorta or its branches + ↑ ESR >20 mm/h. Any 3 criteria = >90% sensitivity. |
| Imaging | CTA or MRA: shows vessel wall thickening, stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm. FDG-PET: Detects active inflammation before structural changes. |

Treatment: Active inflammation: High-dose prednisone 1 mg/kg/day → taper. Steroid-sparing: Azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate. Refractory: Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6, TAKT trial: effective) or anti-TNF.
Tip: 🇮🇩 Indonesian relevance: Takayasu arteritis is more prevalent in Southeast Asia including Indonesia. Young Indonesian woman with absent radial pulse + arm BP discordance + elevated inflammatory markers = Takayasu until proved otherwise. Screen for coronary ostial disease in all Takayasu patients (renal artery involvement → renovascular HTN).
front: Takayasu arteritis — clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and cardiovascular management

TEVAR: Endovascular stent-graft deployment to exclude aortic pathology from circulation without open thoracotomy

| Indication | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Complicated Type B dissection | Class I — malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, refractory pain/HTN |
| Thoracic aortic aneurysm (descending) | ≥60 mm or symptomatic. TEVAR preferred over open repair for focal infrarenal or descending disease (Class I in suitable anatomy). |
| Penetrating aortic ulcer (symptomatic) | Class IIa |
| Uncomplicated Type B (INSTEAD trial) | Class IIb — pre-emptive TEVAR may improve remodelling |

| TEVAR complication | Prevention/Management |
| --- | --- |
| Spinal cord ischaemia (paraplegia) | Major risk (2–5%). Spinal cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure. Prevention: CSF drainage, MAP target ≥80 mmHg, staged procedure, avoid covering left subclavian without revascularisation. Treatment: ↑ MAP + CSF drainage. |
| Endoleak (Type I, II, III) | Type I/III: Re-intervention needed. Type II: Usually benign (collateral flow) — observe unless growing. Annual CT surveillance lifelong. |
| Stroke | Embolic from aortic arch manipulation. Cover left subclavian → left arm/posterior circulation ischaemia unless revascularised. |
| Device collapse / migration | Long-term structural failure — CT surveillance at 1 month, 6 months, then annually. |
front: TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair) — indications, technical principles, and complications

Giant cell arteritis (GCA): Large vessel vasculitis predominantly in adults >50 years (mean age 75). Affects temporal artery, aorta, and branches. Highest risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm.

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Aortic involvement in GCA | Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) in 18–30% of GCA over lifetime. Risk of TAA is 17× higher than general population. |
| Diagnosis | Temporal artery biopsy (gold standard). Ultrasound of temporal artery: "Halo sign" (dark hypoechoic rim). CTA/MRA showing aortic wall thickening. FDG-PET: active aortitis (↑ uptake in aortic wall). |
| Cardiovascular manifestations | TAA (ascending most common in GCA). Aortic dissection. Coronary artery GCA (rare but catastrophic). Upper extremity claudication from subclavian stenosis. |

Treatment: High-dose prednisolone 40–60 mg/day → ↓ constitutional symptoms within days. Taper slowly over 1–2 years. Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6): GIACTA trial — ↑ sustained remission + ↓ cumulative steroid dose. Class I for relapsing or steroid-resistant GCA.
Warning: TAA surveillance in all GCA patients: Annual CTA/MRA for at least 5 years after diagnosis (high TAA incidence). Surgical thresholds same as standard TAA guidelines. Repair while on steroids — high surgical risk but acceptable given aneurysm risk. Stop smoking, control BP aggressively.
front: Giant cell arteritis cardiac involvement — aortitis, thoracic aortic aneurysm, and management

Acute decompensated HF (ADHF): The first 6 hours of management are critical — the "ABCDE" of acute HF

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| A — Assess haemodynamic profile | Warm vs cold (peripheral perfusion). Wet vs dry (congestion). Forrester profile: warm+wet = most common (90%); cold+wet = cardiogenic shock; warm+dry = euvolaemic HF; cold+dry = very low CO without congestion. |
| B — Breathlessness relief | IV furosemide 40–80 mg IV (or 2× oral dose if already on diuretic). Oxygen if SpO₂ <90% (but avoid hyperoxygenation in CO₂ retainers). IV NTG for hypertensive AHF (reduces preload + ↓ ventricular filling pressures rapidly). |
| C — Circulation: Identify and treat cause | ACS? (ECG + troponin + early PCI if STEMI). New AF? (rate control). Hypertensive emergency? (↓ BP). Infection? Mechanical complication? |
| D — Decongestion monitoring | Urine output >100 mL/h = adequate diuresis. Daily weight. Renal function 48h after diuretic. Electrolyte monitoring (K⁺ and Mg²⁺). |
| E — Early GDMT + discharge planning | STRONG-HF: Start/continue/uptitrate GDMT before discharge (ACEi/ARNi + BB + MRA + SGLT2i). SOLOIST/EMPULSE: SGLT2i safe to start in hospital → ↓ 30-day readmission. Discharge planning: weight monitoring instructions, diuretic titration plan, nurse-led HF follow-up within 2 weeks. |

| Risk factor | Weight |

| CKD (eGFR <60) — most important | Primary risk factor. Risk ↑ exponentially as eGFR falls <30. |
| DM + CKD | Synergistic ↑ risk |
| Dehydration / low BP | ↓ Renal perfusion → contrast more concentrated in tubules |

LVH regression with antihypertensive therapy: LV mass can be reduced 10–15% over 12–18 months with effective BP lowering

| Antihypertensive class | LVH regression (meta-analysis ranking) |
| --- | --- |
| ARBs | 13.3% ↓ LV mass index — BEST in class for regression (LIFE trial: losartan significantly ↓ LVH vs atenolol despite similar BP lowering) |
| Calcium channel blockers | 11.5% ↓ LV mass |
| ACE inhibitors | 10.3% ↓ LV mass |
| Diuretics | 8% ↓ LV mass |
| Beta-blockers | 5.9% ↓ LV mass — least effective for LVH regression (despite effective BP lowering) |

LIFE trial (2002): Losartan vs atenolol in HTN + LVH → Similar BP reduction but: 13% ↓ MACE with losartan + 25% ↓ new-onset AF. Established LVH regression beyond BP reduction as an independent mechanism of ARB benefit.
Tip: LVH regression reduces: SCD risk, AF risk, HF development, diastolic dysfunction progression. The relationship between LVH and CV risk is steep — regression of LVH independently predicts ↓ events even after accounting for BP changes. LVH on ECG or echo = very high CV risk → very aggressive treatment target (<130/80 mmHg).

Duke Treadmill Score (DTS): Validated prognostic tool from Bruce protocol treadmill test
DTS = Exercise time (min) − (5 × max ST deviation, mm) − (4 × angina index [0=none, 1=limiting, 2=test-stopping])

| DTS score | Prognosis | 5-year mortality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ≥5 | Low risk | ~0.25%/year |
| −10 to +4 | Moderate risk | ~1.25%/year |
| ≤ −11 | High risk | ~5%/year |

High-risk findings on exercise testing (indicating severe CAD or high mortality risk):

- ↓ Exercise capacity <5 METs (very poor prognosis)
- ST depression ≥2 mm in multiple leads at low workload (<5 METs)
- ST elevation in non-Q leads (transmural ischaemia)
- Sustained VT/VF during or after exercise
- ↓ SBP >10 mmHg from rest (exertional hypotension = severe LV dysfunction)
- Failure to achieve 85% MPHR with angina = "chronotropic incompetence"

Warning: Absolute contraindications to exercise stress testing: Acute MI (<48h), unstable angina, uncontrolled HF, haemodynamically significant arrhythmia, symptomatic severe AS, acute myocarditis/pericarditis, acute aortic dissection, uncontrolled HTN (SBP >200/DBP >110). Relative CI: LBBB (cannot interpret), LMS disease, significant valve disease, severe HCM with LVOTO, physical inability to exercise.
front: Exercise testing — Duke treadmill score, contraindications to stress testing, and high-risk findings

COMPLETE Trial (NEJM 2019): Complete revascularisation vs culprit-only revascularisation in STEMI + multivessel disease

| Design | n=4,041 STEMI patients with ≥1 non-culprit coronary stenosis ≥70%. Randomised to: (1) Complete revascularisation — staged or same sitting. (2) Culprit-only PCI — non-culprit lesions deferred indefinitely. |
| --- | --- |
| Primary endpoint | CV death + new MI at median 3 years |
| Result | 22% ↓ primary endpoint in complete revascularisation group (7.8% vs 10.5%). Mainly driven by ↓ new MI. |
| Timing of non-culprit PCI | Either staged during same hospitalisation OR staged at 45-day follow-up — both equally effective. No need to do everything in one sitting (allows haemodynamic recovery). |

ESC 2022 STEMI guidelines: Complete revascularisation (staged, same hospitalisation) — Class I. Changed practice: All STEMI patients with multivessel disease should have non-culprit lesion PCI during same hospitalisation (when haemodynamically stable).
Tip: SHOCK trial exception: In cardiogenic shock, do NOT routinely stent non-culprit lesions acutely (CULPRIT-SHOCK trial: ↑ 30-day mortality + ↑ RRT with immediate multivessel PCI in cardiogenic shock). In CS: cull-prit only acutely → staged revascularisation when stabilised.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §4.4.3.1 · ESC 2023 §10.3.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §7.4.1
front: Post-STEMI complete revascularisation — COMPLETE trial: should all non-culprit lesions be treated?

Primary prevention = aspirin in people with NO established cardiovascular disease or prior CV event

| Trial | Population | Aspirin dose | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ARRIVE (2018) | Moderate CV risk (10-year ASCVD 10–20%) | 100 mg OD vs placebo | No ↓ MACE. ↑ GI bleeding 2×. Trial underpowered (lower actual event rate than expected). |
| ASCEND (2018) | DM patients without CVD | 100 mg OD vs placebo | 12% ↓ MACE (significant) BUT 29% ↑ major bleeding. Absolute benefit and harm EQUAL — net neutral effect. |
| ASPREE (2018) | Healthy elderly (≥70 years) without CVD | 100 mg OD vs placebo | No ↓ MACE. ↑ Major bleeding (38%). INCREASED all-cause mortality in aspirin group (driven by ↑ cancer — unexplained). |

Current recommendations (ESC 2021, ACC/AHA 2019):

- Aspirin in primary prevention NOT recommended for most patients — bleeding risk = CV protection
- ESC: Consider only in selected patients at very high CV risk if low bleeding risk (individual decision)
- ACC/AHA: Aspirin for primary prevention only if age 40–70 + high CV risk + low bleeding risk — discuss risks/benefits with patient
- Age ≥70: Do NOT use aspirin for primary prevention (ASPREE)
- All patients with ESTABLISHED ASCVD: Aspirin Class I (secondary prevention)

Tip: The primary/secondary prevention distinction is absolute. Never deny aspirin to someone with established MI/stroke/PAD (secondary prevention). Conversely, routine aspirin in healthy people to prevent their first MI is no longer supported — the bleeding risk has caught up with the CV benefit in the modern era of statins and BP control.
front: Aspirin primary prevention — current evidence and recommendations after ARRIVE, ASCEND, ASPREE

| ACE inhibitor cough | More frequent in East and SE Asian patients (prevalence ~30–40% vs ~10–15% in Europeans). Genetic variant in KCNK6 gene may explain | Consider ARB as first-line instead of ACEi in Asian patients with HTN + HF or nephropathy to improve adherence |
| Metabolic syndrome phenotype | Normal BMI but high visceral fat (intra-abdominal adiposity) — "metabolically obese normal weight". Lower BMI thresholds for obesity in Asians (25 kg/m² = overweight Asian vs 30 kg/m² European) | Use Asia-Pacific BMI thresholds. Metabolic syndrome is highly prevalent even at "normal" Western BMI. Lifestyle intervention targets visceral fat. |
| CYP2C19 loss-of-function | ~50% of SE Asians carry LOF allele → ↓ clopidogrel activation | Ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel in ACS for Indonesian/SE Asian patients (especially if genotyping not available — assume LOF) |

NBG (NASPE/BPEG Generic) Code: 5-letter code for pacemaker function (usually first 3 positions used clinically)

| Position | Meaning | Options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I — Chamber paced | Where pacemaker delivers pacing stimulus | A (atrium), V (ventricle), D (both/dual) |
| II — Chamber sensed | Where pacemaker detects intrinsic activity | A, V, D (dual), O (none — asynchronous) |
| III — Response to sensing | What happens when pacemaker detects intrinsic beat | I (inhibit), T (trigger), D (dual — inhibit + trigger), O (none) |
| IV — Rate modulation | Adapts rate to activity/respiration | R (rate-responsive), O (none) |
| V — Multisite pacing | Pacing at multiple sites | A, V, D, O |

| Common mode | Meaning | Use case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| VVI | Paces ventricle, senses ventricle, inhibits when native beat detected | AF with bradycardia (no atrial activity to sense). AV block with AF. |
| VVIR | VVI + rate modulation | Same as VVI but adapts HR to activity |
| DDD | Paces both chambers, senses both, inhibits/triggers appropriately | Sinus node disease + AV block. Maintains AV synchrony. |
| DDDR | DDD + rate modulation | Chronotropic incompetence + AV block |
| AAI(R) | Paces atrium only; senses atrium | Sinus node disease with normal AV conduction |
| DOO | Asynchronous dual-chamber pacing (no sensing — continuous pacing regardless) | Used during surgery to avoid electromagnetic interference pausing pacemaker |
front: Pacemaker NBG code — how to decode VVIR, DDD, DDDR, and what each letter means

back:
DDD: Paces atrium AND ventricle, senses atrium AND ventricle, inhibits pacing OR triggers atrial-tracked ventricular pacing

| Mode | Situation | ECG appearance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AS-VS (atrial sense, ventricular sense) | Native sinus rhythm with native AV conduction. No pacing needed — both chambers inhibited. | Normal sinus P waves, native QRS. No pacing spikes. |
| AS-VP (atrial tracked ventricular pacing) | Native sinus rhythm + AV block. P wave sensed → triggers ventricular pacing after programmed AV delay. | Normal P waves + paced QRS (wide, LBBB morphology from RV pacing). No atrial spike. |
| AP-VS (atrial pacing, ventricular sensing) | Sinus bradycardia with intact AV conduction. Atrial pacing rate falls below lower rate limit → pace atrium → native conduction. | Atrial pacing spike + native QRS (narrow if intact conduction). |
| AP-VP (atrial and ventricular pacing) | Both sinus bradycardia AND AV block. Both chambers need pacing. | Atrial pacing spike + AV interval + ventricular pacing spike + wide LBBB QRS. |

Tip: Rate-responsive (DDDR): Accelerometer or minute ventilation sensor detects activity → ↑ atrial pacing rate → tracks to ventricle. Prevents chronotropic incompetence in exercise. AV delay: Usually 120–200 ms. Shorter if rapid AV delay for physiological sensing. MVP (managed ventricular pacing): Algorithm promotes native conduction over RV pacing — reduces RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.
Warning: Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia (PMT): Retrograde conduction from paced ventricle → RA sensed as AS → triggers VP → retrograde again → endless loop tachycardia. Rate = upper rate limit (typically 120–130 bpm). Treatment: Apply magnet (→ DOO mode → breaks loop), extend PVARP, adjust AV delay.
front: DDD pacemaker function — the four modes of operation and their ECG appearance

back:
ICD discrimination: Two or three detection zones programmed based on heart rate — therapy escalates with faster rates

| Zone | Typical rate | Default therapy | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monitor zone (optional) | 130–150 bpm (below VT zone) | Detection only, NO therapy | Log SVT episodes for physician review |
| VT zone | 150–190 bpm (tailored) | Anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) first → low-energy cardioversion (10–15 J) → high-energy shock (35 J) | ATP terminates 90% of monomorphic VT without pain. SVT discrimination algorithms active. Longer detection time (30–40 beats) to reject SVT. |
| Fast VT / VF zone | >200 bpm | Immediate high-energy shock (35 J + escalating). ATP may be attempted for fast VT before shock. | High rate → less time for arrhythmia discrimination. Immediate defibrillation priority. |

ATP (Anti-tachycardia pacing): Series of pacing stimuli faster than the tachycardia → captures and terminates re-entry. Ramp (acceleration) vs burst (fixed). Painless. Terminates 90% of slow-moderate VT.
Warning: Inappropriate ICD shocks: Most common cause: SVT (AF or sinus tachycardia) detected as VT/VF. Also: T-wave oversensing, lead fracture (noise), electromagnetic interference. PREVENTION: Optimal programming — longer detection time, SVT discrimination algorithms (morphology, stability, onset). Inappropriate shocks ↑ mortality → aggressive programming optimisation is priority. High-rate zones (VF zone >210 bpm) reduce inappropriate therapy without increasing VT mortality (MADIT-RIT trial).
front: ICD detection zones and therapies — how to programme ATP, low-energy shocks, and high-energy shocks

| EMI source | Risk to pacemaker/ICD | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MRI | Device heating, reed switch activation, programming changes, asynchronous pacing. Previously a CI, now manageable. | MRI-conditional devices (post-2011): can have MRI at 1.5T and 3T with proper settings. "Legacy" devices: conditional MRI possible with expert supervision. Inform MRI team of device. Pre-MRI: reprogram to asynchronous mode (DOO/VOO). Non-MR-conditional leads: still carry risk — defer unless clinically essential. |
| Monopolar diathermy/electrosurgery | Sensing electrosurgery current as VF → inappropriate shock; inhibition of pacing in pacemaker-dependent patient | Use bipolar diathermy whenever possible. If monopolar needed: apply magnet over ICD (→ shocks disabled) or programme to asynchronous mode. Grounding plate far from device. |
| External defibrillation | Damage to leads if paddles/pads over device. Post-shock: device reprogramming. | Pads ≥8 cm from device. Post-defibrillation: interrogate device for appropriate function. |

Remote cardiac monitoring (RCM): Daily automatic transmission of device diagnostics to physician — does not require in-person visit

| Component | What is transmitted |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous heart rhythm | 24h rhythm analysis, AT/AF burden, VT/VF episodes, ATP deliveries, ICD shocks |
| Device diagnostics | Battery voltage, lead impedances, sensing thresholds, pacing percentage |
| Fluid index (implanted sensors) | Some devices: Thoracic impedance measurement (OptiVol/Compass) → ↓ intrathoracic impedance = ↑ fluid → early warning of decompensating HF |
| AF detection | Subclinical AF (AHRE — atrial high-rate episodes): Duration >5–6 min at >180 bpm → flag for anticoagulation assessment (ASSERT, CRYSTAL-AF data) |

Evidence for remote monitoring: IN-TIME trial: Daily remote monitoring vs standard care in ICD patients → 34% ↓ all-cause mortality at 1 year. ALTITUDE study: Remote monitoring → 50% ↓ mortality vs clinic-only follow-up.

| Actionable alert | Clinical response |
| --- | --- |
| Sustained VT/VF treated by ICD | Same-day clinical review + AAD optimisation |
| Lead impedance out of range (very high = fracture; very low = insulation failure) | Urgent device check + consider lead revision |
| New AF burden >5 min daily | Assess anticoagulation need (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) |
| OptiVol fluid alert (threshold crossed) | Adjust diuretics + consider early HHF prevention intervention |
front: Remote monitoring of cardiac devices — what it does, clinical benefit, and what alert thresholds trigger action

back:
CRT response: Defined by ≥5–10% absolute increase in LVEF + clinical improvement (NYHA class ↓) at 3–6 months after CRT implant

| Response category | Definition | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Super-responder | LVEF improvement ≥10–15% + normalisation of LVEF (>50%) + NYHA class I/II | ~20–30% |
| Responder | LVEF ↑ 5–10% + symptomatic improvement (NYHA class ↓ ≥1) | ~50–60% |
| Non-responder | No LVEF improvement + no or minimal symptomatic benefit | ~30–40% |

Predictors of CRT response: LBBB morphology (best predictor), QRS duration ≥150 ms, non-ischaemic aetiology, female sex, ischaemic CMP with viable lateral wall (LGE negative), LVEDD <75 mm, not severely dilated RV.

| CRT optimisation strategies | Details |
| --- | --- |
| AV delay optimisation | Echocardiographic (iterative method or Ritter method): optimise LV filling time (maximise A-wave before MV closure). Typical optimal AV delay 100–160 ms. |
| VV interval optimisation | LV pre-excitation (LV pace 20–40 ms before RV) often optimal. Interlead timing optimised by echo or electrogram analysis. |
| LV lead position | Posterolateral LV vein preferred (targets latest-activating wall in LBBB). Avoid apex of LV (no benefit vs RV pacing). CMR identifies optimal lead position (latest activation site). |
| Upgrade from RV-only pacing | Patients with RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy (CMP from chronic RV pacing) → upgrade to CRT → significant EF improvement expected |
front: Cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) response — what is super-response, non-response, and optimisation strategies

SGLT2i CV benefits are multifaceted — not just through glucose lowering (benefit seen in non-diabetic populations)

| Mechanism | CV effect |
| --- | --- |
| Glucosuria + natriuresis | ↓ Plasma volume → ↓ preload → ↓ filling pressures in HF (diuretic-like effect without RAAS activation) |
| NHE-1 inhibition (Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger) | ↓ Intracellular Na⁺ → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ via NCX → improved cardiomyocyte function + ↓ harmful Ca²⁺ overload. Cardioprotective independent of glucose. |
| ↑ Ketone bodies (mild ketonaemia) | Ketones are a "super fuel" for ischaemic/failing heart (more ATP per O₂ molecule than glucose). Cardiac ketone oxidation ↑ efficiency. |
| ↓ Uric acid | SGLT2i promote uricosuria → ↓ uric acid → anti-inflammatory + vasodilatory effects |
| ↓ Sympathetic activation | SGLT2i → ↓ neural adrenergic tone (possibly via ↓ renal afferent nerve activity) |
| Erythropoiesis stimulation | ↑ Haematocrit (mild) via renal EPO-stimulating effect → ↑ O₂ carrying capacity |
| Renal haemodynamics | ↓ Glomerular filtration pressure (afferent arteriole constriction via tubuloglomerular feedback) → ↓ proteinuria → renal protection → indirect CV benefit |
| Body weight ↓ | Loss of calories as glucosuria + modest diuresis → ↓ adipose → ↓ metabolic syndrome drivers |

Tip: The HEART is the organ most sensitive to NHE-1 inhibition — the direct cardioprotective effects of SGLT2i may be the primary mechanism behind HF hospitalisation reduction, rather than natriuresis alone. This explains why benefit is seen even in euglycaemic HF patients (DAPA-HF 42% non-DM cohort: same benefit).

Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DBCM): LV dysfunction in DM patients NOT explained by CAD, HTN, or other identifiable cause

| Pathological mechanism | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Intracellular lipid accumulation | Insulin resistance → ↑ free fatty acid uptake by cardiomyocytes → lipotoxicity → mitochondrial dysfunction |
| Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) | Hyperglycaemia → AGE formation on collagen → myocardial stiffness → diastolic dysfunction |
| Microvascular disease | Endothelial dysfunction in coronary microvasculature → impaired myocardial perfusion → chronic ischaemia without epicardial CAD |
| Autonomic neuropathy | Cardiac sympathetic denervation → impaired heart rate variability + reduced exercise response |
| Oxidative stress + inflammation | ↑ ROS from AGEs + ↑ mitochondrial dysfunction → apoptosis + fibrosis |

| Diagnostic features | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Early stage | Diastolic dysfunction (Grade I or II) on echo. Normal EF. ↓ e' velocity. ↑ E/e' ratio. Often preclinical. |
| Advanced stage | LV hypertrophy + further diastolic dysfunction. Some patients develop systolic dysfunction (↓ EF). HFpEF phenotype most common. |
| CMR | Diffuse ↑ T1/ECV (myocardial fibrosis). ↓ GLS (before EF ↓). Coronary microvascular dysfunction on perfusion CMR. |

Correct: SGLT2i and GLP-1RA benefit in DBCM: SGLT2i reduce diastolic dysfunction markers + ↓ HHF in DM + HFpEF. GLP-1RA improve myocardial glucose metabolism. Treatment of DBCM is primarily through optimal glycaemic control + SGLT2i + HF-specific GDMT.
front: Diabetic cardiomyopathy — pathophysiology, diagnosis, and distinction from other causes of LV dysfunction

back:
Hypoglycaemia is an independent predictor of CV events and mortality in T2DM — blood glucose <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL)

| CV mechanism of hypoglycaemia-induced harm | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Sympathetic surge | ↓ Glucose → catecholamine release → ↑ HR + ↑ BP + ↑ arrhythmia risk. AF trigger. QTc prolongation from catecholamines. |
| Platelet activation | Hypoglycaemia → ↑ thromboxane → ↑ platelet aggregation → ↑ MI/stroke risk |
| Endothelial dysfunction | Acute hypoglycaemia → ↑ oxidative stress → ↑ inflammation → acute vascular injury |
| Electrolyte shifts | Catecholamines → ↓ K⁺ (hypokalaemia) → ↑ QT → ↑ VT/VF risk (especially at night) |
| Direct cardiac ischaemia | ↑ MVO₂ from tachycardia + ↓ O₂ supply → ST depression during severe hypoglycaemia |

High-risk drugs for hypoglycaemia:

| Drug | Hypoglycaemia risk |
| --- | --- |
| Insulin (all types) | Highest risk |
| Sulfonylureas (glibenclamide, glipizide, gliclazide) | High — especially glibenclamide (longest-acting, most hypoglycaemia). Gliclazide MR: lower risk. |
| SGLT2i, GLP-1RA, DPP4i | Very low risk of hypoglycaemia when used alone (glucose-dependent action) |

Warning: In cardiac patients (especially post-MI or with arrhythmia risk): AVOID sulfonylureas — ↑ hypoglycaemia + pharmacological cardiac side effects (some sulfonylureas close cardiac KATP channels → impair ischaemic preconditioning). Prefer SGLT2i + metformin + GLP-1RA in high-CV-risk DM patients.
front: Hypoglycaemia and cardiovascular disease — mechanisms of harm and how to avoid it in cardiac patients

| Amiodarone + digoxin | Amiodarone inhibits P-gp and CYP3A4 → ↑ digoxin levels | Digoxin toxicity (bradycardia, AV block, GI symptoms). Reduce digoxin dose by 50% when adding amiodarone. |

Drug-induced long QT syndrome (DILS): Any drug that inhibits IKr (hERG K⁺ channel) → ↑ APD → ↑ QTc → EADs → torsades de pointes

| Drug category | High-risk drugs (class 1 QT risk) |
| --- | --- |
| Antiarrhythmics | Quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide, amiodarone (mild), dronedarone |
| Antibiotics | Azithromycin (Z-pack), clarithromycin, erythromycin, fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin >> ciprofloxacin) |
| Antifungals | Fluconazole, voriconazole, ketoconazole |
| Antipsychotics | Haloperidol (IV especially), ziprasidone, quetiapine, droperidol, thioridazine |
| Antiemetics | Ondansetron (IV > oral), metoclopramide, domperidone |
| Antihistamines | Terfenadine (withdrawn), astemizole (withdrawn) — old antihistamines |
| Psychiatric | Citalopram/escitalopram (dose-dependent), tricyclic antidepressants |

Risk amplifiers (make QT prolongation from drugs more dangerous): ↓ K⁺, ↓ Mg²⁺, ↓ Ca²⁺, bradycardia, female sex, LVH/HF, baseline long QTc, combining ≥2 QT-prolonging drugs, drug-drug CYP interactions (↑ drug levels)
Warning: Before prescribing a QT-prolonging drug: Check baseline ECG (QTc ≥500 ms = avoid). Check K⁺ and Mg²⁺ (correct if low). Check drug interactions. Use crediblemeds.org for risk classification. Monitor ECG at baseline + 1 week after starting. Stop immediately if QTc >500 ms or ↑ >60 ms from baseline.
front: Drug-induced QT prolongation — mechanisms, high-risk drug combinations, and screening approach

| Interaction | Effect on INR | Mechanism | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Amiodarone | ↑↑↑ INR (can double or triple) | Inhibits CYP2C9 + CYP3A4 → ↓ warfarin metabolism. Persistent for months after amiodarone stopped (long t½ 40–60 days) | Reduce warfarin 30–50%. Monitor INR weekly × 4–6 weeks. |
| Antibiotics (broad spectrum) | ↑ INR | Gut flora eradication → ↓ vitamin K production + ↓ warfarin metabolism by some antibiotics | Check INR within 3–5 days. Usually transient. |
| Metronidazole / Fluconazole | ↑↑ INR | CYP2C9 inhibition → ↑ S-warfarin (active) levels | Reduce warfarin ~40% during course; restart original dose after. |
| NSAIDs + aspirin | ↑ Bleeding risk (not INR) | Additive antiplatelet + GI mucosa damage → ↑ GI bleed risk. NSAIDs also displace warfarin from protein binding → transient ↑ free warfarin. | Avoid NSAIDs. Use paracetamol for analgesia. |
| Vitamin K-rich foods (spinach, kale, broccoli) | ↓ INR | Dietary vitamin K cofactor for clotting factors I, II, VII, IX, X → opposes warfarin effect | Counsel consistent intake — not avoidance. Change in dietary pattern affects INR more than absolute amount. |
| Rifampicin / Carbamazepine | ↓↓↓ INR | CYP induction → ↑ warfarin metabolism → ↓ anticoagulation | May need 3–5× usual warfarin dose. Monitor INR very frequently. |
| Statins (specifically fluvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin) | ↑ INR (mild) | CYP2C9 competition → mild ↑ warfarin levels | Monitor INR when starting statin. |
| Alcohol (binge drinking) | ↑↑ INR acutely | Hepatic CYP inhibition by acute alcohol → ↑ warfarin levels. Chronic alcohol → CYP induction → ↓ INR. | Consistent, moderate alcohol intake tolerable. Binge drinking → erratic INR. |
front: Warfarin drug and food interactions — top 10 interactions to know and INR management approach

FH: Autosomal dominant disorder causing severely elevated LDL from birth → premature ASCVD (coronary disease in 40s in men, 50s in women if untreated)

| Dutch Lipid Network criteria (score) | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Family history: 1st-degree relative with premature CVD (men <55y / women <60y) OR known FH | 1 |
| Personal history: premature coronary disease or peripheral artery disease | 2 |
| Physical exam: Tendon xanthomas on patient | 6 |
| DNA: Pathogenic LDL receptor / APOB / PCSK9 mutation | 8 |
| LDL-C ≥8.5 mmol/L (330 mg/dL) | 8 |
| LDL-C 6.5–8.4 mmol/L (251–329 mg/dL) | 5 |
| LDL-C 5.0–6.4 mmol/L (193–250 mg/dL) | 3 |

Dutch Score: >8 = Definite FH. 6–8 = Probable FH. 3–5 = Possible FH. Score not sensitive for PCSK9 GOF mutation (may underclassify).
Treatment targets in FH: Very high risk (ASCVD or DM or >1 major RF): LDL <55 mg/dL. High risk (no ASCVD): LDL <70 mg/dL. Typically requires: High-intensity statin + ezetimibe + PCSK9 inhibitor.
Tip: Cascade screening: When proband identified → screen ALL first-degree relatives. Reverse cascade: screen children of known FH (paediatric FH from age 2). Universal cholesterol screening at age 9–11 years detects FH early. In Indonesia: FH is underdiagnosed — any LDL >190 mg/dL deserves FH evaluation.
front: Familial hypercholesterolaemia — Dutch and Simon Broome criteria, genetic testing, and cascade screening

Lp(a): LDL-like lipoprotein with an additional apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] protein attached. Genetically determined (largely) — not responsive to diet or statin.

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Structure | LDL particle + apo(a) attached to apoB100 via disulfide bond. Apo(a) structurally similar to plasminogen → competes with plasminogen → ↓ fibrinolysis. |
| Atherogenic mechanisms | ↑ Oxidised phospholipids + ↓ fibrinolysis + direct vascular inflammation. Promotes aortic valve calcification (AS). Independent CV risk factor. |
| Normal / elevated thresholds | ESC/EAS: Lp(a) >50 mg/dL (125 nmol/L) = elevated. Highest risk: Lp(a) >180 mg/dL (450 nmol/L) ≈ lifelong risk equivalent to heterozygous FH. |
| Measurement | Once-in-lifetime measurement sufficient (genetically stable). ESC recommends measuring at least once in all adults. |
| Conditions with ↑ Lp(a) | Hypothyroidism, CKD, nephrotic syndrome (↓ clearance). ↓ With: PCSK9 inhibitors (~25% ↓), niacin (rarely used), LDL apheresis (55% ↓). |

Emerging Lp(a)-specific therapies:

| Drug | Mechanism | Reduction | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pelacarsen (AKCEA-APO(a)-LRx) | Antisense oligonucleotide targeting apo(a) mRNA | 80% ↓ Lp(a) | Phase III HORIZON trial (ongoing) |
| Olpasiran | siRNA targeting apo(a) mRNA | 90%+ ↓ Lp(a) | Phase III OCEAN(a) trial (ongoing) |
| Muvalaplin (small molecule) | Disrupts apo(a)-apoB interaction → prevents Lp(a) particle assembly | 60–80% ↓ | Phase II positive |

Triglycerides (TG): Normal <1.7 mmol/L (150 mg/dL). Mild-moderate: 1.7–5.6 mmol/L. Severe: >5.6 mmol/L. Very high (pancreatitis risk): >10 mmol/L

| TG level | Primary risk | Treatment goal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <5.6 mmol/L (moderate) | ↑ Residual CV risk, ↑ remnant cholesterol | Lifestyle + statin (reduces TG indirectly). Fibrate or omega-3 may help. |
| 5.6–10 mmol/L (severe) | ↑ Pancreatitis risk begins | Very low fat diet + fibrate or omega-3. Alcohol cessation. DM control. |
| >10 mmol/L (very severe) | High pancreatitis risk (acute pancreatitis TG-mediated) | Urgent TG lowering: NPO + insulin infusion (IV) ± plasmapheresis for acute pancreatitis. Long-term: fenofibrate + very low fat diet. |

| Drug | TG ↓ | CV outcome evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fenofibrate (fibrate) | 40–55% | ACCORD-lipid: fenofibrate + statin vs statin alone → no ↓ MACE. Fibrates do NOT reduce CV events when added to statin in unselected patients. |
| Omega-3 FA (EPA+DHA, 4g) | ~30% | STRENGTH (omega-3 CA): ↑ AF risk, no CV benefit → withdrawn. |
| Icosapentaenoic acid (EPA only, Vascepa, 4g) | ~20% | REDUCE-IT: 25% ↓ MACE in statin patients with TG 1.5–5.6 mmol/L. Significant CV benefit. Mechanism debated (some CV benefit beyond TG ↓). |

Tip: REDUCE-IT vs STRENGTH: Both tested omega-3 additions. REDUCE-IT used EPA-only (icosapentaenoic acid) vs STRENGTH used EPA+DHA. Only EPA-only showed CV benefit — DHA may blunt EPA's benefit. The mineral oil control in REDUCE-IT was controversial (mineral oil itself may have raised CV events in control group).
front: Hypertriglyceridaemia — severe vs mild-moderate, pancreatitis risk, fibrate vs omega-3 vs icosapentaenoic acid

Non-HDL cholesterol = Total cholesterol − HDL-C. Represents ALL atherogenic lipoproteins: LDL + VLDL + IDL + Lp(a) + chylomicron remnants

| Measurement | Formula | Target (ESC 2019) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-HDL-C | Total cholesterol − HDL-C | Very high risk: <85 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L). High risk: <100 mg/dL. Moderate risk: <130 mg/dL. |
| Remnant cholesterol | Total cholesterol − LDL-C − HDL-C (= non-LDL, non-HDL cholesterol) | No formal target yet; elevated (>30 mg/dL or >0.8 mmol/L) associated with ↑ CV risk independent of LDL |
| ApoB | Measured directly — reflects total number of atherogenic lipoprotein particles (each particle has one apoB) | Very high risk: <65 mg/dL. High risk: <80 mg/dL. Better than LDL for risk in DM/metabolic syndrome/hypertriglyceridaemia. |

Tip: Why non-HDL matters: LDL-C can be low but remnant particles (VLDL remnants, IDL) remain elevated — seen in DM, metabolic syndrome, hypertriglyceridaemia. These patients have high residual risk despite "normal" LDL. Non-HDL and ApoB capture this. Fasting not required for non-HDL (unlike LDL which requires 12h fast for accurate calculation).
Tip: In Indonesia/Southeast Asia: Atherogenic dyslipidaemia (↑ TG + ↓ HDL + normal LDL) is the dominant pattern — common with obesity, metabolic syndrome, DM. Treating LDL alone may miss the real risk. Non-HDL and TG measurement essential.
front: Non-HDL cholesterol and remnant cholesterol — why they matter beyond LDL, and treatment targets

back:
LDL apheresis: Extracorporeal procedure removing LDL and other atherogenic lipoproteins from blood — used when pharmacotherapy insufficient

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Blood drawn from patient → plasma separated → passed over LDL-adsorbing column (dextran sulphate or immunoadsorption) → LDL absorbed → cleaned plasma returned. Session duration ~2–4h, typically every 1–2 weeks. |
| LDL reduction per session | 60–75% per session. Average reduction over cycle: ~50–55% (LDL rebounds between sessions). |
| Also removes | Lp(a) (~55% per session), fibrinogen, CRP — anti-inflammatory + anti-thrombotic effects beyond LDL lowering. |

Indications:

| Indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Homozygous FH — usually inadequate response to maximum drug therapy (LDL receptor absent/dysfunctional → drugs don't work) | Class I — start as young as possible (from 5–7 years of age) |
| Severe heterozygous FH + ASCVD + LDL >2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) despite maximal therapy | Class IIa |
| Very high Lp(a) + progressive ASCVD despite maximal LDL-lowering | Class IIb |

Tip: Lomitapide (MTP inhibitor) and evinacumab (ANGPTL3 inhibitor): New agents specifically for HoFH. Lomitapide ↓ LDL 50% in HoFH. Evinacumab (mAb against ANGPTL3) ↓ LDL ~50% in HoFH regardless of LDL receptor genotype — effective even in null mutations. Neither available in most resource-limited settings including Indonesia.
front: LDL apheresis — indications, mechanism, and when it is used in homozygous FH and refractory cases

back:
CAST (Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial, NEJM 1989) — the most important NEGATIVE cardiovascular trial ever published

| Design | Post-MI patients + frequent PVBs (on Holter) → antiarrhythmic therapy vs placebo |
| --- | --- |
| Rationale | PVBs → VT/VF → SCD. Hypothesis: Suppress PVBs → reduce SCD. Class IC drugs (flecainide, encainide, moricizine) highly effective PVB suppressors. |
| Shocking finding | CAST stopped early: 2.5× ↑ mortality in patients taking flecainide or encainide despite ↓ PVBs. PVB suppression was HARMFUL in post-MI patients. |
| CAST II | Moricizine arm: Also ↑ mortality. Trial stopped. |

Mechanistic explanation: IC antiarrhythmics cause "proarrhythmia" — slowing of conduction in ischaemic tissue creates re-entry circuits → VT/VF. PVBs in post-MI are a MARKER of risk, not the cause. Eliminating PVBs doesn't eliminate the substrate.
Warning: Lessons from CAST — enduring prohibitions: 1. Class IC drugs (flecainide, propafenone) are CONTRAINDICATED in any structural heart disease (post-MI, LV dysfunction, HF). 2. Arrhythmia suppression is NOT equivalent to mortality reduction. 3. Surrogate endpoints (PVBs) can be misleading — always require outcomes trials. 4. "If it ain't broke, don't fix it" — asymptomatic PVBs post-MI do NOT require treatment with antiarrhythmics.
Tip: CAST was the catalyst for the evidence-based medicine revolution in cardiology and the requirement for large-scale RCTs for drug approval. Before CAST, antiarrhythmics were routinely prescribed based on mechanism and electrophysiological effect — afterwards, only survival benefit mattered.
front: CAST trial — what it showed about antiarrhythmic drugs and why it changed cardiology forever

ABI = Ankle systolic pressure / Brachial systolic pressure. Measured using handheld Doppler.

| ABI value | Interpretation | Clinical significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| >1.4 | Non-compressible vessels (calcified) | False normal — seen in DM, CKD, elderly. Use toe-brachial index (TBI) instead. TBI <0.6 = significant PAD. |
| 1.0–1.4 | Normal | No significant PAD |
| 0.9–0.99 | Borderline (low normal) | Mildly ↑ CV risk. Likely mild PAD. |
| 0.7–0.89 | Mild PAD | Intermittent claudication typical |
| 0.4–0.69 | Moderate PAD | Claudication + possible rest pain |
| <0.4 | Severe PAD / Critical limb ischaemia | Rest pain, tissue loss. High amputation risk. |

ABI as CV risk marker: ABI ≤0.9 → ↑ MACE risk comparable to known CAD. ESC 2016: PAD patients should be treated as "very high CV risk" regardless of symptoms → statin + antiplatelet mandatory.
Tip: Fontaine classification: Stage I = asymptomatic. Stage IIa = claudication >200 m. Stage IIb = claudication <200 m. Stage III = ischaemic rest pain. Stage IV = tissue loss (ulceration/gangrene). Rutherford classification (6 stages) is more widely used in vascular surgery research.

| Smoking cessation | All PAD patients | Single most important modifiable risk factor. Smoking cessation → halves disease progression rate. Counselling + nicotine replacement + pharmacotherapy (varenicline). |
| Statin therapy | All PAD patients (Class I) | High-intensity statin regardless of LDL. ↓ MACE + ↓ limb events. Atorvastatin 40–80 mg OD. |
| Antiplatelet therapy | All symptomatic PAD (Class I) | Aspirin 75–100 mg OD OR clopidogrel 75 mg OD (CAPRIE: clopidogrel slightly superior to aspirin in PAD). VOYAGER-PAD: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + aspirin → 15% ↓ MACE/limb events post-revascularisation. |
| BP control | All PAD patients with HTN | Target <130/80 mmHg. ACEi or ARB preferred (↓ vascular events). Beta-blockers NOT contraindicated in PAD (former concern about ↓ limb flow disproved). |
| Supervised exercise therapy | Claudication (Class I) | Structured supervised exercise programme × 12 weeks → ↑ walking distance >150% (superior to angioplasty alone for claudication). ACC/AHA strongly recommended before revascularisation for claudication. |
| Cilostazol | Claudication (Class IIa) | PDE3 inhibitor → ↑ cAMP → vasodilation + anti-platelet → ↑ walking distance. Dose 100 mg BD. Contraindicated in HF (↑ mortality in HF — any PDE3 inhibitor). |
| Endovascular revascularisation (PTA ± stent) | Lifestyle-limiting claudication despite maximal medical therapy + favourable anatomy; CLI; rest pain; tissue loss | Iliac lesions: best long-term results with stenting. Femoro-popliteal: PTA ± drug-coated balloon/stent. Below-knee: poor durability; reserved for CLI/limb salvage. |
| Surgical bypass | Complex anatomy, CLI, failed endovascular | Aortobifemoral bypass for aortoiliac disease. Femoro-popliteal/tibial bypass for infrainguinal. Prosthetic (PTFE) vs vein grafts (saphenous vein preferred below knee). |
front: PAD management — medical, supervised exercise, and revascularisation: which patients need which approach

back:
CLTI (previously CLI): Chronic ischaemic rest pain + tissue loss (ulcer or gangrene) = limb at immediate risk of amputation

| WIFI classification (Wound, Ischaemia, Foot Infection) | Grades 0–3 each |
| --- | --- |
| W — Wound | 0 = no ulcer/gangrene; 1 = small shallow ulcer; 2 = deep to tendon/capsule; 3 = gangrene involving forefoot or heel |
| I — Ischaemia | 0 = ABI ≥0.8; 1 = ABI 0.6–0.79; 2 = ABI 0.4–0.59; 3 = ABI <0.4 |
| FI — Foot Infection | 0 = none; 1 = mild; 2 = moderate (cellulitis + systemic signs); 3 = severe (systemic sepsis, extensive tissue involvement) |

Management priorities: Revascularisation + wound care + infection control + offloading + metabolic optimisation

| Intervention | Priority |
| --- | --- |
| Urgent revascularisation | Endovascular (below-knee angioplasty) or surgical bypass to restore inline pulsatile flow to foot. Angiosome concept: revascularise the artery supplying the ulcer bed. |
| Wound care | Debridement, off-loading (total contact cast), dressings (appropriate moisture management), hyperbaric oxygen (adjunct for non-healing wounds) |
| Infection control | Broad-spectrum antibiotics for infected wounds. Bone involvement (osteomyelitis) → probe-to-bone test + MRI + long-term antibiotics ± surgical debridement |
| Diabetes management | Tight glycaemic control (↓ infection risk, ↑ wound healing) |
| Primary amputation | If non-reconstructible anatomy, uncontrolled sepsis, or non-viable foot (dementia, non-ambulatory, severe comorbidities) |
front: Critical limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) — definition, WIFI classification, and limb salvage principles
