Carotid stenosis measurement: NASCET method (most widely used) = (1 − residual lumen / distal normal lumen) × 100%

| Stenosis degree | Duplex Doppler velocity |
| --- | --- |
| <50% | PSV <125 cm/s, EDV <40 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio <2 |
| 50–69% | PSV 125–230 cm/s, EDV 40–100 cm/s, ratio 2–4 |
| ≥70% | PSV >230 cm/s, EDV >100 cm/s, ratio >4 |

| Scenario | Recommendation | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Symptomatic ≥70% stenosis (TIA or stroke within 6 months) | CEA (Class I) within 2 weeks of event | NASCET: CEA ↓ 2-year stroke from 26% → 9% vs aspirin alone (absolute risk reduction 17%) |
| Symptomatic 50–69% | CEA (Class IIa) — benefit less than for ≥70% | NASCET: Moderate but significant benefit |
| Asymptomatic ≥70% (very fit, low surgical risk) | CEA or CAS (Class IIa) — controversial | ACST, ACAS: Small benefit of CEA in high-grade asymptomatic stenosis. Modern medical therapy (dual antiplatelet + statin) has significantly reduced stroke risk in asymptomatic stenosis — re-evaluation ongoing (CREST-2). |
| CEA vs CAS for symptomatic stenosis | CEA preferred (Class I for surgically eligible). CAS (Class IIa) if technically difficult surgery or high operative risk | CREST: CEA ↓ peri-procedural MI; CAS ↓ cranial nerve injury. Stroke rates similar. 30-day stroke + death: CAS slightly higher in elderly (>70 years). |
front: Carotid artery disease — stenosis measurement, symptomatic vs asymptomatic thresholds, and CEA vs CAS evidence

back:
Acute limb ischaemia (ALI): Sudden ↓ or cessation of limb perfusion within 14 days — vascular emergency
6 Ps of ALI: Pain · Pallor · Pulselessness · Paraesthesia · Paralysis · Polar (cold)

| Rutherford grade | Findings | Urgency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I (Viable) | No sensory/motor deficit. Audible Doppler arterial + venous signals. | Not immediately threatened. Diagnostic workup + intervention within hours to days. |
| IIa (Marginally threatened) | Minimal sensory deficit (toes). No motor deficit. Audible venous Doppler. | Threatened — urgent revascularisation within 6 hours. |
| IIb (Immediately threatened) | Rest pain + sensory + motor deficit. Audible venous Doppler barely. | EMERGENCY — revascularise immediately (within 1–2 hours) |
| III (Irreversible) | Profound sensory + paralysis + absent venous Doppler. Skin mottling. | Not salvageable — primary amputation to prevent reperfusion injury |

| Cause | Treatment preference |
| --- | --- |
| Embolism (cardiac source — AF, recent MI) | Surgical embolectomy (Fogarty catheter) — Class I for grade IIb. Rapid clot removal from proximal vessel. |
| Thrombosis in situ (PAD background) | Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) — better for in-situ thrombosis with complex anatomy. Also for recently placed bypass graft occlusion. |
| Grade IIb or III | Immediate surgical revascularisation. No time for thrombolysis (takes 12–24h to work). |
front: Acute limb ischaemia — 6 Ps, Rutherford grading, and thrombolysis vs embolectomy decision

COMPASS (NEJM 2017): Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + aspirin vs aspirin alone in 27,395 patients with stable CAD or PAD

| Endpoint | Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg + Aspirin | Aspirin alone | RRR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primary (CV death/MI/stroke) | 4.1% | 5.4% | 24% ↓ (p<0.001) |
| All-cause mortality | 3.4% | 4.1% | 18% ↓ |
| Major bleeding | 3.1% | 1.9% | ↑ (70%) — BUT ICH and fatal bleeding not significantly different |

PAD subgroup: 24% ↓ MACE + 46% ↓ MALE (major adverse limb events) including acute limb ischaemia. VOYAGER-PAD (post-revascularisation PAD): Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + aspirin → 15% ↓ MACE/MALE vs aspirin alone after peripheral revascularisation.
Correct: ESC 2017/2019: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + aspirin 100 mg OD — Class IIa recommendation for patients with stable CAD or symptomatic PAD without high bleeding risk. This "vascular dose" rivaroxaban is now standard practice in many high-risk atherosclerotic patients (ABI <0.9, multivessel CAD, post-PAD revascularisation).
Warning: Absolute contraindications to COMPASS regimen: Prior ICH, ischaemic stroke within 1 month, severe CKD (eGFR <15), active bleeding, concomitant full-dose anticoagulation. Relative CI: History of bleeding peptic ulcer, age >80 (↑ bleeding risk in elderly).
front: COMPASS trial — rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BD + aspirin in stable atherosclerosis

Duration based on provoked vs unprovoked VTE + recurrence risk + bleeding risk

| VTE type | Duration | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PE or proximal DVT — major transient risk factor (surgery, trauma, hospitalisation, immobilisation) | 3–6 months | Reversible trigger — low recurrence after anticoagulation stopped |
| PE or proximal DVT — minor transient risk factor (travel, pregnancy, minor surgery, OCP) | 3–6 months | Lower recurrence than unprovoked but higher than major trigger |
| First unprovoked proximal DVT or PE | Minimum 3–6 months; consider extended/indefinite if low bleeding risk (Class IIa) | 5–10%/year recurrence risk off anticoagulation. Males + elevated D-dimer 1 month after stopping = high recurrence → extend. |
| Second unprovoked VTE | Indefinite (Class I) | Very high recurrence risk: ~15%/year. Benefit-risk favours long-term anticoagulation unless very high bleeding risk. |
| VTE + cancer (CAT — cancer-associated thrombosis) | Indefinite or until cancer remission | DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban) preferred over LMWH now (SELECT-D, ADAM VTE). Exception: GI cancer + increased GI bleeding risk → LMWH preferred. |
| VTE + antiphospholipid syndrome | Indefinite | High recurrence risk. Warfarin preferred (DOACs show ↑ arterial thrombosis in APS triple-positive — RAPS, TRAPS trials). |

Tip: D-dimer strategy: Measure D-dimer 1 month after stopping anticoagulation for first unprovoked VTE. If normalised: may stop. If elevated: recurrence risk high → extend indefinitely (Vienna Prediction Model, HERDOO2 score).
front: VTE treatment duration — how to decide between 3 months, 6 months, and indefinite anticoagulation

HIT: Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia caused by antibodies to platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes → paradoxical THROMBOSIS (not just bleeding)

| 4T Score component | 2 points | 1 point | 0 points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thrombocytopenia severity | >50% fall OR nadir ≥20 | 30–50% fall OR nadir 10–19 | <30% fall OR nadir <10 |
| Timing of platelet fall | Days 5–10 after heparin start (or <1 day if prior heparin in last 30 days) | Consistent but not clear (days 5–10); or >10 days | <4 days without recent heparin |
| Thrombosis or other sequelae | New thrombosis, skin necrosis, anaphylaxis post-heparin bolus | Progressive thrombosis or recurrent thrombosis while on heparin | None |
| Other cause of thrombocytopenia | None apparent | Possible alternative | Definite alternative |

4T score interpretation: 0–3 = Low probability (<1%). 4–5 = Intermediate (10–35%). 6–8 = High (>35%). Confirm with serotonin release assay (SRA — gold standard) or PF4/heparin ELISA.
Warning: MANAGEMENT: STOP ALL heparin IMMEDIATELY (UFH and LMWH). Start non-heparin anticoagulant at therapeutic doses (despite low platelets — thrombotic risk overwhelms bleeding risk): Argatroban (IV DTI, renally safe) preferred if renal failure. Fondaparinux (alternative, indirect Xa inhibitor). Bivalirudin for cardiac surgery. NEVER give warfarin acutely (↑ warfarin-induced skin necrosis from early protein C/S depletion before thrombin inhibition). AVOID platelet transfusion (fuel for thrombosis). Transition to warfarin only after platelet count >150 × 10⁹/L.
front: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — 4T score, pathophysiology, and management

APS: Autoimmune prothrombotic disorder characterised by antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) + thrombosis or obstetric complications

| Sapporo/Sydney revised criteria | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical criteria (≥1 required) | Vascular thrombosis (arterial, venous, or microvascular) OR Pregnancy morbidity (≥3 early miscarriages, or ≥1 late fetal loss, or premature birth with pre-eclampsia) |
| Laboratory criteria (≥1 on ≥2 occasions, ≥12 weeks apart) | Lupus anticoagulant (LA). Anti-cardiolipin antibody (aCL) IgG/IgM titre >40 GPL/MPL. Anti-β2-glycoprotein I (anti-β2GPI) IgG/IgM >99th percentile. |

Triple-positive APS (LA + aCL + anti-β2GPI): Highest recurrence risk → indefinite anticoagulation (10–15%/year recurrence off anticoagulation)

| APS anticoagulation | Drug | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Venous thrombosis — APS | Warfarin (INR 2–3). RAPS/TRAPS/ASTRO-APS trials: DOACs ↑ thrombotic events vs warfarin in triple-positive APS. | Warfarin remains the anticoagulant of choice for APS. DOACs show significantly higher stroke/thrombosis rates in high-risk APS (triple positive). |
| Arterial thrombosis — APS | Warfarin INR 3–4 + aspirin 100 mg. Or Warfarin INR 2–3 + aspirin. | Higher target in arterial APS |
| Obstetric APS (no thrombosis) | Low-dose aspirin + LMWH prophylaxis during pregnancy | Prevention of pregnancy complications; no full anticoagulation needed for obstetric-only APS |
front: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) — diagnostic criteria, thrombotic risk, and anticoagulation management

CDT for PE: Direct infusion of thrombolytic agent into thrombus via catheter in pulmonary artery — offers reperfusion with potentially lower ICH risk than systemic thrombolysis

| CDT vs systemic thrombolysis (tPA) | CDT | Systemic tPA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dose of thrombolytic | Much lower (e.g. tPA 0.5 mg/h × 12–24h = 12–24 mg total) | 100 mg over 2h (standard dose) |
| ICH risk | Lower (~1%) than systemic | ~2–3% ICH rate |
| Efficacy (RV improvement) | Good — ULTIMA trial: Ultrasound-assisted CDT (EKOS) → RV/LV ratio ↓ significantly at 24h | More rapid restoration of flow for massive PE |
| Bleeding (non-ICH) | Access site haematoma more common (large catheter needed) | Lower access site bleeding |

SEATTLE II trial: Ultrasound-accelerated CDT (EKOS) in intermediate-high risk PE → ↓ RV/LV ratio + ↓ sPAP at 48h. Safe — major bleeding in only 10%.

| Indication | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Intermediate-high risk PE (RV dysfunction + ↑ troponin) failing anticoagulation alone | Class IIa — CDT as step-up therapy before considering systemic thrombolysis |
| High-risk PE with relative CI to systemic thrombolysis | CDT as alternative when prior stroke/recent surgery creates risk for systemic tPA |
| High-risk PE with haemodynamic instability | Systemic tPA is still first-line (faster); CDT for failed systemic thrombolysis |
front: Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) for PE — when to use, ULTIMA and SEATTLE II data

Cancer-associated thrombosis: VTE in patients with active cancer. High recurrence risk (3× general population) AND high bleeding risk

| Trial | Comparison | Results |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLOT (2003) | Dalteparin (LMWH) vs warfarin for 6 months in cancer VTE | 52% ↓ recurrent VTE with dalteparin vs warfarin. Established LMWH as first-line for 10+ years. |
| SELECT-D (2018) | Rivaroxaban vs dalteparin in cancer VTE (n=406) | 4% vs 11% recurrent VTE (rivaroxaban better). BUT: 6% vs 4% major bleeding. ↑ GI bleeding with rivaroxaban (especially colorectal/gastric cancer). |
| ADAM VTE (2020) | Apixaban vs dalteparin in cancer VTE | 3.4% vs 14.1% recurrent VTE (apixaban dramatically better). No significant ↑ major bleeding with apixaban. Better GI safety vs rivaroxaban (less GI mucosa drug concentration). |
| CARAVAGGIO (2020) | Apixaban vs dalteparin (large n=1,170) | Apixaban non-inferior to dalteparin for efficacy + similar major bleeding. Confirmed apixaban as DOAC of choice. |

ESC/ISTH 2022 recommendation: DOACs preferred over LMWH for CAT (Class I) EXCEPT: GI malignancy at ↑ bleeding risk (upper GI cancer, colorectal cancer) → LMWH preferred to avoid GI bleeding. Also: GU cancer, urinary tract tumours → LMWH preferred.
Tip: Apixaban > rivaroxaban for CAT due to lower drug concentration in GI lumen → lower GI bleeding risk. Both superior to LMWH in most cancers for VTE recurrence reduction.
front: Cancer-associated thrombosis (CAT) — DOAC vs LMWH, SELECT-D, ADAM-VTE, and special situations

back:
Most thrombophilias do NOT change management decisions — testing is often unhelpful and may cause anxiety. Test only when results will CHANGE management.

| Test results that change management | Impact |
| --- | --- |
| Antiphospholipid syndrome (LA, aCL, anti-β2GPI) | Indefinite anticoagulation; DOACs avoided (warfarin preferred); obstetric APS requires different management |
| Antithrombin III deficiency | Inherited thrombophilia; heparin may be less effective (↓ AT-III → ↓ UFH/LMWH activity); consider genetic counselling |

| Test results that rarely change management | Comment |
| --- | --- |
| Factor V Leiden mutation | Heterozygous: mild ↑ VTE risk; duration extension rarely warranted. Homozygous: significant — may influence duration. |
| Prothrombin G20210A | Similar to FVL — mild increase |
| Protein C/S deficiency | Family members need screening; duration decision similar to unprovoked VTE |
| MTHFR mutation | Not a thrombophilia risk factor — no management change. Do NOT test for MTHFR. |

Warning: TIMING of testing: Acute VTE on anticoagulation → FALSE results: Warfarin ↓ Protein C/S; Heparin ↓ AT-III levels; DOACs affect LA assays. Test ≥3 months AFTER stopping anticoagulation for most inherited thrombophilias. APS antibodies: test during acute event is acceptable (but retest at 12 weeks to confirm persistence). Pregnancy affects Protein S — test after delivery and off OAC.
front: Thrombophilia testing — when to screen, what to test, and which findings change management

DTB (Door-to-Balloon): ≤90 min from first medical contact. First medical contact to device: ≤120 min.

| Component | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Antiplatelet loading | Aspirin 300 mg PO (or 500 mg IV if needed) PLUS P2Y12: Ticagrelor 180 mg (preferred in SE Asia — CYP2C19 LOF 50% prevalence). Or Clopidogrel 600 mg. Or Prasugrel 60 mg (CI: prior stroke/TIA, age ≥75, weight <60 kg). |
| Anticoagulation during PCI | UFH 70–100 units/kg IV (target ACT 250–350s). OR Bivalirudin 0.75 mg/kg bolus → 1.75 mg/kg/h (preferred if HIT risk or high bleeding risk). Do NOT use fondaparinux alone (catheter-related thrombosis risk). |
| Infarct artery strategy | Open culprit artery FIRST. Staged non-culprit PCI during same hospitalisation (COMPLETE trial: Class I). DES preferred (↓ restenosis). DAPT 12 months post-STEMI. |
| Access site | Radial preferred (MATRIX trial: ↓ bleeding + ↓ MACE vs femoral). |
| GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors | Class IIb — consider for large thrombus burden or no-reflow. Not routinely needed with ticagrelor loading. |

Warning: Failed fibrinolysis (ST elevation >50% at 90 min): Rescue PCI immediately. REACT trial: Rescue PCI superior to repeat lysis or conservative management. Never repeat streptokinase (antigenicity).

Ref: PERKI 2024 §3.2.1 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §5.1, §5.2.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §5.2.1

Mechanical complications: Days 3–7 post-MI (myocardial softening + necrosis). High mortality without urgent surgery.

| Complication | Clinical clue | Echo finding | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acute VSD | New harsh pansystolic murmur at LLSB + haemodynamic collapse + step-up in O₂ saturation at RV (right heart cath) | Colour Doppler: LR jet through septum | IABP (↓ afterload → ↓ LR shunt). Vasodilators (NTG). Emergency surgical closure (or transcatheter device as bridge). Anterior MI → apical VSD. Inferior MI → posterior VSD (worse prognosis). |
| Papillary muscle rupture (acute severe MR) | New systolic murmur (may be soft!) + flash pulmonary oedema. Posterior PM most vulnerable (single blood supply from PDA). | Flail MV leaflet + severe MR + giant V waves on PCWP trace | IABP + IV NTG/SNP (↓ afterload → ↓ MR fraction). Urgent MV repair/replacement. MitraClip as bridge in extreme surgical risk. |
| Free wall rupture | Sudden haemodynamic collapse + PEA post-MI | Pericardial blood/tamponade + haemopericardium | Immediate pericardiocentesis (temporary bridge). Emergency cardiac surgery. Mortality >90% without surgery. |

Warning: Free wall rupture + acute tamponade in post-MI setting: DO NOT hesitate — call cardiac surgery IMMEDIATELY. Pericardiocentesis buys minutes only. Unlike isolated pericardial effusion from pericarditis, free wall rupture has continued bleeding into pericardium — drainage alone is not curative.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §3.6.3 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §12.2.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §9.1

🇮🇩 Pharmaco-invasive strategy: Standard of care in Indonesia where primary PCI not available within 120 min of first medical contact

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Diagnosis | STEMI criteria met (≥2 leads with ST elevation meeting criteria) + time from symptom onset <12h + no CI to fibrinolysis |
| 2. Antiplatelet loading | Aspirin 300 mg PO + Clopidogrel 300 mg PO (ticagrelor NOT used with streptokinase — limited data + ↑ bleeding). Note: Clopidogrel 300 mg for age ≤75y; 75 mg if >75y. |
| 3. Anticoagulation | UFH: 4,000–5,000 units IV bolus → 1,000 units/h infusion (target APTT 50–70s). Or enoxaparin: 30 mg IV bolus → 1 mg/kg SC q12h (age <75). 0.75 mg/kg SC q12h if age ≥75. |
| 4. Streptokinase infusion | 1.5 million units IV over 60 min in 100 mL normal saline. Allergic pre-medication: hydrocortisone 200 mg IV. |
| 5. Assess reperfusion at 90 min | ST resolution ≥50% + chest pain relief + reperfusion arrhythmia (AIVR) = successful. If NOT: rescue PCI immediately (REACT trial). |
| 6. Transfer for angiography | Even if reperfusion successful: Transfer to PCI centre for routine angiography 2–24h post-fibrinolysis (ESC 2023) (pharmaco-invasive strategy). STREAM trial confirms non-inferiority to primary PCI. |

Warning: Streptokinase absolute CI: ICH any time. Ischaemic stroke <6 months. Structural CNS lesion. Active internal bleeding. Suspected aortic dissection. Significant head/facial trauma <3 months. Streptokinase: Only give ONCE in a lifetime (antibodies form → anaphylaxis on re-exposure). Document in patient records.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §3.2.2 · PNPK 2026 Bab III.C.2.b · ESC 2023 §5.3 · ACC/AHA 2025 §5.3

GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors (GPI): Block the final common pathway of platelet aggregation (fibrinogen bridge between activated platelets). Reserved for high-risk PCI scenarios.

| Drug | Mechanism | Half-life | Reversal | Best use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tirofiban | Small molecule non-peptide | 2h | Platelet function recovers in 4–8h after stopping | NSTEMI: PRISM-PLUS trial. ACS patients not yet catheterised ("upstream"). PCI with large thrombus burden. |
| Eptifibatide | Cyclic peptide (KGD sequence) | 2.5h | Platelet function recovers in 4–6h | Similar to tirofiban. ESPRIT/IMPACT II trials. |
| Abciximab | Monoclonal antibody fragment (c7E3 Fab) | 10–30 min plasma; platelet-bound 24–48h | Platelet transfusion needed for rapid reversal (platelet-bound → long duration) | Primary PCI with large thrombus. No longer recommended for NSTEMI "upstream" (EARLY-ACS: no benefit, ↑ bleeding). |

Current ESC 2023 recommendations:

- GPI NOT recommended routinely in ACS managed with DAPT + anticoagulation
- GPI Class IIb: Bailout during PCI (massive thrombus, no-reflow, acute vessel closure despite DAPT)
- GPI NOT recommended "upstream" before angiography in NSTEMI (EARLY-ACS, ACUITY: ↑ bleeding without ↓ MACE)
- When GPI needed: Prefer tirofiban or eptifibatide (reversible) over abciximab (prolonged platelet inhibition)

Warning: GPI + bivalirudin: ISAR-REACT 4: No benefit of GPI + bivalirudin vs GPI + UFH. Use UFH with GPI if GPI selected. Major bleeding risk ↑ significantly with GPI — weigh carefully.

Ref: ESC 2023 §6.1.3 · ACC/AHA 2025 §4.3.4

back:
No-reflow: TIMI flow 0–1 in infarct artery after successful mechanical recanalisation, without dissection or spasm. Caused by microvascular obstruction (MVO).

| Mechanism | Contributing factor |
| --- | --- |
| Distal embolisation | Thrombus/plaque debris displaced distally during PCI → microvascular plugging |
| Ischaemia-reperfusion injury | Free radical burst + Ca²⁺ overload + mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening at reperfusion |
| Microvascular vasospasm | Catecholamine surge + endothelial dysfunction → arteriolar constriction |
| Neutrophil plugging | Activated neutrophils plug capillaries at reperfusion |

Treatment (intracoronary drugs are primary):

| Drug | Dose (intracoronary) | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adenosine | 24–48 mcg IC bolus (repeat × 2–3) | ↓ Reperfusion injury (INOS trial: IC adenosine ↓ MVO on CMR). Vasodilation + anti-inflammatory. |
| Sodium nitroprusside | 100–200 mcg IC (carefully — ↓ BP) | NO donor → powerful coronary vasodilation → ↑ microvascular flow |
| Verapamil | 100–200 mcg IC | CCB → coronary arteriolar vasodilation + ↓ vasospasm |
| Nicardipine | 200 mcg IC | DHP CCB → ↓ microvascular vasospasm. Faster than verapamil. |
| GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor | Abciximab or tirofiban IC | Dissolve platelet-rich thrombus in microvasculature |

Tip: Prevention of no-reflow: Thrombus aspiration (selective use — TASTE trial: no routine benefit in STEMI but useful for massive thrombus burden). Direct stenting (skip pre-dilation to avoid embolisation). Avoid excess wire manipulation. Embolic protection devices (distal protection) for saphenous vein graft PCI.

Ref: ESC 2023 §9.1.5

| Score | Components | Use |

| TIMI Risk Score (0–7 for NSTEMI/UA) | Age ≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, known CAD (stenosis ≥50%), ST deviation ≥0.5 mm, ≥2 angina events in 24h, aspirin use within 7 days, ↑ cardiac markers. 1 point each. | TIMI ≥3 → ↑ benefit from early invasive strategy. TIMI 0–1: Low risk. Quick, simple, widely used. |

Calculated by nomogram or online calculator. | Best validated for predicting in-hospital and 6-month mortality. ESC 2020: GRACE >140 = high risk → early invasive (<24h). GRACE 109–140 = intermediate → ≤72h. GRACE <109 = low → selective. Superior to TIMI for risk stratification. |

DOSE trial: High-dose furosemide (2.5× oral daily dose) → more fluid loss + symptom relief vs low-dose. Continuous infusion vs bolus: equal efficacy.

| Parameter | Target / Action |
| --- | --- |
| Starting IV dose | Furosemide-naive: 40–80 mg IV bolus. On oral furosemide: Give 2–2.5× daily oral dose as IV (e.g., 40 mg OD PO → 80–100 mg IV bolus). |
| Adequate response definition | Urine output >100–150 mL/h in first 6h. Weight loss 0.5–1.0 kg/day. Spot urine Na⁺ at 2h: >50 mEq/L = responding; <50 = poor response → increase dose. |
| K⁺/Mg²⁺ replacement | Replace K⁺ to ≥4.0 mEq/L and Mg²⁺ to ≥0.9 mEq/L. Check every 12–24h during IV diuresis. |
| Renal function monitoring | Creatinine every 24–48h. Mild ↑ creatinine (<0.5 mg/dL) = tolerable — do NOT stop diuretics for mild AKI if decongestion needed. |
| Diuretic resistance (spot UNa <50 at 2h) | Double dose → if still inadequate → add metolazone 2.5–10 mg PO 30 min before furosemide (sequential nephron blockade) |

Warning: Diuretic resistance cascade: (1) ↑ IV furosemide dose → (2) Switch to continuous infusion → (3) Add metolazone → (4) Bumetanide or torsemide → (5) Albumin + furosemide (if hypoalbuminaemia) → (6) Ultrafiltration only if truly refractory (CARRESS-HF: UF not superior to step-up pharmacotherapy).

NIV in acute HF: ↓ Work of breathing + ↑ alveolar recruitment + ↓ preload + ↓ afterload. 3CPO trial: CPAP/BiPAP → ↓ dyspnoea + ↓ intubation (no mortality difference vs O₂).

| Mode | Setting | Best for |

| CPAP | PEEP 5–10 cmH₂O titrated to SpO₂. FiO₂ adjusted separately. | Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (most effective for pure volume overload). Simpler device. First choice for APO. |
| BiPAP | IPAP 12–18 cmH₂O, EPAP 4–8 cmH₂O. FiO₂ adjusted. | APO + COPD overlap (hypercapnia). Severe respiratory muscle fatigue. Better ventilatory support. |

Tip: NIV initiation: Semi-recumbent 45°. Start CPAP 5 cmH₂O → titrate. Reassess at 30 min: if SpO₂ improving + RR ↓ + mental status ↑ → continue. If no improvement in 30–60 min → intubate. Combine with IV NTG + IV furosemide for synergistic effect in hypertensive APO.

Tolvaptan: Selective oral V2 receptor antagonist (vasopressin antagonist) → free water excretion (aquaresis) WITHOUT Na⁺ loss → ↑ serum Na⁺ + ↓ congestion

| Comparison | Furosemide (loop diuretic) | Tolvaptan (vaptan) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Urine composition | Hypertonic (Na⁺-rich) → can worsen hyponatraemia | Hypotonic (dilute, Na⁺-poor) → ↑ serum Na⁺ |
| Electrolyte effect | K⁺ + Mg²⁺ loss | No electrolyte loss (pure water removal) |
| Best use | Volume overload with normal Na⁺ | Volume overload + hyponatraemia (Na⁺ <130 mEq/L) |

EVEREST trial: Tolvaptan in ADHF × 60 days. Short-term: ↓ dyspnoea, ↑ weight loss, ↑ serum Na⁺. Long-term: NO ↓ mortality or HHF. Tolvaptan approved for short-term symptomatic relief in ADHF + significant hyponatraemia (Na⁺ <125 or symptomatic 125–135 mEq/L).

| Practical protocol | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Dose | 15 mg OD PO → uptitrate to 30 or 60 mg if needed |
| Critical monitoring | Serum Na⁺ at 4–8h after first dose. Target Na⁺ rise ≤10–12 mEq/L per 24h (avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome — too-rapid correction). Stop immediately if Na⁺ rises too fast. |
| Contraindications | Anuria. Volume depletion. Hypernatraemia. Need for very rapid Na⁺ correction (give hypertonic saline instead for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with neurological compromise). Hepatic impairment (↑ drug levels). |

CRITICAL RULE: When in doubt → TREAT AS VT. Verapamil given to VT = cardiovascular collapse and death.
Brugada algorithm (stepwise — stop at first positive criterion → VT):

| Step | Criterion | If YES |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | No RS complex in ALL precordial leads? | VT (100% specific) |
| 2 | R-to-S nadir >100 ms in any precordial RS complex? | VT |
| 3 | AV dissociation present? | VT (pathognomonic — visible in only 25% of VT) |
| 4 | Morphology criteria in V1 + V6 don't fit typical BBB pattern? | VT |
| All NO | — | SVT with aberrancy (but treat as VT if uncertain) |

Additional VT clues: Concordance (all precordial same polarity). Fusion or capture beats. QRS >160 ms without typical BBB. New axis deviation vs sinus ECG.

| Haemodynamic status | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Unstable VT (any) | Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion 100–200 J. Sedate if conscious. Then AAD to prevent recurrence. |
| Stable VT | IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min → 1 mg/min × 6h → 0.5 mg/min × 18h. Or IV lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg bolus → 1–4 mg/min. Or IV procainamide (avoid if ↓ EF). Elective cardioversion if drugs fail. |

VT storm: ≥3 sustained VT episodes in 24h requiring termination. 30-day mortality 30–50%. Emergency management:

| Step | Intervention | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Deep sedation (propofol 1–2 mg/kg or midazolam + opioid) | ↓ Sympathetic tone → breaks the storm. General anaesthesia for severe agitation or instability. |
| 2 | Correct reversible triggers: K⁺ >4.5, Mg²⁺ >0.9, pH, hypoxia, ischaemia | These lower VT threshold |
| 3 | IV amiodarone: 150 mg over 10 min → 1 mg/min × 6h → 0.5 mg/min × 18h | First-line AAD. Reduces VT recurrence. |
| 4 | IV beta-blocker: Metoprolol 5 mg q5min × 3 OR esmolol infusion 50–300 mcg/kg/min | ↓ Sympathetic drive — HIGHLY effective for sympathetically-driven storm. Combine with amiodarone. |
| 5 | IV lidocaine (if ischaemic VT): 1–1.5 mg/kg bolus → 1–4 mg/min | Na channel block more effective in ischaemic substrate |
| 6 | Left stellate ganglion block (SGB) | ↓ Cardiac sympathetic innervation → breaks refractory storm when pharmacology fails |
| 7 | Urgent catheter ablation (same admission) | VANISH trial: Ablation > AAD escalation for VT recurrence. Ablate identifiable re-entry circuit → ↓ VT burden >60%. |

Warning: ICD storm perpetuation: Repeated shocks → ↑ sympathetic activation → more VT. Programme ATP aggressively; consider external defibrillator to override ICD shocking during pharmacological management of storm.

TdP = QT prolongation (acquired or congenital) + pause → EAD → R-on-T → polymorphic VT with "twisting" QRS axis. Mechanism is OPPOSITE to ischaemic polymorphic VT.
Step-by-step TdP management:

| Step | Action | Dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | STOP offending drug IMMEDIATELY | Remove QT-prolonging drug (sotalol, quinidine, azithromycin, haloperidol, etc.) |
| 2 | IV MgSO₄ (even if Mg²⁺ normal) | 2 g (8 mmol) IV over 2 min → repeat if needed → 1 g/h infusion × 24h. Magnesium stabilises membrane and suppresses EADs. |
| 3 | Potassium replacement | Target K⁺ ≥4.5–5.0 mEq/L. IV K⁺ 20–40 mEq/h with continuous ECG monitoring. |
| 4 | Overdrive pacing (if recurring) | Temporary pacing at 90–100 bpm → shortens QT (QT ↓ with faster HR) → eliminates pauses → prevents TdP initiation |
| 5 | Isoprenaline infusion (if bradycardia-driven TdP, no ischaemia) | 2–10 mcg/min IV. ↑ HR → ↓ QT → ↓ TdP. Bridge to pacing. |
| 6 | Defibrillation if degenerated to VF | 200 J unsynchronised |

Warning: AMIODARONE IS CONTRAINDICATED IN TdP — it prolongs QT further → worsens TdP. This is a high-yield exam trap: TdP treatment = MgSO₄ + overdrive pacing + isoprenaline. NOT amiodarone, NOT sotalol, NOT any class III AAD. Contrast: Non-TdP polymorphic VT (ischaemic) → amiodarone + beta-blocker + urgent PCI.

POAF: Most common complication post-cardiac surgery (20–40% CABG, 40–60% valve surgery). Peak: 2nd–3rd post-op day.

| Prevention | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Pre/peri-op amiodarone (Class IIa) | ↓ POAF 50%. Consider for high-risk patients (prior AF, valve surgery, elderly). |
| Continue pre-op beta-blocker (Class I) | NEVER stop BB before cardiac surgery. Abrupt cessation → rebound tachycardia + ↑ POAF risk. |
| Colchicine 0.5 mg BD (Class IIa) | COPPS-2 trial: Colchicine started 48h pre-op → 45% ↓ POAF. Anti-inflammatory mechanism. |

POAF treatment:

- Correct electrolytes (K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥1.0)
- Rate control: IV metoprolol 5 mg q5min OR amiodarone IV if BB contraindicated
- Most POAF self-terminates within 24–48h — rhythm control if persists
- DC cardioversion for POAF >48h (sinus rhythm preferred in surgical population)

Anticoagulation in POAF: HIGH bleeding risk post-surgery in first 48–72h. Start OAC when haemostasis secure (usually day 2–3) if POAF persists. If POAF spontaneously converts <24h in low-risk patient: OAC decision based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Most POAF resolves within 1 week — if persistent, treat like non-surgical AF.
front: Postoperative AF — prevention, treatment, and anticoagulation decision after cardiac surgery

back:
Typical atrial flutter: Re-entry circuit around tricuspid valve → "sawtooth" flutter waves at 250–350 bpm in inferior leads (II, III, aVF). 2:1 AV conduction → ventricular rate ~150 bpm (CLASSIC finding).

| Management component | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Rate control | BB or non-DHP CCB (verapamil/diltiazem). Harder to rate control than AF (fixed 2:1 block often giving 150 bpm; difficult to get <100 without high drug doses or block conversion to AF). Target <100 bpm. Digoxin as second-line add-on. |
| Cardioversion | Atrial flutter very sensitive to DC cardioversion. Start at 50–100 J biphasic (much lower than AF). Success >90% at first shock. Anticoagulation same as AF: ≥3 weeks OAC before if duration ≥48h (or TOE to exclude thrombus → cardiovert + 4 weeks post-CV OAC). |
| Catheter ablation (Class I) | CTI (cavo-tricuspid isthmus) ablation: 90–95% cure rate for typical flutter. RF ablation of CTI interrupts the flutter circuit. Strongly preferred over chronic antiarrhythmic drugs. Ablation is first-line DEFINITIVE treatment for symptomatic typical flutter. |
| Anticoagulation | Same as AF: CHA₂DS₂-VASc-guided OAC. Atrial flutter carries similar stroke risk to AF — do NOT assume flutter is "safer" and skip anticoagulation. |

Tip: Carotid sinus massage / adenosine in flutter: Slows ventricular rate temporarily (increases AV block) → reveals "sawtooth" flutter waves that were hidden at 2:1 → useful DIAGNOSTIC manoeuvre. Adenosine 6 mg IV → 3:1 or 4:1 block briefly → see flutter pattern. Does NOT terminate flutter (only terminates re-entry SVTs not depending on AV node).

S3 = rapid early-diastolic filling of a dilated/volume-overloaded ventricle (HF, MR; normal in youth).

SCAI 2019 Classification: Five stages from "At Risk" to "Extremis"

| Stage | Name | Clinical criteria | Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | At Risk | No signs/symptoms. Risk factors: large MI, severe HF history. | Optimise GDMT; monitor |
| B | Beginning | Haemodynamic instability WITHOUT hypoperfusion: SBP <90 or HR >100. No end-organ damage. | IV fluids if depleted; close monitoring |
| C | Classic CS | Tissue hypoperfusion: CI <2.2, PCWP >15, cold extremities, oliguria, lactate ↑, AMS. Requires intervention beyond fluid. | Vasopressors + inotropes; IABP; urgent revascularisation if ACS |
| D | Deteriorating | Failing initial CS treatment within 30 min despite ≥1 vasopressor + inotrope. | Escalate MCS: Impella CP/5.0 or VA-ECMO |
| E | Extremis | Cardiac arrest (CPR ongoing) or profound refractory shock. Lactate >8, pH <7.2. | ECPR (VA-ECMO during CPR); palliative care discussion |

Tip: Mortality: Stage C ~40%, Stage D ~60%, Stage E >70%. Trajectory (escalating vs stabilising) matters as much as absolute stage. Shock team model (cardiology + cardiac surgery + critical care) → earlier MCS escalation → ↑ survival.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §4.3.2 · ESC 2023 §7.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §8.1, §8.2

VA-ECMO: Drains venous blood → oxygenator → pump → arterial return. Provides full cardiopulmonary support. Bridge to decision/recovery/LVAD/transplant.

| Critical LV venting problem | Solution |
| --- | --- |
| ECMO fills aorta with oxygenated blood retrograde → ↑ afterload → LV cannot eject → LV distension → ↑ LVEDP → pulmonary oedema | Vent the LV: IABP (↓ afterload, most common), Impella (direct LV decompression), or LA drainage cannula |
| Harlequin/north-south syndrome: When LV partially recovers + pulmonary oedema persists → upper body (brain, heart) gets desaturated LV output while lower body gets ECMO-oxygenated blood | Switch to VAV-ECMO (additional venous cannula for upper body) or improve native lung function aggressively |

Warning: ECLS-SHOCK trial (NEJM 2023): VA-ECMO before PCI in CS-STEMI → NO improvement in 30-day mortality vs standard care, with ↑ major bleeding and ↑ limb ischaemia. Conclusion: VA-ECMO should NOT be used routinely in SCAI C CS-STEMI. Reserve for SCAI D/E (refractory to conventional therapy).
Tip: VA-ECMO indications: Refractory CS (SCAI D/E) on ≥2 vasopressors. Massive PE cardiac arrest (bridge to embolectomy). ECPR for refractory cardiac arrest. Expert centre only — not routine CS treatment.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §4.3.2 · ESC 2023 §7.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §8.1, §8.2
front: VA-ECMO in cardiogenic shock — patient selection, the LV venting problem, and ECLS-SHOCK findings

RV failure management: ↑ RV contractility + ↓ PVR + optimise preload + maintain RV coronary perfusion

| Target | Intervention |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ RV contractility | Dobutamine (β₁ inotropy + mild ↓ PVR). Milrinone (best for RV — ↓ PVR + ↑ contractility). Norepinephrine (↑ MAP → ↑ RV coronary perfusion — critical in dilated RV). |
| ↓ PVR (pulmonary vasodilation) | Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) 10–40 ppm — gold standard: selective pulmonary vasodilation without systemic hypotension. Inhaled iloprost (prostacyclin). IV sildenafil (systemic hypotension risk — use cautiously). |
| Optimise RV preload | Cautious fluids (250 mL boluses). Avoid volume overload → interventricular dependence → LV compression. Avoid excess diuresis (RV preload-sensitive). |
| Maintain RV coronary perfusion | RV perfuses in systole AND diastole. Target DBP ≥40 mmHg. NE to maintain MAP. Sinus rhythm (AV synchrony critical). |
| RV-specific MCS | ProtekDuo: Dual-lumen catheter in PA pumping from RA → PA (similar to right-sided Impella). Used for acute RV failure post-LVAD implant or post-cardiotomy. |

Tip: RV MI specific: Volume loading is KEY (unlike LV failure). Give 500 mL–1 L saline rapidly. Avoid NTG (drops preload → precipitous ↓ CO). Reperfuse RCA urgently. Avoid diuretics until volume-responsive.
front: RV failure acute treatment — inotropes, pulmonary vasodilators, RV preload, and ProtekDuo

Positioning: Inlet 3.5–4 cm below aortic annulus (in LV). Confirmed by fluoroscopy + pressure waveform.

| Trial | Key finding |
| --- | --- |
| IABP-SHOCK II | IABP vs medical therapy in CS-STEMI → NO survival benefit at 30 days or 12 months. IABP downgraded from Class I → Class III (no benefit) for routine CS-STEMI. |
| PROTECT III | Impella CP-guided haemodynamic support for complex high-risk PCI → 30-day MACE 14.1%. Registry data (no sham control). |

LVAD (HeartMate 3): Magnetically levitated centrifugal pump. LV apex → pump → ascending aorta. MOMENTUM 3 trial: 77% 2-year survival vs 63% HeartMate II. 0 pump thrombosis in 2 years.

| Selection criteria | Contraindications |
| --- | --- |
| EF ≤25%, NYHA III–IV despite optimal GDMT, VO₂ max ≤14 mL/kg/min, not transplant candidate, expected survival >1 year | Significant RV failure (RV cannot handle ↑ preload from LVAD). Fixed PVR >8 WU. Moderate-severe AR. Mechanical AV valve. Active infection. Severe irreversible extra-cardiac organ failure. |

Key complications:

| Complication | Mechanism / Management |
| --- | --- |
| GI bleeding (most common) | Pulseless (continuous) flow → arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in GI tract. Octreotide, thalidomide, iron supplementation, endoscopy. |
| Stroke | Embolic (device-related thrombus) or haemorrhagic. Maintain INR 2–3. Aspirin 81 mg. Best predictor: prior stroke. |
| Driveline infection | Chronic percutaneous driveline → portal of entry. Daily dressing changes. IV antibiotics for infection. Source of sepsis in LVAD patients. |
| RV failure post-LVAD | 20–40% of patients. LVAD ↑ LV output → ↑ RV preload → RV cannot handle. May require temporary RVAD (ProtekDuo). |

Tip: 🇮🇩 LVAD not available in Indonesia — patients referred abroad. BPJS does NOT cover LVAD. It is the practical long-term alternative to cardiac transplant for eligible Indonesian patients who cannot travel for transplant.

TVP: RV apex catheter pacing. Rate 60–80 bpm. Output 2× capture threshold. Sensitivity 1–3 mV.

| Indication | Urgency |
| --- | --- |
| Complete AV block + haemodynamic compromise | Immediate |
| Symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine | Urgent (transcutaneous bridge while arranging TVP) |
| TdP from pause-dependent long QT | Immediate — overdrive pace at 90–100 bpm to prevent pauses |
| Trifascicular block pre-surgery | Prophylactic |

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failure to capture (spike without QRS) | Lead displacement; high threshold; low output | ↑ mA output; reposition; check impedance |
| Failure to sense (competitive pacing) | Sensitivity set too low | ↑ Sensitivity (↓ mV threshold); reposition. Risk: R-on-T → VF |
| Hiccups with pacing | Phrenic nerve stimulation | Reduce output if capture maintained; reposition lead |

Tip: Transcutaneous pacing: Bridge while arranging TVP. Painful — needs sedation/analgesia. Confirm MECHANICAL capture (palpate pulse with each spike — electrical capture ≠ mechanical capture). Set rate 60–80 bpm, mA 50 → titrate until capture.

Heart transplant: Only curative treatment for end-stage HF. Limited by donor availability (median wait 6–18 months). Not available in Indonesia — patients referred abroad.

| Listing criteria (Class I) | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Peak VO₂ ≤14 mL/kg/min | Or ≤12 mL/kg/min on BB. Objective exercise capacity. Predicts 1-year mortality >50% without transplant. |
| Refractory HF | NYHA IV recurrent HHF ≥3/year on max GDMT + CRT/ICD. INTERMACS class 1–4. |
| Refractory angina/arrhythmia | Not amenable to revascularisation or ablation. High SCD risk despite ICD. |

| Absolute contraindications | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| Irreversible PH: PVR >5 WU despite vasodilators | Donor RV fails against elevated PVR → primary graft failure. Trial vasodilators first → if PVR ↓ <3 WU: list. |
| Active malignancy (not in remission) | Immunosuppression → tumour progression |
| Active substance abuse | Non-compliance + organ damage |
| Active systemic infection | Immunosuppression → fatal sepsis |
| Severe irreversible extra-cardiac organ failure | Consider combined organ transplant if reversible |

Bridge strategies to transplant:

- Bridge to transplant (BTT): LVAD implant → patient stabilised while waiting for donor
- Bridge to candidacy (BTC): Patient too ill to list → LVAD → recovery → re-evaluate for transplant
- Bridge to decision (BTD): VA-ECMO/Impella as acute bridge while reversibility assessed

Tip: Post-transplant immunosuppression (triple therapy): Tacrolimus (or ciclosporin) + Mycophenolate mofetil + Prednisolone. Main causes of death: 1st year = primary graft failure + infection. After year 1 = allograft vasculopathy (CAV) + malignancy. Annual coronary angiography for CAV detection (develops in 50% at 5 years).
front: Heart transplant listing — UNOS criteria, absolute contraindications, and bridge therapies

back:
IABP: Balloon inflates in DIASTOLE (↑ coronary perfusion pressure) and deflates in SYSTOLE (↓ afterload → ↑ forward CO). Counter-pulsation timed to ECG or pressure trigger.

| Haemodynamic effects | Magnitude |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ Diastolic BP (inflation → ↑ aortic root pressure) | ↑ 20–40 mmHg diastolic pressure → ↑ coronary perfusion |
| ↓ Afterload (deflation → ↓ aortic pressure at systolic onset) | ↓ SVR ~10–15%, ↑ CO ~20% |
| ↓ Myocardial oxygen demand | ↓ Wall stress from ↓ afterload → ↓ MVO₂ |
| ↓ PCWP | Mild ↓ from ↓ afterload → ↓ filling pressures |

| APPROPRIATE IABP uses | CONTRAINDICATIONS to IABP |
| --- | --- |
| Refractory ischaemic chest pain pre-CABG (short-term bridge). Post-cardiac surgery low output. Mechanical MI complications (VSD, acute MR) — bridge to surgery. Prophylactic during high-risk PCI (limited evidence). | Severe AR (diastolic inflation → ↑ regurgitant volume). Aortic dissection. Severe PAD (limb ischaemia). Coagulopathy (relative). LVOTO/HCM (can worsen dynamic obstruction). Dynamic LVOTO in Takotsubo. |

Warning: IABP-SHOCK II trial: IABP + primary PCI + optimal medical therapy vs PCI + OMT WITHOUT IABP in CS-STEMI → NO difference in 30-day mortality (39.7% vs 41.3%). IABP is no longer recommended as routine in CS-STEMI (Class III — no benefit). Downgraded from Class I. Use only for specific haemodynamic situations (mechanical complications, refractory ischaemia) — not as routine CS management.

Ref: PERKI 2024 §4.3.2 · ESC 2023 §7.2 · ACC/AHA 2025 §8.1, §8.2

Hypertensive emergency: SBP >180/DBP >120 mmHg WITH acute target organ damage. Treat IV in monitored setting. Avoid too-rapid BP reduction (autoregulation set higher in chronic HTN).

| TOD | BP target (first hour) | First-line drug |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypertensive encephalopathy | ↓ MAP 10–15% in 1h, then 25% in 24h | IV nicardipine or IV labetalol |
| Ischaemic stroke | Only treat if >220/120. Lower to 185/110 if thrombolysis planned. | IV labetalol or nicardipine (careful titration) |
| ICH | SBP <140 mmHg (INTERACT-2/ATACH-2) | IV nicardipine, IV labetalol. Avoid SNP (↑ ICP) |
| Acute HF / pulmonary oedema | ↓ MAP 10–15% in 1h | IV NTG + IV furosemide. Avoid BB (negative inotropy in HF) |
| ACS | SBP <140 mmHg | IV NTG + IV metoprolol/labetalol. Avoid hydralazine (reflex tachycardia ↑ MVO₂) |
| Aortic dissection (Type A or B) | SBP 100–120 mmHg + HR <60 bpm within 20 min | IV labetalol (FIRST — rate control before vasodilation). Then add nicardipine/SNP if needed. Vasodilator ALONE → reflex ↑ HR → ↑ wall shear stress → ↑ dissection propagation. |
| Eclampsia | SBP <160, DBP <105 | IV labetalol or IV hydralazine or IV nicardipine. IV MgSO₄ for seizure prevention (not BP). |
| Phaeochromocytoma crisis | ↓ MAP 25% in 1h | IV phentolamine (α-blocker) FIRST. Then add BB. NEVER BB first (paradoxical ↑↑ BP from unopposed α). |

Massive PE = high-risk PE: SBP <90 mmHg ≥15 min OR requiring vasopressors OR cardiac arrest. 5% of PE but mortality 25–50%.

| Intervention | Protocol |
| --- | --- |
| Systemic thrombolysis — first-line for massive PE | Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h. Ultra-accelerated (cardiac arrest): 0.6 mg/kg IV (max 50 mg) over 15 min. Or Streptokinase 250,000 IU over 30 min → 100,000 IU/h × 12–24h. |
| UFH during/after thrombolysis | Start UFH immediately on diagnosis. PAUSE during alteplase infusion → resume WITHOUT bolus 2h after when APTT <80 sec. |
| Vasopressors | NE 0.1–0.3 mcg/kg/min to maintain MAP ≥65. Bridge to reperfusion — not definitive treatment. |
| Fluids | Maximum 500 mL bolus. Avoid large-volume resuscitation (↑ RV afterload from volume overload). PE causes RV failure from obstruction — more volume doesn't help. |
| VA-ECMO for PE arrest | ECPR during cardiac arrest → bypass for reperfusion. Allow thrombolysis to work during ECMO. Survival 50–60% in selected patients at ECMO centres. |
| Surgical embolectomy | Indications: Thrombolysis CI or failed, intracardiac thrombus, large clot in transit. Open surgery under CPB removes proximal clot. Mortality 6–35%. |

Correct: Post-thrombolysis care: (1) Monitor for bleeding (especially neurological symptoms → stop → CT head). (2) Compressible bleeding (access sites): Apply pressure 30 min. (3) Start DOAC 24h post-thrombolysis (not simultaneously — ↑ ICH risk). (4) Repeat echo 48h to assess RV recovery. (5) Consider IVC filter if anticoagulation CI with recurrent PE.
front: Massive PE treatment — alteplase 100 mg protocol, VA-ECMO for arrest, and post-lysis care

PPCM: EF <45%, new HF in last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum without prior cardiac disease. Pathomechanism: Oxidative stress → 16kDa prolactin fragment → endothelial apoptosis → cardiomyopathy.

| Treatment | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist) | ↓ Prolactin → ↓ 16kDa fragment → blocks PPCM mechanism. IPAC/BRO-HF: bromocriptine ↑ full LV recovery (52% vs 32%). Dose: 2.5 mg OD × 1 week → 2.5 mg BD × 6 weeks (extended protocol in severe PPCM). Requires: LMWH anticoagulation (↑ thrombosis risk peri-partum). Must STOP breastfeeding (suppresses lactation). |
| Standard HF therapy (postpartum) | ACEi/ARNi: Start postpartum (CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy). BB: Carvedilol/metoprolol safe in breastfeeding. Diuretics: Furosemide safe. SGLT2i: AVOID (insufficient safety data in breastfeeding). |
| Anticoagulation | LMWH during pregnancy + postpartum (hypercoagulable state + ↑ risk LV thrombus if EF severely ↓). OAC (warfarin) postpartum if LV thrombus visualised. |
| ICD/WCD | Defer ICD × 6–12 months (EF often recovers). WCD as bridge. ICD if EF remains <35% at 6 months despite optimal therapy. |

Warning: Drugs CONTRAINDICATED in PPCM breastfeeding: ACEi (captopril acceptable, but lisinopril/enalapril in breast milk → neonatal hypotension). Amiodarone (neonatal iodine toxicity + thyroid). Spironolactone (insufficient safety data). All DOACs (excreted in breast milk). Contraceptive counselling essential — subsequent pregnancy risk 20% recurrence even with recovered EF.

back:
Takotsubo: Catecholamine-mediated apical LV ballooning + basal hypercontractility. Most common in post-menopausal women after emotional or physical stress.

| Treatment | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Supportive care | Most resolve within 2–4 weeks. ACEi (LV recovery). Diuretics for congestion. BB (carvedilol — controversial as catecholamine levels already high, but helpful for rate control and recovery). |
| Anticoagulation | LMWH/heparin in acute phase (apical akinesis → LV thrombus risk). OAC if thrombus detected. Stop when EF recovers (>50%). |
| LVOTO treatment | If dynamic LVOTO present (20–25% of cases): IV fluids + IV BB (metoprolol). Phenylephrine (pure α-agonist) for hypotension — safe because does not stimulate β receptors. NOT vasodilators or inotropes. |

Warning: DRUGS HARMFUL IN TAKOTSUBO: (1) Catecholamines (dobutamine, dopamine, adrenaline): β₁ stimulation → ↑ apical stress → worsens ballooning. Adrenaline can TRIGGER Takotsubo — documented cases from epinephrine anaphylaxis treatment. (2) Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP): Contraindicated if LVOTO present. IABP deflation in diastole worsens dynamic obstruction. Safe alternatives for cardiogenic shock in Takotsubo: IV fluids (if LVOTO) → levosimendan (Ca²⁺ sensitiser — avoids β-receptor stimulation). VA-ECMO if refractory shock.
front: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy — why catecholamines are harmful and alternative management of haemodynamic compromise

IV-to-Oral conversion rules:

- Furosemide IV → oral: Double the IV dose (50% bioavailability). IV 40 mg → PO 80 mg OD

Tip: TRANSFORM-HF trial (NEJM 2023): Torsemide vs furosemide at hospital discharge → No difference in mortality or HHF at 60 days. Resistant HTN: BP uncontrolled on ≥3 antihypertensives (including optimal-dose diuretic). First exclude: White coat HTN (24h ABPM), non-adherence, drug causes, secondary HTN.
Secondary HTN screen in resistant HTN:

- Primary hyperaldosteronism: Aldosterone:renin ratio (most common cause ~20%)
- OSA: STOP-BANG ≥3 → polysomnography
- Renal artery stenosis: Duplex Doppler/CTA
- Phaeochromocytoma: 24h urinary metanephrines or plasma metanephrines
- Cushing's: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
- CKD: Creatinine + urine ACR

Optimise medications then add spironolactone:

| Drug | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Spironolactone 25–50 mg OD (4th drug) | PATHWAY-2: Best 4th drug for resistant HTN. ↓ 24h SBP by 8.7 mmHg more than placebo, and superior to doxazosin and bisoprolol. Monitor K⁺ (hyperkalemia risk, especially with CKD or RAS blocker). |
| Renal denervation (RDN) | SPYRAL HTN-OFF: RDN ↓ daytime SBP by 5 mmHg vs sham at 3 months. RADIANCE SOLO: Similar. Modest effect (~5 mmHg). ESC 2023: Class IIb adjunct at expert centres. Not first-line. Catheter-based RF ablation of renal sympathetic nerves. |

Tip: Chlorthalidone superiority over HCTZ in resistant HTN: Chlorthalidone has 24h duration (vs 6–8h HCTZ) and stronger natriuretic effect → more BP reduction per dose. ALLHAT used chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg. If patient on HCTZ 12.5–25 mg: Switch to chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg as "step 3" drug intensification (may drop SBP 10–15 mmHg on this switch alone).

When to check anti-factor Xa levels (DOAC levels):

- Extremes of body weight (<50 kg or >120 kg)
- Severe CKD at the boundary of use
- Suspected DOAC overdose or toxicity
- Peri-procedure decision-making (is drug still on board?)
- Recurrent thromboembolic or bleeding events despite DOAC
- Drug interactions suspected to ↑/↓ DOAC levels

Anti-Xa levels for rivaroxaban/apixaban/edoxaban: Peak (2–4h post-dose) and trough (12h or 24h post-dose) levels. DOAC levels NOT required for routine monitoring — unlike INR for warfarin. Use anti-Xa assay calibrated for specific DOAC (not same assay as LMWH monitoring).
Tip: Very elderly (>80 years): Apixaban has best evidence and dose reduction criteria (SCr + age + weight). Lower ICH risk vs warfarin in all elderly. ARISTOTLE subgroup >75: Apixaban → 42% ↓ stroke + 54% ↓ ICH vs warfarin. Apixaban preferred DOAC in frail elderly.

Digoxin: Cardiac glycoside. Inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → ↑ contractility (positive inotropy) + ↑ vagal tone → ↓ AV conduction (rate control).

| Indication | Evidence / Class |
| --- | --- |
| Rate control in AF + HFrEF (when BB/CCB contraindicated or insufficient) | Class IIb. Effective at rest (vagal-mediated AV block); less effective during exercise (vagal tone ↓). |
| Symptom control in HFrEF (sinus rhythm) on optimal GDMT | DIG trial: ↓ HHF, neutral mortality. Class IIb as add-on therapy for persistent symptoms. Target plasma level 0.5–0.9 ng/mL. |

Dosing and monitoring:

| Parameter | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Starting dose | 0.125 mg OD (elderly, CKD, low body weight). 0.25 mg OD (young, normal renal function, large body habitus). |
| Therapeutic range | 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (lower end preferred — post-hoc analyses show ↑ mortality at >1.0 ng/mL) |
| Check level | 12h after last dose (steady state after 5–7 days). Check at initiation, after dose change, or if toxicity suspected. |
| Toxicity signs | GI: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia (earliest signs). Visual: Yellow-green halos (xanthopsia). Cardiac: Bradycardia, AV block, bigeminy, VT/VF. |

Warning: Critical drug interactions: Amiodarone (↑ digoxin level 2×), Verapamil (↑ level 50–70%), Dronedarone (↑ level 2.5×), Clarithromycin/erythromycin (↑ level via P-gp inhibition). When adding amiodarone → HALVE digoxin dose immediately + re-check level in 7–10 days. Hypokalaemia ↑ digoxin toxicity even at therapeutic plasma levels (↑ receptor affinity). Monitor K⁺ closely with concurrent diuretics.
front: Digoxin in modern cardiology — dosing, therapeutic range, monitoring, and interactions

SGLT2i CV benefits are largely glucose-independent — proven in non-DM HF populations (DAPA-HF: 42% of patients non-diabetic → same HF benefit)

| Mechanism | Cardiovascular effect |
| --- | --- |
| Glucosuria + natriuresis | ↓ Plasma volume → ↓ preload → ↓ filling pressures without RAAS activation (unlike conventional diuretics) |
| NHE-1 inhibition (Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger) | ↓ Intracellular Na⁺ → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ via NCX → ↓ harmful Ca²⁺ overload → ↑ cardiomyocyte function. This is the PRIMARY cardiac mechanism — independent of glucose. |
| Ketone metabolism | ↑ Serum ketones → "super fuel" for heart (more ATP/O₂ vs glucose) → ↑ cardiac efficiency, especially in ischaemic/failing myocardium |
| Tubuloglomerular feedback | ↑ NaCl delivery to macula densa → afferent arteriole constriction → ↓ intraglomerular pressure → ↓ proteinuria → renal protection (renal benefit independent of glucose) |
| ↓ Sympathetic activation | Possible ↓ renal afferent nerve activity → ↓ central sympathetic output |
| Erythropoiesis | ↑ Haematocrit (mild) via ↑ renal EPO → ↑ O₂ delivery |

Clinical implication: Use SGLT2i in ALL HFrEF patients regardless of DM status (Class I). Can start in-hospital (EMPULSE). Safe in eGFR ≥25 for HF indication (lower threshold than for glycaemic benefit).
Tip: SGLT2i in HFpEF: DELIVER (dapagliflozin) and EMPEROR-Preserved (empagliflozin): both ↓ HHF + CV death in HFpEF (EF >40%). Effect size smaller than HFrEF but significant. ESC Class IIa for HFmrEF/HFpEF. Now the first drugs shown to benefit ANY EF stratum of heart failure.
front: SGLT2i mechanism in heart failure beyond glucose lowering — why they work in non-diabetics

Ivabradine: Selective If-channel (funny current, HCN channel) inhibitor in SAN → ↓ heart rate WITHOUT negative inotropy. Pure rate reduction.
SHIFT trial (NEJM 2010): HFrEF (EF ≤35%), sinus rhythm, HR ≥70 bpm, NYHA II–IV on max tolerated BB. Ivabradine vs placebo → 18% ↓ composite (CV death or HHF). ↓ HHF 26%.

| Indication (ESC Class IIa) | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Patient criteria | Sinus rhythm. HR ≥70 bpm despite maximum tolerated BB. EF ≤35%. NYHA II–IV. |
| Ivabradine is ADD-ON to BB | NOT a replacement for BB. If patient cannot tolerate any BB at all → ivabradine can be used as alternative rate-lowering agent to target HR ≤70 bpm. |
| Contraindications | AF (only works on SAN → no rate slowing in AF — may actually ↑ ventricular rate!). Sick sinus / AV block without PPM. SBP <90. Cardiogenic shock. |

Dosing: Start 5 mg BD. Target: Resting HR 55–60 bpm. Uptitrate to 7.5 mg BD if HR ≥70. Reduce to 2.5 mg BD if HR <50 or symptoms.
Tip: Practical use: Patient on bisoprolol 5 mg OD + HR still 75 bpm + SBP 95 mmHg (cannot ↑ BB further due to hypotension) → ADD ivabradine 5 mg BD → reduce HR further → ↓ HHF risk. This is the key scenario where ivabradine provides additional benefit beyond current BB dose.
front: Ivabradine in heart failure — SHIFT trial, indication, and how to select patients

Hyperkalaemia is the most common reason GDMT (especially MRA) is reduced or stopped. K⁺ binders now allow GDMT continuation.

| K⁺ level | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <5.0 | Continue all GDMT. Dietary K⁺ counselling (avoid bananas, coconut water, potatoes, oranges). |
| 5.0–5.5 | Low-K⁺ diet. Consider K⁺ binder. Reduce spironolactone dose 50%. |
| 5.5–6.0 | HOLD MRA. K⁺ binder. Reduce ACEi/ARB dose. Recheck in 5–7 days. |
| >6.0 mEq/L | EMERGENCY: ECG immediately. IV calcium gluconate (peaked T, wide QRS). IV insulin 10 units + 50 mL 50% dextrose. IV salbutamol nebulisation. IV bicarbonate if acidaemic. Dialysis if refractory. |

Potassium binders enabling GDMT continuation:

| Agent | Dose | Onset | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patiromer (Veltassa) | 8.4 g OD → titrate to 25 g OD with food | 7–24h | DIAMOND: Patiromer → ↑ spironolactone use in HFrEF with K⁺ ↑ history → ↓ HHF. Allows GDMT continuation. |
| Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC, Lokelma) | 10 g TID × 48h → 5 g OD maintenance | 1–6h (faster) | HARMONIZE-OUTCOMES: SZC → ↑ GDMT maintenance in HF. Preferred if faster onset needed. |

Warning: ECG signs of severe hyperkalaemia requiring immediate treatment: Peaked T waves (K⁺ ~5.5–6). PR prolongation + flat P waves (K⁺ ~6.5). Wide QRS (K⁺ ~7). Sine wave pattern → VF imminent (K⁺ >8). IV calcium gluconate does NOT lower K⁺ — it protects the heart while other agents work. Always give calcium first if ECG changes present.
front: Hyperkalaemia management in heart failure — potassium binders and GDMT continuation strategies

back:
Residual inflammatory risk: Patients on optimal statin therapy still have elevated hsCRP → ↑ MACE. Colchicine targets this pathway.

| Trial | Drug/Population | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| COLCOT (NEJM 2019) | Colchicine 0.5 mg OD started within 30 days of MI, added to standard secondary prevention | 23% ↓ composite MACE (CV death/resuscitated arrest/MI/stroke/urgent hospitalisation for angina). NNT 42 at 23 months. |
| LoDoCo2 (NEJM 2020) | Colchicine 0.5 mg OD in stable established CAD | 31% ↓ MACE vs placebo. Confirmed colchicine benefit in chronic stable CAD (not just post-MI). |
| CANTOS (NEJM 2017) | Canakinumab (anti-IL-1β) 150 mg SC q3 months in post-MI + hsCRP ≥2 | 15% ↓ MACE. Proof of concept that inflammation is causal. BUT: ↑ fatal infections + cost (~$16,000/year) → NOT clinically adopted. |

ESC 2021: Colchicine 0.5 mg OD — Class IIa for post-MI secondary prevention if tolerated.

| Colchicine practical considerations | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Dosing | 0.5 mg OD (lower than gout dose of 1–1.2 mg). Start within 30 days of MI. |
| Side effects | GI (diarrhoea, nausea) in ~10% → take with food. Usually mild and transient. |
| Drug interactions | P-gp + CYP3A4 inhibitors (amiodarone, diltiazem, dronedarone, ketoconazole) → ↑ colchicine levels → toxicity. Reduce colchicine dose or use with caution. |
| Contraindications | eGFR <30 (renally cleared → toxicity). Severe hepatic disease. Pregnancy. Breastfeeding. |
front: Anti-inflammatory post-MI treatment — COLCOT, LoDoCo2, and using colchicine for CV risk reduction

back:
STICH trial (NEJM 2011, extended follow-up STICHES 2016): Surgical revascularisation for ischaemic cardiomyopathy with low EF

| Feature | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Population | Coronary artery disease + EF ≤35% (n=1,212). Randomised: CABG + OMT vs OMT alone. Excluded: Left main >50% stenosis. |
| Primary endpoint | All-cause mortality |
| STICH result (median 56 months) | CABG vs OMT: all-cause death 36% vs 41% (HR 0.86, p=0.12 — NOT significant at initial follow-up) |
| STICHES extended follow-up (10 years) | CABG vs OMT: all-cause death 59% vs 66% (HR 0.84, p=0.02 — SIGNIFICANT). CABG ↓ CV death + ↓ all-cause death at 10 years. Late divergence in survival curves. |
| Key lesson | Benefit of CABG in ischaemic CMP emerges LATE (5–10 years). Short-term studies may miss the survival benefit. In suitable surgical candidates with ischaemic CMP + viable myocardium → CABG improves long-term survival. |

STICH viability sub-study: Patients with viable myocardium (nuclear imaging/dobutamine echo) did NOT have greater benefit from CABG vs those without viability. Challenged the dogma of "revascularise if viable" — viability testing alone does not reliably identify who benefits from CABG in ischaemic CMP.
Tip: Current ESC recommendation: CABG Class I for patients with ischaemic CMP + significant coronary disease + symptoms of angina OR viable myocardium + suitable anatomy. The STICHES 10-year data provide Class I evidence for CABG in EF ≤35% + multivessel CAD.
front: STICH trial — CABG vs medical therapy in ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF ≤35%)

back:
Coronary vasospasm: Transient focal coronary artery spasm → transmural ischaemia → dynamic ST elevation (not fixed) → resolves with NTG or spontaneously

| Treatment | Drug | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First-line (prevention) | Non-DHP CCBs | Diltiazem 120–360 mg/day CR or Verapamil 240–480 mg/day. Prevent vasospasm by blocking smooth muscle Ca²⁺. DHP CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine) also effective — verapamil/diltiazem preferred for dual AV nodal benefit if arrhythmia present. |
| Add-on | Long-acting nitrates | Isosorbide mononitrate at bedtime for nocturnal episodes. Nitrate-free interval in morning to prevent tolerance. |
| Acute attack | Sublingual GTN (NTG) | Terminates acute vasospasm episode within 2–5 min. |

Warning: DRUGS WORSENING VASOSPASM: (1) Non-selective BB: Unopposed α-adrenergic → vasoconstriction → ↑ spasm. RELATIVE CI. (2) Aspirin (high dose): Inhibits prostacyclin (vasodilator) → may worsen. Low-dose aspirin usually continued. (3) Triptans (sumatriptan etc.): Serotonin agonists → coronary vasoconstriction → spasm trigger. (4) Cocaine: Potent coronary vasospasm. ABSOLUTE CI — even recreational use. (5) Ergotamine: Potent vasoconstrictor — can precipitate life-threatening spasm. (6) 5-fluorouracil (chemotherapy): Coronary vasospasm and MI — known cardiac toxicity.
Tip: VT/VF during spasm: EMERGENCY. Immediate defibrillation. IV NTG (relieve spasm). IV verapamil or diltiazem (prevent recurrence). Consider EP study + ICD if recurrent VF. Some patients need ICD despite "benign" vasospastic diagnosis — VF during spasm carries high SCD risk.
front: Coronary vasospasm treatment — drugs, what to avoid, and Prinzmetal angina management

back:
Cardiac rehabilitation (CR): Comprehensive secondary prevention programme. Class I for HFrEF (↓ HHF) and post-MI (↓ mortality). Dramatically underutilised globally including Indonesia.
HF-ACTION trial (NEJM 2009): Exercise training in HFrEF → 11% ↓ all-cause mortality/HHF (modest but significant when adjusted for prognostic factors). ↑ 6MWD + ↑ QoL. Safe — no ↑ adverse events.

| CR component | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Exercise training | Aerobic exercise 3–5×/week, 20–45 min per session at 50–70% VO₂ peak or Borg RPE 11–13/20. Progression over 12 weeks. Resistance training incorporated from week 4. |
| Patient education | Medication adherence, daily weight monitoring, sodium restriction, fluid management, symptom recognition and action plan, diet (Mediterranean pattern). |
| Risk factor management | Smoking cessation, BP targets, DM optimisation, lipid management, weight management. |
| Psychological support | Depression screening (PHQ-9 at baseline). Cognitive-behavioural therapy or counselling for anxiety/depression in HF (prevalent ~40% of HF patients). |
| Evaluation | 6-minute walk test at baseline and 12 weeks. LVEF at 3–6 months post-MI. Exercise stress test to guide training intensity. |

Tip: 🇮🇩 Indonesian CR barriers: Only available at large academic hospitals (RSUP level). BPJS covers CR at designated centres but coverage patchy. Telerehabilitation (smartphone-guided exercise + virtual clinic check-ins) emerging as scalable model. CR participation rate in Indonesia: ~5–10% of eligible patients. National PERKI advocacy needed to expand CR access.
front: Cardiac rehabilitation in heart failure — evidence, what the 12-week programme includes, and Indonesian context

back:
PFO closure: Transcatheter device (Amplatzer PFO Occluder) sealing inter-atrial communication → prevents paradoxical embolism → ↓ cryptogenic stroke recurrence

| Ideal patient for closure (ESC 2020 Class IIa) | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Age 18–60 years | Evidence strongest in younger patients (reduced competing stroke etiologies) |
| Cryptogenic ischaemic stroke or TIA | All other causes excluded (AF, large vessel disease, small vessel disease, hypercoagulable states) |
| PFO confirmed on TOE | With or without atrial septal aneurysm (ASA). Larger shunt (grade 2+) or ASA present → ↑ benefit from closure (CLOSE trial) |
| Minimum 6 months after stroke | Brain stable; no acute haemorrhagic transformation risk |

Evidence: REDUCE: 45% ↓ recurrent stroke. CLOSE: 0% vs 6% at 5 years (ASA + large shunt). RESPECT: 45% ↓ stroke (per-protocol). DEVICE CHOICE: Amplatzer PFO occluder most evidence.
Post-closure anticoagulation:

| Period | Regimen |
| --- | --- |
| 0–45 days | Warfarin (INR 2–3) + aspirin 81 mg (device endothelialisation requires temporary OAC) |
| 45 days (TOE check) | If adequate seal + no DRT: Stop warfarin → DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) × 6 months |
| After 6 months | Aspirin 81–100 mg monotherapy LIFELONG |
| If AF develops post-closure | OAC (DOAC) based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc + rate control |

Warning: 3–5% develop new-onset AF after PFO closure (device irritation of right atrium). Usually transient within 6-month blanking period. Manage with rate control + anticoagulation during blanking. Reassess OAC need at 6 months if sinus rhythm maintained.
front: PFO closure for cryptogenic stroke — patient selection, procedure, and post-closure anticoagulation

STICH trial: CABG + OMT vs OMT alone in ischaemic CMP (EF ≤35%). n=1,212 patients with CAD + EF ≤35%.

| STICH result | STICHES (10-year follow-up) |
| --- | --- |
| All-cause death: 36% CABG vs 41% OMT (p=0.12 — NS at 56-month median) | All-cause death: 59% vs 66% (HR 0.84, p=0.02 — SIGNIFICANT). Benefit emerges LATE. |
| CV death + HHF: CABG ↓ significantly | Confirmed CV benefit at 10 years. CABG = Class I for ischaemic CMP + suitable anatomy. |

STICH viability sub-study: Counterintuitive finding — Patients with viable myocardium did NOT show greater benefit from CABG than those without. Challenged "revascularise if viable" dogma. Viability testing alone does NOT reliably identify CABG benefit.

| Practical decision for CABG in ischaemic CMP | Factors supporting CABG |
| --- | --- |
| Class I indications (ESC 2019) | Significant angina symptoms on OMT + suitable anatomy. EF ≤35% + multivessel CAD + expected survival >1 year. |
| SYNTAX score | Low SYNTAX (<22): PCI vs CABG roughly equivalent in survival. High SYNTAX (>32): CABG clearly superior. |
| Completeness of revascularisation | Complete revascularisation achievable: ↑ benefit over incomplete. CABG more often achieves complete revascularisation than PCI in multivessel CAD with low EF. |
| Concomitant surgical procedure | Need for MV repair/replacement, LV reconstruction → prefer CABG + concomitant surgical procedure |
front: Revascularisation in ischaemic cardiomyopathy — STICH trial and the viability debate

back:
Cardiac amyloidosis: Two types need distinct treatment. ATTR (transthyretin) amyloidosis → stabilise or silence TTR. AL (light chain) amyloidosis → eliminate plasma cell clone.

| Drug | Mechanism | Trial | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tafamidis (Vyndaqel/Vyndamax) | TTR stabiliser → prevents tetramer dissociation → ↓ amyloid fibril formation. ATTR-CM only. | ATTR-ACT: 29% ↓ all-cause mortality + 32% ↓ CV hospitalisation vs placebo. Benefit larger in NYHA I–II. | Disease-modifying. Does not clear existing amyloid but prevents progression. Start EARLY (NYHA I–II). Tafamidis 20 mg OD (hATTR) or 61 mg OD (wtATTR). Vyndamax 61 mg OD. |
| Patisiran (Onpattro) | RNA interference → silences hepatic TTR mRNA → ↓ TTR production by >80% | APOLLO: Patisiran in hATTR polyneuropathy (cardiac endpoints secondary). ↓ NT-proBNP + ↑ cardiac function vs placebo. | IV q3 weeks. Now ATTR-CM specific trials ongoing. Greater TTR ↓ than stabilisers. |
| Vutrisiran (Amvuttra) | siRNA → silences TTR mRNA. Subcutaneous q3 months (vs IV patisiran q3 weeks). | HELIOS-A: Non-inferior to patisiran for polyneuropathy. ↓ NT-proBNP + cardiac benefits. | SC q3 months — ↑ convenience vs IV patisiran. |
| Acoramidis | TTR stabiliser (more potent than tafamidis) | ATTRibute-CM: Acoramidis vs placebo → significantly ↓ mortality + HHF at 30 months. Better than tafamidis in TTR stabilisation. | Oral OD. Expected to replace tafamidis as first-line TTR stabiliser. |

AL amyloidosis treatment: Daratumumab-based regimens (anti-CD38 mAb) + bortezomib + dexamethasone → suppress plasma cell clone → ↓ free light chains → ↓ amyloid production. Cardiac toxicity of chemotherapy is itself a management challenge in AL amyloidosis.
Warning: AVOID in cardiac amyloidosis: Digoxin (binds to amyloid fibrils → ↑ toxicity at normal doses). Verapamil/diltiazem (↑ negative inotropy in stiff non-compliant LV → haemodynamic collapse). High-dose beta-blockers (similar concern — titrate cautiously). All medications that lower BP or HR must be started very carefully.
front: Cardiac amyloidosis treatment update — tafamidis, patisiran, vutrisiran, and what to monitor

back:
ASD closure: Recommended when Qp:Qs ≥1.5 with RV volume overload, regardless of age. Transcatheter device closure (Amplatzer) preferred for secundum ASD with adequate rims.

| ASD type | Closure approach | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Secundum (75% of ASDs) | Transcatheter (Amplatzer Septal Occluder) if rims ≥5 mm | Rims provide anchoring. Success rate >95%. |
| Primum (15–20%) | Surgical only | Adjacent to MV/TV — cleft mitral valve repair often needed concomitantly |
| Sinus venosus (5–10%) | Surgical only | Often with PAPVD requiring surgical re-routing of anomalous PV |
| Large secundum (≥38 mm defect) or insufficient rims | Surgical | Too large for device / inadequate anchoring |

Transcatheter procedure: TOE guidance + fluoroscopy. Device size = defect diameter + 8–14 mm. Rim assessment: Must have ≥5 mm all around EXCEPT aortic rim (deficient aortic rim acceptable — aorta provides structural support). Device deployed from RA side → straddles septum → confirm position → release.
Post-ASD closure antiplatelet protocol:

- Aspirin 100 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg DAPT × 6 months (device endothelialisation period)
- After 6 months: Aspirin 100 mg OD lifelong (unless AF warrants OAC)
- New-onset AF post-closure: OAC based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc

Warning: Eisenmenger ASD: PVR ≥5 WU → closure CONTRAINDICATED. Close the ASD → removes pressure relief valve → acute RV failure. Screen ALL ASD patients with PA pressure assessment before closure. RHC mandatory if TOE shows elevated RVSP or clinical signs of pulmonary HTN.
front: Atrial septal defect closure — transcatheter vs surgical, rim assessment, and DAPT protocol

back:
WATCHMAN: Transcatheter left atrial appendage (LAA) occlusion device. Alternative to long-term OAC in AF patients with high stroke risk + contraindication or major reluctance for OAC.

| Ideal candidate | Feature |
| --- | --- |
| Non-valvular AF + CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 (male) or ≥3 (female) | High stroke risk requiring anticoagulation |
| Contraindication to long-term OAC | Prior ICH, serious GI bleeding, frequent falls, strong patient preference to avoid OAC |
| Expected survival >1 year | Device benefit accrues over time |
| Suitable LAA anatomy | LAA ostium diameter 17–31 mm (WATCHMAN FLX). TOE for sizing. |

Evidence: PROTECT-AF: WATCHMAN non-inferior to warfarin for stroke. ↓ Haemorrhagic stroke vs warfarin. PREVAIL confirmed. PRAGUE-17: WATCHMAN vs NOACs → similar composite events at 3.5 years.
Post-WATCHMAN anticoagulation protocol:

| Phase | Regimen |
| --- | --- |
| 0–45 days | Warfarin (INR 2–3) + aspirin 81 mg (device endothelialisation requires anticoagulation) |
| 45-day TOE check | Adequate seal + no DRT → Stop warfarin → DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) × 6 months |
| After 6 months | Aspirin 81–100 mg OD lifelong (or reassess if DRT or new AF indication for OAC) |

Warning: Device-related thrombus (DRT): Occurs in ~4% at 45-day TOE. If DRT found: Continue OAC until TOE confirms resolution. DRT → stroke risk. Annual TOE surveillance recommended by some guidelines. New-onset AF post-closure: Still requires OAC (device seals LAA but AF itself causes atrial body thrombus in addition to LAA thrombus).
front: WATCHMAN LAA closure — patient selection, procedure, and post-closure management

back:
PAH treatment: Risk stratification at diagnosis AND at follow-up determines initial therapy and escalation. Target: LOW RISK at follow-up.

| Risk parameter | Low risk (target) | High risk (needs escalation) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WHO functional class | I or II | III or IV |
| 6-minute walk distance | >440 m | <165 m |
| NT-proBNP/BNP | NT-proBNP <300 ng/L (BNP <50 ng/L) | NT-proBNP >1400 ng/L (BNP >300 ng/L) |
| Haemodynamics (RHC) | RAP <8 mmHg, CI >2.5 L/min/m², SvO₂ >65% | RAP >14, CI <2.0, SvO₂ <60% |
| Cardiac imaging | No pericardial effusion, TAPSE ≥20 mm, RVEF ≥54% | Pericardial effusion, TAPSE <15 mm |

Initial treatment strategy:

| Risk at baseline | Initial therapy |
| --- | --- |
| Low–intermediate risk (WHO I–II) | Upfront dual combination: ERA + PDE5i (ambrisentan + tadalafil — AMBITION Class I) |
| High risk (WHO III–IV) | Triple combination: ERA + PDE5i + subcutaneous/IV prostacyclin analogue (epoprostenol or treprostinil). Consider lung transplant evaluation from outset. |
| Vasoreactive testing positive (calcium-sensitive) | High-dose CCB (diltiazem, amlodipine, nifedipine) → if sustained response (WHO class I–II + near-normal mPAP) → continue CCB. Only 10% of IPAH respond. |

Tip: Sequential add-on: If low-risk not achieved on dual therapy at 3–6 months → add prostacyclin analogue. GRIPHON: Triple therapy (oral selexipag + ERA + PDE5i) → 40% ↓ morbidity/mortality vs dual therapy. Triple combination now recommended for intermediate-high risk PAH not achieving low-risk status on dual therapy.
front: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) risk stratification and treatment intensification — low vs high risk approach

back:
Cardiac rehabilitation: Multidisciplinary 12-week supervised programme. Class I for post-ACS, post-cardiac surgery, and HFrEF. ↓ Mortality 25% + ↓ HHF + ↑ QoL.

| Phase | Timing | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase I (Inpatient) | During hospitalisation (days 2–7 post-MI or post-surgery) | Gentle mobilisation (sitting → standing → walking corridors). Patient education: medications, symptom recognition, activity guidance. Psychological assessment. Smoking cessation counselling. |
| Phase II (Early outpatient) | Weeks 2–4 post-discharge | Supervised exercise (low intensity). Baseline assessments: 6MWT, resting ECG, echo (if not recent), PHQ-9. Risk stratification for exercise. Individual exercise prescription. |
| Phase III (Formal CR programme) | Weeks 4–16 (typically 12-week programme) | Supervised aerobic exercise 3×/week: 20–45 min at 50–70% VO₂ peak (Borg 11–13/20). Progressive intensity increase. Resistance training from week 4–6. Education sessions: diet, stress management, sexual activity guidance, return to work. Monthly case management reviews. |
| Phase IV (Long-term maintenance) | After formal programme | Community-based exercise programme. Annual review with CR team. Telerehabilitation for those unable to attend. |

Key outcome measures:

- VO₂ peak (CPEX test): Best objective measure of cardiorespiratory fitness. Target: ≥10% ↑ from baseline.
- 6-minute walk test (6MWT): Clinically practical. Target: ≥30 m improvement.
- Depression screen (PHQ-9): Treat depression → ↑ CR engagement and cardiac outcomes.
- QoL (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire, SF-36)
- CV risk factor control: BP, LDL, HbA1c, BMI, smoking status

Ref: PERKI 2024 §6.1 · ESC 2023 §13.1 · ACC/AHA 2025 §10.5.3
front: Cardiac rehabilitation programme structure — what happens week by week and key outcome measures

back:
Electrical cardioversion: Synchronised DC shock → depolarises all cardiac cells simultaneously → allows sinus node to take over. SYNCHRONISED for AF/flutter/SVT/stable VT. UNSYNCHRONISED (defibrillation) for VF/pVT.

| Arrhythmia | Energy (biphasic) | Sync |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Atrial fibrillation | Start 120–200 J. Escalate if needed (200 J, then 360 J equivalent). | SYNC ON |
| Atrial flutter | Start 50–100 J (flutter easier to terminate) | SYNC ON |
| SVT | Start 50 J | SYNC ON |
| Stable monomorphic VT | Start 100 J. Escalate to 200 J. | SYNC ON |
| Unstable VT (immediate) | 200 J immediately without delay for sedation if severely compromised | SYNC ON |
| VF or pulseless VT | 200 J biphasic (360 J monophasic) | SYNC OFF (defibrillation) |

Electrode positions:

- Anteroposterior (AP): Right sternal edge + left posterior infrascapular → BEST for AF (higher success rate)
- Anteroapical (AA): Right infraclavicular + cardiac apex (5th ICS mid-axillary) → Standard position

Sedation protocol: Propofol 1–1.5 mg/kg IV (preferred — rapid onset + short duration). OR Midazolam 2–5 mg IV + fentanyl 50 mcg IV. Have defibrillator, intubation equipment, resuscitation drugs available. Nil by mouth ≥4h if elective.
Warning: THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE: DO NOT synchronise for VF. VF has no R waves → device will not fire → patient dies. When in doubt about rhythm: Use SYNC ON for any regular or organised rhythm. Use SYNC OFF only for VF or chaotic disorganised rhythm. Press "SYNC" button and CONFIRM it's on before delivering shock.
front: Electrical cardioversion (DC cardioversion) technique — synchronisation, energy selection, and sedation
