back:
Acute severe MR: Normal LV receiving large regurgitant volume → ↑↑ LA pressure → flash pulmonary oedema. Forward flow reduced (→ cardiogenic shock).

| Problem | Target | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ↑ LA pressure → pulmonary oedema | ↓ Preload | IV furosemide + IV NTG (venodilator) |
| ↑ SVR → ↑ regurgitant fraction | ↓ Afterload | IV nitroprusside (SNP) — most potent afterload reducer. ↓ SVR → ↑ forward flow → ↓ regurgitant fraction. Requires arterial line. |
| ↓ CO from ↑ regurgitation | ↑ Forward flow | IABP: ↓ afterload → ↑ forward CO. BUT: Caution in papillary muscle rupture with biventricular failure — IABP diastolic deflation can worsen RV filling. |
| Definitive treatment | Repair or replace MV | Emergency MV surgery. MitraClip as bridge in extreme surgical risk. |

Warning: DO NOT give positive inotropes (dobutamine) as first-line in acute MR without afterload reduction. ↑ Contractility WITHOUT ↓ SVR = ↑ regurgitant fraction (more flow goes retrograde). First: Afterload reduction (SNP/NTG) ± IABP → forward CO improves. Add inotropes only if truly low-output state persists after afterload reduction.
front: Acute severe MR treatment — why afterload reduction is the key and why IABP is NOT always safe

back:
Prosthetic valve thrombosis (PVT): Thrombus on mechanical or bioprosthetic valve → obstruction or embolisation. Causes: Subtherapeutic anticoagulation (most common), low flow states, pregnancy.

| Scenario | First-line treatment (ESC 2021) |
| --- | --- |
| Left-sided PVT + haemodynamic instability / CS | Emergency surgery (Class I). Fibrinolysis ONLY if surgery unavailable or prohibitive risk. |
| Left-sided PVT + no instability + small thrombus (≤0.8 cm²) | Optimise anticoagulation (UFH) × 72h → reassess by TOE. If no improvement → fibrinolysis or surgery. |
| Left-sided PVT + large thrombus (>0.8 cm²) + stable | Surgery preferred. Fibrinolysis alternative if surgical risk very high. |
| Right-sided PVT (any) | Fibrinolysis preferred over surgery (lower embolic risk from right-sided; surgery riskier). |

Fibrinolysis protocol for PVT (slow regimen — safer):

- Alteplase 25 mg IV over 6h (slow infusion). Repeat if needed after 24h TOE reassessment.
- Or: Streptokinase 500,000 IU over 20 min → 1,500 IU/min × 10h
- TOE monitoring: Check thrombus resolution every 6–12h. Stop when resolved.
- Major risks: Stroke 10–15%, ICH 2–5%, major haemorrhage

Warning: Re-anticoagulate AFTER fibrinolysis: Do NOT stop anticoagulation once PVT treated — the underlying condition (subtherapeutic anticoagulation, atrial stasis) caused the thrombus. Restart UFH → warfarin. Increase INR target if event occurred at therapeutic INR.
front: Prosthetic valve thrombosis — fibrinolysis vs surgery algorithm with LFLG prosthetic valve

back:
Acute AR: Normal LV suddenly receives large regurgitant volume → rapid ↑ LVEDP → pulmonary oedema + ↓ forward CO. No time for compensatory LV dilatation.

| Acute AR feature | Why different from chronic AR |
| --- | --- |
| Small LV (normal sized) | No time for compensatory dilatation — non-compliant LV → ↑ LVEDP faster |
| Short diastolic murmur | LVEDP rises so fast → aortic + LV pressures equalise early in diastole → murmur ends before S1 |
| Tachycardia as compensation | ↑ HR shortens diastole → ↓ time for regurgitation per beat → compensatory mechanism |
| Causes | IE (aortic valve destruction), Type A aortic dissection, trauma, prosthetic valve failure |

| Intervention | Role | Critical point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IV vasodilators (NTG/SNP) | ↓ SVR → ↑ forward flow → ↓ regurgitant fraction | First-line haemodynamic support |
| IV diuretics | ↓ Preload → ↓ pulmonary oedema | Moderate doses — avoid excess |
| IABP | ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED | IABP inflates in DIASTOLE → ↑ aortic diastolic pressure → ↑ AR regurgitant volume → worsens AR dramatically. Can precipitate acute decompensation. |
| Emergency cardiac surgery | AV repair/replacement (or aortic root replacement if dissection) | Definitive — urgent. Acute severe AR is fatal without surgery. |

- Act on a change: echo (TTE and TOE) and fluoroscopy or CT for leaflet motion
front: Prosthetic valve sounds: what is normal and what is an alarm?

back:
- Scratchy, superficial, **up to three components**: atrial systole, ventricular systole, rapid ventricular filling (early diastole)
- Best at the left sternal border with the **diaphragm**, patient **sitting forward**, breath held in expiration
- Varies from hour to hour; may persist despite an effusion
- Pleural rub disappears when the breath is held; a pericardial rub does not
front: Pericardial friction rub: components and how to hear it?

back:
- Measure the **vertical height** of the top of the internal jugular pulsation above the **sternal angle**
- Add about **5 cm** (sternal angle to mid right atrium) = RA pressure in **cm H2O**
- Caveat: the true distance is often 8-10 cm at 30-60 degrees (CT data), so the +5 cm rule underestimates RA pressure
- Divide by **1.36** for mmHg
- Raised: more than **3 cm** above the sternal angle (RA pressure above about 8 cm H2O)
- Sit the patient up if the JVP is very high (the top may be hidden behind the jaw)
front: How do you estimate right atrial pressure from the JVP, and when is it raised?

back:
| Jugular venous | Carotid |
|---|---|
| Not palpable; soft, double (biphasic) inward movement | Palpable, single, outward thrust |
| Obliterated by light pressure above the clavicle | Not obliterated |
| Level falls on inspiration and changes with posture | Unaffected by respiration and posture |
| Rises with abdominal pressure (abdominojugular) | Unaffected |
front: Internal jugular venous pulsation versus carotid pulse: how do you tell them apart?

back:
| Finding | Cause |
|---|---|
| Absent a wave | Atrial fibrillation |
| Giant a waves (every beat) | Tricuspid stenosis, PS, pulmonary hypertension, RVH |
| Intermittent cannon a waves | AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT) |
| Regular cannon a waves | Junctional rhythm, AVNRT, VT with 1:1 retrograde conduction |
| Giant cv wave, lost x descent | Severe tricuspid regurgitation |
| Steep y descent | Constriction, restrictive cardiomyopathy, severe TR |
| Absent y descent | Tamponade |
| Slow y descent | Tricuspid stenosis |
| JVP rises on inspiration | Kussmaul sign: constriction, restriction, RV infarction |
front: JVP waveform abnormalities and their causes?

back:
- Patient at the angle where the top of the JVP is visible; firm, sustained pressure over the mid-abdomen for about 10-15 s, patient breathing normally (no Valsalva)
- **Positive**: a sustained rise of the JVP (commonly quoted as 3 cm or more) throughout the compression that falls abruptly on release
- Meaning: the right heart cannot accommodate the extra venous return: raised left-sided filling pressure or RV dysfunction, constriction, TR
- A brief rise that returns to baseline during compression is normal
front: Abdominojugular (hepatojugular) reflux test: technique and meaning?

back:
| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | Very faint, heard only with effort |
| 2 | Faint but heard at once |
| 3 | Moderately loud, no thrill |
| 4 | Loud **with a thrill** |
| 5 | Heard with the stethoscope edge just touching the chest |
| 6 | Heard with the stethoscope off the chest |
Diastolic murmurs are graded 1-4.
front: Levine grading of systolic murmurs?

back:
[[figure:pe-murmur-identification-algorithm]]
- **Ejection (mid-systolic, crescendo-decrescendo)**: AS, PS, HCM, flow murmurs, ASD (pulmonary flow)
- **Holosystolic (plateau, S1 to S2)**: MR, TR, VSD
- **Late systolic**: MVP (after a click), papillary muscle dysfunction
- **Early diastolic decrescendo**: AR, PR (Graham Steell)
- **Mid-diastolic rumble**: MS, TS, flow across AV valves (VSD, ASD, MR), Austin Flint, atrial myxoma
- **Continuous**: PDA, AV fistula, ruptured sinus of Valsalva, venous hum
front: Classify systolic and diastolic murmurs by timing and shape.

back:
[[figure:pe-phono-aortic-stenosis]]
- **Late-peaking** ejection murmur
- **Soft or absent A2** / single S2; paradoxical splitting
- **Pulsus parvus et tardus**; narrow pulse pressure
- Sustained apex, S4
- **Unreliable**: loudness and thrill (fall with low flow)
front: Bedside markers of severe aortic stenosis (and the unreliable one)?

back:
- **Short A2-opening snap interval** (high LA pressure opens the valve earlier)
- **Long** diastolic rumble (persists to S1 even with long cycles)
- Signs of pulmonary hypertension: loud or palpable P2, RV heave, Graham Steell murmur, functional TR
- Soft S1 and absent opening snap: heavily calcified, immobile leaflets (not milder MS)
- Loudness of the rumble does not grade severity
front: Bedside markers of severe mitral stenosis?

back:
[[figure:pe-phono-pda-continuous]]
- **PDA** (left infraclavicular, peaks at S2)
- Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm, coronary AV fistula, aortopulmonary window, surgical systemic-pulmonary shunt, collaterals (coarctation), mammary souffle
- **Venous hum**: above the right clavicle, louder in diastole and sitting up; **disappears** when supine, on turning the head towards the side of the hum (turning away accentuates it), or with light pressure over the internal jugular vein
- To-and-fro murmurs (AS + AR, VSD + AR) are not continuous: there is a gap at S2
front: Continuous murmur: differential diagnosis and how to exclude a venous hum?

back:
[[figure:pe-pulse-collapsing]]
- **Corrigan**: visible, forceful carotid pulsation; water-hammer pulse
- **de Musset**: head bobbing with each beat
- **Muller**: systolic pulsation of the uvula
- **Quincke**: capillary pulsation in the nail bed
- **Traube**: pistol-shot sound over the femoral artery
- **Duroziez**: systolic bruit with proximal and diastolic bruit with distal compression of the femoral artery (diastolic flow reversal)
- **Hill**: popliteal SBP exceeds brachial by > 20 mmHg (> 60 mmHg often quoted for severe AR; poorly validated)
- **Becker**: retinal arterial pulsation
All need a large stroke volume and wide pulse pressure; they are absent in acute AR.
deck: Peripheral Signs of AR & Eponymous Signs
front: Peripheral (eponymous) signs of chronic severe aortic regurgitation?

back:
| Feature | Austin Flint | Organic MS |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Normal or soft | Loud (mobile leaflets) |
| Opening snap | Absent | Present |
| Amyl nitrite | Softer (less AR) | Louder (more flow, tachycardia) |
| Presystolic accentuation | May be present | Present in sinus rhythm |
Austin Flint mechanism: AR jet hitting the anterior mitral leaflet, plus premature mitral closure as LV diastolic pressure rises.
[[figure:pe-phono-mitral-stenosis]]
deck: Peripheral Signs of AR & Eponymous Signs
front: Apical diastolic rumble in a patient with AR: Austin Flint murmur or organic mitral stenosis?

back:
- **Normal**: 5th intercostal space, at or inside the midclavicular line, less than 2.5 cm across (about one intercostal space), brief
- **Sustained / heaving, not displaced**: pressure overload (AS, hypertension, HCM)
- **Displaced, diffuse, hyperdynamic**: volume overload (chronic AR, MR, VSD, PDA)
- **Tapping**: palpable loud S1 of mitral stenosis
- **Double or triple**: HCM (palpable S4 + bifid systolic impulse)
- **Dyskinetic / ectopic**: LV aneurysm after anterior MI
- Impalpable: obesity, COPD, large effusion, dextrocardia (check the right side)
front: Apex beat: normal and abnormal characters?

back:
- **RV lift / heave**: RV pressure or volume overload (pulmonary hypertension, PS, ASD, MS with PH); sustained and **synchronous** with the apical impulse
- **LA expansion** in severe MR: the LA lies behind the heart and pushes it forward in late systole, so the lift peaks **after** the apical impulse
- Time the lift against the apex or the carotid upstroke
front: A left parasternal lift: RV or left atrium?

back:
- A **thrill** = a murmur of **grade 4 or more** (Levine)
- Systolic thrill: aortic area and suprasternal notch (AS), lower left sternal border (VSD), upper left sternal border (PS)
- Diastolic thrill at the apex: MS (felt in the left lateral position)
- **Palpable P2** (2nd left intercostal space): pulmonary hypertension
- **Palpable S1** (tapping apex): mitral stenosis
- Palpable presystolic impulse: S4 in LVH or HCM
